We place that nourishment of his within our reach, he who is more clearly visible by night than by day, more visible by day than to one whose life is spent.
From him comes a life that holds fast, like firm protection for a son.
May the ageless fires, consuming both what is shared and what is unshared, spread forth; may the ageless fires spread forth.
For he, roaring loudly like the host of Maruts, is the one who finds the fertile fields; he is the one who finds the flowing waters.
He takes up the offerings, the consumer, the banner of the sacrifice, according to his worth.
And when he, the exultant and joyous one, is roused, all men delight in his path, as men do in a path for glory.
When the *kīstas*, seeking heaven, offered him worship, the Bhr̥gus called upon him with reverence; the Bhr̥gus, rubbing [the fire-sticks], were his worshippers.
Agni is the lord of riches, he who is their pure sustainer.
May the wise one win the beloved secret chambers; may the wise one win them.

We invoke you, the lord of all people, the common husband of them all, for our enjoyment—him who is borne by true songs, for our enjoyment. We invoke the guest of men, by whose presence one feels as if in the lap of a father.
And may all these immortals come to our life-giving strength; may the offerings reach the gods, and [grant us] life.

O Agni, you are born as the most powerful by your might, the most vigorous for the service of the gods, like wealth for the service of the gods. For your exhilaration is most vigorous, and your mental power is most splendid.
Therefore, O undecaying one, they attend upon you, like obedient servants, O undecaying one.

Let a hymn of praise go forth for your great Agni, who by his might is powerful, who awakens at dawn, and who seeks out cattle—let it go forth for Agni. When the one bearing oblations calls out to him in all lands, he, like a singer, awakens before the flames; he is the ancient Hotṛ-priest among the flames.

Appearing most near to us, O Agni, bring [wealth] together with the gods through your gracious wisdom—bring great riches through your gracious wisdom. O mightiest one, make for us a great vision to enjoy this;
O Maghavan, churn out great heroic power for those who praise you, like a fierce one by his own strength.
This Agni was born in the support of Manu, the most excellent invoker according to the vow of the yearning ones, according to his own vow;
he who hears all, like wealth for one seeking friendship, for one seeking renown;
the undeceived invoker has sat down in the place of *iḷā*, encircled in the place of *iḷā*.
I send him forth, the accomplisher of sacrifice, along the path of Truth with reverence and an oblation, at the assembly of the gods with an oblation.
Through his bringing of nourishment, he does not grow old by this form of his—
Mātariśvan, who brought that god from afar for Manu, from the distance, as light.
By his even path he instantly traverses the earthly realm; the bull, bellowing repeatedly, casts forth his seed as he bellows.
Beholding with a hundred eyes, the god is swift among the woods. Agni establishes his seat upon the lower ridges and upon the highest ridges.

He, the wise one, the domestic priest, in every house Agni takes heed of the sacrifice and the rite; by his mental power he takes heed of the sacrifice. By his mental power the Ordainer is implored; he has beheld all created beings.
From whence the guest adorned with clarity was born, the bearer, the Ordainer, was born.
When they join him through wisdom in his powers, Agni is like the Maruts in his bounty; he is for the impetuous one, as food is for the hungry.
For he indeed promotes the gift of riches by his greatness. May he protect us from misfortune and from assault, from the curse and from evil assault.

The all-pervading, far-reaching, and wealthy steward has taken [the sacrificial ladle] in his right hand; like one who crosses over, he does not loosen [his grasp]; through desire for glory, he does not loosen it.
For every one who strives, you have been brought as an oblation among the gods.
For every doer of good, Agni grants a boon; he opens wide the doors.

He has been established as the most gracious one in the human community; Agni is the noble lord of the people among the sacrifices, the dear lord of the people among the sacrifices. He rules over the oblations of men that have been prepared with *iḷā*. May he protect us from the malice of Varuṇa, from the malice of the great god.

They praise Agni as the Hotṛ-priest, the bestower of wealth; they have established him as the beloved, most wise steward; they have established him as the bearer of oblations. The gods, seeking riches, have established the all-encompassing, all-knowing, worshipful sage as the Hotṛ-priest—the delightful one for their protection, the delightful one with songs, as they seek riches.
O Indra, that chariot which you, the impetuous one, lead forward from behind for the winning of the prize—O blameless one, you lead it on;
you instantly make it victorious for our assistance and according to your will. O blameless and impetuous one, accept this speech of ours, as we, the wise ones, offer it to you.
Hear us, O Indra, you who are to be honored by men in every battle when the call to arms is raised; you are there with the men for the sake of swift victory.
You, who with heroes win the light of heaven, and with inspired singers overcome for booty—that powerful one, the lords have sought to win like a prize-winning steed, like a vigorous courser.
For you, O wondrous one, cause the bull-like skin to swell; you ward off every stingy mortal, O hero, you exclude the mortal.
Indra, I declare this to you, to Dyaus, to Rudra who is self-glorious, to Mitra and Varuṇa—this far-reaching hymn, this far-reaching hymn for the sake of their great mercy.

We desire Indra for our protection—the friend who grants all life, the ally who overcomes in battles, the ally who overcomes in battles. May our sacred prayer (*brahman*) protect us in every conflict;
for no enemy can strike you down, you who strike down every enemy, you who strike him down.
Bend down the overweening pride of anyone with your most sharpened kindling-sticks, with your aids—O fierce one, with your fierce aids!
Lead us as you did of old; O hero, you are considered blameless.
As a bearer, carry us across all [difficulties] for the sake of Pūru; as a bearer, bring us hither with your mouth.

I would proclaim this to the future Soma-drop, who, like one to be invoked, possesses the impulse that stirs the prayer; the demon-slayer, he whose prayer stirs the prayer. May he himself drive away from us the ill-wisher with his weapons, the evil-minded one.
May the one who pronounces evil flow downward, may he flow away like a tiny speck of dust.
May we win that through thoughtful invocation; may we win wealth, O Lord of Wealth, with excellent heroic power—wealth that is delightful and full of heroic power.
May we approach the ill-minded one with auspicious thoughts and with nourishment.
With true invocations of glory, let us worship Indra, the worthy of sacrifice, with invocations of glory.

Forward and ever forward for us be your aid, O Indra, through your own glorious powers, for the complete removal of the ill-minded, the shattering of the ill-minded! May that [hostile power] which has approached us with its devouring jaws destroy itself;
let it be struck down, let it not carry us away; let the wasting fire, once cast forth, consume it.

O Indra, come to us with abundant wealth by a path free from danger; go before us by a path devoid of demons. Be with us in the distance, be with us at home. Protect us from afar and from near at hand with your aids; ever protect us with your aids.
O Indra, may you grant us wealth that overcomes the foe; may your greatness accompany you, the fierce one, for our great protection, as one seeks a friend for aid.
O most powerful protector, O immortal, be the helper of whatever chariot there may be.
O wielder of the stone, harm no one other than us; O wielder of the stone, harm even him who seeks to harm us.
Protect us from calamities, O Indra, you who are well-praised; as a god, you are forever the warder-off of the ill-minded, the warder-off of the malevolent.
You are the slayer of the wicked *rakṣas* and the protector of a sage such as I.
For thus did your progenitor beget you, O Vasu; he begot you, the slayer of *rakṣases*, O Vasu.

O Indra, come to us from afar, as a lord of the virtuous comes toward the assemblies, as a king comes to his home; we invoke you while offering oblations at the pressed juice, like sons invoking their father for the winning of booty— most bountiful one, for the winning of booty.
Drink the Soma pressed by the stones, O Indra, poured from the vessel like a bull to a watering-place, like a thirsty bull;
for thy exhilaration, for thy beloved draught, for thy most powerful nourishment.
Let the bay steeds bring thee hither as they bring the sun, as all the days bring the sun.
He found the treasure hidden in the cave of heaven, like the embryo of a bird enveloped within the rock, within the infinite rock.
Like one desiring to win the stall of cattle, Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the best of the Aṅgirases, threw open the doors;
Indra threw open the doors of the enclosed nourishment, the enclosed nourishments.
Firmly grasping the thunderbolt in his two hands, Indra whetted it like a sharp blade for hurling; he whetted it for the slaying of Ahi.
Enveloped in power, in strengths, and in majesty, O Indra, you hew down the forest trees like a carpenter, you hew them down like an axe.
O Indra, you have released the rivers to flow at will toward the ocean, like chariots, like prize-seeking chariots. From here they have harnessed their aids for a common, inexhaustible purpose—
like milch-cows yielding all things for mankind, yielding all things for the people.
Seeking wealth, these Āyus have fashioned this speech for you, as a skillful craftsman fashions a chariot; they have fashioned you for favor.
O Sage, adorning you like a noble steed for the sake of booty in battles, we have made you like a courser for strength, for the winning of riches—for the winning of all riches.
O Indra, O dancer, you shattered ninety forts for Pūru Divodāsa, the great donor, with your thunderbolt for the sake of the donor, O dancer;
the fierce one brought down Śambara from the mountain for Atithigva.
Distributing great wealth by your might, you [took] all wealth by your might.
Indra, who possesses a hundredfold aid, protected the Aryan sacrificer in battles, in all contests for light, in the struggles for booty.
Governing for Manu, he subdued those without holy vows; he made the black skin subject to him.
Like a skillful worker, he burns up every thirsty foe; he utterly consumes the malicious one.
The Sun, having been born with power, forced forward his wheel; at the onset of the day, the ruddy one steals away the voice.
As the sovereign lord, he steals it away, when Uśanas came from afar for help, O Sage.
Like Manu, he wins all blessings; like all the days, he is the conqueror.
O you of heroic deeds, destroyer of forts, protect us with your powerful guardians through our new hymns;
O Indra, being praised by the Divodāsas, may you increase like the sky grows with the days.
For to Indra has Dyaus, the Asura, bowed down; to Indra has the great Earth bowed with her vast expanses, in the winning of splendor, with her vast expanses.
All the gods, acting in harmony, have placed Indra at their head.
For Indra let all the libations of men be offered—let them be the gifts of men.
For at all the libations, those who desire the bull urge you on—each separately, seeking the light of heaven, each separately.
We set you, like a ship that carries us across, at the pole of our strength;
the Āyus distinguish Indra with sacrifices, the Āyus honor Indra with hymns of praise.
Couples seeking your aid have spread themselves out for you, O Indra, as they strive to win the stall of cattle; they have come to you, O Indra, as they strive to win the stall.
When you bring together two people who seek cattle and who seek the light of heaven, you, O Indra, manifest your thunderbolt—the bull that accompanies you, the companion that accompanies you.
The Pūrus knew of this heroic deed of yours, O Indra, when you overthrew the autumnal fortresses, overthrew them with conquering might.
O Indra, Lord of Strength, you chastised that mortal who did not sacrifice;
exhilarated, you stole away the vast earth and these waters—these very waters.

Then indeed they celebrated this heroic deed of yours, O Bull, in the exhilarations of the soma, when you, desiring to help, protected those who sought your friendship; when you, desiring to help, protected them.
You performed a great deed for them so that they might prevail in battles.
Seeking glory, they won various rivers; seeking glory, they won them.
And may he take pleasure in this dawn of ours; indeed, be mindful of our hymn and our oblations with our invocations, at the winning of the light with our invocations.
O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, when you, the bull, intend to slay the adversaries, listen to this prayer of mine, the most recent of this worshipper, the most recent of all.

O Indra, growing strong and well-disposed toward us, O hero of many births, slay with your thunderbolt that mortal who acts as an enemy, that mortal who seeks to harm us. Listen, you who are most renowned for hearing;
let malice be far from our path, let every ill-will be driven away.
O Maghavan, with you as our protector, O Indra, may we overcome those who attack us and conquer those who seek to harm us, as we won wealth in former times.
On this most proximate day, speak now in favor of the one who presses the Soma;
at this sacrifice, may we, seeking booty, distribute the prize won in battle—the prize won in battle.
In the winning of light, bring [the prize] in the speech of the filler, for those who wake at dawn, in their own adornment, for the active one, in their own adornment.
Indra slew [the foe], as is well known; he is to be praised head by head. May your gifts be directed toward us; may the gifts of the auspicious one be auspicious.
That ancient offering of yours has shone forth as of old, at that sacrifice where they made you the chooser and the dwelling place; you are the chooser, the dwelling place of the *ṛta*.
Proclaim that now once again! They see within with their rays.
Indeed, Indra is known as the seeker of cattle, the seeker of cattle for those who dwell in kinship.
Now indeed, as in the past, this deed of yours is to be proclaimed—that you opened the pen for the Aṅgirases, O Indra, opening the pen as you gave your aid.
Toward them, and toward us, in the same direction, may you conquer and fight.
To those who press the Soma, deliver up every one who is lawless, even the one who is wrathful and lawless.

When the Hero, with his powers of will, has caused the people to look upon one another, they strive for wealth when it is staked; seeking glory, they press forward, seeking glory. To him they sing for long life accompanied by progeny in their time of distress, with power;
Indra’s thoughts desire a dwelling-place, as the thoughts of men go toward the gods.
O Indra and Parvata, you two who fight from the front, strike down each one who would attack us; strike him down with the thunderbolt, strike him down!
May it reach the one who stays far away, that dense thicket which he seeks to attain.
O Hero, may you, the destroyer, crush our enemies on every side; crush them completely!
I purify both heaven and earth with cosmic order; I burn away the great, Indra-less deceivers.
Where the enemies were struck down after being hemmed in, they lay shattered all around at Vailasthāna.
O wielder of the stone, having overwhelmed even the heads of the sorceresses, crush them with your wide-footed stride, with your great wide-footed stride.
O Maghavan, strike down the host of these sorceresses;
[strike them] at Vailasthānaka, at Armaka, at Mahāvailastha, and at Armaka.
Of those fifty-three [stanzas] which you have scattered with your strides—that indeed pleases you; that little thing indeed pleases you.
O Indra, crush the Piśāci, the one with tawny-tipped hair and made of metal;
strike down every demon.
O great Indra, break them down; hear us! For heaven has glowed with fear, as the earth does at the dread of thee, O wielder of the stone, as if from the heat of the sun, O wielder of the stone.

For thou movest with thy most powerful, fierce, and impetuous weapons. O hero, thou art not slain by men; thou art unassailable, O hero, with thy thrice-seven brave warriors, O hero, with thy brave warriors.
For the one who presses [the Soma] wins an abode of abundance; for the one who presses indeed overcomes his enemies, the enemies of the gods.
The one who presses, an unimpeded seeker of strength, desires to win thousands. To the one who presses, Indra gives enduring wealth; he gives enduring wealth.
May the swift, rushing [horses] bring you here, O Vāyu, toward the offerings for the first draught of Soma—for the first draught!
May your *sūnṛtā* (joyous bounty), knowing [our intent], stand erect according to our mind.
Come with your chariot drawn by teams of horses (*niyutvant*) to grant us gifts, O Vāyu—to grant the gifts of the sacrifice!
May the exhilarating drops, O Vāyu, gladden you—those well-prepared, heaven-seeking draughts made by us, prepared with milk, seeking the heavens.
For when they are prepared for the sacrifice, our aids attend upon our skill;
may the teams of horses come together for the giving, and may our prayers invoke him, yea, our prayers.
Vāyu yokes the two ruddy steeds; Vāyu yokes the two tawny ones; Vāyu yokes the two swift ones to the chariot at the pole to draw, the best at drawing at the pole to draw.
Awaken Purandhi, as a lover awakens a sleeping woman.
Make the two worlds visible; clothe the dawns for glory, clothe the dawns for glory.

For you the bright dawns in the distance spread out their auspicious garments within your wondrous rays—wondrous garments within your new rays. For you the cow that milks all things yields every treasure.
From your flanks you brought forth the Maruts, from the flanks of heaven.
For you the bright, pure, and swift [Soma drops], fierce in their exhilarations, have sped toward the stirring of the waters; they have sped toward the stirring of the waters.
The weary thief, seeking his fortune, prays to you for speed in the chase.
You protect [us] from every world by your law; you protect us from the divine power by your law.

O Vāyu, you alone, without predecessor, deserve the first draught of these pressed Soma juices; you deserve the draught. And from the clans who offer oblations and have turned toward you, all the milch-cows yield for you the milk-mixture; they yield the clarified butter, the milk-mixture.
The sacrificial grass is strewn; come to us for the feast with a thousand teams, O Lord of teams, with hundreds of teams, O Lord of teams!
For the gods have directed themselves toward you, the god, for the first draught.
The sweet-pressed juices have stood forth for you; they have stood forth for exhilaration, for the sake of inspired will.
For you this Soma flows, purified by the stones, clothed in desirable riches, it flows around the vessel; clothed in brilliance, it flows.
This portion of yours among living men—Soma is offered among the gods.
O Vāyu, bring your teams; come seeking us; enjoying [the offering], come seeking us.
Come to our sacrifice with your teams of horses, by the hundreds and by the thousands, for the enjoyment of the offering, O Vāyu, for the enjoyment of the oblation!
This is your seasonal portion, accompanied by the sunbeams along with the sun.
Brought by the *adhvaryu* priests, the bright libations have been offered; O Vāyu, the pure juices have been offered.
May your chariot, drawn by teams of horses, bring you both for our protection, toward the well-prepared offerings for your enjoyment, O Vāyu, toward the oblations for your enjoyment.
Drink of the sweet juice; for the first draught has been set apart for you both.
O Vāyu, come with brilliant bounty; and Indra, come with bounty!
May our prayers turn you both toward the sacrifices; they have cleansed this vigorous drop, like a swift, prize-winning steed.
Drink of these, O you who desire us; come hither to us with your speed!
Indra and Vāyu, you two are the givers of strength; drink of the juices pressed by the stones for your exhilaration.
These Soma juices, pressed here in the waters for you both, have been offered by the *adhvaryu*s; O Vāyu, the bright drops have been offered.
These swift ones have been poured out for you both across the filter;
seeking you, the Soma juices have passed through the sheep’s wool, past the woolly fleece.
O Vāyu, pass by all those who sleep; go to that place where the pressing-stone speaks, and go to the house, O Indra, go there!
The *sūnṛtā* has become visible; the clarified butter flows. Come to the sacrifice with a full team of horses, O Indra, come to the sacrifice!
Here, O Vāyu, you two carry that offering of honey to which the swift ones resort at the *aśvattha* tree; may they be swift for us.
Together the cows bring forth [milk], the barley ripens; your milch-cows do not fail, O Vāyu, your milch-cows do not fail.
O Vāyu, these which are yours—mighty-armed and full of strength—fly within the rivers like bulls; the bulls increase in greatness.

Even those that are not swift on the desert plain, even those that are agile yet have no home in the mountains, are as difficult to restrain as the rays of the sun; they are difficult to restrain by the hands.
Bring forth the highest, great homage—the oblation and the prayer—to the two attentive ones who are gracious, the most sweet to those who are gracious.
Those two sovereign kings, to whom the clarified butter is offered, are praised at every sacrifice. Thus their dominion is invincible from any quarter; their divinity is never to be assailed.
A wider path has been seen for the broad expanse; the way of *ṛta* has been aligned with the rays, the eye [of Mitra] with the rays of Bhaga.
The celestial dwelling of Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa is revealed.
Then they two bestow great, praiseworthy vitality—great, laudable vitality.
They attend day by day upon Aditi—the luminous, the sustainer of the earth, the radiant one—remaining ever-watchful day by day.
The two Ādityas have attained a luminous dominion; they are the lords of bounty.
Of these two, Mitra and Varuṇa are the stirrers of the people, as is Aryaman, the stirrer of the people.
May this Soma, becoming most propitious for Mitra and Varuṇa, be a sharer in the drinking-feasts—a god sharing among the gods.
May all the gods, being of one accord, take pleasure in it today. O Kings, you who uphold the cosmic order (*ṛta*), grant us that which we ask of you; grant us that which we implore.

The man who serves Mitra and Varuṇa with devotion—him, the unassailable, they protect from distress; the mortal who offers oblations, they protect him from distress. Aryaman guards him who acts uprightly according to the law;
he who honors their law with hymns, he who adorns their law with songs of praise.
Homage to the lofty heaven, to the two worlds, to Mitra, and to the bounteous Varuṇa, the compassionate one, the bounteous one!
Praise Indra and Agni; praise the heavenly Aryaman and Bhaga.
Living long, may we be united with offspring; may we be united with the protection of Soma.
Through the protection of the gods, may we, accompanied by Indra and sharing our own glory with the Maruts, be esteemed.
May Agni, Mitra, and Varuṇa grant us shelter; may we and the patrons attain that.
We have pressed [the juice] for you; come hither with the stones! These exhilarating Soma-draughts are mixed with milk, these exhilarating Soma-draughts.
O two Kings who touch the heavens, come here toward us!
These bright Soma-draughts, mixed with milk, are for you both, O Mitra and Varuṇa; they are mixed with milk.
Come hither to these drops, O [Aśvins], the pressed Soma juices mixed with curds, the pressed juices mixed with curds. And at the awakening of the Dawn, together with the rays of the Sun,
the juice has been pressed for Mitra and Varuṇa to drink— the lovely one, for the sake of the Truth to drink.
Like a cow that yields milk at dawn, they milk that stalk for you with the stones; they milk the Soma with the stones.
Come toward us, come hither, for the drinking of the Soma.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, this Soma has been pressed by the men for you; it is pressed for your drinking.
On and on is celebrated the greatness of Pūṣan, he who is born with many powers; the praise of this mighty one does not falter, his hymn of praise does not falter.
Seeking favor, I sing to him whose aid is near, the source of bliss.
He who has drawn to himself the mind of every man—the liberal god, the liberal one, has drawn it to himself.
For I urge you forward, O Pūṣan, as one would a swift steed on its course with hymns of praise, so that you may overcome our adversaries; like a camel, carry us across our enemies.
Since I, a mortal, call upon you, the god who brings bliss, for friendship, make our songs of praise glorious; in the contests for booty, make them glorious.
O Pūṣan, those who, being praiseworthy through their wisdom and existing by your favor, have enjoyed the benefits of your friendship—yes, they have enjoyed them through your wisdom.
Following that most recent [gift] of yours, we seek you for wealth.
O you of wide renown, do not be angry; be swift in our course, be swift in every contest for booty!

O Lord of the Unborn Horses, be well-disposed toward us for our gain; do not be angry, O Bounteous One, you who possess the Unborn Horses, for those who desire glory, O Lord of the Unborn Horses! O Wondrous One, may we turn you hither with effective hymns of praise.
For I do not disregard you, O glowing Pūṣan; I do not deny your friendship.

Let there be *śrauṣaṭ*! With my prayer, I place Agni at the forefront; now we choose that divine host, we choose Indra and Vāyu. Since a newer [hymn] has been offered when the sacrifice was prepared at the navel of Vivasvat, may our prayers go forth toward the gods, even as our prayers do.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, when you two took that untruth away from the Truth by your own will, by the will of Dakṣa, by your own will—
then indeed in your dwellings we beheld the golden [seat],
through our prayers, through the mind, through our own eyes, through the eyes of Soma.
O Aśvins, those seeking the gods invoke you with hymns of praise, just as men raise a shout; the living call upon you for their oblations.
O possessors of all wealth, all glories and nourishments rest in you both. Your fellies on the golden chariot, O wonder-workers, scatter drops of moisture—on the golden chariot.
O wonder-workers, you have been perceived; you open up the firmament. For you, at the morning rites, they harness the chariot-steeds that are free from dust, at the morning rites.
O wonder-workers, we place our station upon the seat of your golden chariot.
Like two travelers on a path, you traverse the mid-air, directing it straight, directing the mid-air.
O Lords of Power, with your powers, favor us by day and by night! May your bounty never fail us; may your bounty never fail us at any time.
O Bull Indra, these Soma drops, drunk by the bull, are pressed; they are pressed by the stones, bursting forth—pressed for you, bursting forth.
May they exhilarate you for the sake of giving great and wondrous bounty.
O you who are borne by songs, being praised with hymns, come hither; as one who is very gracious, come unto us.
O Agni, hear us! Being praised, you shall speak to the worshipful gods, to the worshipful kings.
Since you, O gods, gave that cow to the Aṅgirases, Aryaman milks her along with the fashioner; he knows her well along with me.
May those manly deeds of yours never turn away from us; may your glories never grow old, nor may our strongholds ever decay.
Whatever wondrous, immortal, and ever-new sound you have sent forth age after age—O Maruts, bestow that upon us, and whatever is difficult to overcome, grant that which is hard to surpass.

Dadhyañc, the ancient Aṅgiras, Priyamedha, Kaṇva, Atri, and Manu—these my ancestors know; Manu knows them. Their lineage extends to the gods, and our kinships are with them. Following their path, I bow down with my song; I bow down with my song to Indra and Agni.
Let the Hotṛ sacrifice; let the seekers win what is desirable. Bṛhaspati, the seer, sacrifices with bulls—bulls rich in many boons.
We have ourselves grasped the far-reaching song of praise from the pressing-stone.
The one of excellent wisdom has established the non-giving ones; the one of excellent wisdom has established many dwellings.
O gods who are eleven in heaven, who are eleven upon the earth,
and who are eleven dwelling in the waters by your greatness— O gods, may you graciously accept this sacrifice.
To Agni, who sits upon the altar, whose abode is dear, and who shines with beautiful luster—bring forth a seat for him as if it were a nourishing draught.
Clothe the pure one with my prayer as if with a garment; he whose chariot is light, who is bright-hued, and the dispeller of darkness.
The twice-born one speeds toward the threefold food; what was consumed grows again within the year.
With the mouth and tongue of the one, the noble bull prevails; with the other, the elephant-like one strips the trees.
Moving in the black waters, his two co-dwellers tremble; both mothers hasten toward the infant.
With forward-tongued, scattering, thirst-quenching, and alluring power, he is the one who increases his father’s strength.
For Manu who acts like a man, they are yoked— those swift-runners seeking release, with black furrows, impetuous,
not moving in unison, agile, gliding swiftly, wind-driven, and fleet.
Then his flames rush forth at will, scattering the black monster and assuming a great form,
when he goes along stroking the vast earth, panting, thundering, and roaring.
Adorning himself, he stoops over the brown [mares]; bellowing loudly, he approaches them like a bull toward his wives.
Displaying his vigor, he beautifies his own body; like a terrifying beast with sharp horns, he rushes about, difficult to seize.
He, the spreading one, the pervading one, gathers them together; knowing them as his own kin, he lies with them eternally.
They grow again and go toward their divine nature; together with their parents, they assume another form.

The long-haired maidens, having been dead, stood up erect again for the sake of the living man, as they sang together. Releasing them from old age, he goes along roaring, generating further life-force and invincible vitality.
Licking the upper garment of his mother, he indeed goes forth across the expanse with his powerful, bold warriors.
Bestowing strength upon all that has feet, licking them constantly, the tawny one indeed follows along his paths.
O Agni, shine among our patrons, you who are like a snorting bull, the master of the house;
you have caused the mother-cows with their calves to glow, flickering all around like a coat of mail in battles.
O Agni, may this well-composed [prayer] be dearer to you than a poorly composed one, even more so than a beloved thought.
With that pure, bright radiance of your body which shines forth, do you win for us wealth.
O Agni, grant for our chariot and for our house a boat with constant oars and feet;
a boat that shall carry across our heroes, our wealthy patrons, and our people, and which shall be our protection.
O Agni, may you graciously accept our hymn; may Heaven and Earth and the self-praising Rivers grant it favor.
Seeking cattle and barley for our long life, may the ruddy ones choose for us the best boon.
Truly, that beautiful splendor of the god has been established for the sake of majesty, since he was born from strength;
when he inclines toward it, the prayer succeeds, and the flowing streams of *ṛta* have led him forward.
The nourishing, wondrous form, full of food, dwells eternally; a second [form] is in the seven auspicious mothers;
for the milking of this bull, the young women have brought forth a third, the one who provides tenfold wisdom.
When the wise lords, by their power, brought him forth from the depths with the form of the buffalo;
when Mātariśvan churned him who was hidden in secret for the sake of the distillation of honey, following the ways of ancient times.
When he is led forth from the highest place of his father, he rises wondrously upon the nourishing plants;
when both parents promote his birth, then the youngest one becomes bright with fervor.
Then he entered the mothers, in whom the pure one, unhurt, grew far and wide;
when he had climbed up after the former ones that were born of old, he runs down into the newer, lower ones.
Then indeed they choose him as the Hotṛ-priest in the rites for heaven; seeking fulfillment, they strive toward him as if toward Bhaga.
When, praised by many, he moves with wisdom and power among the gods, he goes at all times to the mortal’s praise to provide sustenance.
When he, the worshipful one, urged by the wind, has spread out like a quivering serpent at its sloughing-off, unrestrained;
then, in the flight of that burning one who leaves a black trail, whose birth is pure, he traverses the mid-air along his path.
Like a chariot that has gone forth, fashioned by skillful craftsmen, he hastens to heaven with his ruddy limbs;
then those black ones, his swift-moving steeds, flee from his brilliance like birds from the onset of a hero.
For by you, O Agni, Varuṇa whose vows are firm, Mitra, and the bounteous Aryaman have been made strong;
since you were born all-pervading, encompassing them with your power in every way, as the felly encompasses the spokes.
O Agni, youngest one, you bestow wealth and the company of the gods upon the one who exerts himself and presses the soma;
as such, O youthful son of strength, we now establish you, the possessor of great wealth, like Bhaga in our song of praise.
For us, you shall bestow wealth that is self-sustaining, a household blessing, and enduring strength—like Bhaga and Dakṣa—just as one holds together the reins.
He who, being of noble will, governs both worlds like reins, and proclaims the praise of the gods according to the Eternal Order (Ṛta).
And may the Hotṛ of brilliant luster, with swift horses, the joyous one with a shining chariot, hear us.
May that unerring Agni lead us by the best paths toward desirable wealth, prosperity, and greater well-being.
Agni has been lauded with powerful hymns, as he bestows further sovereignty;
may both these wealthy patrons and we ourselves spread forth beyond [all obstacles], just as the sun disperses the mist.
O Agni, kindled, bring the gods today to the one who extends the ladle;
spin out the ancient thread for the donor who has pressed the soma.
O Tanūnapāt, you measure out for me the sacrifice rich in ghee and full of sweetness,
belonging to an inspired singer like me who exerts himself as a donor.
Pure, purifying, and wonderful, he sprinkles the sacrifice with honey;
Narāśaṃsa, the god worthy of worship among the gods, thrice [comes] from heaven.
O Agni, being praised, bring hither Indra— the wondrous, beloved one—
for this hymn of mine, O fair-tongued one, is directed toward you.
Spreading the sacrificial grass with outstretched ladles at the well-performed sacrifice, I prepare for Indra a wide, sheltering seat that most amply accommodates the gods.
May the great, purifying, and much-desired divine doors, which increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*), be opened wide for the gods to pass through.
May Night and Dawn, the two neighboring ones who are praised, well-adorned, the mighty mothers of the Eternal Order (Ṛta), sit upon the sacrificial grass with favor.
The two divine Hotṛ-priests, the sages with lovely tongues who love to chant—
may they today perform for us this successful sacrifice that reaches the heavens.
Pure among the gods, the Hotrā offering is entrusted to the Maruts;
may Iḷā, Sarasvatī, and Mahī sit upon the sacrificial grass, they who are worthy of worship.
May Tvaṣṭṛ, who is well-disposed toward us, release for us that wondrous seed— abundant in many ways and by its own nature— for our prosperity and for wealth, at our very center.
Releasing [the oblations] by yourself, O Vanaspati, sacrifice to the gods;
Agni, the wise god among the gods, prepares the offerings well.
To Vāyu, who is accompanied by Pūṣan and the Maruts, and by all the gods— to Indra, who is moved by the Gāyatrī, offer the oblation with the cry of Svāhā!
Come to the offerings consecrated with Svāhā to partake of them;
O Indra, come, hear our call, for they invoke you at the sacrifice.
I bring forward a more powerful, newer hymn for Agni; I offer a prayer of speech to the Son of Strength.
He who is the Son of the Waters, beloved along with the Vasus, has sat down upon the earth as the seasonal Hotṛ-priest.
Being born in the highest heaven, Agni became manifest to Mātariśvan;
by the power and the greatness of him as he was kindled, his flame caused both Heaven and Earth to shine forth.

His flames are brilliant and ageless; the rays of him who is fair to behold, of beautiful countenance, and of splendid luster—those whose power is light, O Agni, stir themselves like rivers rushing over the night, unceasing and ageless.
Him whom the Bhr̥gus have sent forth, the all-knowing one, at the navel of the earth by the power of the world—
stir that Agni with your songs in his own home, he who alone rules over wealth like Varuṇa.

He whom no one can restrain, like the roar of the Maruts, like an army let loose, or like a celestial thunderbolt—Agni eats and chews with his sharpened jaws; like a warrior against his enemies, he subdues the forests.
Will Agni indeed be a hero for our hymn? Will the Vasu, together with the Vasus, fulfill our desire?
Will he, the impeller, truly speed our prayers toward gain? Him of the radiant countenance, I praise with this prayer.
To Agni, whose face is ghee and who sits at the yoke of the Cosmic Order (ṛta), they reach out as if to a friend when he is kindled.
Kindling him, the one who is not harsh, shining brightly in the assemblies, shall lift up our prayer toward the radiant light.
O Agni, being vigilant, protect us with your vigilant, auspicious, and powerful guardians;
O Desired One, with those who are undeceived, undaunted, and unwinking, protect our offspring on every side.
The Hotṛ goes forward to his office by means of his creative power, holding aloft the pure-hued prayer;
he moves toward the ladles turned to the right, which first touch his primary station.
The milking-streams of Truth have lowed toward him, encompassed within the womb of the god, in his seat;
when he dwelt distributed in the lap of the waters, then he sucked the self-sustaining powers by which he moves.
Desiring to win that same wondrous form, the two of equal age strive together, each seeking their common goal.
Then, like Bhaga, he is to be invoked; like a charioteer gathering the reins, he has drawn them together toward us.
Him whom two of equal age serve, a pair dwelling together in the same womb and sharing the same home;
he who is grey-haired yet born young by day as if by night, moving through many human generations, remains undecaying.
The ten fingers and our prayers impel him; we mortals call upon the god for aid.
From the dry land he speeds down the slope; with those who advance toward him, he has established new ways of knowledge.
For you, O Agni, rule over the celestial realm, and you, by your own power, over the earthly, like a herdsman of cattle.
These two great, shimmering, golden, and winding ones, adorned with splendor, have taken their seats upon the sacred grass.
O Agni, graciously accept and take pleasure in this word, O delightful one, self-sustained, born of *ṛta*, and of noble power!
For you face every direction, you are beautiful to behold, and like a dwelling-place rich in food, you are joyous to look upon.
Ask him; he has gone there. He knows it; as one who is wise, he moves; indeed, he moves. In him are the commands; in him are the sacrifices. He is the lord of strength, of powerful vigor.

They ask him, yet he does not inquire of them; for what he has grasped with his own wise mind, he does not forget, neither the first nor the later word. Unconfused, he acts in accordance with his will.

To him indeed go the sacrificial ladles; to him go the swift mares. He alone shall hear all my words—he who has many commands, the overcomer, the accomplisher of sacrifice, whose protection is flawless. As a child, he has assumed vigorous strength.
When he has come together with them, he moves about as one who has just been born;
he hastens with his companions toward the glowing heat for joy and delight, when the longing ones approach him as he stands firm.
Like a wild beast of the waters or a forest-roamer, he has been placed upon the highest skin.
Agni, the wise one who knows the *ṛta* and is true, has proclaimed the ways to mortals.

I praise Agni, the three-headed and seven-rayed, who is never-failing in the lap of his parents; he who sits within him as he moves, yet remains firm, and has filled all the luminous realms of heaven.
The great bull has grown toward these two; undecaying and far-reaching, he stands with his protection extended.
He plants his footsteps upon the ridges of the wide earth; his ruddy flames lick the udder.
Moving together toward their common calf, the two well-fashioned milch-cows wander in all directions;
unceasingly measuring out their paths, they bestow all great insights upon us.
The wise poets lead him to his station; guarding with various hearts the one who does not age, they looked all around, desiring to win the river. Sūrya became manifest to them, to the men.
Worthy to be beheld, victorious throughout the quarters, to be invoked for the great and the small so that they may live—
since he, the bounteous one visible to all, has become manifest in many places through these days for the sake of these embryos.
How, O Agni, have those who purify themselves offered to you with the strength of Ayu, aspiring for prizes?
When the gods, establishing both seed and offspring, took delight in the chant of the Eternal Order (Ṛta).
O youngest one, self-sustained lord, take heed of this my speech, most bountiful and well-offered!
One person reviles, another praises; I, your worshipper, praise your very body, O Agni.

O Agni, those guardians who, seeing him blind, protected Māmateya from distress—those doers of good deeds the omniscient one protected; though the enemies sought to harm them, they did not succeed in harming them.
O Agni, whoever—being stingy, malevolent, and hostile—harms us with duplicity, may that heavy spell recoil upon him; may he destroy his own body with his evil words.
Or rather, O powerful one, whatever mortal harms another mortal through duplicity—he, being praised, protect him from that; O Agni, let none of us be delivered over to misfortune.
When Mātariśvan, having entered it, stirred him— the Hotṛ who belongs to all waters and all gods,
whom they established among the human clans, brilliant like the sun, resplendent for the sake of beauty.
They did not deceive him who gave us this prayer; Agni has taken pleasure in that protection of mine.
May they accept all the works of this singer who brings forth his hymn of praise.
Him whom the worshipful ones have seized in his eternal dwelling and established with hymns of praise—
him they lead forward, grasping him in their sacrifice, hastening like horses yoked to a chariot.
The wondrous one destroys many things with his jaws; then, radiant, he shines within the forest.
Then the wind blows after his flame day by day, like the arrow of an archer shot at its mark.

Him whom neither enemies nor those seeking to harm can injure while he is still in the womb—him, blind and sightless, they cannot deceive by their looking on; his own constant friends have protected him.
He, the lord of the house, seeks great wealth; he stands at the station of powerful riches.
The pressing-stones have indeed served him as he hastens toward us.
He who is the bull among men, as he is for the two worlds (heaven and earth), whose flow is drunk by the living through his glories— he who, having sped forth, has settled in his place of origin.
He who shone upon the unassailable city, like a courser, a sage, a steed of the clouds;
like the sun, resplendent and hundredfold in essence.
The doubly-born one, shining brightly, has taken his stand over the three luminous realms and all the regions,
the most excellent sacrificer, in the gathering place of the waters.
This is that Hotṛ priest who, having a twofold birth, possesses all desirable things through his desire for glory—
the mortal who has offered oblations to him with well-prepared gifts.
O Agni, as a liberal donor, I have called upon you many times; indeed, I am your friend, like one who has found refuge under the protection of a great impeller.
Even at the sacrifice of one who possesses wealth but lacks breath, or of the stingy one who never bestows gifts,
or of the godless man who flees— never do you favor them.
O Agni, that mortal is like the moon, great and most exalted in heaven; may we, as thy worshippers, ever advance before thee.
Him whom those seeking cattle have brought forth with skillful labor among the waters at the sacrifice—like a friend—with their devotion;
at his might and song, the two worlds, heaven and earth, trembled; he is the beloved, the worshipful one, the protection of all beings.

When those [deeds] of yours for the Soma-pressing Purumīḷha were indeed set forth like friends by the self-sustaining ones, then you two found the will and the path for the singer; and hear, O bulls, of the one who dwells in the house.
The peoples have adorned your birth from the two worlds, O Bulls, to be proclaimed for great skill;
since you bring [the oblation] for the sake of *ṛta* and for the steed, you enjoy the sacrifice through the invocation and the labor.
That people, O Asuras, is dear to you both who, as upholders of *ṛta*, proclaim the lofty *ṛta*.
You two harness the efficient power of the vast heaven for the sake of the waters, like a bull to the pole.
In this great rite, you two fulfill the desire by your greatness; the dustless, impetuous milch-cows are in their stall.
They low toward the sun at its setting and at the break of dawn, like swift birds.
The long-haired maidens have sung out to you both for the sake of the sacred Law (*ṛta*), O Mitra and Varuṇa, where you two chant the path.
Release [the waters] by yourselves; cause our prayers to swell. You two rule over the inspired thoughts of the sage.

Whosoever, striving with sacrifices, offers to you both—the sage who as Hotar-priest performs the sacrifice, accomplishing the prayer—unto him you two indeed come; you enjoy the rite; come toward our songs and our favor, being well-disposed toward us.
With sacrifices and with cattle, they first anoint you two, the upholders of *ṛta*, as if by the impulse of the mind.
They bring songs to you with concentrated thought; with an undeluded mind, you have attained wealth.
O Heroes, you bestow wealthy vigor; with your wondrous powers you have attained wealth and greatness from this world.
Neither the heavens nor the days, nor the rivers, nor even the Paṇis have attained your divinity or your bounty.
You two clothe yourselves in fat garments; your thoughts are flawless, indeed like continuous streams. You have struck down all falsehoods; O Mitra and Varuṇa, you abide by the cosmic order (*ṛta*).
Not even one among them has clearly understood this: the true mantra, uttered by the seer, is powerful and fierce.
The four-edged, terrible [thunderbolt] strikes that which has three edges; thus, the first revilers of the gods have been worn away.
The footless one goes forth, the first among those with feet; O Mitra and Varuṇa, who among you perceives this?
The embryo bears the burden of this very world; he fulfills the *ṛta* and overcomes the *anṛta*.
We behold him as he goes forth, the lover of maidens, never falling down;
he clothes himself in wide-spreading, impenetrable garments—the beloved abode of Mitra and Varuṇa.
Born without a horse, without a rein, the steed neighs loudly as he flies with his back uplifted;
the youths have delighted in the unconscious prayer, praising the foundation in Mitra and Varuṇa.
May the milch-cows, who favor the son of Mamatā, cause him who loves sacred prayer to swell at this very udder.
Knowing the ways, let him beg for food; seeking to win her over with his mouth, he shall deliver Aditi.

O gods Mitra and Varuṇa, may I turn you both toward the enjoyment of our oblation with reverence and for your protection. May our sacred prayer be victorious in battles; may we have divine rain that leads us safely across.
We worship you two, the great ones, with common accord, O Mitra and Varuṇa, with oblations and salutations— with clarified butter,
O you who are dripping with ghee— since the Adhvaryus bring [these offerings] to you through our prayers as it were.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, this well-fashioned hymn is offered to you as a presentation, not as a mere performance;
when the Hotṛ priest anoints you in the assemblies, the patron, seeking your favor, O mighty ones, desires to worship you.
The cow Aditi has swelled with milk for the one who acts according to the *ṛta*, for the person who offers the oblation, O Mitra and Varuṇa.
When he serves you in the assembly, honoring you, that man becomes like a human *hotṛ* priest who has presented the oblation.
Moreover, among the exhilarating clans, may the cows and the divine waters cause the soma-juice to swell for you both.
And so, O ancient Lord of the house, enjoy this; drink of the milk of the ruddy cow.
Now I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu, who measured out the earthly realms;
he who, striding thrice with wide-gazing steps, propped up the highest dwelling place.
Viṣṇu is praised for that heroic deed: like a terrifying beast, roaming and dwelling in the mountains, he in whose three wide strides all worlds abide.
Let this hymn go forth as strength for Viṣṇu, the dweller on the mountains, the wide-striding bull—
he who alone has measured out this long, extended common dwelling-place with only three steps.
He whose three steps, filled with honey, rejoice in imperishable self-sustenance;
he who alone has supported the threefold earth and the sky, and all existing beings.
May I attain that beloved domain of his, where men devoted to the gods rejoice;
for there, indeed, in the highest footstep of Viṣṇu of the wide stride, is the kinsman and the fountain of honey.
We desire to go to those abodes of yours where the many-horned, tireless cattle are;
for there, indeed, the supreme station of the wide-striding Bull shines forth abundantly.
Sing forth with prayer to the drinking of your soma-juice for the great Hero and for Viṣṇu—
those two undeceivable ones who stand upon the ridges of the mountains like two horses on a straight path.
Truly, the brilliant encounter of you two, the impetuous ones, O Indra and Viṣṇu, protects you, the drinkers of the pressed juice;
for you ward off the missile of the archer Kṛśānu that is aimed at a mortal.
These [streams] increase his great manly power; he brings down the two parents for the sake of seed and enjoyment.
The son establishes the lower and the higher name of the father, and a third name in the luminous realm of heaven.

We celebrate each of those manly deeds of his, the seated one, the protector, the harmless, the bounteous giver— He who, with only three strides, strode across the earthly realms for the wide-striding one to live in spacious freedom.

Two indeed are the strides of him who beholds the light; having gazed upon them, the mortal stirs with zeal. But no one dares to approach his third stride, not even the winged birds that fly through the air.
Together with the ninety-four names, he has set the wheel in motion like a revolving disc;
the youth of great stature, measuring himself out with the singers, returns to the battle-cry.

Be gracious like a friend, O you who are invoked with clarified butter, you of far-reaching splendor, whose course is swift and who are wide-extending. Therefore, O Viṣṇu, even by the wise your praise is to be honored, and your sacrifice is to be perfected by the one possessing oblations.
He who offers worship to Viṣṇu— the ancient, most recent, and most bounteous ordainer—
who proclaims the great birth of this Great One, he shall indeed surpass even his equal through his glorious renown.
O singers, fulfill that ancient one according to your knowledge, him who from birth is the embryo of the Eternal Order (*ṛta*).
Knowing his very name, proclaim it; O Viṣṇu, may we share in your great favor.

King Varuṇa, the Aśvins, and the Maruts, the wise ones, follow that will of his, the ordainer. Viṣṇu, accompanied by his friend, maintains supreme skill that finds the day and opens the stall of cattle.

Viṣṇu, the divine ordainer who has come forth for companionship to the well-doing Indra, being himself a greater doer of good, has quickened the Ārya who dwells in the three abodes; he has caused the sacrificer to partake in his share of the Eternal Order (*ṛta*).
Agni has been awakened; Sūrya rises from the earth; the radiant Dawn has shone forth greatly with her light.
The Aśvins have yoked their chariot to travel; the god Savitṛ has impelled every living being apart.
When you two, O Aśvins, harness your bull-like chariot, sprinkle our dominion with ghee and honey;
quicken our prayer in the battles, and may we share in the spoils in the contest for heroes.
May the well-praised chariot of the Aśvins come hither—three-wheeled, carrying honey, drawn by swift horses;
may that three-seated, wealthy vehicle, possessing all prosperity, bring welfare to our bipeds and quadrupeds.
O Aśvins, bring nourishment to us; sprinkle us with your honeyed whip.
Prolong our lives, wipe away our sins, drive off our enemies, and be our companions.
You two place the embryo within moving creatures; you two are within all existing worlds. O Ashvins, you two, the bulls, have set in motion Agni, the waters, and the lords of the forest.
You two indeed are physicians with your medicines; and you are charioteers with your skill in driving.
Furthermore, O fierce ones, you bestow sovereign power upon that man who, possessing oblations, worships you with his mind.
O Vasus and Rudras, you of many insights, increasing in power, O bulls, grant us your favor in our desire!
For you, O wonder-workers, when the son of Ucathya praised your wealth, you sped forth with your ungrudging aids.
Who shall offer oblation to you both for this very favor, since you, O Vasus, bestow wealth upon him who honors you with reverence at the station of the Cow?
Awaken for us abundant and opulent inspirations, as you two move with a mind that fulfills every desire.
When your chariot, harnessed for the sake of the son of Tugra, was placed as a protector in the midst of the surging flood;
then may I come unto your protection and refuge, like a hero to the battlefield with flying steeds.
May Upastuti protect me from the son of Ucathya; may these two winged ones not suck me dry.
May the ten-fold piled fuel not consume me, when, bound by you, it devours the earth itself.
The rivers, most motherly, did not swallow me up when the Dāsas cast me down bound fast;
when Traitana hewed at his head, the Dāsa himself gnawed away his own breast and shoulders.
Dīrghatamas, the son of Mamatā, having grown old in the tenth age,
becomes the Brahman-priest and charioteer of the waters as they go toward their goal.
I praise with sacrifices at the assemblies the two great ones, Heaven and Earth, who increase the cosmic order and are wise;
they who, sons of the gods, possessing wondrous deeds, together with the gods, bestow desirable boons through such inspired thought.
And I think of the mind of the guileless father and the great inherent power of the mother;
through their invocations, the two parents of noble seed have made the world wide for progeny, and through their vastness, they have established immortality.
Those sons, skillful in their work and wondrous in their deeds, brought forth the two great parents so that they might be first perceived.
You two, O unswerving ones, guard the station of the son—the truth of both the stationary and the moving according to the cosmic law (*dharman*).
Those masters of illusion, possessing excellent wisdom, have measured out the two sisters who share a common womb, a pair dwelling together in one abode.
As sages of brilliant splendor, they extend a new thread after each new one across the sky within the ocean.
Today we meditate upon that desirable gift of Savitṛ at the impulse of the god.
O Heaven and Earth, with your benevolent mind, bestow upon us wealth consisting of treasures, a hundredfold.
For they, Heaven and Earth, are the source of all prosperity, observers of cosmic order (*ṛta*), and the sustainers of the realm of space, wise seers.
Between these two divine powers of noble birth, the pure god Sūrya moves according to the eternal law (*dharman*).
The wide-extending, mighty, and inexhaustible Father and Mother protect all beings;
the two world-halves are most courageous and beautiful, since the Father has clothed them in forms.
He, the wise son of his two parents, the bearer of oblations, purifies the worlds by his creative power.
From the dappled cow and the bull of excellent seed, he milks for all days the bright milk of this [soma].

This one among the active gods is the most active, who brought forth the two worlds that are beneficial to all; he, through his skillful wisdom, measured out the two realms and has firmly established them with imperishable supports.
O Heaven and Earth, being praised by us, you two of great power, bestow upon us great glory and lofty dominion;
with that whereby we may ever extend ourselves over the peoples, send forth to us praiseworthy strength.

Has the eldest come to us, or has the youngest? What mission does he perform as messenger, and what have we said? We have not reviled the cup which is of noble lineage; O Agni, brother, we have indeed praised the excellence of this wooden vessel.
"Make one chalice into four; that is what the gods told you, and that is what I have come to tell you.
O sons of Sudhanvan, if you will do exactly this, you shall become worthy of sacrifice together with the gods."
When you spoke to Agni the messenger, saying, "A horse must be made, and a chariot must be made here;
a cow must be made, and two youths must be made"—O brothers, we approach you now that those things have been accomplished.
Having performed that deed, O Ṛbhus, you asked: "Where has he gone who came to us as a messenger?
When he had announced that the four chalices had been made, Tvaṣṭṛ then hid himself among the divine women.
"Let us slay them," so Tvaṣṭṛ said, "those who have reviled the cup from which the gods drink. When the Soma is pressed, they assume other names; with other names the maiden has preserved them.
Indra yoked his two bay horses; the Aśvins [yoked] their chariot; Bṛhaspati brought the multiform [cow].
As Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, and Vāja, you went to the gods; being skillful-handed, you attained your share of the sacrifice.
From the hide you brought forth the cow by means of your insights; those who were old, you made young again.
O sons of Sudhanvan, you fashioned horse after horse; having yoked the chariot, you went to the gods.
"Drink this water," you said; "or rather, drink this rinsing-water of *muñja* grass.
O sons of Sudhanvan, if you do not find pleasure in that, then indeed you shall rejoice at the third libation.
"The waters are most abundant," said one; "Agni is most abundant," said another.
One proclaimed her who strikes terror to many. Speaking the Truth, you fashioned the cups.
One drives away the lame cow that drinks the water; another carves the meat brought on the carving-board.
One carries away the dung until sunset; what indeed did the two parents do for their sons?
On the heights you created grass for him, and in the valleys, by your skillful work, O heroes, you created water;
since you lay down in the house of Agohya, O Ṛbhus, you do not follow after that which is here today.
When you crept around the worlds with eyes closed, where indeed were your dear parents then?
You cursed him who seized your foreleg; to him who spoke out against you, you spoke back in reply.
Having slept, O Ṛbhus, you asked this: "O Agohya, who has awakened us here?
The goat declared the dog to be the awakener; today, after a full year, he has opened his eyes.
By day the Maruts travel; Agni here travels upon the earth; this Vāta travels through the mid-air;
Varuṇa travels with the waters and the oceans, seeking you, O sons of strength.
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Āyu, Indra, Ṛbhukṣan, and the Maruts not look with disdain upon us,
as we proclaim in the assembly the heroic deeds of the prize-winning steed, born of the gods.
When they lead forth from the mouth the seized offering of the goat, which is covered with a brilliant garment and wealth,
the bleating, multiform goat goes forward well-directed toward the beloved path of Indra and Pūṣan.

This goat, the portion for Pūṣan, is led before the vigorous horse; it belongs to all the gods. When the beloved sacrificial cake is brought with the steed, Tvaṣṭṛ quickens it for the sake of glorious renown.
When men lead the horse, fit for oblation and the path of the gods, three times around according to the seasons—
at that moment, the goat, Pūṣan’s first portion, goes forth, announcing the sacrifice to the gods.
The Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Āvayāj, the Agnimindha, the Grāvagrābha, and the wise Śaṃstṛ—
with this well-prepared, well-offered sacrifice, fill the channels of the belly.
May those who hew the sacrificial posts, those who carry the posts, and those who carve the *caṣāla* for the horse’s post,
as well as those who prepare the cooking-vessel for the steed— their approval may further us.
He has come near; my prayer has been well-placed for him, he whose back is smooth, toward the regions of the gods.
The inspired seers rejoice after him; we have made him a good kinsman in the prosperity of the gods.

Whatever tethering-rope, halter, or head-stall belongs to the prize-winning steed, whatever cord or rein is upon his head, or whatever grass has been placed in his mouth as fodder— may all these of yours be among the gods.
Whatever of the horse’s raw flesh the fly has eaten, or whatever is smeared upon the sacrificial post or the axe,
whatever is on the hands of the slaughterer or on his nails— may all of that be yours among the gods.
Whatever undigested food from the belly escapes, and whatever odor there is of raw flesh—
let the immolators make that well-prepared, and let them cook the sacrificial victim until it is thoroughly cooked.

Whatever from your body, as it is being cooked by the fire, drips down toward the spit when you are impaled—let that not rest upon the earth, nor upon the grass; let it be offered to the longing gods.
Those who look upon the horse as cooked, those who say of it, "It smells good,
take it away," and those who wait for a portion of the steed's meat— may even their approval further us.
The inspection of the flesh-cooking cauldron, the vessels for pouring the broth,
the warming covers for the pots, the hooks, and the carving-boards— all these attend to the horse.
The stepping forth, the sitting down, the rolling over, and the tethering-post of the steed;
that which he drank and that which he ate as fodder—may all these of yours be among the gods.

Let not the smoke-scented fire crackle against you; let not the glowing cauldron, smelling of fat, break apart. O gods, accept this horse—sacrificed, welcomed, praised, and consecrated with the cry of *vaṣaṭ*.
The garment they spread beneath the horse, the upper covering, the golden ornaments, the halter, and the foot-rope— these dear things they present to the gods for the steed.
Whatever of yours was pained when you were exhausted by great effort, or by the heel, or by the whip—
just as one offers the oblation with a ladle at the sacrifices, all those [pains] of yours I soothe with a sacred prayer (*brahman*).
The axe meets the thirty-four ribs of the horse, the steed of the friend of the gods.
Make its limbs free from injury; following the joints, carve it apart with skill, proclaiming each section as you go.
One is the dissector of Tvaṣṭṛ’s horse; two are the guides, and such is the season. Those of your limbs which I prepare in due order, those very portions I offer as balls of meat into the fire.
Let not your dear self burn you as you enter it; let not the axe linger upon your body.
Let not the greedy, unskilled dissector, passing over the flaws, mangle your limbs with the knife.
Verily, you do not die here, nor do you suffer harm; you go to the gods by easy paths.
Your two bay steeds and the two spotted mares have become yoked; the vigorous steed has taken his place at the pole of the donkey.
May the prize-winning steed grant us abundance in cattle, abundance in horses, heroic sons, and wealth that nourishes all;
may Aditi grant us sinlessness, and may the horse, accompanied by our oblation, win for us sovereign power.
When you first neighed at birth, rising from the ocean or from the primordial waters,
with the wings of a hawk and the forelegs of a deer— O steed, your great birth is worthy of praise.
Yama gave him; Trita harnessed him; Indra was the first to mount him. The Gandharva grasped his reins; O Vasus, you fashioned the horse from the sun.
You are Yama; you are Āditya, O steed; you are Trita by your secret vow.
You are parted from Soma by an interval; they say you have three bonds in heaven.
They say you have three bonds in heaven, three in the waters, and three within the ocean.
O steed, may Varuṇa be gracious to me even as he is where they say is your highest place of birth.
O Steed, here are your grooming-stations; here are the places where the hooves of the winner are set down. Here I have seen your auspicious reins, which the guardians of *ṛta* protect.
I recognized you as yourself from afar with my mind, like a bird flying down from heaven;
I beheld your head, the winged one, speeding along easy paths that are free from dust.
There I beheld thy supreme form, striving for food at the station of the cow;
when the mortal has provided enjoyment for thee, then, O most voracious one, thou hast swallowed the plants.
After you, O steed, comes the chariot; after you, the young man; after you, the cattle; after you, the fortune of maidens.
After you, the troops have sought your friendship; after you, the gods have measured out your heroic power.
Golden-horned, with iron hooves, swift as thought—Indra was inferior to him.
The gods themselves came to eat his sacrificial food, he who first mounted the steed.
With their flanks rounded and their middles slender, the divine coursers, like heroes, rush together;
like swans they draw up in rows when the horses have reached the celestial racecourse.
O steed, your body is winged; your mind is swift-gliding like the wind.
Your horns are fixed in many places; they move flickeringly in the forests.
The vigorous steed has come toward the place of instruction, meditating with a mind directed toward the gods.
The goat, his kin, is led before him; behind him follow the sages and the singers.
He has approached the highest dwelling place, the steed toward his father and mother;
for today he shall go to the gods as the most beloved, and then he bestows desirable boons upon the donor.
Of this lovely, gray-haired Hotṛ-priest, his middle brother is Ashna;
his third brother has ghee upon his back. Here I beheld the Lord of the People, who has seven sons.
Seven yoke the one-wheeled chariot; a single horse draws it, bearing seven names.
Three-naved is the wheel, undecaying and invincible, upon which all these worlds rest.
Upon this seven-wheeled chariot stand the seven; seven horses draw it. Seven sisters sing together toward it, where the seven names of the cows are deposited.
Who has seen the first-born being, when that which is boneless supports the bony?
Where indeed is the life-force, the blood, and the soul of the earth? Who has approached the wise man to ask this?
As a simpleton, I ask with my mind, not knowing: where are these footsteps of the gods placed?
Upon the young calf have the sages stretched out seven threads to weave.
Unaware, I ask the wise seers here for knowledge, not knowing myself—
what indeed is that One in the form of the Unborn who has propped apart these six worlds?
Let him who truly knows it speak here of this beautiful bird’s hidden station:
from its head the cows milk forth milk; clothed in their covering, they have drunk the water with their feet.
The mother distributed her portion to the father according to the Eternal Law (ṛta); for in the beginning, she united with him through meditation and the mind.
She, loathing the essence of the embryo, was pierced; then those who offered homage approached her with their prayer.
The Mother was yoked to the pole of the sacrificial fee; the Embryo stood within the enclosures.
The Calf lowed as he beheld the Cow of all forms across the three distances.
Bearing three mothers and three fathers, he stands alone, erect; they do not cause him to weary.
Upon the back of that heaven, they deliberate in speech that knows all things, yet does not move all.
This twelve-spoked wheel of *Ṛta* revolves around the sky so as not to decay;
here, O Agni, seventy-two pairs of sons have taken their stand.
They say that the Father has five feet and twelve forms, rich in moisture, in the further half of heaven;
but others say he is the Far-Sighted One, fixed upon the seven-wheeled, six-spoked lower [chariot].
Upon the five-spoked wheel as it revolves, all living beings stand supported. Its axle, though bearing a heavy burden, does not grow hot; from of old its nave has never been shattered.
The wheel with its rim has turned, ageless; ten yoked [horses] carry it upon the outstretched [chariot].
The eye of Sūrya moves through the mid-air, enveloped; in it all beings are fixed.
Of those born together, they say the seventh was born alone; these six are the twin seers, born of the gods.
Their desired offerings are established according to their stations; for the Sustainer, they tremble, transformed according to their forms.
Those who are women, they call men; he who has eyes sees them, yet the blind does not discern them. The son who is a seer perceives them; he who understands them shall be the father of his father.

Beneath the further shore and beyond this near one, the Cow has risen up, bearing her calf with her foot. Whitherward has she gone? To which region has she departed? Where indeed will she give birth, for she is not within the herd?
Who here can declare it, acting like a seer—how he who knows his father below this [world], or how he who is beyond this [world] below? Whence was the divine mind born? RV_1,164.18c–d.
Those who are hitherward, them they call away; those who are away, them they call hither.
O Indra and Soma, those things which you two have fashioned carry [the world] like yoked horses at the pole of the firmament.
Two birds, united and friends, cling to the same tree. Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating.
Where the well-winged ones, without blinking, cry out together toward their share of immortality at the assemblies—
there the wise guardian of the entire world, the lord, has entered me, the simple one.
On that tree whereon all the fair-winged ones, eating honey, settle and procreate—of that tree they say the fruit at the top is sweet; he who does not know his father shall not attain it.
That which is the Gāyatra placed upon the Gāyatra, or that from which they fashioned the Triṣṭubh out of the Triṣṭubh,
or the Jagatī-foot placed upon the Jagatī— those who know this have attained immortality.
With the *gāyatrī* he measures out the *arka*; with the *arka*, the *sāman* in the *triṣṭubh* meter; with the *vāka*, the *vāka*.
With the two-footed and four-footed syllable, they measure out the seven voices.
With the *jagatī* he propped up the river in heaven; with the *rathantara* he beheld the sun.
They say there are three kindling-sticks of the *gāyatrī*; from there it surpassed [all] by its greatness and majesty.
I call hither this well-milking cow; may the skillful milker milk her.
May Savitṛ impel for us the most excellent impulse. The Gharma has been heated; that indeed I shall proclaim aloud.
Muttering "hiṅ," the mistress of treasures has come hither, seeking her calf with her mind.
May this inviolable cow yield milk for the two Aśvins; may she increase for our great good fortune.
The cow has lowed after her blinking calf; she has made the "hiṅ" sound for the sake of measuring his head.
Lowing toward the warm milk in her mouth, she utters her cry and yields her milk with her streams of milk.

This is that which bellows, by which the cow is encompassed; she utters her lowing, resting upon the cleft of the cloud. By her insights she has indeed brought the mortal low; becoming lightning, she cast off her covering.
The breathless one lies within the moving, living, and firm [world] in the midst of the dwellings.
The living spirit of the dead moves by its own powers; the immortal shares a common womb with the mortal.
I beheld the Herdsman, who never rests, moving hither and thither along his paths;
clothed in converging and diverging rays, he revolves repeatedly within the worlds.
He who made this does not know it; he who saw it is indeed far removed from it.
Enveloped within his mother’s womb, he who possesses abundant offspring has entered into destruction.
Heaven is my father, my progenitor; there is my navel. This great earth is my kin, my mother. Between the two upturned bowls is the womb; therein the father placed the seed within the daughter.
I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth; I ask where the navel of the world is.
I ask you about the seed of the stallion; I ask about the highest heaven of speech.
This altar is the furthest limit of the earth; this sacrifice is the navel of the world.
This Soma is the seed of the potent horse; this Brahman is the highest heaven of speech.

Seven half-germs, the seed of the world, abide by the command of Viṣṇu in the established order; through their insights and their mind, those wise ones, as encompassers, surround everything on every side.
I do not discern what this is that I am; hidden and girded, I move with my mind. When the first-born of Order come to me, then I obtain a share of this speech.
Moving westward and eastward, held by its own nature, the immortal shares a common womb with the mortal.
These two, eternal and moving in opposite directions, pass along; people perceive one, but they do not perceive the other.
In the syllable of the Ṛgveda, in the highest heaven, upon which all the gods have settled—what will he do with the Ṛgveda who does not know that? But those who know it, they sit together here.
O blessed one, may you indeed have abundant good pasture; and may we also be blessed. Eat grass at all times, O inviolable one, and drink pure water as you wander.
The ruddy one has lowed, fashioning the waters; she who is one-footed, two-footed, four-footed, eight-footed, and nine-footed, consisting of a thousand syllables, is in the highest heaven.
From her the oceans flow forth; by her the four quarters of space live.
From her flows that imperishable syllable (akṣara); upon it everything depends for life.
From afar, I saw the smoke consisting of *śaka* wood, spreading outwards beyond this lower world.
The heroes cooked the dappled bull; these were the first ordinances (*dharmāṇi*).
Three long-haired ones appear in due season; one of them shears his hair within the year.
One surveys the universe with his powers; the speed of one is seen, but not his form.
Speech has been measured out in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them.
Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech is what humans speak.
They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni; and he is the divine, fair-winged Garuḍa.
Being one, the sages call him by many names; they call him Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan.
The tawny-winged birds fly up to heaven, clothed in the waters along their black path;
they have returned from the seat of Cosmic Order, and from them indeed the earth is moistened with clarified butter.
Twelve are the fellies, one the wheel, and three the naves; who indeed has understood that?
Into it are fixed together thirty spokes, sixty that are unshakable as if immovable.

O Sarasvatī, that breast of yours which is inexhaustible, which is a source of bliss, by which you nourish all desirable things— that which bestows jewels, finds wealth, and grants excellent gifts— bring it here for us to suck.
With sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; those were the first ordinances. These great ones attained the firmament where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide.
This same water rises up and flows down through the days;
Parjanya quickens the earth, and the fires quicken the heavens.
The divine, well-winged, great bird, the offspring of the waters, the beautiful one among the plants;
him who satisfies us from all sides with rains, Sarasvant, I invoke for protection.

By what auspicious power have the Maruts, of equal age and common birthplace, joined together? With what intention have they come from where? From where do these bulls roar forth their strength, seeking wealth?
Whose prayers have the youthful Maruts accepted? Who has turned them toward his sacrifice?
Like hawks gliding through the mid-air, by what great thought may we cause them to pause?

From where do you come alone, O Indra, you who are so mighty, O Lord of the Good? What is it thus that you ask, meeting with the radiant ones? Tell us that, O Lord of Bay Steeds, which is yours among us.
My sacred prayers, my thoughts, and the pressed juices are auspicious; my strength stirs, and the pressing-stone is set forth for me.
They invoke you and long for you with their hymns; these two bay steeds carry you toward us.

Therefore, uniting with these our closest companions, adorning our bodies with our own powers, we now harness these [steeds] with great majesties; for you, O Indra, have indeed conformed to our self-nature.
Where was that self-power of yours, O Maruts, when you left me alone in the slaying of Ahi?
For I am indeed fierce, powerful, and mighty; with my weapons, I have struck down every enemy.
O Bull, you have performed many deeds for us with our allied and equal manly powers.
For we shall indeed accomplish many things, O most mighty Indra, through our resolve whenever we, the Maruts, so desire.
O Maruts, with my own Indra-power I slew Vṛtra, having become mighty through my own fury.
With the thunderbolt in my arm, I made these all-glittering waters easy to traverse for Manu.
Nothing, O Maghavan, is superior to you; indeed, no one among the gods is known to be your equal.
Neither one being born nor one already born can attain you. Do what you must do, O exalted one!

Though I am but one, let my power be manifold; whatever I, daring in spirit, shall accomplish through my wisdom—O Maruts, I am indeed known as fierce; Indra alone is the lord of those things which I have shaken down.
