O Maruts, you have gladdened me here with this hymn, since you, O heroes, have fashioned for me this glorious prayer—
this prayer for Indra, the bull, the great sacrificer, for my sake, as friends for a friend, for my own body with your own bodies.
Truly, these Maruts, shining toward me, bringing blameless glory— having beheld you, O moon-colored ones, you have pleased me and you shall please me even now.
Who here, O Maruts, has magnified you? Come forward, O friends, toward your friends! May you, the wondrous ones, cause our prayers to be heard; be mindful of these my true words.

Since the inspired wisdom of Mānya has brought us here to serve you, as a poet brings his gift to one worthy of worship—O Maruts, turn hither toward this sage; let the singer recite these sacred prayers for you.
This is your hymn, O Maruts, this is the song of the poet Māndārya, the son of Māna. May it bring offspring for our own bodies; may we find strengthening food that bestows long life.
Let us now proclaim the ancient greatness of that impetuous host, the herald of the Bull.
Like kindling wood on your march, O Maruts of mighty roar, like warriors in battle, O Śakras, display your powers!
Constantly bringing sweetness like a son, they play at play in the sacrificial assemblies, impetuous in their vigor.
The Rudras reach out with their protection to the one who bows; being self-strong, they do not neglect the one who has prepared the oblation.
To him who has offered oblations, the immortal helpers have granted abundance of wealth;
for him the Maruts, like well-disposed friends, sprinkle many regions with refreshing milk.

Those who have clothed themselves in the regions with their powers, your swift-moving steeds have rushed forward. All beings tremble with fear; even the dwellings shake at your brilliant march when your spears are extended.

When your brilliant, impetuous [horses] make the mountains roar, or when the manly ones shake the back of heaven, every lord of the forest fears at your onset; the plants bow down as if they were chariot-riders.
O fierce Maruts, with your benevolence, you whose hosts are unharmed, fulfill our desire for favor!
Wherever your lightning, with its gnashing teeth, bites, it releases the cattle like a well-aimed bolt.

Those who bestow firm support, whose gifts are inexhaustible, who are unrestrained and well-praised in the assemblies—they sing their song of praise so that they may drink the intoxicating draught; for they know the first heroic deeds of the Mighty One.
O Maruts, protect with your hundred-armed strongholds that man from treachery and evil whom you have favored;
O fierce, powerful, and exuberant ones, preserve the person from reproach for the sake of the prosperity of his offspring.
O Maruts, all auspicious things are placed upon your chariots; as if in rivalry with one another, your powers are set there.
Rings are upon your shoulders for your journeys, and your axle revolves between the two wheels.
Many auspicious things are upon their manly arms; upon their chests are golden ornaments, impetuous and glittering.
Upon their shoulders are these [spears], and upon their fellies are sharp razors; like birds spreading their wings, they have displayed their splendors.
Great by their greatness, far-reaching and pervasive, visible from afar like the heavens with their stars;
sweet-toned, fair-tongued, resonant with their voices—the Maruts, mingled with Indra, cry out in praise.
O well-born Maruts, that is your greatness; long is your bounty, like the ordinance of Aditi.
Even Indra does not, through abandonment, frustrate that [bounty] for the person of good deeds to whom you have granted it.

O Maruts, that kinship of yours in a former age, when you, the immortals, frequently favored our hymn of praise—with this prayer you granted hearing to Manu; together with your wondrous deeds, O heroes, you have made yourselves known.
O Maruts, swift ones, by means of your abundant wealth may we flourish for a long time;
when men extend their efforts in the assembly, through these sacrifices may I attain that desired goal.
This hymn for you, O Maruts, this song of the poet Māndārya, the son of Māna—may it bring offspring for our own bodies; may we find strengthening food that bestows long life.

A thousand are your aids for us, O Indra; a thousand are the most praiseworthy refreshments, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. May a thousand riches come to delight us; may thousandfold strengths come unto us.

May the Maruts come toward us with their aids— those most excellent ones from the lofty heaven, possessed of wondrous power— especially when their teams of horses, reaching even to the furthest limit, carry them across the ocean.
Among them the well-placed, butter-dripping [ladle] has settled, like a spear with golden sheath close at hand;
moving in secret like a woman among men, the speech gathers together like an assembly in a hall.
The brilliant, tireless Maruts have mingled with the youthful [waters] as if with their common property;
the terrible gods did not push away heaven and earth, but took pleasure in strengthening for friendship.
When the divine Rodasī, with loosened locks and manly spirit,
was pleased to accompany him, she— like Sūryā, with her brilliant countenance— ascended the chariot of her worshipper like the swift onset of a cloud.
The youths established the young woman, united for glory, the one firm in the assemblies;
when your hymn, O Maruts, accompanied by oblations, sang the song as the Soma was pressed, he paid you honor.

I proclaim that which is worthy of being proclaimed: the true greatness of these Maruts, when they, of virile mind and full of self-confidence, carry along even firm and fortunate women as their companions.
Mitra and Varuṇa protect [us] from blame; Aryaman punishes those who are unworthy of praise.
Even the unshakable and firm things are moved; the Maruts, who grant choice boons, have caused them to grow.
O Maruts, there is indeed no limit to your power; even from afar, they have reached the very end of our strength.
Having increased through their bold might, they have boldly encompassed our enemies like a surging wave.
May we today be the dearest to Indra, and may we call upon him tomorrow in the assembly;
may we be so in the past, and may he follow us through the great days—may R̥bhukṣan favor us, O heroes.
This is your hymn, O Maruts, this is the song of Māndārya, the son of Māna, the poet. May it bring offspring for our own bodies; may we find strengthening food that bestows life-sustaining power.
Sacrifice after sacrifice, you who are swift in equal measure; with every prayer, O gods, you take hold of us as we seek the divine.
May I turn you hitherward for our well-being, for the greatness of both worlds, and for your protection with well-fashioned hymns.
Like self-born bulls, those who are self-strong, the shakers have been born for food and for light;
they are like thousandfold waves of the waters, worthy of praise with the mouth, like oxen and stallions.
Like Soma juices pressed out, with their stalks satiated, they sit within our hearts like those who offer worship;
upon their shoulders there clings something like a clinging creeper, and in their hands are joined both the ring and the dagger.
The self-yoked [horses] have come down from heaven at will; O immortals, urge yourselves on with the whip!
Born of many powers, free from dust, the Maruts with their glittering spears have shaken even the firmest things.
O Maruts, who among you trembles by his own power like a tongue between the jaws, flashing with spears?
Like the discharge of arrows on the path of a journey, you are many-impelled, like the sun's steed day by day.

Where indeed is the farthest limit of this great space, and where its near side, O Maruts, when you have come hither? When you cause that which is compact to fall asunder like something fragile, you fly with the stone through the shimmering ocean.
Like a victorious onset, O Maruts, is your stormy host—mighty, radiant, and crushing;
like the bounty of a liberal giver is your auspicious gift, wide-reaching and flashing like the power of the Asuras.
The rivers roar against the tires [of their chariots] when they send forth their thunderous voice from the clouds;
the lightnings smile down upon the earth when the Maruts sprinkle the ghee.
Pṛśni brought forth for the great battle the brilliant host of the tireless Maruts;
those companions brought forth the formidable being, and then they beheld their own vigorous power.

This hymn for you, O Maruts, this song of the poet Māndārya, the son of Māna—may it bring offspring for our own bodies; may we find strengthening food and a community that bestows life-sustaining gifts.
Even though you are great, O Indra, since you are the protector of these [Maruts] from even great hostility;
as such, O wise ordainer, being mindful of the Maruts, win their favors for us, for they are most dear to you.

O Indra, those Maruts have yoked their teams for all the peoples, knowing how to ward off the hostilities of mortals; the onset of the Maruts is like a laugh in the winning of the light-giving, foremost prize.

O Indra, that spear of yours has been fixed for us; the Maruts drive on every side our formidable power. For even Agni, blazing brightly when fanned by the wind, bestows refreshments like waters upon an island.
O Indra, do you grant us that wealth, like a gift bestowed by most powerful liberality;
may those hymns of yours which have been pleasing, O Vāyu, cause them to swell with strength like the breast of honey.
In you, O Indra, are the most bountiful riches that lead every one who follows the *ṛta*;
may those Maruts be gracious to us, they who of old were like gods seeking a path.
Go forth toward the men who bestow gifts, O Indra; exert yourself in the great earthly dwelling.
For now their broad-based spears stand like women at a ford, displaying their manly prowess.
One hears the approaching roar of these terrible, tireless Maruts,
who with their aids swoop down like debt-collectors upon the mortal who attacks them in battle.
O Indra, with the Maruts, bestow upon us for all people wealth consisting of cattle and other spoils;
O God, being praised by the gods, you are praised in turn. May we find strengthening food that grants life-sustaining gifts.
There is nothing now, nor will there be tomorrow; who knows that which is mysterious?
One must tread cautiously upon the mind of another, for even what has been learned may perish.
O Indra, why do you wish to strike us? The Maruts are your brothers;
act rightly with them, and do not slay us in the encounter.
"O brother Agastya, being our friend, why do you disregard us? For we know how your mind is disposed; you simply do not wish to give to us."
Let them prepare the altar; let them kindle the fire in front.
There, we two shall extend for you the sacrifice, the manifestation of immortality.
O Lord of Wealth, you rule over riches; O Lord of Friends, you are the most liberal among friends.
O Indra, consult with the Maruts, and then consume the oblations in due season.
With this homage and with this hymn, I approach you; I beg for the favor of the swift ones. O Maruts, being gracious through your wisdom, lay aside your anger and unyoke your horses.

O Maruts, this hymn of yours, fashioned with the heart and mind, has been offered to you with reverence, O Gods. Come hither, taking pleasure in our thought, for you are indeed the ones who increase our homage.

May the Maruts, being praised, be gracious to us; and may Maghavan, the most beneficent, being praised, grant us happiness. May our beloved forests stand upright; O Maruts, may we conquer all the days in our desire for victory.
Fleeing from this powerful Indra, O Maruts, trembling with fear, I said:
"The oblations were prepared for you; we have sent them far away—be gracious to us!"

By whom even the Mānasas are made mindful at the dawning of the eternal mornings through his power—may he, the bull, together with the Maruts, bestow fame upon us; may he, the fierce one, the steadfast giver of victory, be mighty with his own fierce ones.
O Indra, protect the men who are more powerful; through the Maruts, become one whose wrath is averted.
Endowed with excellent wisdom and victorious, may we find a strengthening community that bestows life-sustaining gifts.
May your journey be wondrous, and wondrous your aid, O bounteous Maruts, who shine with the splendor of serpents.
Far away from us, O bounteous Maruts, let that rushing arrow of yours be; far away the stone which you hurl.
O bounteous ones, spare the people of Tṛṇaskanda;
raise us up that we may live.
Sing the *sāman* like the bird that soars through the atmosphere; let us praise that which has grown strong and is full of light.
The milch-cows, unharmed, stand upon the sacred grass, as they seek to reach the divine dwelling.
The bull shall sing with the bulls who offer sweat as their oblation; like a wild beast, he shall devour that which he would otherwise pass over.
The exhilarating priest, praised by all, brings forth his thoughts; the worshipful youth bears the pair of offerings.
May the Hotṛ-priest reach the measured seats as he goes; may he bear the germ of the earth through the autumns.
Let the horse neigh as he is led, let the bull bellow; let the Voice move between the two worlds like a messenger.
Those who seek the gods bring forth for him deeds more effective than his own, heroic exploits;
may Indra, of wondrous luster, take pleasure in them, standing in his chariot as one easy to approach, like the two Nāsatyas.
Praise that Indra indeed, who is a warrior, who is the hero, the bounteous lord, who stands upon the chariot;
he who fights even against those facing him, who possesses the bull, and who is the dispeller of even the dense darkness.
Since he thus prevails in greatness over men, the two worlds, heaven and earth, are not sufficient for him as a girth-belt;
Indra has encompassed the earth like a stronghold, and he, the self-sustaining lord, bears up the sky like a diadem.
In battles, O hero, for you who are chosen by the virtuous and who travel most widely—
to honor you, the one whom the united hosts of men, even the patrons themselves, rejoice in with their strengths during the exhilaration of Soma.
For thus indeed are the libations auspicious for you in the ocean, when the divine waters rejoice in them.
Every cow has become pleasing to you, even when you, through your inspired thought, visit the people who are patrons.
May we be his good friends through these praises, like those of men who possess excellent protection;
may Indra abide in our hymns of praise, as one swift in action brings forth our songs of laudation.
Like men vying with one another in praise, may Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, be on our side;
like those seeking a friend, they serve the Lord of the City with well-guided sacrifices, seeking him as their mediator.
For indeed, any sacrifice that offends Indra, even if it proceeds crookedly with a wandering mind,
brings him home— just as one reaches a watering-place when thirsty, or as a long road finally leads to the goal for one who has reached his destination.
O Indra, do not abandon us here in the battles along with the gods, for you, O impetuous one, possess the power to overcome.
Even the great host of the bounteous Maruts, whose youthful company is attended by the hymn of the sacrificer, praises him.

This hymn of praise is for you, O Indra; by this, O Lord of Bay Steeds, find a path for us. O God, turn toward us for our well-being. May we find a strengthening community that grants life-sustaining gifts.
O Indra, king of kings, you and the gods—protect us, O Asura!
You are the lord of the good, the bountiful one who delivers us; you are the true one, the possessor of wealth, the giver of strength.

O Indra, you shattered the seven autumnal fortresses, the refuge of the Dānus who spoke with insults; O blameless one, you released the waters of the flood and delivered Vṛtra over to the young Purukutsa.

O Indra, much-invoked one, with those [helpers] by whom you now encompassed the unaging, hero-wedded Ajas and the heavens, you, like a lion in its lair, performed deeds for the sake of Agni, the insatiable Tūrvayāṇa, while dwelling in the house.
O Indra, may they remain for you in this same womb for the praise of your greatness through the thunderbolt;
when you released the floods and drove down the cattle by battle, you stood with your two bay horses and boldly seized the spoils of war.
O Indra, carry Kutsa, in whom you take delight; let the two bay horses of Vāta, swift as thought, draw you.
Let the Sun’s wheel roll forward in the encounter; may he with the thunderbolt in his arm go forth against the rivals.
O Indra, lord of the bay horses, grown strong through the pressing-stones, you have struck down the non-givers who were hostile to Mitra—
those who, while seeing Aryaman together with Ayo, were yet destroyed by you as they carried away their offspring.
The sage whispered, O Indra, for the winning of the sun; he made the earth a cushion for the Dāsa.
Maghavan performed three wondrous deeds of bounty; he cast Kuyavāc into a pitless place within the dwelling.
These ancient deeds of yours, O Indra, have become new again; you brought down many clouds for the sake of light.
You shattered the godless fortresses as if they were unbaked clay; you bent down the weapon of the godless oppressor.
O Indra, you, the shaker, sent forth the shaking waters so that they flowed like rivers;
when you, O hero, carried them across to the ocean, you brought Turvaśa and Yadu safely across.

O Indra, may you be ours at all times, the most secure protector of men among heroes. As such, grant us victory over all our rivals; may we find a strengthening community that bestows life-sustaining gifts.
O Lord of the Bay Steeds, your exhilarating, intoxicating drink has been drunk for your greatness, like [the contents] of a large vessel.
O Bull, your juice is a bull, a prize-winning steed that wins a thousandfold.
May your exhilarating, bull-like, and most excellent intoxication come to us— O Indra, the immortal one, the victorious, the winner of spoils, and the subduer of hostile armies.
For you, O hero, are the winner; you urge on the chariot of man. As one who is victorious, burn away the lawless Dasyu with your flame, as if burning a vessel.
O Sage, as the sovereign lord, you stole the wheel of the sun by your might;
with the steeds of Vāta, bring Kutsa as a weapon against Śuṣṇa.
For most powerful indeed is your exhilaration, and most brilliant is your wisdom;
as a slayer of Vṛtra and a finder of wide space, may you consider yourself the best winner of horses.
Just as you were for the ancient singers, O Indra, like water for one who thirsts, so do I repeatedly invoke you with this hymn of praise. May we find this strengthening food that bestows long life.
Make us exhilarated for the attainment of wealth; O Indu, as a bull, enter Indra.
Raging in your fury, you drive away the enemy; you find no one standing against you.
Direct our songs toward him who alone moves among the peoples—
he whom the self-power (svadhā) follows as a bull follows the sown barley, plowing it.
In whose two hands are all the treasures of the five peoples;
be on the watch for him who seeks to harm us and strike him down like a thunderbolt from heaven.
Slay the one who offers no libation, the difficult-to-reach one who brings you no joy.
Bestow upon us his possession; even a patron takes note of this.
O Indu, you have protected him whose strength is twofold, who has been present at the songs of praise;
O Indu, you have furthered Indra, the prize-winner, in the contests for booty.
Just as you were for the ancient singers, O Indra, like water for one who thirsts, so do I repeatedly invoke you with this hymn of praise. May we find this strengthening food that bestows long life.
The bull among men, the protector of the people, the king of the tribes, Indra, invoked by many—
praised and seeking glory, come hither to me with your protection, having yoked your two vigorous bay steeds!
O Indra, those bulls of yours, the stallions yoked by prayer, the coursers with powerful chariots—mount upon them; come hither with them! We invoke you, O Indra, when the Soma is pressed.
Mount the bull-chariot; O Bull, the Soma is pressed for you and the sweet juices are poured out.
Having yoked the two bulls, O Bull among the peoples, come toward me along the downward slope with your two bay steeds.
This sacrifice goes to the gods; this is the sacrificial food; these are the prayers; this, O Indra, is the Soma.
The sacred grass is strewn; come hither, O Śakra, sit down and drink; unyoke your two bay horses here.
O Indra, well-praised, come hither toward the sacred formulations (*brahmāṇi*) of the poet Mānya.
Singing our praises, may we find the light of day through your protection; may we find nourishment, a secure dwelling, and one who bestows life-giving gifts.

O Indra, whatever readiness of ear you have, by which you have become a helper for those who sing your praises—do not consume our desire as it grows; may I obtain all the works of the living man from you.
O Indra, King of kings, let them not deceive us, whatever two sisters may do in the womb;
even the waters have sped toward him with swift motion—may Indra come to us with friendship and vital strength.
Indra, the hero, is the victor with his men in battles; he hears the invocation of the singer who implores him.
He brings the chariot near to the donor; he raises up our songs when he manifests himself.
Thus, through the men, Indra has become renowned for his glorious fame; he, the devourer of nourishment, has come to the side of those who possess friends.
In the assembly where food is praised and words are spoken, the hymn of the sacrificer brings about all-encompassing success.
With you, O Maghavan Indra, may we overcome our enemies who consider themselves great.
You are our protector; you indeed have been for our increase. May we find this strengthening food that bestows long life.
"Many autumns have I spent in toil, through nights and mornings that wear one out;
old age diminishes the beauty of our bodies. Yet, let husbands still come to their wives."

For even those who were the first observers of the *ṛta*, who spoke the truths together with the gods—they too have passed away, for they did not reach the end. Now let the wives come together with the bulls.
The toil of the gods is not in vain, for they protect us; may we overcome all our rivals.
Here let us proclaim the victory in this battle of a hundred ways, as we two, a harmonious pair, have come together to fight.
Desire has come upon me from this side, born from that side, from wherever it may be—from the obstructing river.
Lopāmudrā leads forth the bull; the unwise woman suckles the wise one as he pants.
I now address this Soma, drunk within my heart from close at hand:
whatever sin we have committed, may he graciously forgive it; for mortal man has many desires.
Agastya, digging with his spades and desiring offspring, progeny, and strength—
the fierce seer nourished both classes [of people] and attained true blessings among the gods.
Your well-governed horses traverse the realms when your chariot speeds around the watery expanses.
Your golden fellies spray forth moisture; drinking of the sweetness, you accompany the dawns.
You two reach across the steed when he, the manly one who strives in sacrifice, speeds forward;
when your sister, praised by all, brings you for the sake of strength, you, drinkers of the honeyed draught, are implored for nourishment and food.
You two placed the milk within the raw cow; you brought down the ancient essence of the cow.
When the pure, oblation-bearing one, like a cleansing ladle, offers sacrifice between the two fire-sticks that consume the wood.
You two indeed chose the honeyed *gharma* for Atri, like a flood of water for its course.
O Aśvins, heroes, that [work] of yours for the sake of cattle proceeds toward the sweetness, like the wheels of a chariot.
O Wonder-Workers, may I turn you both hither for the sake of giving, as the aged Tugrya did with his longing for cattle;
the waters and the two worlds attend upon your greatness, and your swift axle, O Holy Ones, has worn away from distress.
When you two, O bounteous givers, yoke your teams of horses, you release Purandhi by your own powers;
like the wind, the patron hastens and exerts himself; like one of noble vows, he wins the prize for the great [sacrifice].
For we indeed, as your praisers, truly celebrate you both; the niggardly man, though intent on his own gain, is cast aside.
And so it is, O blameless Aśvins, that you, the bulls, protect the one who stands near the gods.
For you two, O Aśvins, indeed day after day, even at the winning of the flowing stream of Virudra,
Agastya— most praised among men among men— made himself known by thousands, like one who strikes with a weapon.

When you two speed forth with the greatness of your chariot, you go swiftly like the *hotṛ* of a man. Bestow upon our patrons, O Nāsatyas, wealth consisting of fine horses; may we be possessors of riches.

O Aśvins, we invoke today that chariot of yours with new hymns for our well-being—the chariot with uninjured fellies, which traverses the sky. May we find a strengthening community that bestows life-sustaining food.
When, as the two most beloved ones, you perform the office of the *adhvaryu* priest and pour forth the waters with food and riches—
this sacrifice has offered praise to you both, O dispensers of wealth, protectors of men.
May your pure, water-drinking horses— divine coursers with the speed of the wind,
swift as thought, vigorous, and smooth-backed— bring you both, O self-ruling Aśvins, hither.

May your chariot, like a rushing torrent, come with its wide seat for our well-being—swift as thought, the first to arrive, worthy of worship, and the one who must be invoked. You two are the riders of that bull-like vehicle.
Born here and there, they have lowed together with their stainless bodies and their own names.
One of you two is the victorious lord of the well-sacrificing one; the other is considered the fortunate son of heaven.
May your tawny, towering steed, moving downward according to our will, come to our dwellings;
may the two bay steeds of the other nourish us with strengths, O Aśvins, as they stir the regions with their neighing.
Like a bull, the autumnal showerer comes forth for you both; he moves along, sending forth many refreshments of honeyed sweetness.
By the ways of the other, they have been nourished with strengths; like surging rivers, they have come to us.
An ancient song has been released for you two by the wise one, O Aśvins, flowing in three ways at the pressing. You who are praised, protect the suppliant; hear my call as you come on your journey.
Moreover, this song of yours, belonging to the radiant one of wondrous appearance, swells in the assembly where the triple sacrificial grass is spread for the sake of men.
O showerers, the bull-like cloud has overflowed for you; bestowing gifts upon man, it is like the pouring out of kine.
O Aśvins, like Pūṣan, the one rich in wisdom honors you both as one honors Agni or Uṣas;
when I, praising you with my desire for wide space, invoke you, may we find a strengthening community that bestows life-sustaining gifts.
This ritual wisdom has come into being; now prepare yourselves! O wise ones, rejoice in the chariot drawn by stallions.
You who quicken the prayer, you who are worthy of worship, you who possess the wealth of Viśpalā, you two sons of heaven, pure in your vows for the sake of the pious man.
For you two are most like Indra, worthy of praise, most like Maruts, most wondrous in your deeds, the best of charioteers among those who drive chariots.
You carry a full chariot laden with honey; with that, O Aśvins, you come to the donor.
O wonder-workers, what do you do here? What do you sit for, when any person whatsoever who offers no oblation exalts himself?
Pass him by; let the life of the niggard decay. Bestow light upon the inspired singer who utters his hymns.
Crush the dogs that snarl from all sides; slay the enemies; O Aśvins, you have understood these [prayers].
Make every word of the singer rich in treasure; O Nāsatyas, protect both my hymns of praise.
You two fashioned this winged boat, endowed with life, for the son of Tugra upon the rivers;
with which, with a godward mind, you two carried him forth, flying well through the great flood.
The son of Tugra was cast down into the waters, abandoned in the bottomless darkness;
four ships, beloved by the belly [of the ocean], sent forth by the Aśvins, carry him across.
What tree was that which stood firm in the midst of the ocean, which the son of Tugra, when in distress, embraced?
Like the feathers of a swift-flying bird, O Aśvins, you carried him away for the sake of glory.
O Nāsatyas, O Heroes, may that hymn which the Mānas have uttered for you follow after you.
From this Soma-offering seat today, may we find a strengthening community that bestows life-sustaining gifts.
Yoke that [chariot] which is swifter than thought, O Mighty Ones, which has three seats and three wheels;
with it you come to the dwelling of the pious man, and with its triple-layered structure you fly like birds on their wings.

The well-rolling chariot moves as it approaches the earth, when you two, possessed of wisdom, stand ready for the strengthening food. May this beautiful song attend your wondrous form; O Daughters of Heaven, you two attend upon the Dawn.

Mount your well-rolling chariot, which follows your sacred laws, O possessors of oblations; with that chariot, O Nāsatyas, you come to the dwelling to provide for us, for our offspring, and for ourselves.
Let not the wolf nor the she-wolf harm you; do not avoid us, nor cast us aside. This portion is set out for you, this song; O wonder-workers, here are your vessels of honeyed draughts.
Gotama, Purumīḷha, and Atri, bearing oblations, call upon you both for protection, O wonder-workers.
Like one who goes straight toward a pointed-out direction, come to my call, O Nāsatyas.
We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness; our hymn of praise has been offered to you both, O Aśvins.
Come hither by the paths traveled by the gods; may we find strengthening food and a community that bestows life-sustaining gifts.
We invoke you both today, and we shall invoke you again when the dawn breaks with our hymns,
O Nāsatyas, wherever you may be— O Sons of Heaven, most bountiful to the liberal patron.

O Bull-like ones, rejoice well among us; slay the Paṇis while delighting in the flowing waters. Hear me through the invocations of my hymns, O Heroes, you who are seekers and perceivers with your ears.
For the sake of glory, O Pūṣan, like gods who have fashioned arrows, the Nāsatyas brought the bridal procession of Sūryā.
Your lofty steeds, born of the waters, speed along like the worn-out ages of the mighty Varuṇa.
O lovers of sweetness, may that gift of yours be ours; further the hymn of the poet Mānya, when the people, O bounteous givers, rejoice in you for the sake of glory and heroic power.
This hymn has been fashioned for you both, O Aśvins, with well-wrought praise by the Mānas, O bounteous lords.
Come on your path for our offspring and for ourselves, rejoicing in the house of Agastya, O Nāsatyas.
We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness; our hymn of praise has been offered to you both, O Aśvins.
Come hither by the paths traveled by the gods; may we find strengthening food and a community that bestows life-sustaining gifts.
Which of these two is the earlier, which the later? O sages, how were they born? Who truly knows?
They both support the universe by their own power; as for their name, the two days roll on like wheels.
The two footless ones, moving much, bear as their offspring the many-footed embryo that moves;
like an eternal son in the lap of his parents, O Heaven and Earth, protect us from evil.
I invoke the unassailable gift of Aditi—unconquered, heavenly, free from death, and accompanied by homage.
O Heaven and Earth, bring that forth for the singer; O Heaven and Earth, protect us from evil.
May we follow the two world-halves, Heaven and Earth, who do not grow weary and who grant protection, the parents of the gods; O both worlds, you gods, protect us from evil with both kinds of days.
When the two young maidens, sisters and twins, come together at the same place in the lap of their parents;
when they kiss the navel of the world—O Heaven and Earth, protect us from evil!

I invoke with the help of the gods the two wide, great, and lofty seats, the two mothers who by the cosmic order (ṛta) bestow immortality and possess beautiful countenances. O Heaven and Earth, protect us from evil!
The two wide, broad, vast, and far-reaching ones I address with reverence at this sacrifice—those two auspicious ones who bestow great protection; O Heaven and Earth, guard us from evil.

Whatever offense we may have committed against the gods, or against a friend, or even against our own kinsman—the prayer now offered shall be their means of atonement. O Heaven and Earth, protect us from evil!
May both noble praises protect me; may both assist me with their aid and favor. Even against the stingy enemy, O most bountiful gods, may we, rejoicing in this, find nourishment.
I, the wise one, have proclaimed this Truth to Heaven and Earth so that it may be heard far and wide.
May they protect me from reproach and from misfortune in the encounter; may Father and Mother guard me with their aids.

O Heaven and Earth, O Father and Mother, let this which I address to you here be true. O lowest of the gods, through your protections, may we find this strengthening community that bestows life-sustaining food.
May Savitṛ, the god who belongs to all men, come to our sacrifice with nourishments and fair praise;
so that you, O youths, may gladden us at the close of day, and that the whole world may be mindful of us.
May all the gods come to us, united—Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa.
May they all be our strengtheners, so that they may make our power easy to wield and never falter.
I praise with hymns Agni, your most beloved guest, the victorious one who is well-pleased;
so that Varuṇa may be of good fame for us, and the unassailable patron may bring us strengthening food.

I approach you both with homage, O Dawn and Night, you who desire to win, like a cow easy to milk; on the same day, measuring out the hymn of praise between the two forms of milk in this single udder.
And may Ahi Budhnya grant us joy; like a river swelling with milk for her young, the Sindhu flows toward us—by whom we shall speed the Son of the Waters, whom the mind-swift, bull-like steeds carry.
And may Tvaṣṭṛ come toward us, together with the patrons, at the time of the pressing, being well-disposed;
may Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, the protector of the people, the most powerful among men, come here to us.
And our hymns, yoked with horses, lick him like cows licking their young calf;
our songs embrace him, the most fragrant of men, as wives embrace their husbands.
And may the Maruts, with their increased armies, together with Rodasī, sit down with one mind upon us—
those who have spotted horses, whose chariots are like rushing streams, who destroy the enemy, and who are gods bound by friendship.
When they have manifested themselves through their greatness, they harness their teams with a well-fashioned hymn. Then, like a bolt on a fair day, their armies drench every enemy with their rain.
Bring the Aśvins forward for protection; bring Pūṣan forward, for they are self-strong. Viṣṇu is free from malice, as are Vāta and Ṛbhukṣan; may I turn the gods hither for their favor.

O worshipful ones, may this our devotion toward you be one that nourishes and provides a seat; may it strive among the gods for wealth. May we find strengthening food and a community that bestows life-sustaining gifts.
Now I shall praise Food, the great upholder of the cosmic order and source of power,
by whose might Trita shattered Vṛtra limb from limb.
O sweet Soma, O honeyed Soma, we have chosen you;
be our protector.
Come near to us, O Soma, as a father, auspicious with your auspicious aids; you who bring delight, who are not to be hated, a friend most gracious and free from duplicity.
O Food, those juices of yours are spread throughout the regions,
resting like the winds in heaven.
These [gifts] of thine, O *pitu*, bestow [wealth]; O most sweet *pitu* of thine, the delicious juices of thy flavors surge forth like those with powerful necks.
In thee, O Food, the mind of the great gods is set;
by thy beautiful banner it has been made manifest, and through thy protection thou hast slain the serpent.
O Soma, when you have gone there to the light of the mountains, O Food, come here indeed as our nourishment, sufficient for us to enjoy.
Whatever essence of the waters and plants we consume,
O Vātāpi, become fatness for us.
O Soma, whatever portion of ours consists of milk, of barley, or of grain— O Vātāpi, become fat with that!
O herb, become a gruel-offering; be plump, kidney-shaped, and expansive. O drinker of the wind, be indeed fat.
O Soma, we have refined you with our words, as cattle prepare their offerings;
you are the feast-companion for the gods, you are the feast-companion for us.
Enkindled today, you shine as a god among the gods, O conqueror of thousands;
as a messenger and a sage, carry the oblations.
Tanūnapāt, for the one who goes toward the *ṛta*, the sacrifice is anointed with honey;
may he bestow thousandfold nourishments.
Being invoked and worthy of praise, bring here the gods who are worthy of sacrifice;
O Agni, you are the winner of thousands.
With power they have strewn the eastward-pointing sacrificial grass, yielding a thousand heroes,
where you, O Ādityas, shine forth in splendor.
The Virāj, the Samrāj, the Vibhvīs, the Prabhvīs, and those that are many and more numerous—
these Doors have flowed with clarified butter.
For they, well-adorned with golden ornaments and beautiful forms, shine forth with splendor; may the two Dawns sit here in this place.
For the two divine Hotṛ-priests, the sages of eloquent speech, are indeed the first;
may they perform this sacrifice of ours.
O Bhāratī, Ilā, Sarasvatī— whatever goddesses of yours I invoke here,
do you all impel us toward glory.
For Tvaṣṭṛ, the lord, has generated all forms and all cattle;
worship for their increase.
O Lord of the Forest, by your own power release the path for the gods;
may Agni make the oblations sweet.
Agni, the leader of the gods, is anointed with the Gāyatra;
he shines forth amidst the utterances of Svāhā.
O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God who knowest all ways;
keep away from us the sin that leads astray, and we shall offer thee the most abundant word of homage.

O Agni, as one who is ever new, carry us across all difficulties with blessings; may you be a broad, vast, and spacious fortress for us, and grant well-being and health to our children and descendants.
O Agni, keep disease away from us; let those who do not protect with fire attack other peoples.
O worshipful God, together with all the immortals, grant us the earth again for our well-being.
Protect us, O Agni, with your unfailing guardians, shining brightly in your beloved dwelling.
O youngest one, may no fear reach your singer now, nor in the future, O powerful one.
O Agni, do not deliver us over to the malevolent, to the one who seeks to harm us, to the enemy, or to misfortune.
Do not give us up to the one who bites, nor to the one who gnaws, nor to the one who injures us; O Lord of Might, spare us!

O Agni, born of Truth, may one like you, being praised, grant protection to our bodies. You indeed ward off all those who wish to harm or revile us; for you, O God, are the one who discerns them clearly.
O Agni, you who know both kinds, you approach at the onset of the day, O worshipful one, for the sake of man;
at the arrival of the evening, you become one to be exhorted for the sake of humanity, like a stallion to be groomed by those who desire you.
We have uttered our invocations to this victorious Agni, the son of Manu.
May we, together with a thousand seers, win a thousandfold; may we find strengthening food that bestows long life.
Magnify with new hymns Bṛhaspati, the unassailable bull whose tongue is sweet;
he who is the leader of songs, radiant, whose praise the gods and mortals alike listen to when it is being chanted.
To him, the seasonal hymns resort, he who has been released like the outpouring of those seeking the gods;
for Bṛhaspati, moving straight toward the wide spaces, became all-pervasive through the cosmic order, even as Mātariśvan.

He extends his arms like Savitṛ toward the hymn of praise, the rising salutation, and the song of glory; by his power, he is one who must be honored daily, terrible like a wild beast, yet free from malice and full of might.

His fame resounds in heaven and upon the earth; like a swift steed, he, the wise possessor of power, restrains [the foe]. Like the weapons of wild beasts, these [missiles] of Bṛhaspati go forth toward the heavens, possessing serpent-like magic power.
O Bṛhaspati, those wicked Pajras who, regarding you as a mere vessel for libations, live off your blessings—do not grant your favor to the evil-minded; rather, punish the scorner.
Like a well-trodden path leading to good pasture, like a beloved friend who is difficult to restrain;
those who are unassailable look upon us—they have stood there, uncovering what was veiled.

To whom the hymns of praise go together like rivers, like streams flowing toward the ocean with their banks as wheels—he, Bṛhaspati, the wise and eager vulture, beholds both within: the waters and the crossing.

Thus has the great, many-born, and mighty god Bṛhaspati been established as the bull. May he, when praised by us, bestow wealth in heroes and cattle; may we find a strengthening community that grants life-sustaining gifts.
Like the *kaṅkata* bird, not like the *kaṅkata*, and like the *satīnakaṅkata*—
these two, called "the swarms," unseen, have smeared themselves.
She kills those who have not yet been seen when she approaches, and she kills them as she departs;
moreover, she kills while pounding, and she grinds them while grinding.
The *śarāsa*, *kuśarāsa*, *darbha*, and *sairyā* grasses, as well as the *mauñja*,
*adṛṣṭa*, and *vairiṇa*— all these together have been smeared down.
The cows have settled in their pen; the wild beasts have entered their lairs;
the lights of men have gone out; and the unseen ones have smeared themselves [with darkness].
These very ones have appeared at evening like thieves;
though unseen before, you have now become seen by all and fully perceived.
Heaven is your father, Earth your mother, Soma your brother, and Aditi your sister;
unseen yet seen by all, stand still and rest yourselves well.
Those that are on the shoulders, those that are on the limbs, those that are needle-like, and those that are prickly— whatever invisible things you are here, all of you together, perish!
The sun rises in the east, seen by all, as the slayer of the unseen;
crushing all unseen beings and all female sorceresses.
Yonder sun has flown up, consuming many things;
the Āditya, visible from all mountains, is the slayer of the unseen.
I hang the poison in the sun; I place the skin-bag in the house of the one who possesses the spirituous liquor.
May it surely not kill us, nor may we die; its range is for the non-dead. For you, O honeyed one, the steed of the bay-hued [Indra] has made you sweet with honey.
This tiny little bird has swallowed your poison;
it shall surely not die, nor shall we die. Its range is a league away, yet the honey-dweller has made you sweet with honey.
The thrice-seven little sparks have eaten the flower of the poison. Even they do not die, nor shall we die; its range is far, yet the honey-dweller has made thee sweet with honey.
Of the ninety-nine new [stems] that cause the growth of poison, I have grasped the names of them all. O enemy, his range is gone; he who stood upon the bay horses has made you honey-sweet with honey.
The thrice-seven peahens, the seven sisters who are virgins— they have carried away your poison, just as women with water-jars carry off water.
So small is the *kuṣumbhaka* worm; I shatter it with a stone.
Thereupon the poison has turned away, following the distant enclosures.
The Kuṣumbhaka, as it was rolling down from the mountain, said this:
"The venom of the scorpion is sapless; O scorpion, your venom is sapless."
O Agni, you are born from the heavens; you, the one eager to blaze, are born from the waters and from the stone;
you are born from the forests and from the plants; O Lord of men, you are born pure from men.
O Agni, yours is the office of the Hotṛ, yours the seasonal office of the Potṛ; yours is the office of the Neṣṭṛ, and you are the Agnīdh for the one who follows the Ṛta.
Yours is the office of the Praśāstṛ; you act as the Adhvaryu; you are both the Brahman and the Gṛhapati in our home.
O Agni, you are Indra, the bull among the virtuous; you are Viṣṇu, the wide-striding, worthy of homage.
You are the Brahman, the winner of wealth, O Brahmaṇaspati; you, O Ordainer, are accompanied by Purandhi.

O Agni, you are King Varuṇa, whose laws are firm; you become Mitra, O wonder-worker, worthy of praise. You are Aryaman, the lord of the virtuous, whose enjoyment is shared; you are Aṃśa, O God, who distributes portions at the assembly.
O Agni, as Tvaṣṭṛ, you bestow great heroism upon the worshipper; O you of Mitra-like greatness, the divine wives are your kin.
You, the swift impeller, grant us excellent horses; you, rich in wealth, are the host of heroes.
O Agni, you are Rudra, the Asura of the great heaven; you are the host of Maruts; you rule over nourishment.
You travel with the ruddy winds, O friend of the house; as Pūṣan, you yourself protect those who worship you.
O Agni, you are the giver of wealth to him who serves you; you, O God, are Savitṛ, the bestower of treasures.
You are Bhaga, O Lord of men, and you rule over all riches; you are the protector in the home for him who has devoted himself to you.

O Agni, the clans seek you out in the home as their lord; they strive toward you, the king who is easily found. O you of beautiful countenance, you rule over all things; you are equal to ten hundred thousand.
O Agni, men seek you as a father with their sacrifices; they seek you, the radiant one, for brotherhood through their labor.
You become a son to him who honors you; as a most gracious friend, you protect us from assault.
O Agni, you are Ṛbhu, to be honored nearby; you are the lord of strength and of wealth consisting of cattle.
You shine forth according to your skill for the sake of giving; you are the one who instructs and extends the sacrifice.

O divine Agni, you are Aditi to the donor; you, as Hotrā Bhāratī, grow strong through our song. You are Iḷā for a hundred winters for the sake of skill; O Lord of Wealth, you are Sarasvatī, the slayer of Vṛtra.
O Agni, well-maintained, you are the highest vital power; in your desirable hue, in your very appearance, there is splendor.
You are the great, furthering strength; you are abundant wealth, wide on every side.
O Agni, the Ādityas have made you their mouth; the pure ones have made you their tongue, O Sage. Those who bestow gifts attend upon you at the sacrifices; in you the gods eat the offered oblation.
In thee, O Agni, all the guileless immortal gods eat the offered oblation with their mouths;
through thee, mortals make their drink savory. Thou hast been born as the pure embryo of the plants.

O Agni, well-born god, you are equal to them and even surpasses them in your might; you exceed them, O god, when your power spreads here through its greatness across both heaven and earth, the two world-halves.

O Agni, those wise patrons who bestow upon their singers a gift preeminent in cattle and adorned with horses—lead both us and them toward greater prosperity; may we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly.

Increase Jātavedas by means of sacrifice; worship Agni with oblation and with continuous song—the one who is kindled, the one who provides excellent nourishment, the leader of men, the celestial Hotṛ, seated at the pole within the sacrificial assemblies.

The nights and dawns have lowed toward you, O Agni, as milch-cows toward their calf in the stalls. Like the chariot-pole of heaven, you shine through the human generations, O possessor of many boons, illuminating the nights in succession.

The gods have established him at the foundation of the region, the doer of wondrous deeds, the messenger between heaven and earth— Agni, who is like a chariot known to all, with brilliant radiance, and who, like Mitra, is to be praised among the people.
Him, growing in his own home within the mid-air, they have placed like a shining moon in the cleft;
him who flies through the mists of Pṛśni, observing with his eyes, he who, like a guardian, watches over both races of men.
He, the Hotṛ-priest, encompassing the entire sacrifice, him men honor with oblations and with song.
With golden jaws, flickering among the growing plants, he makes himself manifest throughout heaven and earth like the sky with its stars.
O Agni, being kindled for our well-being, shine upon us with wealth, bestowing riches as you burn.
Bring both heaven and earth to us for our prosperity, O divine Agni, so that the oblations of man may be accepted.
O Agni, grant us great gifts; grant us thousandfold wealth. Open up for us the doors of booty as if with fame.
Make heaven and earth favorable through our prayer; make the bright light shine forth like the dawns.
Kindled along the nights of the dawns, he shines like the sun with his ruddy luster;
Agni, the priest of men who performs the sacrifice well, is the king of the tribes and the gracious guest of the Āyu.
Thus, O Agni, ancient one, has human prayer been made to swell among the immortals in the high heavens;
like a cow yielding milk for the singer within the enclosures, it has itself impelled toward us hundredfold nourishment in many forms.
O Agni, may we, through our horse or through our sacred prayer (*brahman*), distinguish ourselves above these people.
May our splendor shine forth high over the five tribes, like the sun, invincible.

Be mindful of us, O powerful one, worthy of praise, you in whom the well-born patrons find their strength; you, O Agni, to whom the prize-winners come with sacrifice, shining brightly in your own home among our constant offspring.
O Jātavedas Agni, may we both—the singers of praise and the wise patrons—be under your protection.
Grant us wealth that is excellent, most radiant, abundant, rich in progeny, and blessed with noble offspring.

O Agni, those wise patrons who bestow upon the singers a gift preeminent in cattle and adorned with horses—lead both us and them toward greater prosperity; may we, blessed with heroic sons, speak aloud at the assembly.
Kindled on the earth, Agni has been established; he stands facing all living beings.
May Agni—the purifier, the wise god from of old, the worthy Hotṛ—sacrifice to the gods.
Narāśaṃsa, anointing the stations, equal to the three heavens in greatness, possessing self-radiance—
sprinkling the oblation with a mind that drips ghee, may he anoint the gods at the head of the sacrifice.
Praised with our mind, O Agni, as is your due, sacrifice to the gods today before the human [priest].
Bring hither the unshakable host of the Maruts; O men, worship Indra who sits upon the sacred grass.

O divine *barhis*, increasing, rich in heroes, spread upon this altar for the sake of wealth and easy to maintain—sit upon it, O Vasus, anointed with clarified butter; sit here, O all you gods, Ādityas, worthy of sacrifice!
May the divine doors, wide-opening and easy of access, be thrown open as they are invoked with salutations.
May they, spacious and ageless, spread themselves out, purifying their glorious and hero-producing hue.
Excellent are the deeds of you two who have grown great from of old, Dawn and Night, like two joyful weavers;
weaving together the stretched-out thread, you two who face each other are the well-milking, milk-laden ornaments of the sacrifice.
The two divine Hotṛ-priests, the first and most wise, shall sacrifice with the Ṛc verse in a straight manner, being more beautiful;
sacrificing to the gods at the proper times, they anoint themselves upon the navel of the earth, over the three ridges.
May Sarasvatī, who perfects our devotion; may the goddess Iḷā, and Bhāratī, who overcomes all;
may these three goddesses, by their own inherent power, sit upon this sacred grass and protect us with an unassailable refuge.
Tawny-hued, well-nourished, bestowing vital strength, a hero is born through obedience, one who loves the gods.
May Tvaṣṭṛ open up offspring for us as our central bond; then may he go to the path of the gods.

May the Lord of the Forest stand by, releasing [the victim]; may Agni, through his insights, prepare the oblation. May the divine immolator, knowing well, lead the thrice-anointed offering to the gods.
Ghee is mixed; ghee is his source; he rests in ghee; ghee is his abode. According to your wont, bring [the gods] here; rejoice; O Bull, carry away the oblation consecrated with Svāhā!
I invoke for you Agni, the brightly shining, the one worthy of perfect praise, the guest of the people, the one well-provided with offerings—
he who, like Mitra, is to be cherished, the god among the godly folk, Jātavedas.
Worshipping him in the gathering place of the waters, the Bhr̥gus twice established him among the clans of mankind.
May this Agni, the messenger of the gods, whose horses are swift, surpass all the worlds.
The gods established Agni among the human clans as a beloved one, like friends who wish to dwell together. May he shine upon the longing nights—he who is to be honored in the home of the donor.
His nourishment is delightful like that of his own kin; for beautiful is the sight of him when he speeds forth, eager to act.
He who repeatedly extends his tongue among the plants shakes off his tail-bristles like a chariot-horse.
When those praising me for my forest-conquering power proclaimed a monstrous form to the Uśij, he displayed himself with wondrous light, he who, though aged, suddenly became young again.
He who shines upon the forests like one parched with thirst, he has roared like water on a path, or like a chariot;
he whose path is black, the glowing and delightful one, has become manifest, smiling like the sky through the clouds.
He who has spread himself over the broad earth, burning it, goes like a cattle without a herdsman, self-guided;
Agni, the radiant one, heating the thickets, with his blackened path, has made the earth savory as it were.
Now, at the recitation of your ancient favor, this prayer has been proclaimed at the third assembly.
O Agni, grant us great wealth consisting of heroic sons, abundant food, strength, and a lineage of noble offspring.
O Agni, just as through you the Gṛtsamadas have won the nearby [treasures] hidden in secret, so may they,
possessing good heroes and overcoming their enemies, bestow that vital strength upon the patrons who sing your praise.
The conscious Hotṛ has been born as a father for the protection of the fathers;
may we be able to harness him, the noble wealth manifest before us, who possesses the prize of victory.
In whom the seven rays are extended, the leader of the sacrifice—
he, like Manu, as the Potṛ priest, impels that entire divine eighth [ray].
Whether he has run forth after them or whether he has uttered the sacred prayers (*brahmāṇi*),
he encompasses all poetic insights (*kāvyā*) as the felly encompasses the wheel.
For together with the pure one, the pure Praśāstṛ has been born through his mental power;
knowing his firm ordinances, he grows like branches.
These milch-cows, seeking their own color, have followed him, the Neshtri;
would that the sisters who have come hither might grant us what is better than the three [worlds]?
When the sister has come near the mother, bringing clarified butter,
the Adhvaryu rejoices at their arrival like grain at the rain.
May he himself prepare the priest for his own nourishment;
may we truly win the hymn and the sacrifice, and we have offered them.
So that the wise one may prepare it properly for all the worshipful gods—
this sacrifice, O Agni, which we have performed, rests within you.
O Agni, accept this my fuel-stick and this my attendance; truly, hear these songs of mine.
With this [hymn], O Agni, son of strength, seeker of horses, we would worship you with this well-spoken hymn, O well-born one.
As such, O lover of songs, we who seek wealth and desire to serve thee, shall honor thee with our hymns, O bestower of riches.
May he become our wise patron, O Maghavan, Lord of Wealth, Bestower of Riches;
drive away from us all those who hate us.
May he [grant] us rain from heaven; may he [grant] us unassailable strength;
may he [grant] us thousandfold nourishments.
O youngest messenger, being praised with our song for the sake of the one who seeks help, come hither, O most excellent sacrificer and Hotṛ-priest.
For you, O Agni, O sage, go between both races as one who knows; you are like a messenger belonging to the people, like a friend to a friend.
As one who knows, satisfy us; as one who is wise, worship in due order, and sit down upon this sacred grass.
O Agni, youngest descendant of Bharata, bring us the most excellent, radiant,
and much-desired wealth, O Vasu.
May the hostility of neither god nor mortal master us; deliver us from that and from our enemies.
And through you, may we cross over all enemies, as one crosses over streams of water.
O Agni, pure, purifying, and worthy of worship, you shine forth mightily;
you are offered oblations of clarified butter.
O Agni, descendant of Bharata, you are ours, being invoked with offerings of heifers, bulls, and eight-footed mares.
Consumer of wood, with clarified butter as his libation, the ancient, excellent Hotṛ-priest,
the wonderful son of strength.
Like one seeking booty, now praise the yoking of Agni’s chariots—
he who is most glorious and bountiful.
He who is a good leader for the donor, who, being ageless, causes the enemy to age; he whose countenance is beautiful when invoked with oblations.
He who is praised for his splendor in his homes at evening and at dawn—
he whose sacred law is never violated.
He who shines forth with his flame like the sun with its light, resplendent and anointed with ageless [rays].
Following Atri, they have strengthened Agni with hymns according to his own sovereignty;
he has assumed all splendors.
Through the aid of Agni, Indra, Soma, and the gods, may we remain unharmed; may we overcome those who attack us.
The Hotṛ, knowing his place, has sat down upon the seat of the Hotṛ—resplendent, shining, and most skillful;
Agni, the most excellent, whose wisdom protects his unfailing vows, who brings a thousandfold wealth, and whose tongue is pure.
You are our messenger, and you are our protector from afar; O Bull, you are the leader to greater wealth.
O Agni, for the extension of our offspring and our own bodies, be a watchful guardian, shining with undiminished light.
Let us worship you in your highest birth, O Agni; let us worship with hymns in your lower dwelling-place.
From whatever womb you have arisen, I sacrifice to that; into you, when well-kindled, the oblations have been poured.
O Agni, most skilled in sacrifice, worship with the oblation; quickly acknowledge the gift and the bounty.
For you are the lord of riches among all treasures; you are the inspirer of the pure word.

Both kinds of wealth of yours, O wonder-worker, are never exhausted as you are born day after day. Make your singer, O Agni, possessed of food; make him the lord of wealth consisting of noble offspring.

With your excellent host, O Agni, be well-disposed toward us; you are the best sacrificer who brings the gods to the sacrifice for our well-being. As an undeceived guardian and our protector from afar, shine upon us with splendor and wealth.

Agni is the first to be invoked like a father when he is kindled by man at the place of the sacrificial food; clothed in splendor, immortal, and wise, he is the one to be groomed, the seeker of renown, the prize-winner.
May Agni, of wondrous luster, the immortal and wise one, hear my invocation with all my songs.
Two dark steeds, or two ruddy ones, or two tawny ones draw his chariot; he, the distributor, has fashioned it.
Upon the outstretched [earth] they generated him well-born; Agni became the embryo in many-formed [plants].
Even in the dark night, with his splendors, the wise one dwells unconfined.
I sprinkle Agni with the oblation of ghee, him who dwells facing all beings—
broad, great with transverse vigor, most expansive, impetuous, and visible through his foods.
I offer oblations from every side to him who faces us; may he accept it with a mind free from malice.
Agni, possessed of the beauty of a youth and of a desirable hue, flickers with his body so that one cannot touch him.
O Victorious One, may you accept your portion by choice; with you as our messenger, let us speak like Manu.
With my tongue and eloquence, I repeatedly invoke the perfect Agni, who is rich in honey and the winner of wealth.
Hear our call, O Indra; do not neglect us. May we be yours for the giving of riches, for these offerings increase your strength, seeking wealth as rivers flow.
Release the great waters, O Indra, which you caused to swell—the many ancient ones obstructed by the serpent, O Hero.
Strengthened by hymns, you struck down even the Dāsa who considered himself immortal.
O Hero Indra, in these hymns of praise in which you take delight, and in these Rudrian chants of praise—
these very songs flow forth for you alone, in which you rejoice, like brilliant steeds rushing toward Vāyu.
Increasing your brilliant strength and placing the brilliant thunderbolt in your arms,
O Indra, may you, growing strong and radiant for us, conquer the Dāsa tribes with the help of Sūrya.
The wise one who dwelt in secret, hidden and concealed within the waters, veiled in mystery— him, O Hero,
you slew with your valor, he who had propped up the waters and the sky.
We shall now praise your ancient greatness, O Indra, and we shall praise your recent deeds.
We shall praise the eager thunderbolt in your arms; we shall praise your two bay horses, the banners of the sun.
O Indra, your two bay steeds, seeking booty, have now let out their neighing that drips with ghee.
The earth has spread itself wide in every direction, and even the mountain, though about to move, has grown still.
The mountain sat down, never failing; bellowing, he has cried out together with his mothers.
Strengthening their voice on the far shore, they have spread abroad the breath impelled by Indra.
Indra struck down Vṛtra, the wielder of magic, who lay across the great river;
at the roar of this bull and his thunderbolt, the two worlds, Rodasī, trembled in fear.
The thunderbolt of this bull roared aloud when the mortal man consumed the non-human [strength].
Having drunk of the pressed juice, he brought down the magical powers of the guileful Dānava.
Drink, drink the Soma, O heroic Indra! Let the exhilarating pressed juices delight you.
Filling your two flanks, let them increase your strength; thus the pressed juice has aided Indra, the filler of the city.
O Indra, we have become yours; as inspired singers, may we win wisdom while honoring you according to the Eternal Law.
Seeking your aid, we meditate upon your praise; may we be ready at once for you to grant us wealth.
May we be yours, O Indra, those who, seeking your aid, increase your strength. Grant us that most powerful wealth, rich in heroes, which you, O God, have desired for us.
Bestow a dwelling; bestow friendship upon us; O Indra, bestow upon us the host of Maruts—those who are in harmony with you and, being exhilarated, drink the first draught along with the Vāyus.

May they now come, in whom you take delight; drink the Soma to your satisfaction, O Indra, for strength. You, the deliverer, have truly strengthened us in battles with lofty hymns of praise, even unto heaven.
Those great ones who indeed, O Deliverer, have sought to win your favor with hymns, or those who,
spreading the sacred grass like a household, have come— protected by you alone, O Indra— they have attained the prize.
O Hero, rejoicing indeed among the fierce ones, drink the Soma at the Trikadruka sacrifices, O Indra!
Shaking your beard while being gratified, come with your two bay horses for the drinking of the pressed juice.
Take up that power, O Hero, by which you struck down Vṛtra, the Dānu, and Aurṇavābha.
You disclosed the light for the Ārya; the Dasyu fell at your left hand, O Indra.
May we, overcoming all rivals with your aids, subdue the Dasyus through the Ārya way;
for us, you delivered Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, to Trita as a gift for your friendship.
Of this exhilarating Soma pressed by Trita, Indra—swelling with power—struck down Arbuda; like the sun turning its wheel, Indra, accompanied by the Aṅgirases, rent Vala asunder.
Surely, O Indra, may that wealthy sacrificial gift of yours yield its boon to the singer;
grant gifts to those who praise you, let not our fortune perish. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly.
He who, as soon as born, was the first wise god and surpassed the gods by his power;
at whose breath the two worlds trembled through the greatness of his manly might—he, O people, is Indra.
He who steadied the trembling earth, who set the agitated mountains at rest,
who measured out the wide mid-air, and who propped up the sky— he, O people, is Indra.
He who, having slain the dragon, released the seven rivers; who drove out the cows by breaking open the enclosure of Vala;
who generated Agni between the two stones—he, O people, is Indra, the destroyer in battles.
He by whom all these things were made to pass away, who cast the Dāsa race down into the depths;
he who, like a winning gambler, seized the prize—the prosperity of the enemy—he, O people, is Indra.

When they ask of that terrible one, "Where is he?", and people say of him, "He does not exist," he destroys the prosperity of the enemy like a gambler's stakes; have faith in him, O people—for he is Indra.

He who is the inciter of the weary, he who is the helper of the emaciated, he who is the protector of the suppliant Brahmin and the singer; he who, fair-cheeked, is the guardian of the one who has set the pressing-stones and pressed the Soma—he, O people, is Indra.
He in whose direction are horses, in whose direction are cattle, in whose direction are villages, and in whose direction are all chariots;
he who generated the sun and the dawn, he who is the leader of the waters—he, O people, is Indra.
He whom the two contending armies invoke, the enemies both near and far;
though they have mounted the very same chariot, they call upon him separately—he, O people, is Indra.
He without whom people do not conquer, whom those engaged in battle invoke for protection;
he who has become the counterpart of the universe, who shakes the unshakable—he, O people, is Indra.
He who with his arrow struck down those who repeatedly committed great sins against me while they were unaware;
he who does not grant boldness to the arrogant, he who is the slayer of the Dasyu—he, O people, is Indra.
He who discovered Śambara dwelling in the mountains in the fortieth autumn;
he who slew the dragon Ahi as he displayed his prowess, the Dānu lying in wait—he, O people, is Indra.
He who, the bull with seven rays, the mighty one, released the seven rivers to flow;
he who, thunderbolt-armed, struck down Rauhiṇa as he was scaling heaven—he, O people, is Indra.
Even Heaven and Earth bow down before him; even the mountains tremble at his might.
He who is the Soma-drinker, whose arm is braced, who holds the thunderbolt in his hand—he, O people, is Indra.

He who protects with his aid the one who presses the juice, the one who cooks, the one who recites, and the one who exerts himself; he for whom prayer is the means of growth, for whom the Soma is, and for whom this gift is intended—he, O people, is Indra.
O you who, even against the resistless one, shatter strength for the man who presses the juice and cooks the oblation—you are indeed truly real.
O Indra, may we, your friends forevermore, speak at the assembly with heroic sons.
The Season is the progenitor; born quickly from her, he entered the waters in which he grows. That became a swelling, teeming mass of milk—the first cream of the stalk, worthy of praise.

They come together, carrying milk; they bring nourishment for him who possesses all abundance. The path is common for those rushing down the slopes; that which you performed first—you are worthy of praise for that.
One follows after him as he gives; one goes along, fashioning those forms from those waters.
One endures all the repulsions of the other; you who performed this first deed—you are worthy of praise.
They sit distributing nourishment to the creatures, like wealth that increases for one who approaches;
with insatiable teeth he eats the father’s food—he who performed this first deed, he is worthy of praise.
You made the earth visible to heaven, O slayer of the serpent, when you cleared the paths of the rivers;
as such, the gods have generated you, a god, with hymns like water for a prize-winning steed—you are worthy of praise.
You who bestow nourishment and increase, you have milked the dry from the moist, full of sweetness;
you have established a treasure for Vivasvat. You alone rule over all; worthy of praise are you.
You who, by your law, have established within the gift the flowering and fruit-bearing plants and the flowing rivers;
you who have generated the peerless lightnings from heaven—you, the wide one, encompassing the expanses, are worthy of praise.
You who brought Nārmara together with his wealth to be slain, for the sake of nourishment and for Dāsaveśa;
you who opened the unguarded mouth of Ūrjayantī—even so today, O doer of many deeds, you are worthy of praise.
Whether it was a hundred or ten who were eaten together at once, when you granted your hearing to one and protected him in his outcry;
when you struck down the Dasyus without a cord for Dabhīti, you became a most excellent protector—this is your praiseworthy deed.
All the enclosures have yielded to his manly power; they have granted wealth to him, the achiever.
You have propped up the six regions and the five directions; you have surpassed all others—you are worthy of praise.
O Hero, your valor is well-proclaimed, in that by a single resolve you win wealth;
O Indra, you who have performed all the deeds of Jātūṣṭhira, the powerful one—by these you are worthy of praise.
You brought to a halt the swift-flowing streams to facilitate the crossing for Turvīti and Vayya;
you raised up Parāvṛj who was lying low, and by making the blind and the lame hear, you became worthy of praise.
O Vasu, prepare for us that gift of wealth; great is your store of riches.
O Indra, bestow that wondrous bounty day by day for the sake of glory. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly.
O Adhvaryus, bring Soma for Indra;
pour out the intoxicating juice with the ladles, for the hero is ever desirous of its drink. Offer it to the bull; indeed, this is what he desires.
O Adhvaryus, bring this [Soma] to him who struck down Vṛtra—who had enclosed the waters—just as a thunderbolt strikes a tree;
for he is subject to that [Soma]. This Indra is worthy of drinking it.
O Adhvaryus, him who struck down Dṛbhīka, who drove forth the cows, and who opened Vala for you—
wrap this Indra with Soma-offerings as one wraps the wind in the mid-air with garments, like a swift steed.
O Adhvaryus, urge that Indra toward the offering of Soma— he who slew Uraṇa as he looked upon his ninety-nine arms, and who cast Arbuda down and crushed him.

O Adhvaryus, to that Indra for whom [the gods] slew Svashna, who slew the insatiable Shushna, who [slew] Vyansa, who [slew] Pipru and Namuchi, and who [slew] Rudhikra— to that Indra, offer the oblation of the soma-plant.
O Adhvaryus, bring the Soma for this Indra, who shattered the hundred ancient fortresses of Śambara like stones,
and who scattered the hundred thousand followers of Varcin.
O Adhvaryus, bring the Soma for him who, having slain [the foe], buried a hundred and a thousand in the lap of the earth;
he who struck down the heroes of Kutsa, Āyu, and Atithigva. Bring the Soma for him!
O Adhvaryus, whatever you men desire, bring that to Indra by carrying it with obedience. O performers of sacrifice, bring the Soma purified by the hands to the famous Indra; offer it as an oblation.

O Adhvaryus, perform service for him; having been purified in the wood, bring him forth from the wood. Rejoicing in what is held in the hand, he has lowed toward you; offer the intoxicating Soma to Indra.
O Adhvaryus, fill the liberal Indra with Soma juices, just as one fills a cow with milk.
I know this secret of his; the worshipful one perceives me when I desire to give more.

O Adhvaryus, him who is the king of celestial wealth, of that which is on earth, and of what dwells in the soil—fill him with Soma-offerings as one fills a granary with barley; let this be your work for Indra.
O Vasu, prepare for us that gift of wealth to bestow; great is your store of riches.
O Indra, grant us wondrous glory day after day. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly.
Now, indeed, let me proclaim the great, true deeds of this great and true one.
At the Trikadruka festivals he drank of this pressed juice; in its exhilaration, Indra slew the dragon.
He propped up the vast sky where there was no pillar; he filled the two worlds and the intermediate space.
He supported the earth and spread it out—these things Indra did in the intoxication of Soma.

Like dwellings, he measured out the eastward-flowing channels with his measures; with his thunderbolt, he pierced the channels of the rivers. He released them freely upon paths for long journeys—those deeds Indra performed in the exhilaration of Soma.
Having surrounded his assailants out of fear of being harmed, he cast all their weapons into the kindled fire;
in the intoxication of Soma, Indra performed those deeds—he united them with cattle, horses, and chariots.

He brought to rest that great roaring river as it flowed; he carried those who did not swim across in safety. Having emerged from the water, they set out toward wealth. Indra performed these deeds in the intoxication of Soma.
By his greatness he released the westward-flowing Sindhu; with his thunderbolt he crushed the Dawns.
Severing the powerless with those who possess speed, Indra performed these deeds in the intoxication of Soma.
Knowing the secret hiding place of the maidens, he, the rejected one, rose up appearing openly. Śroṇa stood there; Vyānaṅga looked out. Indra performed those deeds in the intoxication of Soma.
Praised by the Aṅgirasas, Indra split Vala and tore apart the firm foundations of the mountain.
He broke down their artificial enclosures; these things Indra did in the intoxication of Soma.
Having approached Cumuri and Dhuni with sleep, you struck down the Dasyu and protected Dabhīti.
Even Rambhi found gold there; those deeds Indra performed in the exhilaration of Soma.
Surely, O Indra, may that wealthy sacrificial gift of yours yield its boon to the singer;
grant gifts to those who praise you, let not our fortune perish. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly.
To you, the most excellent among the virtuous, I offer a beautiful hymn of praise, like an oblation into a kindled fire.
We invoke for our protection Indra—the ageless one who makes others age, the grown one who is eternally young.
Without whom, the great Indra, nothing exists; in him all heroic powers are concentrated.
He carries Soma in his belly, vast strength in his body, the thunderbolt in his hand, and wisdom in his head.
Neither the two worlds nor the oceans can encompass your power, O Indra; neither the mountains nor the seas can contain your chariot.
No one can withstand your thunderbolt when you fly across many leagues with your swift steeds.
For all bring their will to him, the worshipful, the bold, the bull who attends to them.
As a bull, sacrifice with the oblation, O most wise one; drink the Soma, O Indra, with your bull-like luster.
The vessel of the bull flows forth, a wave of honey, for the bull to drink—the bull who is the source of food.
The two bull-like Adhvaryu priests and the bull-like pressing-stones press out the bull Soma for the bull [Indra].
Mighty is your thunderbolt, and mighty is your chariot; mighty are your two bay steeds, and your weapons are like bulls.
O Bull Indra, you are the lord of the mighty exhilarating draught; satisfy yourself with the bull, the Soma.
Like a ship in a gathering, I approach you with prayer at the libations, bold in my resolve.
Will he not surely take heed of this our word? We pour ourselves out to Indra like a fountain of wealth.
Turn toward us before the distress comes, as a cow, swelling with pasture, turns to her calf;
O Śatakratu, may we once more be united with your favors, as bulls are joined with their mates.
Surely, O Indra, may that wealthy sacrificial gift of yours yield its boon to the singer;
grant gifts to those who praise you, let not our fortune perish. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly.
Sing this new song for him in the manner of the Aṅgirases, when his ancient powers surge forth;
when, in the exhilaration of Soma, he has by force opened all the enclosed cow-pens that were firmly established.
May he be that one who, measuring out his power for the first nourishment, surpassed all greatness;
the hero who, girding his body for battles, fixed the heaven upon his head by his majesty.
You performed your first great heroic deed when, at the beginning, you stirred up your fury through sacred power (*brahman*).
O Lord of the bay horses, by means of him who stands upon the chariot, the swift ones, driven forth, flow together and apart.
Then he, who by his might surpassed all worlds, grew strong as a sovereign lord;
the bearer of light overspread the two worlds with radiance, weaving together and enveloping the turbid darkness.

He, by his might, made firm the mountains facing the east; he turned the waters of the rivers downward. He supported the earth that nourishes all, and by his creative power, he propped up the sky from falling.
That [bolt] was fashioned by his arms for him, which his father made from all that exists, from the very source of creation;
with it, the loudly roaring one struck down Krivi upon the earth so that he might lie there, having pierced him with the thunderbolt.

Like an aged woman dwelling with her parents, I seek you, Bhaga, from our common seat. Grant me a sign; bestow it upon me and bring it hither; give me that portion for my body wherewith you will honor me.
O Indra, we would call upon you, the liberal giver; for you, O Indra, bestow works and spoils of war.
Help us, O Indra, with your wondrous aid; O bull-like Indra, make us more prosperous.
Surely, O Indra, may that wealthy sacrificial gift of yours yield a boon to the singer;
grant it to the praisers, let not our fortune fail us. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly.
