O Dakṣa, O God of wise intellect, for you we mortals have performed these rites at the sacrifice;
take note of every man with his good chariot, and make all that, O immortal Agni, palatable to us.
Flaming forth with your broad radiance, drive away our enemies, the demons, and diseases.
May I abide in the protection of the great Agni, who grants excellent refuge, under the guidance of him who is easily invoked.
Be our protector at the dawning of this very dawn, and be our guardian when the sun has risen.
O Agni, well-born in body, cherish my hymn of praise as you would your own constant offspring, my son.
O Agni, you who behold men, shine forth as a bull, red amidst the many black [nights].
O Vasu, lead us and carry us across distress; O youngest one, make us seekers of wealth.
O invincible Agni, shine forth like a bull, having conquered all strongholds and all blessings;
O Jātavedas, you are the leader of the first sacrifice, the protector, and the excellent guide of the great rite.
O singer, you who are wise, shining toward the gods, bring us many flawless shelters.
Like a prize-winning chariot, O Agni, carry us toward strength; may you bring us the two well-established worlds, heaven and earth.
O Bull, cause us to swell and quicken our strengths; O Agni, make the two worlds yield milk for us.
O God, shining with the gods through your brilliant luster, let not the ill-will of a mortal encompass us.
O Agni, bestow upon the one who invokes you the *iḷā*—the gift of cattle, full of wondrous power, and most enduring.
May there be to us a son, a spreading progeny; O Agni, may that benevolence of yours abide with us.
This Agni is the lord of great heroic power and of great good fortune;
he is the lord of wealth consisting of noble offspring and cattle, and he is the lord of the slaying of Vṛtra.
O Maruts, O heroes, attend to this man who increases your strength, in whom there are riches that augment prosperity—
those who overcome the malicious in battles and who have destroyed the enemy every day.
As such, O bounteous Agni, sharpen us for wealth consisting of excellent heroic power— wealth that is most abundant, rich in progeny, free from disease, and full of vigor, O thou of mighty splendor.
He who has made all worlds his own and has overcome them, he who has established worship among the gods—
he strives for the gods, for heroic strength, and for the praise of men.
O Agni, do not deliver us over to thoughtlessness, nor to lack of heroes, nor to lack of singers, O son of strength; nor to reproach. Drive away our enemies.
O fortunate Agni, grant us strength at this great sacrifice—strength accompanied by progeny.
O one of abundant splendor, unite us with even greater wealth that brings joy and glory.
Being kindled according to the first ordinances, he who possesses all desirable things is anointed with unguents;
Agni—flame-haired, clothed in clarified butter, purifying, and skilled in sacrifice—is prepared for the worship of the gods.
Just as you, O Agni Jātavedas, being wise, performed the office of the Hotṛ for the earth and for heaven, so now with this oblation sacrifice to the gods; like Manu, further this sacrifice today.

Three are your lifespans, O Jātavedas; three are your births from the dawns, O Agni. With these, as the one who knows, worship the favor of the gods, and then become the bringer of peace and prosperity for the sacrificer.

Praising Agni, the radiant and beautiful one, we pay homage to you, O Jātavedas, who are worthy of worship. The gods have made you their messenger, their steward, and the bearer of oblations—the navel of immortality.
O Agni, whatever Hotṛ-priest before you was more skilled in sacrifice, established from of old and bringing bliss by his own nature—
according to his law, O wise one, perform the sacrifice for us, and then establish our rite for the feast of the gods.
O Agni, be well-disposed toward us when we approach you—like a friend to a friend, like a father who is kind.
For the dwellings of men are full of many deceivers; burn up the hostile powers that turn against us.
O Agni, burn up the enemies within; burn away the curse of the distant, stingy foe. O Vasu, you who are observant, burn the thoughtless ones; let your ageless, tireless flames spread abroad.
Desiring [success], O Agni, with fuel and with ghee I offer this oblation for speed and strength;
as much as I am able, praising with a prayer, I offer this divine hymn for the winning of a hundredfold wealth.
O Son of Strength, praised with your flame, bestow great vital power upon those who labor;
O Agni, grant wealth and well-being to the Viśvāmitras. We have cleansed your body many times over.
Bestow wealth, O excellent winner of riches; for such you truly become, O Agni, when fully kindled.
In the dwelling of the fortunate singer, you grant us abundant prosperity; with outstretched arms, you assume wondrous forms.
I choose Agni as the Hotṛ at the sacrificial feast—the skillful sage, all-knowing and infallible.
May he, the most excellent sacrificer, worship among the gods for us; may he win us riches and boons for the sake of wealth and strength.
O Agni, I send forth toward you the ladle filled with oblation, radiant, bestowing gifts, and dripping with ghee.
Moving clockwise and choosing the assembly of gods, he has established the sacrifice together with the bountiful Vasus.

With a more vigorous mind, O Agni, protect us; grant us aid, O giver of good offspring, you who are yourself a giver. In the abundance of the most heroic wealth, may we be the ones to offer fair praises to you, the possessor of riches.
For many are the faces that the worshipful people have placed in you, O Agni, the god.
Therefore, O youngest one, bring hither the host of gods, so that you may sacrifice today to the divine assembly.

When the gods, seating you as the Hotṛ priest at the sacrificial meal for the sake of worship, anointed you—O Agni, as such, be mindful of us here for our protection; bestow glorious renown upon our bodies.
The priest invokes Agni, Uṣas, the Aśvins, and Dadhikrā with hymns at the break of dawn.
May the gods, possessing excellent light, hear us; may they, being of one mind and longing for the sacrifice, attend our rite.
O Agni, born of Truth, three are your strengths, three your abodes, and three are your many tongues. Three also are your bodies beloved by the gods; with these, protect our songs without ceasing.
O Agni Jātavedas, many are your names, O self-dependent god of immortality.
And those many illusions of the masters of illusion, O all-impelling one whose kinship is sought, you have gathered together within yourself.
Agni is the leader of the divine peoples like Bhaga, the god who guards the seasons and upholds the cosmic order.
As the slayer of Vṛtra, the ancient one, and possessor of all wealth, may he carry the singer across all difficulties.
I invoke here Dadhikrā, Agni, and the goddess Uṣas; Bṛhaspati and the god Savitṛ; the Aśvins, Mitra and Varuṇa, and Bhaga; the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas.
O Jātavedas, place this sacrifice of ours among the immortals; enjoy these oblations.
O Agni, Hotṛ-priest, sitting down as the first, partake of the drops of fat and ghee.
O Purifier, drops of fat mixed with ghee drip for you;
according to your own law, bestow upon us the most excellent treasure for the feast of the gods.
For you, O Agni, the wise and true one, the drops of clarified butter drip;
as the most excellent seer, you are kindled; become the protector of the sacrifice.
For thee, O Agni, the lord of power, the drops of fat and ghee drip down, O irresistible one. Praised by the seers, come with thy lofty luster; O wise one, graciously accept the offerings.
The most powerful fat has been extracted from your midst; we offer it to you.
O Vasu, the drops drip upon your skin; accept them, O God, according to the divine portions.
This is that Agni in whom Indra, longing for him, placed the pressed soma within his belly;
having won thousandfold booty like a swift steed, you are praised, O Jātavedas.

O Agni, that splendor of yours which is in heaven, on earth, in the plants, and in the waters, O worshipful one— by which you have stretched out the wide mid-air— that light of yours is brilliant, surging, and beheld by men.
O Agni, you go toward the flood of heaven; you have called upon the gods who are worthy of worship.
You [go] to those waters which are in the luminous realm beyond the sun, and those which stand below it.
May the fires of the soil, in harmony with those of the flowing waters, being free from malice, accept the sacrifice and grant great, disease-free nourishments.
O Agni, bestow upon the one who invokes you the *iḷā*—the gift of cattle, full of wondrous power, and most enduring.
May there be to us a son, a spreading progeny; O Agni, let that benevolence of yours be with us.
Rubbed forth and well-established in his dwelling place, the youthful sage, the leader of the sacrifice—Agni, the ageless one among the aging woods; therein Jātavedas has established immortality.
The two Bharatas, Devaśravas and Devavāta, churned forth the wealthy Agni, the highly skillful one.
O Agni, look out for us with great riches; be our leader through the days to come.
The ten fingers have generated him, the ancient one, well-born among his mothers and dear to them. Praise Agni, the son of Devavāta, O Devaśravas—he who shall be the master of men.
I have established you in the best place upon the earth, in the station of Iḷā, on days that are auspicious.
O Agni, shine with wealth upon the Ṛṣadvatī, the Āpayā, and the Sarasvatī, where men dwell.
O Agni, bestow upon the one who invokes you the *iḷā*—the gift of cattle, wondrous and most constant.
May there be to us a son, a spreading progeny; O Agni, let that benevolence of yours be with us.
O Agni, overcome the hostile armies, casting away those who oppose us;
invincible, crossing over the godless ones, bestow splendor upon the one who brings the sacrifice.
O Agni, you are kindled with the *iḷā* offering, the immortal invoker who is sought for the sacrifice; graciously accept our ritual service today.
O Agni, wakeful son of strength, invoked with oblations, come with your splendor to this sacred grass,
my seat.
O Agni, together with all the Agnis and the gods, magnify our songs at the sacrifices— those who are indeed mindful.
O Agni, grant wealth consisting of heroic sons and abundance to the donor; sharpen us so that we may be rich in offspring.
O Agni, you are the wise son of Heaven, and by your lineage you belong to Earth as the knower of all things.
O conscious one, sacrifice here to the gods individually.
Agni, the wise one, wins heroic powers; he wins booty, adorning himself for immortality.
O you who abound in food, bring those gods here to us.
Agni, the unerring one, shines upon Heaven and Earth, the two immortal goddesses who belong to all people;
he dwells among them with strengths, most resplendent through our homages.
O Agni and Indra, come here to the sacrifice in the house of the donor who has pressed the Soma;
O Gods, do not fail us, for the drinking of the Soma.
O Agni, son of strength, Jātavedas, you who are eternal, you are kindled in the home of the waters;
magnifying the places of assembly with your aid.

Having perceived Agni Vaiśvānara with our minds, we, possessing oblations, sing praise to the one worthy of invocation, the finder of heaven—the bountiful god, the charioteer, the delightful one; seeking wealth, the Kuśikas call upon him with songs.
We invoke that bright Agni for protection—Vaiśvānara, Mātariśvan, the one worthy of praise;
Bṛhaspati for the divine service of men, the inspired singer, the listener, the guest who speeds swiftly.
Like a neighing horse, Vaiśvānara is kindled by the Kuśikas with their wives, age after age.
May that Agni, ever-watchful among the immortals, bestow upon us great heroism, excellence in horses, and treasure.
Let the Vājas go forth with their powers like fires; mingled for glory, they have yoked their spotted deer.
The Maruts, great in strength and all-knowing, the undeceivable ones, make the mountains tremble.
The Maruts, adorned with fire, belonging to all peoples—we implore their fierce and mighty protection.
They, the sons of Rudra, resounding, clothed in rain, like lions in their roaring intent, are the bounteous givers.
We implore with fair praises the host upon host, the troop upon troop: the splendor of Agni and the might of the Maruts.
With spotted deer for steeds, possessing inexhaustible wealth, they come to the sacrifice, wise in the assemblies.
I am Agni, by birth Jātavedas; clarified butter is my eye, immortality is in my mouth. I am the threefold hymn, the measurer of the region; I am the unaging heat, the oblation by name.
With three purifiers he cleansed the hymn, discerning with his heart the thought and the light;
by his own powers he fashioned the most excellent treasure and then beheld heaven and earth all around.
The inexhaustible fountain with a hundred streams, the wise father of all that is to be spoken;
him who rejoices as the *meḷi* in the lap of his parents—O Heaven and Earth, fulfill him whose word is truth.
Forward go your strengths, seeking heaven, accompanied by oblations and the butter-spoon; they approach the gods, desiring their favor.
I praise with song Agni, the wise, the accomplisher of the sacrifice, who is prompt to hear and who bestows what is intended.
O Agni, may we, through your power, be able to overcome the hostilities of the vigorous god Yama; may we cross beyond all enmities.
Being kindled at the sacrifice, Agni the purifier is worthy of praise;
we pray to him whose hair is flame.
Broad-chested, immortal, clothed in clarity, well-invoked with *svāhā*,
Agni is the bearer of oblations for the sacrifice.
Those who press on with zeal, holding forth the ladles and possessing the sacrifice, have thus brought Agni hither with their prayer for his aid.
The immortal god, the Hotṛ, goes before with his creative power,
impelling the assemblies of knowledge.
The prize-winner is placed among the prizes; he is led forward in the sacrifices—the inspired singer who accomplishes the rite.
Worthy of choice, he was fashioned by wisdom; he took as his womb the germ of all beings, the father of Dakṣa, through his own body.
I have established you, the most excellent one, produced by strength through the praise of skill— O Agni, the radiant and longing one.
The inspired singers, seeking to win, kindle Agni with their strengths at the harnessing of the sacred Law— him who is the controller and the one who crosses the waters.
I praise Agni at the sacrifice— the Son of Strength, shining toward heaven, the one possessed of the wisdom of a seer.
Worthy of invocation and homage, visible even through the darkness,
Agni, the bull, is kindled.
Agni, the bull, is kindled like a horse that carries the gods;
him they invoke with oblations.
O Bull, we who are bulls ourselves kindle you, the bull,
O Agni, as you shine forth loftily.
O Agni Jātavedas, accept our oblation, the sacrificial cake,
at the morning pressing, O you who are enriched by prayer.
O Agni, this sacrificial cake has been cooked for you, or perhaps it has been fully prepared;
enjoy it, O youngest one!
O Agni, partake of the sacrificial cake offered on the day before yesterday;
you, O Son of Strength, are established at this sacrifice.
O Jātavedas, O Sage, at the midday libation, enjoy the sacrificial cake here;
O Agni, the wise do not diminish your portion in the assemblies of the sacrifice, for you are the mighty one.
O Agni, son of strength, take pleasure at the third libation in the offered sacrificial cake;
then, through inspired praise, establish among the gods the sacrifice, rich in jewels, watchful among the immortals.
O Agni, increasing one, O Jātavedas, graciously accept this offering, the sacrificial cake, which has been prepared for the day after yesterday.
Here is this fire-drill; here is the means for procreation prepared. Bring hither this mistress of the people; let us churn Agni in the ancient manner.
Jātavedas has been deposited in the two fire-sticks, well-established like an embryo within pregnant women;
day by day Agni is to be praised by wakeful men who bring oblations.
O wise one, bring [the oblation] down upon her who lies extended; having been conceived at once, she has given birth to the bull.
With his ruddy crest and bright radiance, the son of *iḷā* has been born according to the sacred law.
In the place of Iḷā, upon the navel of the earth, O Jātavedas Agni, we establish you so that you may carry our oblation.
O men, churn forth the sage, the guileless, the wise, the immortal, the fair-faced one;
O men, bring forth Agni, the first banner of sacrifice in the east, the most auspicious.
When they churn him with their arms, he shines forth like a prize-winning steed, ruddy among the woods;
brilliant as the unobstructed path of the Aśvins, he sweeps past, burning up the stones and the grass.
Born, Agni shines forth, observant, a prize-winner, a sage praised by seers, bountiful;
him whom the gods established at the sacrifices as the one to be invoked, the all-knowing bearer of oblations.

Sit down, O Hotṛ, in your own place, being wise; establish the sacrifice in the womb of good deeds. As one who pleases the gods, worship the gods with the oblation; O Agni, bestow great vitality upon the sacrificer.
Produce smoke, O friends, like a bull; go toward the prize without failing.
This Agni is the conqueror of armies and possesses heroic sons, by whom the gods overcame the Dasyus.
This is your seasonal birthplace, from which once born you shone forth;
knowing it, O Agni, sit down here, and then cause our songs of praise to flourish.
He is called Tanūnapāt when he is the embryo of the Asura; he becomes Narāśaṃsa when he is born.
When Mātariśvan measured out his form in the mother, he became the rush of the wind in his swift course.
Well-rubbed by vigorous friction, well-placed as the sage, O Agni, perform the sacrifice flawlessly; worship the gods for the one who seeks the gods.
Mortals have brought forth the immortal one—unfailing, swift, with strong jaws;
the ten unwedded sisters, moving together, grasp the newborn male.
The seven-hotted one shone forth from of old when he blazed in his mother’s lap at her udder.
The joyous one does not close his eyes day after day, since he was born from the belly of the Asura.
Armed against enemies like the onset of the Maruts, these first-born of the sacred word know all things. The Kuśikas have offered a glorious prayer; each one in his own home has kindled Agni.
Since we have chosen you here today, O wise Hotṛ, as this sacrifice proceeds;
since you have sacrificed firmly and indeed performed the rites steadfastly, come to the Soma, knowing and perceiving all.
Your Soma-loving friends desire you; they press the Soma and present the sacrificial offerings.
They endure the insults of men, for, O Indra, no wisdom whatsoever exists apart from you.
Not even the furthest regions are distant for you; come hither, O Lord of Bay Horses, with your two bays.
These libations have been prepared for you, the steadfast bull; the pressing-stones are set in motion while the fire is kindled.

Indra, the fair-cheeked, the bounteous, the overcomer, of great host, of mighty deeds, the impetuous— when you, the fierce one, were established among mortals as a protector, where then, O Bull, are those heroic exploits of yours?
For you alone, shaking even the unshakable, go forth slaying the Vṛtras;
heaven and earth, the mountains, stand according to your law as if fixed in their places.
And even in safety, O much-invoked one, you alone, as the slayer of Vṛtra, have spoken firmly with your glories;
for even these two boundless worlds, O Indra, when you grasp them together, are but a handful to you, O Maghavan.
O Indra, let your two bay horses go forth down the slope; let your thunderbolt go forth, crushing the enemies.
Slay those who face you, those who follow behind, and those who flee away; make all truth prevail, and let it be spread abroad.
The mortal to whom you have granted sustenance, even that which was not his portion, shall enjoy domestic wealth.
O Indra, invoked by many, may your benevolent favor be dripping with clarity; your gift brings thousands.
O Indra, much-invoked, you crushed Kuṇāru, who dwelt with Dānu and was handless;
O Indra, with your might you struck down Vṛtra, the footless one who grew arrogant and hostile.
O Indra, you have established in its seat the level, vigorous, great, and boundless earth; the Bull has propped up the sky and the mid-air; let the waters flow here, impelled by you.
O Indra, Vala, who had no foe to restrain him, opened the cow-stall out of fear before you struck;
he made the paths easy to traverse for the release of the cows, while the sounding voices of praise bore up toward the one invoked by many.
Alone, Indra has filled the two world-halves joined together—the earth and the sky.
And from the mid-air, O Hero, as the charioteer of our battle, bring us food and yoked strengths.

The sun does not violate the quarters assigned to him day after day, impelled by the one with bay horses; when he has traversed his paths, he then effects his release with his steeds—this indeed is his [work].
They longed to behold the great and wondrous face of the radiant Dawn as she came from the night;
all recognize her when she arrives in her majesty—the many well-performed deeds of Indra.
A great light is deposited within her flanks; the raw cow moves about bearing the cooked [milk].
Every sweetness is gathered within the cow, which Indra placed there for our nourishment.
O Indra, be firm; the snares have been set. Aid the sacrifice for the sake of the singer and his friends.
Let the mortals of evil magic and wicked intent, the armed enemies, be struck down.
The clamor is heard from the nearby enemies; strike down upon them your most scorching thunderbolt!
Hew them down from below, shatter them, and overcome them! Slay the *rakṣas*, O Maghavan, and deliver them up.
Uproot the *rakṣas* with its very root, O Indra; cut it in the middle and crush its tip.
How far have you pursued the *salalūka*? Cast your burning weapon at the hater of sacred prayer.
For our well-being, O Leader, when you sit with the swift steeds amidst the many great nourishments, may we be winners of vast wealth; may Indra grant us progeny and fortune.
O Indra, bring us glorious fortune; may we take our place at the abundance of your gift.
Like a wide expanse, our desire has spread out; O Lord of Wealth, fulfill it for us with riches.

Satisfy this desire with cattle and horses, and extend it with radiant wealth! Seeking the light of heaven, the wise Kuśikas have fashioned this hymn for you, O Indra, as a vehicle for your praise through their inspired thoughts.
O Lord of Cows, burst open the cow-pens for us; let gains and strengths come to us together.
You are the dweller in heaven, O Bull of true vigor; O Maghavan, be a good giver of cattle to us.
We invoke for our good fortune the bountiful Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the winning of booty—
the fierce one who hears us, who comes to our aid in conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras, and who is the conqueror of riches.
The knowing bearer of the oblation, instructing and honoring the thought of *ṛta*, attained the granddaughter of his daughter;
there, the father, exerting himself toward the outpouring of his daughter, hastened with a willing mind.
He has not left his inheritance to his sister; he made his embryo the storehouse of the winner.
When the mothers generated the bearer, one was the maker of good deeds, the other was the one who cried out.
Agni was born, trembling with the sacrificial ladle, as the sons of the Great One were manifested before the ruddy one.
Great is their embryo; great is that which has been born from them; great is the growth of the one with tawny horses through the sacrifices.
Victorious songs attended him; they recognized the great light emerging from the darkness.
Knowing him, the dawns rose up toward him; Indra alone became the lord of the cattle.
The wise sages, with their minds directed forward, pierced the firm barriers; the seven inspired ones sent them forth.
They found every path of Cosmic Order; knowing them, he entered into them with reverence.
When Saramā found the breach of the mountain, she made the great, ancient path wide for the common goal.
The swift-footed one led the way at the head of the flowing streams; knowing it well, she went first toward the roar.
The wisest one came, seeking friendship; the mountain yielded the embryo for the sake of the pious act.
The youth, eager for the sacrifice, won [the prize] with his companions; then he immediately became an Aṅgiras, singing his praise.
The manifest presence, the counterpart of every being, knows all births and slays Śuṣṇa.
May he, the path-finder from heaven, seeking cattle and singing our praise, as a friend release his friends from reproach.
With minds longing for cattle, they sat down with hymns, creating a path toward immortality;
even now this is their abundant dwelling-place, by which they sought to win the months through the Eternal Law (*ṛta*).
Beholding their own milk, they rejoiced while milking the seed of the ancient one;
their roar heated heaven and earth, and when [the cattle] were born, they established their mastery over the cows and the heroes.
He, the slayer of Vṛtra, released the cows at the birth [of the hymns] through oblations and songs;
for him, the far-reaching noble cow, yielding ghee, milked out honey-sweetness.
For him, their father, they have prepared a dwelling; the skillful ones have indeed looked upon his great, radiant power.
Supporting the two parents with a pillar, they have established the impetuous one standing erect.
When the great Dhiṣaṇā impelled him who grows instantly and pervades both worlds,
he in whom all blameless songs meet together— all powers that are unsurpassed belong to Indra.
I desire your friendship and your powers; many teams go forth to the slayer of Vṛtra.
We have come with a great hymn of praise to the patron; O Maghavan, be our protector.

Having found the great, many-glittering field, Indra then set in motion for his friends the way of movement; shining forth with his men, he brought forth the sun, the dawn, the path, and Agni all at once.
Even the waters, this far-reaching lord of the house, has sent forth toward one goal, all-glittering;
being purified by the seers with their filters, the sweet, swift-flowing streams are urged on through days and nights.
The two dark treasuries of wealth follow after thee, O worshipful Sūrya, through thy greatness,
when thy friends, O Indra, eager for thy love, strive to encompass thy majesty with their straight-flying arrows.

Become the lord of our truthful hymns, O slayer of Vṛtra; be the bull who grants all life and bestows vital strength upon our songs. Come to us with your auspicious friendships, you, the great one, hastening with your mighty aids.
Worshipping him with reverence as did Aṅgiras, I fashion this new hymn for you, O ancient one.
Drive away the many godless deceits; O Maghavan, grant us our own wealth for our gain.
The purifying mists have spread far and wide; carry us safely to the further shore of them.
O Indra, you who are the charioteer, protect us from harm; swiftly, ever more swiftly, make us winners of cattle.
The slayer of Vṛtra, the lord of cattle, has assigned the cows; with his ruddy abodes he has passed through the black one.
Indicating the direction by means of truth, he has thrown open all his own doors.
We invoke the auspicious Maghavan Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the winning of booty;
the fierce one who hears us, for our protection in conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras and is the conqueror of riches.
O Indra, Lord of Soma, drink this Soma, this midday libation which is dear to you. Puffing out your cheeks, O Maghavan, wielder of the *ṛjīṣa*, unyoke your two bay steeds and rejoice here.
O Indra, drink the Soma mixed with milk and curds, the stirred offering, the bright juice; we have given it to you for exhilaration.
Being of one mind with the host of Maruts who perform sacred prayer, together with the Rudras, pour down the rain abundantly.
O Indra, those Maruts who increased your breath, your power, and your might while singing praises—
O wielder of the thunderbolt, O fair-cheeked one, drink at the midday libation together with the troop of the Rudras.
Now the inspired singer has proclaimed their honeyed power: those Maruts who were the host of Indra;
by them, when impelled, he found the vital spot of Vṛtra, though he deemed himself to have no vulnerable point.

O Indra, enjoying the libation like Manu, drink the Soma for perpetual heroic power. O Lord of the Bay Steeds, turn hither through our sacrifices; with your swift steeds, you set the flowing waters in motion.
When you, O Indra, having slain Vṛtra, released the waters so that they might flow like racing mares,
you struck down with your moving weapon the godless one who lay encompassing the goddesses.
Let us worship with homage Indra, the exalted, the vast, the towering, the ageless, the youthful;
he, the worthy of sacrifice, whose greatness the two beloved worlds have not measured, nor do they encompass his majesty.
The many well-performed deeds of Indra—none of all the gods transgress his laws.
He who supported the earth and this heaven, the one of wondrous power who begot the sun and the dawn.
O guileless one, this is your true greatness: that as soon as you were born, you drank the Soma.
O Indra, neither the days, nor the days and nights, nor the months, nor the autumns have restrained the power of you, the mighty.
O Indra, as soon as you were born in the highest heaven, you drank the Soma for exhilaration;
when you entered heaven and earth, you then became the primordial sustainer of the poets.
You slew the serpent as he lay encompassing the waters, O many-born one, you who are more powerful than the one displaying his might;
even the sky did not equal your greatness when you stood upon the earth with one of your two flanks.

For the sacrifice, O Indra, has been your strengthener; it is dear to you, the pressed Soma and the sacrificial food. Being worthy of worship, protect sacrifice with sacrifice; the sacrifice aided your thunderbolt in the slaying of the serpent.

With sacrifice and for aid, I have brought Indra hither; may I turn him toward us for new favor—he who has grown strong through ancient hymns, through those of the middle period, and even through the newest.
Since inspiration has entered me and brought me forth, I shall praise Indra before the decisive day, so that he may carry us across from distress;
him whom both sides invoke like one going in a boat.
His beaker is full; Svāhā! Like a pourer, he has filled the vessel for drinking.
The dear Soma juices have come together toward Indra from the right, for his exhilaration.
Neither the deep-flowing Sindhu nor the mountains obstructed you as you surrounded them, O much-invoked Indra, when, thus impelled by your friends, you shattered even the firm enclosure of cattle.
We invoke for our good fortune the bountiful Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the acquisition of booty;
the fierce one who listens, for our protection in conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras and is the winner of riches.
From the lap of the mountains, longing [to flow], like two mares let loose,
vying with each other, like two bright mother-cows licking their calves, the Vipāś and Śutudrī rush forth with their waters.
Impelled by Indra, seeking his impulse, you two go toward the ocean like two charioteers; meeting together, swelling with your waves, O radiant ones, one of you flows into the other.
I have come toward the Sindhu, the most motherly; we have reached the broad and auspicious Vipāś.
Like two mothers licking their calf, they move together toward their common source.
Swelling with this milk, we move along the god-fashioned womb; our impulse, once set in motion, cannot be turned back—what does the inspired singer desire as he calls aloud to the rivers?
O you who follow the *ṛta*, rest for a moment according to your ways at my Soma-offering word!
Seeking help, the son of Kuśika has called with a lofty hymn toward the river.
Indra, whose arm wields the thunderbolt, has dug us out; he struck down Vṛtra, the dam of the rivers.
The god Savitṛ, the fair-handed, has led us forth; by his impulse we go along the wide expanses.
This heroic deed of Indra is to be proclaimed forever: how he tore apart the dragon;
with his thunderbolt he struck down those who sat around him, while the waters went forth, seeking their course.
O singer, do not forget these words, for future generations will raise their voices to you; O bard, be well-pleased with our hymns, do not cast us down among men—homage be to you!
O sisters, listen well to the singer; he has come to you from afar with wagon and chariot. Bow down low; become easy to cross, O rivers, flowing downward with your currents below the axle.
O *kārū*, let us hear your words as you have come from afar with wagon and chariot. I bow down before you like a swelling woman; like a maiden for her suitor, I am ever devoted to you.

When indeed the Bharatas, seeking cattle, shall cross over you—driven by the people and impelled by Indra—then let the impulse flow forth, urged on in its course; I choose for myself the favor of you who are worthy of sacrifice.
The Bharatas, seeking cattle, have crossed over; the sage has shared in the favor of the rivers.
Swell forth, you who bring nourishment and great wealth; fill your channels and flow swiftly!
May your wave, O Waters, strike against the pins; release the yokes.
Let the two inviolable cows, though they have committed no fault and are free from sin, swell with milk.
Indra, the breaker of forts, has overcome the Dāsa with his hymns; the finder of wealth, bestowing gifts, he has scattered his enemies.
Urged by prayer and increasing in body, the giver of much has filled both heaven and earth.
I send forth the impulse of you, the mighty Makha, fashioning my speech as an offering to the Immortal.
O Indra, you are the first to go among the human settlements and the divine tribes alike.
Indra, whose aim is to destroy, overthrew Vṛtra; whose aim is to transform, he stripped away the guises of the deceivers.
He struck down Vyansa as he burned among the woods, and he made manifest the lowing of the cows of the nights.
Indra, winner of the light of heaven, generating the days, has conquered the hostile armies with his helpers;
he made the banner of the days shine for Manu and found the light for the great battle.
Indra has entered into the impetuous strength with his might, bestowing many manly deeds like a hero; for he has inspired these prayers for the singer, and has heightened this bright color of theirs.
They celebrate the many great deeds well-performed by this great Indra:
with his host he crushed the crooked ones; with his wondrous powers, he of surpassing might, overcame the Dasyus.

In battle, Indra by his greatness created wide space for the gods; he, the true lord, the filler of the people, dwells in the seat of Vivasvat. These deeds of his the inspired poets and sages proclaim with hymns of praise.
Satrāsāha, the most excellent, the giver of strength, who has won the light of heaven and the divine waters—
he who has won the earth and this very sky, after Indra the wise ones rejoice.
Indra has won the steeds and he has won the sun; Indra has won the cow that provides much nourishment.
He has won golden wealth as well; having slain the Dasyus, he protected the Aryan race.
Indra won the plants and the days; he won the trees and the mid-air.
He split Vala and drove away the disputants; then he became the tamer of those who act with hostile intent.
We invoke the auspicious Maghavan Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the winning of booty;
the fierce one who hears us, for our protection in conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras and is the conqueror of riches.
Mount the two bay horses yoked to your chariot; come toward us like Vāyu with his teams.
Drink the soma juice, being let loose among us; O Indra, svāhā! We have offered it to you for your exhilaration.
I yoke to the poles of the chariot the two swift, bay steeds for the one invoked by many,
so that they may speed hither to this sacrifice from every side and bring Indra to us as he hastens toward what has been prepared.
Bring hither the two bulls, O burner; come down here, O self-dependent bull.
Let the two horses swallow [the fodder]; unyoke here the two ruddy steeds. Day by day eat the similar parched grains.
With a sacred prayer, I yoke for you your two swift bay horses, companions joined by prayer, who revel together;
mounting your firm and comfortable chariot, O Indra, come to the Soma as one who is wise and discerning.
Let not other sacrificers detain your two bay steeds, the virile ones with smooth backs.
Pass by them all; we shall prepare for you what is fitting with the pressed Soma juices.
This Soma is for you; come hither! Being well-disposed, drink of it most constantly. Sitting down upon the sacrificial grass at this sacrifice, O Indra, take this drop into your belly.
The sacred grass is strewn for you; O Indra, the Soma is pressed, and the parched grains are prepared for your two bay steeds to eat.
To you, the dweller in that place, the one of many powers, the bull accompanied by the Maruts—to you these oblations are offered.
O men, mountains, and waters, have made this [Soma] sweet with milk for you, O Indra.
Having come to it, O lofty one, drink it with a gracious mind; being wise and knowing, follow your own paths.
O Maruts, those whom you shared in the Soma, who strengthened you and became your host—
being in harmony with them and longing for it, O Indra, drink this Soma with the tongue of Agni.
O Indra, drink of the pressed juice according to your own nature, or drink with the tongue of Agni, O worshipful one.
O Śakra, enjoy the sacrifice offered from the hand of the *adhvaryu* or that of the *hotṛ*, and take pleasure in the oblation.
We invoke for our good fortune the bounteous Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the winning of booty—
the fierce one who listens, who comes to our aid in conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras, and who is the conqueror of wealth.
Place this offering before us for our gain, O Agni, as you ever strive with your aids;
he who has grown great at every libation through his own increasing powers, and who has become renowned by his mighty deeds.
For Indra, the Soma juices have been known since ancient times—those by which he became the skillful R̥bhu, whose joints are strong and who is vast.
Welcome these as they are being offered; O Indra, drink of the bull, the one shaken by the strong ones.

Drink and grow strong; for yours indeed are the pressed Soma-draughts, O Indra—both those of old and these here now. Just as you drank the ancient Somas, O Indra, so drink them today, O Wondrous One, as one who is ever new.
Great is the vessel, overflowing in the gathering; he possesses fierce might and bold strength.
Even the earth could not contain him when the Soma juices exhilarated the Lord of the Bay Steeds.

Great and formidable, he has grown for heroic power; the bull has gathered [strength] through his poetic wisdom. Indra is the bestower of fortune; his cows grant booty, and his sacrificial gifts are born in abundance.
When the rivers went forth according to their impulse, as waters flow toward the ocean like charioteers,
even from that seat Indra is more expansive, when the Soma, the milked stalk, fills him.
Like rivers flowing toward the ocean, bringing well-pressed Soma for Indra, they milk the stalk with their hands using ladles; they purify the honey with a stream through the filters.
Like lakes are his bellies that hold the Soma; he has encompassed many libations. When Indra had consumed the first foods and slain Vṛtra, he chose the Soma.
Bring it hither; let no one hold this back from us, for we know you as the lord of riches.
O Indra, lord of bay horses, bestow upon us that magnificent gift which is yours.
O Indra, Maghavan, wielder of the *ṛjīṣa*, bestow upon us wealth that is abundant and possesses every desirable thing.
Grant us a hundred autumns to live, and grant us, O fair-cheeked Indra, eternal heroic sons.
We invoke for our good fortune the bountiful Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the acquisition of booty—
the fierce one who hears us, who comes to our aid in conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras, and who wins riches.
O Indra, we turn you toward us for the slaying of Vṛtra, for strength, and for victory in battle.
O Śatakratu, may the worshippers turn your mind and your eye toward us,
O Indra.
O Śatakratu, we invoke all your names with every song for the sake of overcoming our adversaries,
O Indra.
With a hundred powers of Indra, the one praised by many and the sustainer of the people, we magnify him.
I invoke Indra, who is invoked by many, for the slaying of Vṛtra and for the winning of booty in battles.
Be victorious in the contests for booty; we implore you, O Śatakratu, O Indra, for the slaying of Vṛtra.
O Indra, grant us victory in the contests for glory, in the struggle for the prize, in the battles, and in the pursuit of renown; overcome those who seek to harm us.
O Indra, Lord of a hundred powers, drink the most invigorating, brilliant, and watchful Soma for our protection.
O Śatakratu, those sensory powers of yours which exist among the five peoples— O Indra, I choose them for you.
O Indra, great renown has come to you; bestow upon us invincible splendor. We cause your vital strength to swell upward.
Come to us from nearby, O Śakra, and also from afar;
O wielder of the stone, come here from whatever world is yours, O Indra.
Like a carpenter, I have fashioned this inspired thought; like a prize-winning steed with a good yoke, I hasten forward.
Touching upon my dearest and most distant goals, I, the wise one, desire to behold the seers.
Ask about the origin of the sages from the *inota*: supported by their minds, they fashioned heaven through their good deeds.
These songs of praise of yours, increasing and impelled by thought, have now come into accordance with the sacred law.

Placing secret things here, they anointed the two worlds for dominion; they measured them out with their measures and extended the wide ones. The two great ones, meeting together, were established for the sake of nourishment.
As he was mounting up, all [the gods] adorned him; clothed in splendors, he moves, self-luminous.
Great is that name of the bull-like Asura; assuming every form, he has taken his stand upon the immortal realms.
The first bull, the elder, brought these many strengthening powers to birth;
O two Kings, sons of Heaven, through the insights of the assembly, you have maintained sovereign power from days of old.

O two Kings, you attend to the three, the many, and all the sacrificial assemblies in the rite; I beheld them there with my mind, having gone in spirit to the Gandharvas who have Vāyu for their hair, as they abide in their sacred law.
Now, by means of the names of this bull and the cow, they have measured out his kinship with the cattle;
clothing themselves in various divine powers (*asurya*), the masters of illusion have fashioned their forms within him.
Truly, no one has surpassed that golden splendor which Savitṛ has extended for me.
With fair praise, he has encompassed the two world-halves that pervade all things; like a maiden, he has veiled his offspring.
You two accomplish the great ancient [work]; may you both be our divine protection. All the wise ones behold the manifold deeds of the one who stands with tongue like a cowherd.
We invoke for our good fortune the bountiful Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the acquisition of booty;
the fierce one who hears us, for our protection in the conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras and is the winner of riches.
The prayer, fashioned from the heart and shaped by hymns of praise, goes forth toward Indra as its lord;
O Indra, you who are ever-watchful at the sacrifice when it is being recited, take note of that which is born for you.
Born from heaven itself, ancient, wide-awake, and being recited at the sacrifice—
clad in auspicious, bright white garments— this is that ancestral prayer of our forefathers, come to us.
Even Yama’s mother has given birth here to the twin Yamās; for the tip of the tongue has arrived, flying hither.
These two born together, slayers of darkness, attend to their wondrous forms at the base of the heat.
Among mortals, there is no one who can revile these who are our fathers, warriors for the sake of cattle.
Indra, the majestic and wondrous one, has made firm for them and released the enclosures of the cow-pens.
Where the friend, together with his friends, the Navagvas, went forth against the cattle with the warriors,
there Indra, with the ten Daśagvas, truly found the sun dwelling in the darkness.
Indra found the honey gathered in the cow, hoofed and with a solid hoof, within the fold of the earth;
hidden, secret, and concealed in the waters, he, the possessor of skill, took it in his right hand.
Discerning the light from the darkness, may we choose it; may we be far removed from misfortune in the encounter.
O Indra, drinker of Soma, increased by Soma, take pleasure in these songs of the most frequent singer.
May light attend the sacrifice for heaven and earth; may we be far from great distress.
For even against the many attacks of a mortal, O Vasus, you are excellent deliverers through your mighty power.
We invoke the auspicious Maghavan Indra in this battle, the most heroic among men in the acquisition of booty;
the one who hears us, the fierce one for our protection in conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras and is the winner of riches.
O Indra, we invoke you, the bull, when the Soma is pressed;
as such, drink of the sweet juice.
O Indra, praised by many, take pleasure in this pressed Soma that finds the power of the mind;
drink and pour it down until you are fully satisfied.
O Indra, Lord of the People, being praised, further our sacrifice accompanied by prayer along with all the gods.
O Indra, lord of the virtuous, these pressed Soma drops flow forth for you; the bright drops seek your dwelling.
O Indra, take the pressed Soma, most excellent, into your belly;
for yours are the celestial drops.
O lover of songs, drink our pressed juice; you are anointed with streams of honey.
O Indra, glory is indeed won through you alone.
The imperishable splendors of the trees attend upon Indra;
having drunk of the Soma, he has grown strong.
Come to us from nearby and from afar, O slayer of Vṛtra;
take pleasure in these our songs.
When you are invoked between the far distance and the near,
O Indra, come here from there.
Come then to us, O Indra, being invoked toward me for the drinking of the Soma;
come with your two bay horses, O wielder of the stone.
The seasonal Hotṛ priest has taken his seat; the sacred grass has been strewn in due order;
the pressing-stones have been yoked at dawn.
O you who are borne by prayers, these prayers are being performed; sit upon the sacred grass.
O Hero, enjoy the sacrificial cake.
Delight yourself in these libations of ours, O slayer of Vṛtra, in these hymns and in the recitations,
O Indra, lover of songs!
Our prayers lick the wide one who drinks the Soma, the Lord of Strength,
Indra, as mother cows lick their calf.
So do you rejoice in the soma-juice for the sake of great bounty from your own body;
do not deliver your worshipper to reproach.
O Indra, we, seeking you and bearing oblations, sing your praises;
and you, O Vasu, are well-disposed toward us.
O Māra, release us; come hither, O lover of bay horses! O Indra, self-sustained one, rejoice here.
O Indra, may the two long-maned horses, dripping with clarity, carry you hither on a comfortable chariot to sit upon the sacrificial grass.
Come to our pressed soma, O Indra, mixed with milk—
the one which, along with your two bay steeds, seeks you out.
O Indra, come to this exhilarating drink, pressed by the stones upon the sacred grass; will you not indeed satisfy yourself with it?
Thus my songs have gone forth from here toward Indra, sent out to turn him hither for the drinking of the Soma.
We invoke Indra here with hymns for the drinking of the Soma; will he not surely come through our songs of praise?
O Indra, these Soma juices have been pressed; take them into your belly, O Śatakratu, O possessor of wealth and horses.
For we know you, O Sage, as the winner of wealth, bold in battles;
therefore, we seek your favor.
O Indra, come with your bulls and drink this pressed juice of ours, mixed with milk and mixed with barley.
For you alone, O Indra, in your own dwelling, I urge the Soma for your drinking;
may this [Soma] delight in your heart.
We Kuśikas, seeking your aid, invoke you, the ancient Indra, for the drinking of the pressed juice.
Come hither, standing upon the chariot-seat; to you belongs the drinking of Soma from days of old.
Release your dear friends and mount the sacred grass; these bearers of oblations call upon you.
Come hither, passing over many peoples and the prayers of the enemy, with your two bay horses to us;
for these hymns, fashioned into songs of praise, call upon you, O Indra, as they take delight in your friendship.
O God Indra, being of one mind with us, come quickly with your bay steeds to our sacrifice which increases through homage;
for I invoke you repeatedly with my prayers, offering oblations of clarified butter at the shared feast of the sweet juices.
And may these two vigorous bay steeds, your companions, well-yoked and fair-limbed, bring you hither.
May Indra, enjoying the libation with parched grain, as a friend hear the praises of his friend.

Would you not make me the guardian of the people? O Maghavan, wielder of the *ṛjīṣa*, would you not make me the king? Would you not make me a seer who has drunk of the pressed juice? Would you not grant me of the immortal wealth?
May the great bay horses, harnessed together, bring thee hither, O Indra, to the shared banquet—
those who from of old reach to the heights of heaven, the well-groomed, vigorous steeds of the Bull.
O Indra, drink of the bull-like juice shaken by the bull, which the falcon brought for you who desired it;
in whose exhilaration you cause the peoples to tremble, and in whose exhilaration you threw open the cow-pens.
We invoke the auspicious Maghavan Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the acquisition of booty;
the fierce one who listens, for our protection in the conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras and is the winner of riches.
May this beloved Soma, pressed by the tawny steeds, be yours;
O Indra, enjoying it with your tawny steeds, come to us and mount your golden chariot.
Delighting in the dawn you caused it to shine; delighting in the sun you caused it to glow.
O Indra, possessor of bay horses, wise and discerning, you increase toward all glories.

Indra, with his bay steeds, has supported the heaven that nourishes the bay steeds and the earth that is the form of the bay steeds; he, the bearer of the bay steeds, sustains abundant food between those two where the bay one moves.
Born as a tawny bull, he illumines the entire radiant realm;
the one with bay horses takes up his tawny weapon, the golden thunderbolt, within his arms.
Indra, with his bay horses, opened the way for the beloved, bright, and pure thunderbolt enveloped in light;
he drew forth the pressed juice with his bay steeds and brought the cows out with his bay steeds.
Come, O Indra, with your pleasant bay horses whose hair is like peacock feathers;
let no one hold you back, as fowlers catch a bird—pass them by like a desert.
The devourer of Vṛtra, the breaker of Vala, the destroyer of forts, the progenitor of the waters;
Indra, the rider of the chariot, the master of the two bay steeds, who shatters even what is firm.
Like deep oceans, you nourish your power;
like cows, O good guardian, the milch-kine have reached the pasture, as streams flow into a lake.
Bring us impetuous wealth, as one who acknowledges his share; O Indra, shake down for us enduring riches, like a man with a hook shakes ripe fruit from a tree.
O Indra, you are long-lived, self-ruling, of consistent purpose, and most glorious in your own renown. Increasing in strength, O much-praised one, be for us the most illustrious of all.

O Indra, renowned and great, the heroic deeds of you— the warrior, the bull, the self-ruling lord, the fierce, the youthful, the aged, the impetuous, and the wielder of the thunderbolt who never grows old— are truly mighty.
Great art thou, O buffalo, by thy manly powers, a seeker of wealth, O fierce one, overcoming others;
sole king of the entire world, do thou both fight and cause the people to dwell in peace.
Shining forth, he has surpassed all measures; unopposed from every side, he has surpassed the gods.
By his might, Indra has surpassed heaven and earth, and the vast, wide mid-air, he who drinks the soma-dregs.
The Soma juices, pressed from of old, enter into Indra— who is wide, deep, formidable by birth, all-encompassing, and the protector of prayers— just as rivers flow into the ocean.
O Indra, that Soma which Earth and Heaven bear for you with longing, like a mother carrying her child—
that very one they urge forth for you, and the Adhvaryus purify it for you to drink, O Bull.
O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, as a bull for the battle, drink the Soma according to your custom for exhilaration.
Pour the wave of the sweet juice into your belly; you have been the king of the pressed juices from of old.
O Indra, united and accompanied by the Maruts, drink the Soma, O wise hero, slayer of Vṛtra!
Slay the enemies, drive away the mockers, and then grant us security from every side.
And according to the seasons, O guardian of the seasons, drink our pressed soma, Indra, together with the gods who are your friends.
The Maruts, whom you shared with, who followed you when you struck Vṛtra, have bestowed their strength upon you.
O Maghavan, those who strengthened you at the slaying of Ahi, those at the battle with Śambara, O Lord of Bay Steeds, and those in the quest for cattle;
those sages who now rejoice after you—drink the Soma, O Indra, together with your host of Maruts.
We invoke here for new protection that Indra, the bull accompanied by the Maruts, who has grown great, the one without enemies, the divine ruler, the all-conquering, the fierce giver of victory.
As soon as he was born, the youthful bull desired to drink of the pressed juice;
drink of the pure draught according to your desire, for this is the first portion of the Soma mixed with milk for you.
On the day you were born, out of desire for him, you drank the mountain-dwelling nectar of the Soma stalk;
your mother, the youthful progenitor, first poured it for you in the house of the great father.
Having approached his mother, he sought food; he beheld the sharp Soma as his udder. Driving away the others, the skillful one moved forward; he of many forms performed great deeds.
Fierce, subduing the swift, possessing overwhelming power, he fashioned his body according to his will;
Indra, having surpassed Tvaṣṭṛ by his very birth, drank the Soma from the vessels of that [demon].
We invoke for our good fortune the bounteous Indra, the most heroic in this battle, the winner of booty;
the fierce one who hears us, for our protection in the conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras and is the conqueror of riches.
Praise the great Indra, in whom all the people who drink Soma have fulfilled their desire;
him, the one of excellent wisdom, fashioned by the two world-halves (Dhiṣaṇās) with vast skill, whom the gods generated as the slayer of Vṛtras.

Him whom no one indeed overcomes in battles—the self-ruling one, the most heroic, who stands upon his bay horses; he who, as the most powerful lord, with his vigorous warriors, has shortened the life of the Dasyu by his wide-reaching strides.
Victorious in battles, crossing over like a steed, pervading both heaven and earth, the bounteous one;
like Bhaga to be invoked in the act of praise, like a father, dear, easy to call upon, and bestowing vital strength.
The upholder of heaven, the back of the mid-air, standing erect like a chariot, Vāyu with his teams of horses and his Vasu-companions;
the illuminator of nights, the progenitor of the sun, who distributes the portion like Dhiṣaṇā, bestowing strength.
We invoke the auspicious Maghavan Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the acquisition of booty;
the fierce one who hears us, for our protection in conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras and wins riches.
Let Indra drink with *svāhā*, he for whom the Soma is intended—having come as the fierce bull accompanied by the Maruts;
may the far-reaching one be satisfied with these foods, and may the oblation fulfill the desire of his body.
I yoke for you the two attendants for speed, whose obedience you have favored since ancient times.
May the bay horses place you here, O fair-cheeked one; drink of this well-pressed, delightful soma.
The singers have established Indra—the one who mingles with the milk, the bringer of a good crossing—for the sake of preeminence and sustenance.
O drinker of the *ṛjīṣa*, exhilarated by the Soma, bestow upon us cattle in many ways.

Delight this desire with cattle and horses, and extend it with moon-bright bounty. Seeking the light of heaven, the wise Kuśikas have fashioned hymns for you, O Indra; with their prayers, they have prepared the vehicle for you.
We invoke for our good fortune the bounteous Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the acquisition of booty;
the fierce one who hears us for our protection in conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras and is the winner of riches.
The lofty hymns have resounded toward Indra, the sustainer of the people, the bountiful one worthy of praise—
him who is magnified by beautiful songs, invoked by many, the immortal one who is celebrated day by day.
Our hymns approach from every side Indra, the lord of a hundred powers, the ocean-like, the mighty hero;
him who wins the prize, the breaker of forts, the swift one who crosses the waters, who dwells with his own power, who overcomes all adversaries, and finds the light of heaven.

In the mine of wealth, the singer is praised; Indra, the faultless one, honors those who laud him. He has indeed taken pleasure in the dwelling of Vivasvat; praise him, the all-conquering slayer of the arrogant foe.
With songs and hymns, do ye with zeal celebrate the Hero, you, the most manly among men.
He of many wiles yields to your force; homage is his, for from of old he alone is the Lord.
Many are his invitations among mortals; the earth bears many riches for him.
For Indra, the heavens, the plants, and the waters guard their wealth—the living forests and the streams.
For you, O Indra, Lord of the Bay Steeds, have they evermore established sacred prayers and songs; be pleased with them!
Be mindful as a kinsman of our newest aid; O gracious Friend, bestow vital strength upon those who sing your praise.
O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, drink the Soma here, just as you drank of the pressed juice at Śaryāta’s sacrifice.
Under your guidance and in your protection, O Hero, the sages who perform fair sacrifices seek to win your favor.
Longing for it, O Indra, drink here our pressed soma with the Maruts as your friends;
for when you were born, O much-invoked one, all the gods surrounded you for the great battle.
In the crossing of waters, O Maruts, this kinsman has gladdened Indra with gifts of wealth;
together with them, let the slayer of Vṛtra drink the pressed Soma of the donor in his own dwelling place.
For this [Soma] has been pressed here with power, O Lord of bounties; drink of it, O lover of songs!
O Soma, let him who shall follow your self-sustaining power restrain his body within the pressed juice; may he, the one worthy of Soma, exhilarate you.
May it reach your two flanks; O Indra, may it reach your head through this prayer; O hero, extend your arms for the sake of bestowing wealth.
O Indra, at dawn, enjoy our offering accompanied by parched grains, by groats, by cakes, and by hymns of praise.
O Indra, enjoy this cooked sacrificial cake and give it your approval;
for you the oblations flow forth.
Eat our sacrificial cake and take pleasure in our songs,
as one desiring a bride approaches a young woman.
O you who are renowned from of old, enjoy our sacrificial cake at our morning libation;
for, O Indra, your power of will is vast.
O Indra, enjoy here at this midday libation the parched grains and the lovely sacrificial cake,
while the praiser and singer, hastening toward his goal and acting like a bull, invokes you with his songs.
At the third libation, O Much-Praised One, grant us the parched grains and the offered sacrificial cake.
O Sage, may we, providing nourishment, honor you who are accompanied by the Ṛbhus and possessed of strength with our prayers.

For you who are accompanied by Pūṣan, we have prepared the groats; for you who possess bay horses and are borne by bay steeds, we have prepared the parched grains. Eat the cake with your troop of Maruts; drink the Soma, O wise hero, slayer of Vṛtra.
Bring forth the parched grains quickly for him, and the sacrificial cake for the most heroic of men.
Day after day, O Indra, may these similar offerings increase you for the drinking of Soma, O bold one!
O Indra and Parvata, bring hither on your lofty chariot desirable refreshments accompanied by brave heroes.
O Gods, enjoy the oblations at the sacrifices; wax strong, rejoicing in the songs of praise and the libation.
Stay well here, O Maghavan; do not depart. Now I shall worship you with well-pressed Soma.
O Indra, O Lord of Might, like a son grasping his father’s garment, I take hold of you with this most sweet song.
Recite, O Adhvaryu! Answer me; let us both prepare an acceptable offering for Indra.
Sit upon this sacrificial grass of the patron; then let the hymn be recited for Indra.
O Maghavan, may he be born at home; for that indeed is your place of origin. Let your harnessed bay horses carry you there.
Whenever we shall press the Soma, let Agni, as your messenger, run swiftly toward you.
Depart, O Maghavan, and come back again; O Indra, brother, your purpose lies in both places:
where the great chariot is stationed and where there is the unyoking of the prize-winning ass.

O Indra, you have drunk the Soma; go home. A beautiful wife and pleasant sport await you in the house, where there is the stationing of a great chariot and the unyoking of the prize-winning steed, accompanied by sacrificial gifts.
These Bhojas, the Aṅgirases, the Virūpas, the sons of Dyaus, the heroes of the Asura—
bestowing riches upon Viśvāmitra at the thousandfold pressing, they have prolonged his life.
Maghavan assumes form after form, creating his own bodies through his powers of illusion;
when he comes from heaven three times in an instant, he, the observer of the cosmic order (*ṛtāvā*), drinks at non-regular times according to his own secret mantras.
The great seer, god-born and impelled by the gods, the observer of men, propped up the billowy river;
when Viśvāmitra brought Sudās [across], Indra took pleasure in the Kuśikas.
Like swans, make a song with the pressing-stones, rejoicing with hymns at the sacrifice when the Soma is pressed;
together with the gods, O wise seers who behold men, drink the Soma-mead, O Kuśikas!
Come hither, O Kuśikas, and take heed! Release the horse of Sudās for the sake of wealth.
May the King slay Vṛtra in the east, the west, and the north; then let him sacrifice at the best place upon the earth.
I have praised Indra, who sustains both these worlds, heaven and earth;
this prayer of Viśvāmitra protects the Bharata people.
The Viśvāmitras have offered this prayer to Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt;
may he indeed make us possessors of excellent wealth.
What do your cows do among the Kīkaṭas? They do not yield the milk-mixture, nor do they heat the sacrificial cauldron.
Bring us the wealth of Pramaganda; O Maghavan, subject Naicāśākha to us!
Sasarparī, driving away want, has lowed loudly; she was given by Jamadagni. The daughter of Sūrya has spread her fame among the gods—immortal and ageless.
Sasarparī quickly brought glory for them among the five peoples;
she, the winged one, bestowing new life, whom the Palastis and Jamadagnis gave to me.
May the two oxen be firm; may the axle be strong; may the two rams not slip apart, nor may the yoke break asunder.
May Indra protect the two poles of the cart; O you whose rim is uninjured, be with us.
Bestow strength upon our bodies, O Indra; bestow strength upon our horses.
Bestow strength upon our children and grandchildren for their life, for you are indeed the giver of strength.

Envelop yourself in the heartwood of the *khadira* tree; bestow vigor upon the *spandana* and the *śiṃśapā*. O axle, be firm; being firmly established, hold us fast; do not let us slip away from this journey.
May this lord of the forest not abandon us, nor may he harm us; may there be well-being for us from our homes until we reach our dwelling and until our release.
O Indra, with your many and most excellent aids today, O Maghavan, O hero, quicken us!
May he who hates us fall low; may our breath desert him whom we hate.
He heats even the axe and hews even the *śimbala* tree;
O Indra, even the cauldron, boiling and bubbling, casts up foam.
O people, they do not understand the arrow; thinking it to be a mere beast, they lead away the red one.
They do not cause the swift horse to run with the swift; they lead the donkey in front of the horses.
O Indra, these sons of Bharata have understood only the way back, not the way forward.
They urge on their own horse as if it were a stranger's; they lead the prize-winning steed around in the race as if he were their own.
For the great assembly, they have repeatedly brought forth this strength for him who is worthy of praise;
may Agni hear us with his domestic fires, and may the imperishable one hear us with his celestial ones.
I sing a great song to the great Heaven and to the Earth; my desire moves about, seeking and knowing.
In the praises of these two, at the assemblies, the gods who honor them rejoice together.
O Heaven and Earth, may your cosmic order (*ṛta*) be truth; be fully present for our great and excellent prosperity.
This homage to Heaven and Earth, O Agni, I offer with nourishment; I seek precious treasure from you both.
For indeed, O you two ancient ones, the truthful speakers have found you both, O Heaven and Earth who follow the cosmic order (*ṛta*).
Even men, seeking to gain the hero’s prize in battle, have praised you both, O Earth, as they sought your favor.
Who truly knows? Who here can declare it? Whither do these paths converge toward the gods?
Their lowest seats have been seen, which are in the highest secret ordinances.
The seer, the watcher of men, has looked upon them as they rejoice in the separately spread womb of *ṛta*.
They have made their dwelling apart like a bird, yet they are in harmony through a common purpose.
Though distinct yet common, dwelling far apart, they stand upon a firm and watchful station;
though becoming young sisters, they nevertheless proclaim their names as a pair.
All these generations are clearly distinguished; though bearing the great gods, she does not waver.
The one moves, yet the whole remains fixed; the winged bird flies abroad, diverse and manifoldly born.
I have come from afar to this ancient kinship of ours, established long ago by our great Father,
the progenitor— wherein the gods, praising us with their rites, stood upon the wide, diverging path between the two worlds.

I proclaim this hymn of praise, O Heaven and Earth; may those whose hearts are soft and whose tongue is Agni hear it—the sovereign Mitra, Varuṇa the youthful, and the Ādityas, the sages who have spread far and wide.

The golden-handed Savitṛ, with his fair tongue, ruling as lord over the three heavens at the assembly, has sent forth his fame among the gods; O Savitṛ, send us all-encompassing prosperity from there.
May Tvaṣṭṛ, the skillful-handed, the possessor of goodly wealth, the upholder of Ṛta, the god, grant us those things for our protection.
O Ṛbhus, accompanied by Pūṣan, rejoice; with the pressing-stones raised, you have fashioned the sacrifice.
The Maruts, with lightning-chariots, armed with spears, sons of heaven, born of *ṛta*, tireless;
may Sarasvatī and the worshipful ones hear us—may they, the swift ones, bestow wealth along with heroic sons.
Hymns and chants go forth to Viṣṇu, the one who is seen in many places, as singers go on the path of Bhaga;
he is the wide-striding, preeminent one, whose many youthful mothers do not neglect him.
Indra, ruling through all his heroic powers, has filled both world-halves with his greatness.
The breaker of forts, the slayer of Vṛtra, the bold host—seizing them, bring us much cattle!
The Nāsatyas are my parents, inquiring after their kin; the Aśvins’ kinship is a beloved name.
For you two are the givers of wealth to us; O undeceived ones, you protect the gift of riches with those who are never stingy.
O sages, that great and beautiful name of yours is truly yours, O gods, since you all exist in Indra.
O much-invoked one, as a friend with your dear Ṛbhus, fashion this prayer of ours for the winning of the prize.
May Aryaman, Aditi, and the worshipful ones—unconquerable are the ordinances of Varuṇa—keep us far from childlessness; may our path be rich in offspring and abounding in cattle.
May the messenger of the gods, sent forth in many ways, declare us sinless in our integrity.
May the Earth, the Sky, and the Waters hear us, as well as the Sun with the stars and the wide mid-air.
May the powerful mountains hear us, who are firm in their foundations and rejoice in the sacrificial food;
may Aditi with the Ādityas hear us, and may the Maruts grant us auspicious protection.
May the path always be easy to traverse and rich in nourishment; O gods, blend the plants with honey.
O Agni, may Bhaga not fail me in your friendship; may I attain the dwelling of wealth abounding in food.
Enjoy the oblations; shine forth with nourishments toward us; measure out for us glorious renown.
O Agni, conquer all those enemies in battles; shine upon us with a benevolent mind throughout all days.
When the first dawns shone forth, the great imperishable syllable was born in the station of the Cow.
Now, upholding the ordinances of the gods, the singular and great divine sovereignty of the gods has manifested.
May the gods not lead us astray here, nor the ancient fathers who know the path, O Agni.
Between the two ancient dwellings, you are the banner; great is the singular divine power of the gods.
My desires fly forth in many directions; I have looked toward the ancient rites with reverence.
When the fire is kindled, let us proclaim the Truth (ṛta); great indeed is the singular divine sovereignty of the gods.
The common king, distributed in many places, lies among the resting ones, moving through the woods.
One bears the calf; the mother dwells [there]. Great is the unique sovereignty of the gods.
He has occupied the earlier ones and follows after the later ones; he is within the young maidens as soon as they are born.
Those who were pregnant give birth without having been impregnated—great indeed is the singular divine power of the gods.
The calf, having two mothers, wanders alone, bound and lying beyond;
these are the ordinances of Mitra and Varuṇa—the great, singular sovereignty of the gods.

The Hotṛ priest with two mothers, the sovereign in the assemblies, moves along the forefront while his foundation dwells below. Those who speak pleasant words bring forth delightful things; great is the singular sovereignty of the gods.
As if toward a hero fighting in the thick of battle, everything approaching is seen turned back; the thought moves within, warding off the cow. Great is the unique sovereignty of the gods.
The gray envoy stirs within; great, he moves among the people with his radiant light. Bearing wondrous forms, he looks upon us; great is the singular divine sovereignty of the gods.
Viṣṇu, the guardian, protects the supreme domain, upholding the beloved, immortal abodes.
Agni knows all those worlds; great is the singular divine sovereignty of the gods.
The twin sisters have made their forms manifold; of these two, one shines black and the other is white. When the dark and the ruddy sisters [unite], great is the singular divine power of the gods.
Where the Mother and the Daughter, both cows yielding nectar, suckle together;
in that seat of the Eternal Order (*ṛta*), I praise you—the singular, great lordship of the gods.
Licking the calf of another, she has lowed; with what world has the cow set down her udder?
She, the *ilā*, swells with the milk of *ṛta*; great is the singular divine sovereignty of the gods.
She clothes herself in many-colored forms; standing erect, she licks a three-year-old calf.
Knowing [this], I move through the seat of Ṛta; great is the singular divine sovereignty of the gods.
Like two footsteps set down by a wonder-worker, one of them is hidden and the other is manifest;
that path leads both together and apart—the singular, great sovereignty of the gods.

Let the milch-cows come lowing—those that are without calves, those that yield nectar, those that are ever-flowing, and those that have never been milked; becoming ever-new young maidens, [they proclaim] the one great divine power of the gods.
When the bull bellows among others, he deposits his seed in another herd;
for he is the protector of the night, he is Bhaga, he is the King. Great is the singular divine sovereignty of the gods.
O people, let us now proclaim the hero’s possession of noble horses; the gods know it.
Six sets of five joined together draw him; great is the singular divine power of the gods.
The divine Tvaṣṭṛ, the impeller of all forms, has nourished the creatures and begotten them in many ways; he is also the master of all these worlds. Great is the singular sovereignty of the gods.
The two great worlds, moving together, have been filled with his wealth; both of them are overspread by his riches.
The Hero is renowned for finding treasures; great indeed is the unique sovereignty of the gods.
And this earth of ours, the all-sustaining one, dwells like a king with Mitra as his ally;
like heroes seated in front for protection, great is the singular divine power of the gods.
The plants and the waters are yours to ward off [evil]; O Indra, the earth bears wealth for you.
May we be your friends, sharing in your favor. Great is the singular divine sovereignty of the gods.

Neither the sorcerers nor the wise can violate those first, firm ordinances of the gods. Neither the two worlds, free from malice, nor the mountains that stand firm can be bent down by their wondrous powers.
One, moving not, supports six burdens; the cows have approached the highest Truth. Three great ones stand above; two are hidden in secret, one is visible.
The bull with three faces, possessing all forms, and with three udders, manifold and rich in offspring;
he who has three aspects rules as the majestic lord—he is the seed-bestowing bull of all eternal things.
The pathfinder of these [waters] has awakened in their presence; I have invoked the beloved name of the Ādityas.
Even the divine waters have stood still for him; though moving separately, they have turned around him.
The rivers have three dwelling places; the sages [are thrice-three]; and the one who is sovereign in the assemblies has three mothers.
Three are the water-bearing maidens, moving toward heaven, who exercise lordship at the sacrifice three times a day.

O Savitṛ, three times from heaven, day after day, impel desirable things toward us; thrice during the day, O Bhaga, bestow wealth and treasures in threefold measure, O Protector, so that we may win them through your inspiration.
Three times from heaven Savitar impels his gifts; the two kings Mitra and Varuṇa, the fair-handed, [join him].
Even the waters and the two wide worlds beg for wealth at the impulse of Savitar.
Three times the highest, difficult to overcome, are the luminous realms; three heroes of the Asura reign over them.
May the gods, who are observers of cosmic order (*ṛta*), vigorous, and invincible, be present thrice at the sacrifice of heaven.
He who discerns has found my inspired thought, like a cow wandering at large, unattended by a herdsman, which has straightway yielded much milk for nourishment; Indra and Agni shall be its praisers.
Indra and Pūṣan, the two bulls with skillful hands, being well-pleased like those of heaven, have milked out the inexhaustible wealth;
since all the gods have taken delight in this [earth], may I here obtain your favor, O Vasus.
The sisters who desire the bull’s power recognize the embryo within him while paying homage. Like lowing cows toward their calf, they move toward him who bears great beauty.
I call upon the well-established Heaven and Earth with my inspired thought, yoking the pressing-stones at the sacrifice.
These offerings of yours, which bring abundant boons to mankind, rise upward—beautiful and worthy of worship.
O Agni, that honeyed and wise tongue of yours which is proclaimed among the gods, reaching far and wide— with that,
seat here all the worshipful ones for our protection, and cause them to drink the honeyed draughts.
O Agni, that wondrous providence of yours which, like a flowing stream from a mountain, nourishes even the gods— O Jātavedas, O Vasu, grant us that benevolence which extends to all people.
The cow of the ancient one yields what is desirable; the son of the Dakṣiṇā moves within her.
Bearing the light, he of radiant course brings the dawn; the hymn of praise has awakened the Aśvins.
Well-yoked, they carry you both toward the cosmic order (*ṛta*); the offerings rise upward like fathers.
Consume the thought of the niggardly man from us; we have brought you under our control—come hither!
With well-yoked horses and a smoothly-rolling chariot, O wonder-workers, hear this cry from the pressing-stone.
Why indeed, O Aśvins, do the ancient sages say that you are the ones most ready to turn back toward us?
Take note of us; come hither by your wondrous ways! All people, O Aśvins, invoke you.
For these honeyed draughts, mixed with milk, have been offered to you like friends at the break of dawn.
O Aśvins, lords of bounty, your praise resounds among the people across many realms.
Come hither by the paths traveled by the gods; O wonder-workers, here are these offerings of honey for you.
Ancient is your dwelling, auspicious is your friendship, O Heroes; your wealth is among the Jahnu people.
Renewing our auspicious friendships, may we now together rejoice in the sweetness of the common bond.
O Aśvins, you who are most skillful, together with Vāyu and his teams of horses, O youthful Nāsatyas, being in harmony,
enjoying the Soma offered on the third day, drink it— O bounteous givers, you who are never-failing!
O Aśvins, abundant refreshments have come toward you, striving with unerring songs of praise;
for your chariot, born of Truth and urged by the pressing-stones, traverses heaven and earth in an instant.
O Aśvins, this Soma, most sweet, is yours; drink it and come to our dwelling. Your chariot, displaying many forms, comes most readily to the appointed place of him who has pressed the juice.
Mitra, speaking, stirs men to action; Mitra has upheld both the earth and the sky.
