Mitra gazes upon the people with unblinking eyes; offer an oblation rich in ghee to Mitra.
O Mitra, O Āditya, may that mortal be foremost who exerts himself for you with sacred observance;
he whom you protect is neither slain nor conquered, and no distress reaches him, neither from near nor from afar.
Free from disease, rejoicing in the sacrificial food (*iḷā*), with measured steps upon the wide expanse of the earth,
and abiding by the ordinance of Āditya, may we remain in the good favor of Mitra.
This Mitra, worthy of homage, most gracious, a king of noble power and a wise ordainer, has been born. May we abide in the favor of that worshipful one, and likewise in his auspicious goodwill.
The great Āditya is to be approached with homage; he who brings men into harmony is most kind to the one who praises him. To that most praiseworthy Mitra, offer this pleasing oblation into the fire.
The aid of the divine Mitra, the sustainer of the people, is winning; his splendor possesses most wonderful renown.
Mitra, who by his greatness has surpassed the heavens in extent,
has surpassed the earth with his glories.
The five peoples have submitted to Mitra for his assistance and power;
he sustains all the gods.
Mitra among the gods and among living beings has provided nourishment for the person who has strewn the sacrificial grass, according to his desired vows.
O heroes, here and here indeed, by your wisdom and kinship, the yearning ones have come to those [powers] with their knowledge;
through those creative powers by which you, O sons of Sudhanvan, changing your forms at every impulse, attained a share in the sacrifice.
By those powers with which you fashioned the chalices, by that insight through which you brought forth the cow from the hide,
and by that mind with which you wrought the two bay steeds— by all this, O Ṛbhus, you attained godhood.
The R̥bhus attained the friendship of Indra; the grandsons of Manu, the skillful workers, have sped forth.
The sons of Sudhanvan won immortality, having performed their labors with sacred rites, being doers of good through their skillful work.
With Indra you travel on the same chariot at the pressed juice; thus, you possess the splendor of the Vasus.
O Ṛbhus, sons of Sudhanvan, your well-wrought deeds and heroic exploits have no equal among those who offer praise.
O Indra, together with the R̥bhus who possess strength, pour down the pressed Soma sprinkled in both hands.
Urged by prayer, O Maghavan, rejoice in the house of the donor along with the sons of Sudhanvan, those heroes.
O Indra, accompanied by the Ṛbhus and the Vājas, exhilarate yourself here for us at this libation with your power, O you who are praised by many!
These pastures have been offered to you; the ordinances of the gods and the duties of men have been established according to the sacred laws.
O Indra, together with the Ribhus, the swift ones, seeking booty, come here to the worshipful hymn of the singer;
with a hundred eager intentions for the sake of the living man, you who have a thousand ways, come to the offering of the sacrifice.
O Dawn, rich in booty, wise one, accept with favor the hymn of the singer, O bounteous lady!
Ancient yet youthful goddess, all-pervading, you move according to your law, O possessor of all boons.
O immortal goddess Uṣas, shine forth with your radiant chariot, sending out pleasant songs.
Let the well-governed horses of broad luster bring you hither—you who are golden-hued.
O Dawn, facing all beings, you stand upright as the banner of immortality.
Moving toward your common goal, turn hither like a wheel, O ever-new one.
Like one weaving a fringe, the bounteous Dawn approaches, the mistress of the dwelling;
generating light, the fortunate and wondrous one has spread from the ends of heaven to the earth.
Bring forth with reverence your hymn of praise toward the radiant goddess Uṣas.
The honey-bearer has established her splendor high in heaven; she of lovely aspect has shone out across the luminous realms.
O observer of the cosmic order, she has been awakened from heaven by our hymns; the wealthy goddess has risen with splendor across the two worlds.
O Agni, seeking desirable wealth, you go toward the approaching, radiant Dawn.
Stirring the foundations of Truth and the dawns, the Bull has entered the two great worlds;
the great creative power (*māyā*) of Mitra and Varuṇa has spread its light in many places like the moon.
These longings of ours, which we have cherished, have not been too much for one like you;
where, O Indra and Varuṇa, is that glory of yours, by which you bring wealth to your friends?
This man, seeking wealth, invokes you two most frequently for eternal protection.
O Indra and Varuṇa, being of one mind with the Maruts, listen to my call from heaven and earth.

O Indra and Varuṇa, may that wealth be ours; O Maruts, may there be for us riches consisting of all-heroic sons. May the Varūtrīs protect us with their shelters; may Hotrā, Bhāratī, and Dakṣiṇā protect us with sacrificial gifts.
O Bṛhaspati, who belongs to all the gods, enjoy our oblations;
bestow treasures upon the donor.
Worship the pure Bṛhaspati with hymns at the sacrifices;
he has willed his unbending might.
Bṛhaspati, the bull of the people, possessing all forms, the invincible and most excellent one.
O Pūṣan, O glowing god, this newest hymn of praise for you is being recited by us to you.
Accept this my song that strives for booty; favor my prayer as a suitor favors a young woman.
May that Pūṣan be our protector, he who beholds all beings and surveys them completely.
We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ;
may he inspire our thoughts.
Seeking strength through the wisdom of the god Savitṛ,
we implore the bounty of Bhaga.
The inspired singers, impelled by their devotion, honor the divine Savitṛ with sacrifices and well-fashioned hymns.
Soma goes forth, knowing the way; he goes to the appointed place of the gods, to sit upon the womb of the Eternal Order (Ṛta).
May Soma provide for us— both for our bipeds and for our four-footed livestock—
food that is free from disease.
Increasing our lifespan and overcoming our adversaries,
Soma has taken his seat at the place of assembly.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, sprinkle our pastures with clarified butter; O you of noble wisdom, moisten the regions with honey.
O you whose praise is wide, who increase through homage, you rule by the greatness of your skill; O you of pure vows, with your most far-reaching [powers].
Praised by Jamadagni, sit in the womb of the Cosmic Order;
drink the Soma, O you who increase the Truth.
For you indeed, O Agni, the gods, ever of one mind, have established you as their divine messenger; with wisdom they have established you.
They have generated the immortal among mortals, the worshipful god among those who seek the gods, the wise one; they have generated every wise god-seeker.
O Agni, turn Varuṇa, your brother, toward the gods with our prayer—he who loves the sacrifice, the eldest who loves the sacrifice;
the Āditya who upholds the cosmic order, the king who sustains the people.
O friend, turn toward your friend, as a wheel follows the swift horse, as a chariot follows its speed—toward us, O wondrous one, with speed!
O Agni, find favor for us with Varuṇa, and with the all-shining Maruts. O radiant one, grant well-being for our offspring and progeny; O wondrous one, grant us well-being!
O Agni, you who are wise, may you ward off from us the wrath of the god Varuṇa;
being the best of sacrificers, the most excellent bearer of oblations, and blazing brightly, release us from all hostilities.
O Agni, be our protector, our closest helper at the dawning of this very morning;
being gracious, appease Varuṇa for us, and grant us mercy; be one who is easily invoked by us.
The sight of this most fortunate god among mortals is most excellent and most wonderful;
it is like the pure, heated ghee of the cow, as desirable as the gift of a divine milch-cow.
Threefold are those supreme, true, and desirable births of this divine Agni.
Enveloped within the infinite, he has come—pure, bright, noble, and shining intensely.
He, the messenger, desires all dwellings; he is the Hotṛ-priest with his golden chariot and his lovely tongue.
With ruddy horses, beautiful and far-shining, he is ever delightful like an assembly rich in food.
Making himself known to men, he is the kinsman of sacrifice; they lead him forth with a great cord.
He dwells in the dwellings of this mortal man, accomplishing his purpose; the god has attained the state of a sharer in wealth.
May that Agni, who knows the way, lead us toward the treasure allotted by the gods which belongs to him—
that which all the immortals fashioned through their wisdom, while Dyaus, the father and begetter, poured forth the truth.
He was born first among the dwellings, at the base of the great [heavens], in the womb of this space;
footless and headless, he hid himself in the lair of the bull, drawing apart the two ends.
The host has first come forth with praise, into the womb of Truth, into the lair of the Bull.
Longed-for, youthful, beautiful, and radiant, the seven dear ones have been born for the Bull.
Here our human fathers sat down, aspiring toward the *ṛta*;
invoking the dawns, they drove forth the cows from within the enclosure, which were well-milking and confined within the rock-stable.
Having seen the rock, they polished it; others around them proclaimed this deed of theirs.
Guided by their flocks, they sang toward the prize; they found the light and yearned for it with their prayers.

With minds longing for cattle, those eager ones (the Uśij) have opened with divine speech the firm, obstructed mountain that held the cows, which were moving about and encompassing it; the heroes have burst open the solid stall rich in cattle.
They conceived the first name of the milch-cow; they found the thrice-seven highest names of the mother.
Knowing that, the hosts of singers acclaimed her; the ruddy dawn became manifest through the glory of the cow.
The evil darkness perished; the sky shone forth; the radiance of the divine Dawn has arisen.
Sūrya has mounted the vast fields, beholding both the upright and the crooked among mortals.
Then, having awakened, they looked out from behind; then indeed they took hold of the treasure allotted by heaven.
All the gods are in all their dwellings; O Mitra and Varuṇa, may there be truth for our prayer.
I would call upon the brightly shining Agni, the invoker, the sustainer of all, the most excellent sacrificer;
he has pierced the pure udder like that of cows, like the purified juice of the stalk poured out.
Aditi among all those worthy of sacrifice, the guest of all human beings—
may Agni Jātavedas, choosing the protection of the gods, be gracious to us.
He who, being immortal and true to the cosmic order (*ṛta*), has been established as the god among gods and the messenger among mortals;
may Agni, the most excellent invoker, blaze forth by his greatness and be stirred by the oblations of man.
O Son of Strength, born here today among us, O Agni, you travel as a messenger between both races of beings,
having harnessed your lofty, straight-tailed, vigorous, and radiant steeds.
The two steeds that increase the strength, the ruddy ones dripping with clarity—swift as thought through the power of Truth, I consider them the swiftest;
yoking your ruddy horses, you move between you gods and the clans of mortals.

Aryaman, Varuṇa, and Mitra among them, Indra and Viṣṇu, the Maruts, and the Aśvins— O Agni, with your fine horses, good chariot, and great bounty, bring these gods hither for the person who offers the excellent oblation.
O Agni, this sacrifice provides cattle, sheep, and horses; it has heroic companions and is forever unassailable.
O Asura, it is rich in nourishment and progeny; it is long-lasting wealth, broad-based, and full of assembly-halls.
O Agni, for him who, sweating, brings fuel for you, or heats his head out of devotion to you—you, being self-strong, become his protector; guard him from every one who seeks to do him harm.

Whoever brings food to you, even when you are not seeking it, and stirs up the delightful guest so that he leaves a remnant—may that pious man kindle you within his home; may wealth be firmly established with that generous giver.
Whoever praises you at evening or at dawn, or who, possessing oblations, makes you his friend— he,
like a well-trained horse in its own stable, you should deliver from distress, O giver of gold.
O Agni, he who offers to you, the immortal one, and performs service for you with uplifted ladle—may he, though striving, not be deprived of wealth; may no distress from the malevolent encircle him.

O Agni, that mortal whose well-performed sacrifice you, the god, have accepted with favor, being bountiful; may his priestly office be pleasing to you, O youngest one, and may we be the strengtheners of him who serves you.
May the wise one distinguish between intention and lack of intention; like a horse’s back, may he separate the straight from the crooked among mortals.
O God, grant us wealth with noble offspring; bestow upon us freedom and protect us from bondage.
The undeceived sages have instructed the seer, establishing him in the dwellings of man;
therefore, O Agni, you shall behold these wondrous ones visible to all, through the movements of the noble one with your feet.

O Agni, youngest one, you who provide excellent guidance to the priest who presses the Soma and serves you—O impetuous one, bring wealth to the one who exerts himself; bring broad, radiant splendor for his protection, O filler of the people.

And now, O Agni, whatever we have done out of devotion to you with our feet, hands, and bodies— like those who fashion a chariot with their skillful work, the wise ones, striving for the goal, have upheld the *ṛta*.
Then may we, the seven sages, be born from the mother Dawn as the first ordainers among men;
may we become the Aṅgirases, sons of Heaven, and, shining brightly, may we shatter the mountain that holds the wealth.
And just as our ancient fathers of old, O Agni, who were longing for the *ṛta*, went toward the pure light, chanting their hymns; so did they cleave the earth and uncover the ruddy dawns.

Performing good deeds, shining brightly, seeking the gods, like smiths blowing upon the birth of iron, O gods, they have come— purifying Agni, strengthening Indra, and surrounding the wide stall of cattle.
O Mighty One, he has looked upon the generations of the gods as one looks upon herds of cattle among a people rich in food;
even the *urvaśīs* of mortals have yearned for him, for the increase of the noble and the nearby living man.
We have worked for you and become skillful; the radiant dawns have dawned forth as the Truth.
They have polished in many ways the flawless Agni, the beautiful eye of the god, which shines with great splendor.
O Agni, O Ordainer, we have uttered these hymns for you, the Seer; may you take pleasure in them. Blaze forth, make us more prosperous, and bestow upon us great wealth, O you who possess many boons!
Bring hither for your protection Agni, the king of the sacrifice, the Rudra, the invoker of heaven and earth who sacrifices with truth—
him of golden form, before the unperceived thunderbolt strikes.
This is the womb which we have prepared for you, like a longing, well-dressed wife for her husband;
may he, enveloped, sit down facing us—these [fingers] of yours, O skillful one, are turned toward us.

O worshipper, recite a hymn of praise to the immortal god who hears us, who is undaunted, who beholds men, and who is most gracious— the one whom I, like a presser of Soma, laud as the extractor of sweetness, even as a pressing-stone.

O Agni, you indeed are our protector through this sacrificial post; be mindful of this *ṛta*, O you who perceive the *ṛta* and possess noble wisdom. When will your hymns of praise be shared in the feast? When will our friendship be established in your house?
How indeed, O Agni, will you report that to Varuṇa? How to Heaven? What offense of ours do you reproach? How will you speak to bountiful Mitra, to Pṛthivī, to Aryaman, and to Bhaga?

When, O Agni, will you speak from the sacrificial hearths as one who grows strong; when to the wind that is powerful and seeks splendor; when to the Nāsatya who moves all around and dwells within; and when, O Agni, to Rudra, the slayer of men?
How shall I speak to the great Pūṣan, the bringer of nourishment; how to Rudra, the skilled sacrificer who bestows oblations;
how to Viṣṇu, the wide-striding, regarding the seed; and how, O Agni, to the lofty arrow?
How [shall I speak] to the host of Maruts, to the Eternal Law? How, being questioned, shall I answer the great Sun?
O Jātavedas, being wise, answer rightly for Aditi and for the Swift One from heaven.
By means of *ṛta*, the *ṛta* established by law, I praise the cow; together with the raw, O Agni, she has swelled with the cooked, honeyed milk.
Though she is black, she has nourished herself with the white, life-sustaining draught.
For by the *ṛta* indeed has the bull been anointed; Agni, the manly one, with the milk of the back.
Without trembling he moved, bestowing vital strength; the speckled bull has milked the bright udder.
Splitting the mountain with Truth, the Aṅgirases shouted together with the cattle. The heroes sat around for prosperity at the dawn; light became manifest when Agni was born.
By the cosmic order (*ṛta*), O Agni, may the immortal, unassailable goddesses, the Waters, with their honey-sweet waves,
flow forth forever to run— like a prize-winning steed urged on at the start of a race.

Let us never go to the sacrifice of anyone who neglects his duties, nor of a neighbor who deceives, nor of a kinsman; O Agni, let us not incur the debt of a crooked brother, nor suffer from the skill of a treacherous friend.
Protect us, O Agni, with your protections, you who are well-protecting and gratified in battle;
flash back against us, shatter the firm distress, and slay the *rakṣas*, even though it has grown very great.

O Agni, be well-disposed toward us through these hymns; O Hero, touch these prizes with our prayers. And, O Aṅgiras, take pleasure in our sacred formulations; may the praise celebrated by the gods resound unto you.
O Agni, Ordainer, I have recited all these secret ways, hidden words, and poetic utterances for you who know them—
these inspired songs and hymns— with my thoughts and prayers.
Display your power like a wide-spreading net; go forth like a powerful king with his elephant.
Rushing along your swift net, you are an archer; pierce the demons with your most scorching shafts.
Your whirling flames fly swiftly; following them, touch [the enemy] boldly, O glowing one.
O Agni, with your tongue of fire, cast forth your heats like winged insects; unfettered, scatter your firebrands in every direction.
Dispatch thy spies in every direction; be thou our most rapid protector, infallible guardian of this people.
O Agni, let no one who plots evil against us from afar or nearby prevail over thee; let no affliction overcome us.
Arise, O Agni! Spread yourself out against [the foe]; burn down our enemies, O you of the sharp weapon!
O kindled one, whoever has practiced hostility toward us, him you shall burn down like dry brushwood.
Stand upright and pierce them; O Agni, manifest thy divine powers against us.
Slacken the firm bows of those impelled by demons, and crush our enemies, whether they be kin or strangers.
O Most Youthful One, he knows your benevolence who has opened a path for such a prayer;
for him, you have shone forth all auspicious days, riches, and the splendors of the noble, opening wide the doors.

O Agni, let him be fortunate and a liberal giver who, throughout his own life and within his home, desires to satisfy you with constant oblations and hymns; for him, may every sacrifice result in auspicious days.
I praise your benevolence; let my voice resound toward you. May this song of mine, like a beloved wife, sing your praise.
O you who possess noble horses and fine chariots, may we adorn you; may you maintain our lordly powers day after day.
May many a person come here to you of their own accord, O dispeller of darkness, as you shine day after day;
may we, joyful and playing, serve you, while we stand amidst the splendors of the people.
O Agni, for him who approaches you with good horses and fine gold on a chariot laden with wealth—
you become his protector and his friend, he who has taken pleasure in showing you hospitality in due order.

Through my kinship and with my words, I break down the great [fortresses]. This [power] has come down to me from my father Gotama. O most youthful Hotṛ, wise one, master of the house, take heed of this our speech.
Sleepless, swift-crossing, most gracious, unwearied, non-violent,
and most tireless— may those guardians of yours, O Agni, sitting together in unison, protect us, O wise one.

Those guardians of yours, O Agni, who, seeing him blind, protected Māmateya from misfortune—they, the omniscient ones, protected those doers of good; though the enemies sought to harm them, they did not succeed in deceiving them.
Through you may we be prosperous; aided by you, under your guidance, may we obtain spoils.
Accomplish both our praises, O upholder of truth; act immediately, O one who is not to be shamed.
With this fuel, O Agni, may we worship you; accept the hymn being recited.
Burn away the malicious Rākṣasas; protect us from malice, from reproach, and from blame, O you who are great as Mitra.
In unison with the bounteous Vaiśvānara, how shall we offer worship to Agni, the great light?
With his perfect and lofty growth, he has propped up the firmament as if it were a supporting pillar.
Do not revile him who, as a god, has bestowed this gift upon me, a mortal— Agni Vaiśvānara, the wise, the immortal, the discerning, the most heroic among men, the youthful and skillful one.
The Sāman is doubly great; he is the mighty bull with sharp horns and a thousandfold seed.
Having found the hidden track of the cow like a lost treasure, Agni has declared his inspired wisdom to me.
May Agni, the bounteous giver, with his sharp-jawed form and most fervent flame,
consume those who violate the ordinances of Varuṇa and the beloved, steadfast laws of the mindful Mitra.
Like brotherless maidens wandering abroad, like women who hate their husbands and are evil-minded,
being wicked, false, and untruthful, they have produced this profound station.
O Agni, Purifier, for me who am so small and yet unyielding, you have boldly placed upon me this great, deep, and mighty hymn— like a heavy burden— as a sevenfold back of nourishment.
May the purifying prayer, through its mental power, reach him who is common to all and equal—
him who is beautiful upon the skin of the earth, fashioned like a young shoot upon the summit of the speckled mountain.
What of this speech of mine is to be proclaimed? They speak of that which is hidden in the secret cave.
When they have opened the doors of the ruddy cows like a flood, he guards the beloved summit of the form, the footstep of the bird.
And this indeed was that great, mighty array, which the ancient cow, the ruddy one, followed;
shining in the station of Truth, he found it hidden away, moving swiftly, hastening on.
Then, shining while dwelling with his parents, he recognized the secret, lovely [form] of Pṛśni;
in the highest station of the mother, near the cow, was the tongue of the extended, virile flame.
I speak the truth with reverence when questioned, O Jātavedas, according to my hope for this world:
you alone rule over all this wealth, whether it be in heaven or upon the earth.
"What wealth is ours from this, and what treasure? O Jātavedas, being wise, declare it to us.
For we have gone, like those seeking a lost track, into the secret depths of this path's furthest end."

What is the boundary, what are the rules? When shall we reach your favor, like swift horses reaching for the prize? When will the goddesses, the wives of the Immortal, extend us with the splendor of the sun, O Dawns?
With speech that is not vigorous, but feeble, deceptive, and trivial, they have not been satisfied.
Therefore, O Agni, what can those who are unarmed say here against you? Let them remain in their powerlessness.
For the glory of this kindled bull, the face of the Vasu has shone forth in the house.
Clothed in brilliance, with a form most beautiful to behold, he has gleamed like a dwelling-place with wealth, O bountiful one.
Stand up erect for us, O Hotṛ of the sacrifice, O Agni, as the most excellent sacrificer among the gods;
for you indeed surpass every thought, and you further even the inspired wisdom of the wise.
The unerring Hotṛ has been seated among the people—Agni, the delightful one, wise in the assemblies.
Like Sūrya, he has extended his radiance upward; like a pillar, he supports the smoke against the sky.

As the well-warmed, bountiful ladle, dripping with ghee, moves to the right, choosing the assembly of the gods, the sacrificial post rises up like a newly-born bull; well-placed and firmly established, it anoints the victims.
Upon the strewn sacrificial grass, while the fire is kindled, the Adhvaryu priest has stood up upright, well-pleased.
Agni, like a herdsman or a Hotṛ-priest, goes around three times from of old, choosing his path.
Agni, the measured-strider, goes around by himself—the Hotṛ, the delightful one with honeyed speech, the observer of Truth.
His flames run like prize-winning steeds; all beings are afraid when he has blazed forth.
Auspicious is your appearance, O Agni of radiant countenance; fair is the sight of you, though you are terrible and manifold.
For your flames cannot be obscured by darkness, nor do soot-stained things bring blemish to your body.
There is no one who has hindered his birth, nor indeed have mother and father been able to restrain him when he desires to go forth.
Then Agni, the purifier, well-established like Mitra, has shone among the human tribes.
Him, Agni, whom the five sisters dwelling together have brought forth twice among the human tribes—
him who awakens at dawn like a sharpened tooth, bright and fair-tongued, keen as an axe.
O Agni, those bay steeds of yours— bathed in ghee, ruddy, straight-moving, swift-moving,
bright-red, powerful, with straight testicles— those wondrous ones have summoned the host of gods.
Those flames of yours, O Agni, which move along— conquering, unwearied, and brilliant—
like hawks hastening toward their goal, they roar loudly like the host of the Maruts.
The sacred prayer has been fashioned for you, O Kindled One; let the reciter proclaim the hymn, and may you distribute the offerings.
Men have seated Agni as the Hotṛ-priest; the yearning ones, paying homage, have established the praise of the living man.
This one has been established here as the first by the ordainers—the Hotṛ, most skilled in sacrifice, to be praised at the rites;
whom Apnavāna and the Bhṛgus caused to shine forth, the wondrous and pervasive one, for every tribe within the woods.
O Agni, when shall the manifestation of you, the god, appear in its proper sequence?
For mortals have indeed seized you, who are to be praised among the people.
Beholding him, the observer of cosmic order and the wise one, like the sky with its stars,
as the bringer of joy to all sacrifices in every house.
The Āyus have brought hither the swift messenger of Vivasvat, who moves toward all peoples— the banner of the Bhr̥gus, for every tribe.
Him, the wise one, they have established as the Hotṛ priest in due succession— him who is delightful, whose radiance is purifying, and who is the best of sacrificers through his seven stations.
Him who has entered into the eternal mothers, who is hidden in the forest,
who is wonderful, placed in a secret cave, yet easily found by those seeking him wherever he may be.
When the gods rejoiced in the separation of the grain in that udder, in the abode of *ṛta*,
great Agni— honored with homage and offered oblations— ever attends the sacrifice as the observer of *ṛta*.
Knowing the duties of the sacrifice as a messenger, and being fully cognizant of both ends of heaven and earth,
you go forth as a messenger from of old, chosen and most wise, knowing the ascents to heaven.
Black is your path, O radiant one; your light shines before you, and your moving flame is the sole marvel of wonders.
When she who was not impregnated conceives a germ, even as soon as you are born, you become the messenger.
The strength of him who was born this very moment is visible when the wind blows after his flame;
he turns his sharp tongue among the dry brushwood and, with his jaws, he rends even solid food apart.
When he has carried away the food with his swift [strength], the mighty Agni makes himself a swift messenger;
consuming [the offerings], he follows the roar of the wind; like a swift horse, he is urged on and incited for the prize.
I impel with my song your messenger, the all-knowing, the immortal bearer of oblations, the most excellent sacrificer.
For he knows the treasury of wealth, the great ascent to heaven;
may he bring the gods here to us.
That god knows how to bend the gods for the one who follows the *ṛta* in his home;
he bestows even the most cherished treasures.
He is the Hotṛ; he, being wise, goes between the two worlds on his mission as messenger, knowing the ascent to heaven.
May we be those who have honored Agni with offerings of oblations—
those who, causing him to thrive, kindle him.
They have become renowned far and wide, having won wealth and heroic powers,
those who have offered worship to Agni.
May riches, much-desired, come to us day by day; may strengths rise up for us.
That inspired poet, through his power over the human races,
pierces through them like a swift arrow.
O Agni, be gracious; you are great, you who have come to this god-seeking people to sit upon the sacred grass.
He, the immortal, difficult to deceive among human clans,
has become the messenger of all, a protector.
He, the delightful Hotṛ, is led around the sacrificial ground during the celestial rites;
and as Potṛ, he sits down.
And Agni is the divine wife at the sacrifice, and he is the master of the house in the home;
and as the Brahman priest, he sits down.
For you come as the invoker of the people who perform the sacrifice,
and [you partake] in the oblations of human beings.
He has entered upon the office of messenger for him whose sacrifice you have accepted,
in order to carry the mortal's oblation.
O Aṅgiras, find pleasure in our ritual; [find pleasure] in our sacrifice;
hear our invocation.
May your unassailable chariot reach us from every side,
you with which you protect those who offer oblations.
O Agni, may we today succeed for you with our hymns—as one would with a horse—with a thought that is auspicious and touches the heart;
may we prosper through our offerings.
For indeed, O Agni, you have become the charioteer of auspicious will, of effective and righteous power, and of the great cosmic order.
Through these our hymns, O Agni, come toward us, like the light of heaven; be well-disposed toward us with all your faces.
Praising you with these songs today, O Agni, let us serve you; your roars thunder forth like those of heaven.
O Agni, your most sweet appearance shines forth even now at this day and even now at this night;
it glows for glory like a golden ornament close at hand.
Like purified ghee, like a stainless body, like bright gold— so does that [splendor] of yours shine, O self-dependent one, like a golden ornament.
For you, O Agni, who observe the cosmic order (*ṛtāvan*), drive away even long-standing enmity from the mortal who thus performs sacrifice.
May our friendship with you gods, O Agni, be auspicious, as may our brotherhood; this is our kinship in this common dwelling, at this same udder.
Auspicious is your face, O powerful Agni; it shines forth nearby like that of the sun. Brilliant to behold, it is seen even by night; in its form, food appears smooth and beautiful to the sight.
O Agni, born of many, being praised with fervor, disclose your inspired thought for the singer;
O radiant one of great power, grant us that abundant prayer which you have cherished together with all the gods.
From you, O Agni, are born poetic insights; from you, inspired thoughts; from you, effective hymns arise.
From you comes wealth adorned with heroes, for the mortal who offers oblations with such devotion.
From you is born the prize-winning steed, the bearer of booty, far-reaching, the performer of aid, and truly powerful;
from you comes wealth impelled by the gods, bringing joy; from you, O Agni, comes the swift, speeding charger.
O Agni, you, the immortal god with the pleasant tongue, the mortals seeking the gods first invite with their prayers— the one who drives away hatred, the domestic lord of the house, the unerring.

Far from us, O Agni, keep away lack of wisdom, far away distress, and far away every evil thought, when you protect us. O Son of Strength, auspicious at evening, O God, he whom you accompany brings well-being.
O Agni, he who kindles you with the sacrificial ladle uplifted, and prepares food for you three times on this very day—
may he, being wise through your power, O Jātavedas, overcome his enemies with glorious splendors.
O Agni, he who, laboring and paying honor, has brought fuel to your great countenance—
he, kindling it at evening and at dawn, prospers and dwells with wealth, slaying his enemies.
Agni rules over great sovereignty; Agni [rules] over booty and supreme wealth. The youngest, self-dependent one, bestows treasure upon the mortal who serves him in succession.
Whatever offense we have committed against you, O youngest one, among men, through lack of thought or by any deed, make us sinless before Aditi; loosen our transgressions on every side, O Agni.
O Agni, even from great sin when it is imminent—from the domain of both gods and mortals—may we, your friends, never suffer harm; grant well-being and prosperity to our children and descendants.
Just as you, O Vasus, worthy of worship, released even the Gaurī cow that was stuck by the foot, so likewise release us from this distress; O Agni, prolong our life further.
Agni has looked back upon the vanguard of the dawns as they shine forth, well-disposed toward the bestowing of treasures.
O Aśvins, come to the dwelling of the pious man; the god Sūrya rises up with his light.
The god Savitṛ has sent his light upward, shaking off the drop like a warrior seeking cattle;
Varuṇa and Mitra follow the sacred law when they cause the sun to ascend in heaven.
Him whom they made for the dispersal of darkness, while seeking security and not resting in their purpose—
him, Sūrya, the all-seeing, the seven great bay mares carry through the entire moving world.

Moving with your swiftest steeds, you go weaving the thread of the sacrifice, O God, spreading out the black garment of the night. The rays of the Sun, violently shaking, have driven away the darkness within the waters like a skin.
Unsupported and unbound, how is it that this one does not fall down, face downward or face upward?
By what inherent power does he move? Who has seen him? As a pillar supporting heaven, he protects the firmament.
Agni Jātavedas, the god, has looked upon the Dawns as they shine with their splendors. O Nāsatyas, wide-striding ones, come hither to this sacrifice of ours on your chariot.
The god Savitṛ has raised his banner aloft, creating light for the entire world;
Sūrya, shining brightly with his rays, has filled heaven, earth, and the intermediate space.
Bringing light, the ruddy ones have come; the great and wonderful Dawn, shining with her rays, the goddess Uṣas goes forth on her well-yoked chariot, awakening us for our welfare.
May those most excellent carriers bring you both here—chariots and horses—at the dawning of the dawn. For these Soma juices are for your sweet draught; O Bulls, rejoice at this sacrifice.
Unsupported and unbound, how is it that this one does not fall headlong or face upwards?
By what inherent power does he move? Who has seen him? As the pillar of heaven, he stands firm and protects the firmament.
Agni, our Hotṛ at the sacrifice, being a prize-winning steed, is led around—
the god worthy of worship among the gods.
Agni goes three times around the sacrifice like a charioteer,
bestowing nourishment upon the gods.
Agni, the lord of booty and the sage, has stepped around the oblations,
bestowing jewels upon the donor.
This [Agni], who is kindled for Devavāta at the city of Sṛñjaya,
is radiant and the subduer of enemies.
May a mortal man indeed be master of this such Agni, the sharp-toothed and bounteous giver.
Him they groom day after day, like a prize-winning steed, like the ruddy child of heaven.
When the prince, son of Sahadeva, awakened me with his two bay horses,
I rose up toward him like one summoned.
And those two worshipful bay horses, presented by the youth Sāhadevya,
I accepted immediately.
O divine Aśvins, may this son of Sāhadeva, Somaka Kumāra, have a long life through you both.
O divine Aśvins, you two make that prince Sāhadevya long-lived.
May the true Maghavan, the consumer of the dregs, come hither; may his bay steeds run toward us.
For him we have pressed the most skillful soma-juice; being praised, may he make his arrival here.
O Hero, descend like one at the end of a journey, so that you may rejoice today at this our libation.
Like Uśanas, the wise priest shall recite a hymn; let him offer a prayer to the conscious Lord of divine power.
Like a sage accomplishing secret rites, when the bull, drinking deeply, shall chant his outpouring;
thus from heaven he brought forth the seven singers, who by day, singing praises, established the sacred ordinances.
When the beautiful light of heaven was found through hymns, they caused the great radiance to shine at the break of day;
the most heroic one, for the sake of men, dispelled the blinding and turbid darkness so that it might be seen.
Indra, the drinker of the *ṛjīṣa*, has grown to immeasurable strength; with his greatness he has filled both worlds.
Even beyond that, his majesty extends further, for he has surpassed all existing beings.
Śakra, knowing all manly deeds, released the waters with his eager friends;
they who by their words even split the rock, the Uśijs opened the stall full of cattle.
You struck down Vṛtra who had obstructed the waters; the earth, being conscious, favored your thunderbolt. You sent forth the oceanic floods; O bold hero, you became their lord through your might.
When you, O Much-invoked One, shattered the rock for the waters, Saramā appeared before you;
as our leader, may you strike out abundant booty, breaking open the cow-pens while being praised by the Aṅgirases.

O Maghavan, you who are mindful of men, come toward the sage for his aid in the winning of light for the one imploring you; speed him with your protections at the invocation for glory. Let the guileful Dasyu, devoid of prayer, fall away.
Come home with a mind intent on slaying the Dasyus; let Kutsa be devoted to your friendship.
Sit down together in your own dwelling, you two of like form; for even a woman who knows the cosmic order may distinguish between you.
You travel on the same chariot with Kutsa, seeking aid, as the goad who masters the two bay steeds of Vāta;
desiring to seize the straight-running prize like a prize to be grasped, the Seer shall be present for the decisive day.
For Kutsa, you struck down the insatiable Śuṣṇa; at the onset of the day, you crushed Kuyava and thousands of Dasyus.
Instantly, with the help of Kutsa, crush the Dasyus and strike off the wheel of the Sun in the encounter.
You delivered Pipru, who was growing exceedingly strong while hunting, into the power of R̥jiśvan, the son of Vidathin;
you struck down fifty thousand black ones and shattered his fortresses as an old age destroys a man.
When the Sun, placing his body near [the earth], manifests the form of immortality;
like a wild elephant putting on its strength, he is as fearsome as a lion as he bears his weapons.
Desiring wealth, our wishes have gone toward Indra, longing for him at the pressing of the juice as if for the winning of light;
seeking glory and striving with hymns, he is like a home, like joy, and like fair-looking prosperity.
Let us invoke that very Indra, who is easy to call upon, he who has performed many heroic deeds;
he who, possessing desirable wealth, swiftly brings booty that is worth seizing to a singer like me.
When the sharp bolt falls amidst the people, O Hero, upon any random occasion;
when the terrible encounter of the noble one occurs, then indeed be the protector of our bodies.
Be the protector of Vāmadeva’s inspired thoughts; be a friend free from malice in the winning of booty.
Having come to you for your providence, O you of wide renown, may you be present for the singer at all times.

With these men who seek you, O Indra, with these liberal patrons, O Maghavan, may we overcome all enemies in every battle, as the heavens do with their splendors; thus, through the nights and many autumns, may we rejoice.

Thus have we fashioned a prayer for Indra, the bull, the vigorous one, just as the Bhr̥gus fashioned a chariot; so that our friendship may never be severed, may he be our fierce protector and guardian of our bodies.
Now, O Indra, being praised and glorified, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers;
a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. Through this inspired thought, may we be masters of chariots, ever victorious.
Great art thou, O Indra; indeed, the earth and the heaven have recognized thy sovereign power with great magnificence.
Having slain Vṛtra by thy might, thou didst release the rivers that had been swallowed by the serpent.
At the birth of your brilliance, the sky trembled; the earth trembled with fear at your own wrath.
The well-founded mountains roared; the desert wastes were dissolved and the waters flowed away.

Splitting the mountain with his might, hurling the thunderbolt, displaying his power with forceful vigor, he struck Vṛtra with the bolt while rejoicing; the waters, their strength now released, flowed swiftly like those whose bull had been slain.
Your father, the Sky, deemed himself a true hero; the maker of Indra performed the most skillful work.
He who begot him—the one with the resonant voice and the excellent thunderbolt—made him immovable from his seat, like the earth from its foundation.
He who alone causes the earth to tremble, the king of the peoples, Indra, invoked by many—
truly all rejoice after him, praising the gift of this divine and bounteous lord.
All Soma juices have become his; all the most intoxicating draughts of the mighty one have indeed become his.
You have truly become the lord of treasures; O Indra, you have established all peoples within your gift.
Then, O Indra, as soon as you were born, you placed all these peoples in their stations;
O Maghavan, with your thunderbolt you tore apart the dragon who lay across the flowing waters.
Indra, the ever-conquering, the bold, the powerful, the great, the boundless bull with the excellent thunderbolt—
he who is the slayer of Vṛtra, the winner of booty, and the giver of riches, the bountiful Maghavan.
This one, chosen and renowned as the sole Maghavan in battles, scatters those who stand arrayed against him;
he brings the prize of victory which he wins—may we be dear to him in his friendship.
He is heard of as winning and slaying; he also drives forth the cattle by battle.
When Indra makes his wrath true, everything firm and everything moving fears him.
Indra has won the cattle, he has won the gold, and he, the bounteous Maghavan, has won the herds of horses—indeed, he who [conquered] many [enemies].
Most heroic among men, with these his helpers, he is the distributor of riches and the gatherer of wealth.
How much does Indra regard his mother? How much his father, the progenitor who begot him? He who sets his strength in motion in moments, like the wind driven by thundering clouds.
He makes the settled man unsettled; the Bounteous Lord raises up the dust in a whirlwind.
Like the sky armed with lightning, he shatters all things; and may the Bounteous Lord bestow wealth upon his praiser.
This one has impelled the wheel of the sun; he has brought Etaśa to rest as he was speeding along.
The black, winding smoke besprinkles him at the base of the skin, in the womb of this mid-air.
Like a sacrificing priest at the black [altar].

Desiring cattle for friendship, O sages, desiring horses, seeking strength, and longing for wives, we bring down Indra— the bull who grants offspring and possesses inexhaustible aid— like a water-jar from a well.

Be our protector, appearing as a kinsman, the observer, and the comforter of those who offer Soma. As a friend, a father, and the most fatherly of fathers, create a world for the one who desires it, bestowing vital strength.
Be the protector and friend of those who seek your friendship; O Indra, being praised, bestow vital strength upon the one who lauds you.
For we have exerted ourselves for you with these ritual labors, magnifying you, O Indra.
When Indra Maghavan is praised, he alone slays many Vṛtras that are irresistible;
dear is his singer, whom neither gods nor mortals can ward off from his protection.
Thus may Indra, the bounteous, the exuberant, the unassailable upholder of the people, make our prayers true;
you, the king by birth, bestow upon us and upon the singer great renown.

Now, O Indra, being praised and now being lauded, swell nourishment for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we be chariot-borne victors, ever-conquering.
This is the ancient path discovered of old, by which all the gods were born. From this very source let him be born when fully grown; let him not cause his mother to perish in that way.
I have not emerged from this; it is a difficult place. I shall go out sideways from the flanks.
Many things yet undone remain for me to do; I will fight with one and question another.
He looked upon his departing mother and said: "I shall not go back; indeed, I shall not go back. In the house of Tvaṣṭṛ, Indra drank the Soma, a hundredfold gift, pressed from the ladles.
What could he accomplish separately, whom she bore for a thousand months and many autumns?
For indeed, there is no likeness of him among those already born, nor among those yet to be born.
Deeming him as if something blameworthy, Indra’s mother hid him in secret, for he was overflowing with heroic power.
Then he rose up, clothing himself in his own raiment; being born, he filled the two worlds, heaven and earth.
These flow along, sounding "alala," crying out like the observers of Truth (*ṛtāvarī*);
ask them: what is this they are saying? Against what rock-bound enclosure do the waters break through?
What indeed do the waters proclaim as the secret names for him? Do they intend to reveal the hidden power of Indra?
Having slain Vṛtra with his mighty weapon, my son has released these rivers.
Even me, the young woman, did not abandon you; even me, Kuṣavā, swallowed you.
Even for my sake, the waters were gracious to the infant; even for my sake, Indra rose up with might.
O Maghavan, even my own shoulder you struck down, having pierced through;
then, having been pierced, he became inferior, as you crushed the head of the Dāsa with your weapon.
The first-calf cow has brought forth for you the ancient, invincible, and impetuous bull, Indra.
The mother has let loose the unlicked calf to wander, he who seeks his own path by himself.
And the Mother looked with favor upon the Great Bull; "O son, these gods are abandoning you," she said.
Then Indra, about to slay Vṛtra, spoke: "O friend Viṣṇu, stride out yet more widely!"
Who made your mother a widow? Who sought to kill you as you were wandering? Which god was merciful to you when you seized your father by the foot and slew him?
In my helplessness, I cooked the entrails of a dog; among the gods I found no one to comfort me. I saw my wife being dishonored, and then the falcon brought the honeyed nectar to me.
Thus, O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, all the gods, the easily invoked protectors,
choose you alone here— the great, exalted one who has grown vast— over both worlds in the slaying of Vṛtra.
The gods released [the waters] like those who have grown old; O Indra, you became the sovereign ruler whose womb is truth.
You slew the serpent who lay encompassing the flood; you dug out the channels that nourish all things.
O Indra, with your thunderbolt you rent asunder at a non-joint the dragon who was not yet satisfied, who was gaping, who was unawakened, who was sleeping,
and who lay across the seven flowing rivers.
Indra shook the earth with his might, as the wind stirs the waters with its force;
longing for power, he split the firm foundations and shattered the peaks of the mountains.
They have run forth toward him like women toward their child; the pressing-stones have sped away together like chariots.
You have satisfied the far-spreading rivers, you have pressed down the waves; O Indra, you have released the obstructed floods.
You [O Indra] stilled the great, all-nourishing earth as it flowed for Turvīti and Vayya;
by means of homage, you brought the surging flood under control and made the rivers easy to cross.
Like roaring rivers, he caused the youthful, flowing waters—knowers of the cosmic order (*ṛta*)—to swell;
he filled the thirsty plains and deserts. Indra brought down the barren cows belonging to the lord of wondrous deeds.
Through many dawns and many celebrated autumns, having slain Vṛtra, he released the rivers;
Indra pierced the obstructed, tightly confined streams so that they might flow across the earth.
O Lord of the Bay Steeds, you brought forth from his dwelling the son of the unwedded woman, whom the ants had not given;
seizing the blind serpent, he opened his eyes, and as he emerged from the fire-pot, his joints were set together.
The inspired sage, knowing them, has proclaimed your ancient deeds to the wise one—
those acts which you, O King, have performed according to your own will as manly and virile exploits.

Now, O Indra, being praised and now being lauded, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we be chariot-borne victors, ever-conquering.

May Indra, the fierce lord of men, the wielder of the thunderbolt, come to our aid from afar or from near at hand; may he, who grants assistance, be victorious over his enemies in the clash of battles with his mightiest powers.
May Indra come toward us with his bay horses, turning hitherward for our protection and for bounty.
May the wielder of the thunderbolt, the bounteous and overflowing Maghavan, stand by this sacrifice of ours in the winning of the spoil.
O Indra, placing this sacrifice of ours before you, you shall grant us our purpose;
like a gambler winning wealth, O wielder of the thunderbolt, may we through you conquer the enemy in battle.

Desiring us and well-disposed, O self-dependent Indra, come indeed to us nearby; drink now of this well-pressed soma, of the offered honey-sweet juice, and exhilarate yourself with the soma from the *pṛṣṭhya* vessel.

Him who has overflowed with abundance through the new seers, like a tree laden with ripe fruit, like a victorious reaper; like a youth full of passion approaching a maiden, I call toward me Indra, the one invoked by many.
Like a mountain, he who is self-strong and lofty, Indra, born from of old for the sake of conquest, fierce;
he who seizes the ancient thunderbolt like a formidable [wielder], filled with wealth like a vessel overflowing with water.
He whose equal there has never been from birth, nor anyone who can obstruct his bounty or his wealth—
showering forth like fierce power, O you invoked by many, grant us riches!
I behold the wealth and the dwellings of the people; you shall open the stall of the cattle. O helper of men, victorious in battles, you are the one who leads us toward a vast heap of riches.

By what power is he heard as the most powerful, by which the lofty one repeatedly performs his various deeds? As the best dispeller of distress for the liberal giver, he then bestows wealth upon the singer.
Do not neglect us; bring it, give that to us—abundant wealth which you have to bestow upon the donor.
When this new gift is praised and this hymn is recited, we shall proclaim it, O Indra, praising you.

Now, O Indra, being praised and glorified, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we be chariot-warriors who ever win the prize.
May Indra come to us for our protection; praised here, may the hero be our companion at the feast.
May he, whose many powers have increased, nourish his sovereign dominion like the sky, so that it may prevail over all.
Here, celebrate his manly deeds— he of abundant splendor and great bounty—
those deeds by which he, whose wisdom is like that of a sovereign in the assembly, is victorious and overcomes the people as a deliverer.
May Indra come from heaven, from earth, swiftly from the ocean or from the watery depths;
may he, accompanied by the Maruts, come for our protection from the sun-bright realm or from afar from the seat of Cosmic Order.
We praise that Indra in the assemblies of sacrifice, who rules over abundant and vast wealth—
he who, with Vāyu, conquers in the raids for cattle and boldly leads us toward greater prosperity.
He who, establishing himself in reverence after reverence, raises his voice, generating it for the sacrifice;
may that Hotṛ-priest, striving with hymns and possessing many boons, bring Indra here to the sacrificial seats.
When, seeking through prayer, they hasten to the pressing-stones in the dwelling of Auśija,
then may the resistless Hotṛ of Pastyas— our great bearer who carries [the oblation] within the enclosures— come hither.
When the strength of the bull Bhārvara truly accompanies him for the sake of the singer’s gift;
when he is in the secret place of Auśija’s dwelling, so that there may be inspiration, refreshment, and exhilaration.
When he uncovers the expanses of the mountain, he quickens the swiftnesses of the waters with his milks;
when the wise ones bring him forth for the sake of strength, he finds the place of hiding of the wild ox and the gayal.
Auspicious are your hands and well-formed your palms, O Indra, which bestow bounty upon the one who praises you.
What is your dwelling? Why do you not exhilarate us? Why do you not rise up to rejoice in giving to us?

Thus indeed is Indra the true sovereign lord of wealth; he slays Vṛtra and creates wide space for the people. O much-praised one, grant us riches through your wisdom; may I partake of your divine protection.

Now, O Indra, being praised and now being lauded, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we be masters of chariots, ever victorious.
Whatever Indra has enjoyed and whatever he desires, that may the great and powerful one accomplish for us.
Maghavan, who goes wielding the stone by his might, accepts our prayer, our hymn of praise, the Soma, and our recitations.
The bull, hurling his four-cornered thunderbolt, the fierce, most manly, and powerful one with his two arms,
has donned the woolly Paruṣṇī for glory— he who has embraced her joints for friendship.
The god who, being born as the most divine among gods, by means of great spoils and mighty strengths,
holding the yearning thunderbolt in his arms, caused the heaven and the earth to tremble with his impetuous force.
All the embankments and the many slopes trembled at his lofty birth—heaven and earth;
the winds roar like men around the moving cow, and the strong one brings together the two parents.
These indeed, O Indra, are your great deeds against the mighty, to be proclaimed at all the Soma-pressings—
that when you, O hero, bold one, having boldly shown your courage, struck the serpent with your thunderbolt through your power.
All those [deeds] of yours are true, O you of many manly powers; from the udder of the bull, the milch-cows flow forth.
Then indeed, out of fear of you, O you whose mind is like a bull, the rivers have rushed forward with speed.
Here, O Lord of the Bay Steeds, those goddesses, your sisters, praise you with their aids, O Indra, when they, being released by you,
flow along your long-reaching course after having been held back.
The exhilarating stalk has been pressed like a river; may the ritual effort and the power of the one who exerts himself come to you.
Toward us, from the one who blazes forth, let the twin rays of the bull, possessing great strength, hasten like a swift rein.
O Victorious One, bestow upon us the highest and most excellent manly powers and all-conquering strengths.
Make the Vritras easy for us to slay; strike down the weapon of the attacking mortal.
O Indra, listen well to us alone; grant us manifold spoils of war.
Send us all abundant blessings; O Maghavan, be a true giver of cattle to us.

Now, O Indra, being praised and lauded, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we be chariot-warriors who ever win the prize.
How has he grown great? Whose priest’s sacrifice does he favor as he approaches the Soma from the udder?
Drinking, desiring, and enjoying the plant, the lofty one has waxed strong for the sake of the radiant wealth.
What hero has attained his shared banquet? Who has partaken of him with his favors? What of him is manifest? What aid has he been for the increase of the one who exerts himself in worship?
How does Indra hear the oblation being offered? How, hearing it, does he know of this [sacrificer’s] aids? What are his ancient manifestations? And how do they call him a fulfiller for the singer?
How may the one who exerts himself with devotion, meditating upon it, attain his wealth through this [hymn]?
May the god, the knower of all things, who has accepted our homage, take pleasure in our rites.
How, at the dawning of this dawn, has the god taken pleasure in the friendship of a mortal? How is his friendship [extended] toward those friends who have stretched out for him a well-yoked desire?
What then is this vessel-like friendship for our friends? When indeed shall we proclaim your brotherhood?
For the sake of glory, the outpourings of his beautiful form are like the most wondrous light from the sun, or like the milk from the cow.
Seeking to destroy the malevolent and destructive one who is devoid of Indra, he sharpens his keen weapons for the assault.
There, as if a fierce creditor collecting debts, he drives away the unknown enemies far from us at the break of dawn.
For the boons of *ṛta* are many; the thought of *ṛta* destroys crookedness.
The hymn of *ṛta*, awakening and shining upon the living man, has pierced the ears of the deaf.
The firm foundations of *ṛta* exist; manifold are the radiant beauties for the sake of beauty.
By means of *ṛta* they impel forth long-lasting nourishment; by means of *ṛta* the cows have entered into *ṛta*.
Upholding the *ṛta*, he wins the *ṛta* itself; the surge of the *ṛta* is swift and seeks cattle.
For the sake of the *ṛta*, the two broad, vast, and deep worlds exist; for the sake of the *ṛta*, the two supreme milch-cows yield their milk.

Now, O Indra, being praised and glorified, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we be chariot-warriors who ever win the prize.
What excellent praise might turn Indra, the son of strength, toward us with his bounty?
For that hero, O people, bestows riches upon the singer; he is the lord of cattle who drives away our adversaries.
He is to be invoked and praised in the slaying of Vṛtra; that Indra is well-praised and true in his bounty.
On his journey, may the bounteous Maghavan bestow wide space upon the mortal who offers prayer and presses the Soma.
Him indeed the men invoke in the encounter; risking their own bodies, they make him their protector, when both sides have come together in mutual sacrifice for the winning of sons and grandsons.
The tribes act with purposeful intent in their striving, O Mighty One, as they exert themselves together for the winning of the waters.
When the warrior clans have come together in battle, then some indeed seek to overcome Indra in the encounter.
Then indeed some shall worship the power of Indra; then let the cooked offering surpass the sacrificial cake;
then let Soma part from those who have not pressed it; then indeed he has taken pleasure to sacrifice to the Bull.
He who presses the Soma for Indra who desires it thus, he wins wide space for himself;
with a focused mind, not turning away, he makes that very person his friend in battles.
He who today shall press Soma for Indra, shall cook the cooked offerings, and shall roast the grains— Indra,
delighting in the hymns of that mindful man, shall bestow upon him virile strength.
When the impetuous one has distinguished the assembly, and when the noble one has looked toward the long contest,
the wife calls out to the bull who has been sharpened by the Soma-pressers within the dwelling.
He traded what was greater for what was less; having sold it, I regretted it when I went back.
He did not overvalue the lesser for the greater; the skillful and clever ones milk out the profit.
"Who will buy this Indra of mine for ten milch-cows? When he has struck down the Vṛtras, then let him give him back to me."
Now, O Indra, being praised and glorified, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers;
a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of Bay Steeds. Through this inspired thought, may we be charioteers who ever win the prize.
Who today, a manly lover of the gods, desiring it, has taken pleasure in the friendship of Indra? Or who, when the fire is kindled and the Soma is pressed, prays for great, decisive aid?
Who has bowed with speech to the one worthy of Soma? Who becomes mindful as the dawns break? Who desires Indra’s alliance, who his friendship, and who his brotherhood? And who seeks the sage for aid?
Who today chooses the protection of the gods? Who prays to the Ādityas and Aditi for light?
Whose pressed stalk of soma do the Aśvins, Indra, and Agni drink with their minds, finding it pleasing?
To him may Agni Bhārata grant protection; may he long behold the sun rising, he who says, "Let us press the Soma for Indra," for the manly hero, the most heroic among men.
Neither many nor few overcome him; Aditi shall grant him wide protection.
Dear to the well-doer, dear to Indra is the pious man, dear the one who offers good aid, and dear is he who possesses Soma.
This hero, the swift-conquering Indra, is easy to serve; he makes the cooked offering his own exclusive possession.
He is neither kinsman, nor friend, nor relative to one who does not press the soma; for him who offers no praise, he is difficult to serve and strikes down those who do not invoke him.
Indra, the drinker of the pressed juice, does not form a friendship with the wealthy miser who does not press the soma.
He takes away his wealth and strikes him naked; he becomes the exclusive possessor for the one who presses the juice and cooks the offering.
The higher ones, the lower ones, and those in the middle call upon Indra; those who are traveling and those who have settled call upon Indra;
those dwelling in peace and those fighting call upon Indra; men seeking booty invoke Indra.
I was Manu and I was Sūrya; I am the seer Kakṣīvat, the inspired singer. I have guided Kutsa, the son of Arjuni; I am the sage Uśanas—behold me!
I gave the earth to the noble one; I gave rain to the mortal who offers oblations.
I led forth the lowing waters; the gods followed my will.
Exhilarated by the soma, I shattered at once the ninety-nine fortresses of Śambara; with you as my ally, I brought the hundredth stronghold to total ruin when I protected Divodāsa Atithigva.
Let that falcon be foremost among the swift falcons, O Maruts,
when the fair-winged bird, by its own inherent power, brings the god-pleasing oblation to Manu without wheels.
When the falcon, trembling, brought it from afar, the wide-pathed one, swift as thought, was released;
he sped quickly with the honeyed Soma, and here the falcon won for himself high renown.
The straight-flying falcon, the bird, bringing the exhilarating intoxication from afar,
has brought the Soma while holding the stalk, accompanied by the gods, having taken it from yonder highest heaven.
Taking it, the falcon brought the Soma—a thousand and ten thousand pressings at once.
Thereupon the wise one abandoned the enemies; in the intoxication of the Soma, the unerring one left behind the foolish.
While still in the womb, I indeed came to know all these generations of the gods. A hundred iron fortresses guarded me; then, like a hawk, I flew forth with speed.
Truly, he did not carry me away against my will; rather, I surpassed him with my skill and heroic might.
With a sudden stride, Purandhi abandoned her hostilities, and waxing strong, he overcame the winds.
When the falcon swooped down from heaven with a cry, or when the winds bore Purandhi hither;
when Kṛśānu, the archer, eager in his mind, released the swift-darting bowstring for him.
Like Bhujyu, the straight-flying [bird] was carried by the falcon from the high ridge of the mountain belonging to Indra’s follower;
his winged feather fell within, even as that bird sped along its course on the journey.
Then Maghavan took up the white vessel, anointed with milk, swelling with the bright juice—the pure essence of honey offered by the *adhvaryu*s—for his exhilaration;
the Hero takes it for his exhilaration, that he may drink.

With you as his ally, O Soma, through that friendship of yours, Indra caused the waters to flow for mankind. He slew the serpent, released the seven rivers, and opened the channels that were as if closed up.
O Indu, with you as his ally, Indra swiftly and by force struck down the wheel of the Sun, which was rolling upon the high ridge; thus was all the life of the great oppressor destroyed.
Indra slew and Agni consumed the Dasyus before midday in the encounter;
with his arrow he struck down many thousands, like those who go astray through lack of resolve in a difficult dwelling.
O Indra, you made the Dasyus lower than all, and you rendered the Dāsa tribes infamous.
You two repelled them and crushed the enemies; you obtained recompense through your weapons of death.
Thus it is true, O bountiful ones: you two, Indra and Soma, have disclosed the wide space of horses and cattle;
you have burst open the enclosures hidden by the stone and have pierced even through the firm earth.
O Indra, being exhilarated, come to our praise with strengths and aids, with your two bay horses;
passing even over the many libations of the noble one, you who are praised with hymns and are of true bounty.
For he, the manly one, comes indeed, perceiving, being summoned by the pressers to the sacrifice—
he who, possessing good horses and considering himself fearless, rejoices together with the heroes who have pressed the Soma.
May he cause his ears to hear, so that he may strive for strength and rejoice according to the beloved direction.
Raining down bounty, the powerful Indra shall make for us fair paths and security.
He who comes with aid to the one imploring him, to the inspired singer thus calling and praising—
may he, the wielder of the thunderbolt, placing swift horses upon his yoke, bring thousands and hundreds.

O Maghavan Indra, may we, your inspired singers, be protected by you; may we be wise patrons, praising you and sharing in the wealth of the lofty heaven—wealth that is desirable and abundant in food—for its bestowal.
O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, there is none superior to you, nor any greater;
indeed, there is no one else like you.
All the peoples have followed you completely, as wheels turn after a chariot;
indeed, you are renowned as great.
Even all the gods together could not withstand you, O Indra,
when you extended the days by night.
And where, for Kutsa who was being oppressed as he fought,
you, O Indra, stole the wheel from Sūrya.
Where you alone, O Indra, fought against all the impetuous gods, you struck down the attackers.
And where, for the sake of a mortal, O Indra, you set the sun in motion,
you protected Etaśa with your powers.
Why indeed, O Vṛtra-slayer, are you so exceedingly wrathful, O Maghavan? It was then that you struck down Dānu.
And this indeed was the heroic deed, O Indra, the manly exploit you performed:
that you slew the daughter of Heaven, she who was ill-disposed toward marriage.
O Indra, you indeed crushed Uṣas, the daughter of Heaven, though she was great and exalting herself.
Uṣas ran away from the wagon, terrified of the crushed [chariot],
when the bull struck her down.
This wagon of hers lies here, well-crushed by the Vipāś;
he has sped away from that distant place.
And by your power, O Indra, you encompassed with your magic the Sindhu, which had spread out over the earth, swelling with its waters.
And with bold courage, you seized the possession of Śuṣṇa when you crushed his fortresses.
And you struck down the Dāsa Śambara, the son of Kulitara, from the lofty mountain, O Indra.
And you slew the hundreds of thousands of the Dāsa Varcin,
like five wheel-rims upon an axle.
And furthermore, Indra, the Lord of a hundred powers, caused that son of the unwedded woman who had been cast away to take his share in the hymns of praise.
Moreover, Indra, the Lord of Might, knowing well, brought across those two, Turvaśa and Yadu, who were unable to swim.
And those two Āryas, O Indra, you slew on the far side of the Sarayu;
you struck down Arṇa and Citraratha.
O Vṛtra-slayer, you have led away the two abandoned ones—the blind and the lame;
that favor of yours is not to be attained.
Indra shattered a hundred fortresses made of stone for Divodāsa, who offered him oblations.
With his weapons, Indra, by means of his magic power, put thirty thousand Dāsas to sleep for the sake of Dabhīti.
O Vṛtra-slayer Indra, you alone are indeed the common protector of cattle,
you who have shaken all these things.
And now, whatever manly deed you shall perform, O Indra, by your power—
may no one today diminish that.
O Āduri, may the god Aryaman grant you what is desirable;
may Pūṣan grant what is desirable, Bhaga grant what is desirable, and the god Karūlatī grant what is desirable.
With what aid will the wondrous one come to us, he who is the friend ever-increasing? With what most powerful host?
Which true one among the exhilarations, most bountiful, shall intoxicate you with the soma-juice?
So that you may break open even firm wealth.
Be truly our protector, O friend of us who sing your praises; may you come to us with a hundred aids.
Turn toward us as a wheel turns for a steed— with the teams of horses belonging to all people.
For you come down the slope of our intentions, as if to your own station;
I have partaken [of the light] together with the sun.
When thy many wrathful impulses and thy wheels, O Indra, have rolled forth together— then [all things] abide in thee and in the sun.
Moreover, they indeed call you, O Lord of Might, the bounteous Maghavan,
the giver who does not hesitate.
And indeed, at once, you bestow abundant wealth upon the one who exerts himself and presses the soma.
For not even a hundred obstructors can restrain your bounty, nor your mighty deeds as you perform them.
May your hundred aids protect us; may your thousand aids protect us;
may all your succors protect us.
Choose us here for friendship and for well-being,
for great and celestial wealth.
Favor us always, O Indra, with abundant wealth;
favor us with all your protections.
For us, open up those water-filled enclosures rich in cattle, like a hunter, O Indra, with your newest aids.
Our chariot, bold and radiant, O Indra, never to be overthrown,
speeds forth seeking cattle and horses.
O Sūrya, among the gods, establish for us a preeminent glory,
most lofty like the sky above.
Come then to our side, O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra;
great one, with your great aids.
O Wondrous One, you are indeed swift and impetuous among those who possess wondrous power;
you perform wonders for our protection.
Even with a few, you slay the more numerous and the swelling foe by your might,
together with those companions who are with you.
O Indra, we are with you; we sing our praise to you.
Protect each and every one of us!
O wielder of the stone, come to us with your wondrous, blameless, and invincible aids.
O Indra, may we truly become the friends of one such as you, who possesses cattle— companions joined for exhilarating vigor.
For you alone, O Indra, rule over the prize consisting of cattle; as such, bestow upon us great nourishment.
O Indra, lover of songs, when you, being praised, desire to bestow wealth upon your worshippers, no one can turn you away from that.
The Gotamas have sung toward you with their song, O Indra, so that you may grant gifts for the sake of spirited strength.
We shall proclaim your heroic deeds, those which you, rejoicing, shattered by attacking the forts of the Dāsas.
The wise ones sing those manly deeds which you have performed,
O Indra, lover of songs, when the soma juices are pressed.
The Gotamas have increased their strength through you, O Indra, bringing hymns of praise;
bestow upon them glory accompanied by heroic sons.
For even though you, O Indra, belong in common to all who exist forever,
we invoke you as such.
O Vasu, turn toward us; O Soma-drinker, Indra, exhilarate yourself with our draughts of soma.
May the hymn of our thoughts bring you hither, O Indra;
turn your two bay steeds toward us.
Eat our sacrificial cake and take pleasure in our songs,
as one desiring a bride approaches a young woman.
We implore Indra for a thousand harnessed steeds;
a hundred jars of Soma.
We cause hundreds and thousands of your cattle to flow toward us;
may your bounty come to us.
Ten golden jars of yours have we received;
you are a bountiful giver, O slayer of Vṛtra.
O bounteous giver, give us much; let not little be ours. Bring much hither;
for indeed, O Indra, you desire to give much.
For you are renowned in many places as a bountiful giver, O hero, slayer of Vṛtra;
grant us a share in your wealth.
O far-seeing one, son of the winner of cattle, I praise your two tawny steeds; do not hold back the cows from them.
Like two young girls, uncovered, on a new wooden seat, small and young,
the two brown ones shine forth during their journeys.
Ready for me is the one who comes at dawn, ready is he who follows after dawn; the two tawny steeds are unfailing on their journeys.

Send forth your voice like a messenger to the Ṛbhus; I pray for the white cow Śvaitarī as a sacrificial covering—those skillful ones who, impelled by the wind, with their swift movements, instantly reached across the sky.

When the Ṛbhus performed service for their parents with their skillful deeds and wondrous powers, then indeed they attained the friendship of the gods; as wise ones, they brought nourishment to the mind.
May those who made their parents young again, who were lying old like worn-out sacrificial posts—
Vāja, Vibhvan, and Ṛbhu, accompanied by Indra and possessing the essence of sweetness— protect our sacrifice.
Since for a year the Ṛbhus guarded the cow, since for a year the Ṛbhus fashioned the skin,
and since for a year they carried her light— by those labors they attained immortality.
The eldest said, "Make two cups," and the younger said, "Let us make three.
The youngest said, "Make four. Tvaṣṭṛ was amazed at these words of yours, O Ṛbhus.
The men spoke the truth, for they indeed accomplished it; the Ṛbhus followed this self-dependent way.
Tvaṣṭṛ, having seen them, was amazed at the four cups shining like the sun.
When for twelve days the Ṛbhus rejoiced in the hospitality of Agohya while resting,
they made the fields fertile, led forth the rivers, established plants upon the desert, and brought the waters to the lowlands.

May those R̥bhus— who fashioned the well-rolling chariot that carries men, and who created the all-speeding, omniform cow— fashion wealth for us, they who are self-strong, skillful in their work, and dexterous-handed.
For the gods took pleasure in their waters, contemplating them with wisdom and mind;
Vāja became the skillful worker among the gods, Ṛbhukṣan that of Indra, and Vibhvan that of Varuṇa.
O Ṛbhus, those who, rejoicing with wisdom and hymns, fashioned for Indra the two well-yoked bay horses—
bestow upon us an increase of wealth and riches, O Ṛbhus, like friends seeking security.

Today they have granted you the drinking of the soma and exhilaration; O gods, it is not without toil that one gains your friendship. Therefore, O Ṛbhus, bestow treasures upon us now at this third libation.
O Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, Vāja, and Indra, come to this sacrifice of ours for the bestowing of treasures;
for now the divine Dhiṣaṇā has ordained your drinking at these days, and your exhilarations have come together.
Knowing your origin, O Ṛbhus, you who possess the treasure of strength, rejoice according to the seasons!
Your exhilarations have come together, as has your abundance; send forth upon us wealth accompanied by noble heroes.
O Ṛbhus, this sacrifice has been prepared for you, which you have accepted as you did from Manu since ancient times.
Delighted, you have turned toward it; you have all become foremost, O Vājas.

Now indeed has there been for you, O heroes, a bestowal of treasures for the mortal who serves and worships you. Drink, O Vājas, O Ṛbhus; the great third libation has been offered to you for exhilaration.
O Vājas, come to us, O R̥bhukṣans; you great heroes are praised for the sake of wealth.
These draughts of yours have come home at the close of days, like cows to their stalls.
O sons of strength, come to this sacrifice, being invoked with reverence;
O wise ones, being of one mind, drink of this honeyed draught for which you are present—bestowers of treasures, accompanied by Indra.
O Indra, in harmony with Varuṇa, drink the Soma; O lover of songs, in harmony with the Maruts.
In harmony with those who drink first and those who drink at the appointed times, in harmony with the divine wives who bestow treasures—drink in harmony with them all.
In harmony with the Ādityas, rejoice; in harmony with the mountains, O Ṛbhus;
in harmony with the divine Savitṛ, in harmony with the rivers that bestow treasures.

The *Ṛbhus* who [honored] the Aśvins, who [honored] their parents, and who by their aid fashioned the cow, the horses, the armor, and the two worlds; those far-reaching heroes who have performed noble deeds.

O *Ṛbhus*, you who bestow wealth consisting of cattle, food, brave sons, treasures, and abundant nourishment— being exhilarated, O first-drinkers, grant that wealth to us and to those who praise your gift.
You were not absent, nor did you fail to satisfy us; O Ṛbhus, you were not excluded from this sacrifice.
Rejoice with Indra, with the Maruts, and with the kings, O gods, for the bestowing of treasures.
Come hither, O sons of strength, O Ṛbhus, sons of Sudhanvan; do not stay away!
For at this libation of yours is the bestowing of treasures; may your exhilarations follow after Indra.
