the two worlds, clothed in their upper garment, have increased through the offerings of clarified butter and the foods of honey.
Crying out, the wise one has brought forth the seven ruddy sisters from the honeyed [substance] so that they may be seen;
born of old, he has halted within the mid-air and, seeking, has found the covering of Pūṣan.
The seers have fashioned seven boundaries; the one who is in distress has stepped beyond only one of them.
The pillar of Āyu stands in the dwelling of the highest, at the parting of the paths, upon the foundations.
The non-existent and the existent in the highest heaven, in the birthplace of Dakṣa, in the lap of Aditi—
Agni is indeed our first-born of Ṛta, the bull and the cow in the earliest age.
This is he, in whose protection and through whose assistance the singer prospers in the favor of Agni— he who,
radiant and encompassed by the flames, moves around the heights with the most excellent beams of light.
Agni, who shines forth with his rays, radiant and eternal, a guardian of the *ṛta* among the gods;
he who has extended his friendship to his friends, unassailable like a swift, well-trained steed.

He who rules over every divine feast, who rules over all life at the dawning of the morning; in him, O Agni whose chariot is unharmed, the one with inspired hymns establishes his offerings with his powers.
Increasing through invigorating hymns and enjoying our songs, he hastens toward the gods with rapid flight;
the joyous Hotṛ, the most excellent sacrificer, Agni, being well-blended, sprinkles the gods with his tongue.
Bring hither with songs and salutations that Agni who trembles like Indra at dawn—
the Jātavedas whom the sages praise with their hymns, the one who bears the oblations of the conquerors.
In whom all treasures have gathered together, like horses with their riders rushing toward the prize in their courses—
O Agni, bring those aids of yours, most desired by Indra, hitherward for our sake.
Then indeed, O Agni, having sat down with greatness, as soon as you were born, you became one to be invoked. The gods followed that intention of yours; then the first helpers increased in strength.

O Agni, bestow upon us well-being from heaven and earth for the sake of sacrifice, O God; may we be united with your insights, O Wonder-worker, and protect us, O God, with your far-reaching blessings.
O Agni, these thoughts born for you celebrate your bounty with cattle and horses; when a mortal has attained enjoyment from you, O Vasu, well-born one, he bestows gifts through his prayers.
I consider Agni to be my father, Agni my kinsman, Agni my brother, and ever my friend.
I worship the face of the great Agni, the bright and worshipful splendor of Sūrya in heaven.
O Agni, our prayers are successful and winning, for you, the eternal Hotṛ, protect them in their home.
May he who is faithful to the *ṛta*, the possessor of ruddy horses and abundant food, grant us desirable wealth through days and nights.

Like a friend established by days, like a long-standing ritual application, the men have generated Agni with their two arms—the ancient priest, the lover of the sacrifice; they have seated him among the people as the Hotṛ.
O God, sacrifice yourself to the gods in heaven; what can a simpleton, lacking in wisdom, do for you?
O God, just as you have sacrificed to the gods according to the seasons, so too, O well-born one, sacrifice to your own self.

O Agni, be our protector and our guardian; be the maker of our strength and the bestower of vitality upon us. Grant us, O most mighty one, the gift of oblations, and protect our bodies with unflagging care.
Agni advances with his lofty banner; like a bull, he bellows toward the two worlds. He has reached even the furthest ends of heaven; the buffalo has grown great in the lap of the waters.
The bull, the hump-backed embryo, has rejoiced; the vigorous, unceasing calf has bellowed. Making the divine powers rise up, he goes forth first among his own dwellings.
He who has grasped the head of his parents; at the sacrifice, they have established him like the wave of the sun.
At his flight, the ruddy ones, whose foundation is the horse, have delighted their bodies in the womb of the Eternal Order.

For at every dawn, O Vasu, you come first; you have become the radiant one between the two twins. For the sake of cosmic order, you have established the seven steps, engendering Mitra for your own self.
You have become the eye and the great guardian of the cosmic order (*ṛta*); you have become Varuṇa when you strive for the sake of *ṛta*.
You have become the Son of the Waters, O Jātavedas; you have become the messenger of him whose oblation you have accepted with pleasure.
You are the leader of the sacrifice and of the mid-world, where you accompany [the gods] with your auspicious teams of horses;
you place your head in heaven, winning the light, and you have made your tongue, O Agni, the bearer of the oblation.
By the will of this [god], Trita, seeking the inspired thought of the supreme father through his own ways, dwelt within the cave;
being attended in the lap of his parents and calling his weapons kin, he goes forth.
Knowing the weapons of his fathers, Trita Āptya, impelled by Indra, went forth to battle;
having slain the three-headed, seven-rayed one, he released the cows even of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son.
O Indra, lord of the virtuous, you struck down with your might the one who was striving for great power and considering himself secure;
seizing the cattle of Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, you tore off his three heads and cast them away.
O Waters, you are indeed the sources of bliss;
grant us strength for great joy and for the sight [of the divine].
Whatever most auspicious essence you possess, grant us a share of it here,
like longing mothers.
To him for whose dwelling you quicken us, to him let us go readily;
O Waters, give us life.
May the divine waters be auspicious for our aid and for our drink;
may they flow toward us with peace and well-being.
Ruling over desirable things, governing the people—
I beg the waters for healing.
Soma has told me that within the waters are all healing remedies,
and Agni, who brings well-being to all.
O Waters, bestow healing medicine as a protection for my body,
so that I may long behold the sun.
O Waters, carry away this whatever evil is in me—
whether it be that which I have committed as treachery, or that which I have sworn falsely, or even any untruth.
Today I have entered into the waters; we have united with their essence.
O Agni, come hither full of milk; endow me with splendor.
O friend, may I win back my friend through friendship, having traveled across even the vast ocean.
May the wise one, meditating further upon the earth, establish the grandson of the father.
Your friend does not desire this friendship, that she who shares the same mark should become of different form.
The sons of the great Asura, the heroes, the upholders of heaven, look out over the wide expanse.
The immortals indeed desire this very thing from you, the offspring of the sole mortal:
let your mind be fixed upon our mind; as a husband to a wife, enter into our body.
What we have never done before, how could we now speak untruth while proclaiming the Truth?
The Gandharva in the waters and the watery maiden—she is our kin, she is our ultimate bond of relationship.
In the womb, the progenitor, the god Tvaṣṭṛ, the impeller who takes all forms, made us two, husband and wife.
No one violates his ordinances; both Earth and Heaven know this of us.
Who knows of this first day? Who has seen it? Who can declare it here?
Great is the ordinance of Mitra and Varuṇa; what then will you say, O reviler, to the men with your words?
Desire for union has come upon me, Yami, so that we may lie together in the same womb. Like a wife yielding her body to her husband, I would even draw back from you as chariot wheels turn away.
They do not stand still, nor do they close their eyes—these spies of the gods who wander here.
O you who incite me, go quickly by another way; with that, tear him apart like the two wheels of a chariot.
May she honor him with nights and days; may she repeatedly measure out the eye of the sun.
Yamī, the twin sister, shares a common kinship with Yama through heaven and earth; let her commit this act of incest.
Truly, those later ages will come when kinswomen shall commit acts unbecoming to kin.
Press thy arm close to the bull; O fortunate one, seek another husband than me.
What is a brother when one becomes protectorless? And what is a sister when Destruction (Nirṛti) overtakes one?
Driven by passion, I utter this much lamentation; unite my body with your body.
"Indeed, I would not have united my body with your body; they call it an evil thing for one who approaches his own sister.
Arrange your pleasures with another than me; O fortunate one, your brother does not desire this."
Alas, O Yama, you are truly pitiable; we have found neither your mind nor your heart.
Surely another shall embrace you, as a girth-strop encircles a harnessed horse, or as a climbing vine clings to a tree.
O Yami, one shall surely embrace another, and another shall embrace you, as a creeper clings to a tree.
Either you must seek his heart, or he yours; therefore, establish a most auspicious bond of harmony between you.

The bull has yielded for the bull the milks of heaven by his milking; the mighty one, the undeceivable son of Aditi, knows all through his wisdom. May he, the worthy of sacrifice, perform the sacrifice according to the seasons for those who are worthy of sacrifice.
May the Gandharva woman and the water-nymph protect my mind within the roar of the river. May Aditi place us in the midst of what is desired; may our eldest brother speak for us first.
Truly, that auspicious, cattle-rich, and glorious Dawn has shone forth for mankind with the light of heaven,
since they have brought forth Agni as the Hotṛ priest for the assembly, according to the will of those who desire him.
Then the hawk, dispatched to the sacrifice, brought down that far-reaching, all-seeing drop;
when the Aryan tribes chose Agni, the wonder-worker, as their Hotar-priest, then indeed was the sage born.
O Agni, you are always delightful to the man who performs the sacrifice well with his oblations, like a pasture for one who thrives;
or when you, having won the prize worthy of praise from the inspired singer who exerts himself, approach with many [attendants].
Raise up the two parents like a lover; he desires fortune and, being beloved, sends it from his heart.
The bearer speaks; the sacrificer performs his work well; the lord of power grows strong and trembles with inspired thought.
O Agni, son of strength, that mortal who attains your favor becomes renowned far and wide;
bestowing nourishment and borne by his horses, he, radiant and powerful, prospers through the days.
O Agni, worthy of sacrifice, when this divine assembly takes place among the gods, O worshipful one;
and when you, self-dependent lord, distribute treasures, grant us here our share of wealth.
Hear us, O Agni, in this common dwelling; yoke your swift chariot of immortality.
Bring hither to us the two worlds, the parents of the gods; let none among the gods be absent, but remain here.
Heaven and Earth, first by the Eternal Law, become listeners with true speech, when the god,
making mortals ready for sacrifice, sits down as the Hotṛ-priest, turning toward his own vital breath.
The god who encompasses the gods by the Eternal Law (*ṛta*), carry our oblation, you who are first among those who perceive.
Having smoke as your banner, kindled with fuel, radiant with light, you are the delightful, eternal Hotṛ-priest, most skilled in sacrifice through your voice.
The cow’s own turn is the immortal nectar of the god; born from that, they have sustained the two wide worlds.
All the gods followed that sacred formula of yours, whereby the dappled cow yields the celestial ghee and water.
I praise you both for your increase, O waters dripping with ghee; O Heaven and Earth, you two worlds, hear my call.
Since the days have gone toward the lack of guidance, may our two Parents here sharpen us with sweetness.
What has the King seized from us? When have we transgressed his decree? Who knows?
For even Mitra himself may lead the gods astray; there is even a cry of reproach against them, like that of those who fail to win the prize.
The name of immortality here is difficult to perceive, when she who shares the same origin becomes manifold in form.
O lofty Agni, protect without fail that man who meditates upon the well-being of Yama.
In which sacrificial assembly the gods rejoice, and at the seat of Vivasvat they take their stand;
they have placed light in the sun and established the nights within the month—those two tireless ones who move around the luminous realm.
In that secret counsel wherein the gods move together, we have no knowledge of it. May Mitra, Aditi, and the divine Savitṛ proclaim us sinless here before Varuṇa.
Hear us, O Agni, in our common dwelling; yoke your swift chariot of immortality.
Bring hither to us Heaven and Earth, the parents of the gods; let none of the gods be far from us here.
I yoke for you both an ancient prayer with homages; let the hymn go forth like a path to the patron.
May all the sons of immortality listen, they who have taken up their stations in the celestial realms.
When you two came together like two sisters striving in harmony, the god-seeking men brought you forward.
Sit down in your own place, you who know it; be seated comfortably for our Soma juice.
I have ascended after the five steps of *rūp*; I follow the four-footed one with my vow.
By means of the syllable (*akṣara*), I measure this out; I purify it upon the navel of *ṛta*.
For the sake of the gods he chose death; for the sake of progeny he did not choose immortality.
They made Bṛhaspati the seer their sacrifice; Yama released his own dear body.

Seven flow for the infant accompanied by the Maruts; the sons have established the *ṛta* for their father. Both worlds indeed belong to him; he rules over both, both strive for him, and both nourish him.
Honor with an oblation Yama, the king, the son of Vivasvat, the assembler of people, who has departed along the great slopes and has spied out the path for many.
Yama was the first to find the path for us; this pasture is not to be taken away, where our ancient fathers have departed, having been born according to their own paths.
Mātali is magnified by the Kavyas, Yama by the Aṅgirases, and Bṛhaspati by the Ṛkvans;
those whom the gods have magnified and those who have magnified the gods—some rejoice with the cry of Svāhā, others with the call of Svadhā.
O Yama, sit down upon this sacrificial grass, in harmony with the Aṅgiras fathers;
let the mantras recited by the seers bring you here, O King, and rejoice in this oblation.
Come with the Angirases who are worthy of sacrifice; O Yama, rejoice here with the Vairūpas.
I invoke Vivasvat, who is your father, that he may sit down upon the sacrificial grass at this sacrifice.
The Aṅgirases are our fathers, the Navagvas, the Atharvans, and the Bhṛgus, who are worthy of the Soma; may we abide in the good-will of those worthy of sacrifice, and in their auspicious favor.
Go forth, go forth by the ancient paths, where our former fathers have gone.
There you shall see both kings rejoicing in their own power—Yama and the god Varuṇa.
Unite with the Fathers, unite with Yama, and with the merit of your sacrifices and good works in the highest heaven.
Leaving behind all that is blameworthy, return again to your home; unite with a new body, full of splendor.
Depart, go away, and creep far from here; the fathers have prepared this place for him.
Yama gives him a dwelling clearly revealed by days, waters, and nights, along with his protection.
Run past the two dogs, the sons of Saramā, the four-eyed brindled ones, by the righteous path;
then approach the benevolent fathers who rejoice in the banquet together with Yama.
O Yama, those two dogs of yours who are the guardians, four-eyed, protectors of the path, and watchers over men—to them entrust this man, O King; bestow upon him well-being and freedom from disease.
The two broad-nosed, honey-colored messengers of Yama, who delight in the life-force of men, wander among the people.
May they today grant us back here a blessed life-force so that we may behold the sun.
Press the Soma for Yama; offer the oblation to Yama. To Yama indeed goes the sacrifice, with Agni as its messenger, well-prepared.
Offer to Yama an oblation rich in ghee and step forward;
may he lead us among the gods to a long life that we may live.
Offer to King Yama the most honey-sweet oblation;
this homage is to the seers born of old, the ancient makers of the path.
It flies with the three *kadruka* cups; the six wide ones are but one great [entity].
The *triṣṭubh*, the *gāyatrī*, and all the meters—these are all established in Yama.
May the lower, the higher, and the middle Soma-loving Fathers rise up—those who have gone to the life-span, who are harmless and knowers of the *ṛta*; may those Fathers protect us in our invocations.
Let this homage be offered today to the fathers who have gone before and those who followed after;
to those who are seated in the earthly realm, or those who are now among the well-fortified tribes.

I have found the benevolent fathers, and the descendant, and the wide stride of Viṣṇu. Those who sit upon the sacrificial grass and partake of the pressed food with the funeral offering—may they be most ready to come here.
O Fathers who sit upon the sacred grass, come hither with your aid; we have prepared these oblations for you, so please accept them.
Come to us with most auspicious protection, and then bestow upon us well-being, health, and freedom from harm.
The Soma-loving ancestors have been invited to their dear offerings placed upon the sacred grass;
may they come, may they listen here, may they speak in our favor, and may they protect us.
Bending your knees and sitting down to the south, may you all favor this sacrifice.
O Fathers, do not harm us for anything, whatever offense we may have committed against you through our human nature.
Sitting in the lap of the ruddy dawns, bestow wealth upon the mortal who offers oblations.
O fathers, grant a share of that treasure to your sons; bestow strength here upon them.
Our ancient fathers, worthy of Soma, the Vasiṣṭhas who have followed after the drinking of Soma—
may Yama, rejoicing with them, desiring [the offerings], eat the oblations according to his desire along with those who desire them.
Those who have thirsted among the gods, panting, who know the office of the Hotṛ, who fashion hymns with their chants—
O Agni, come hither with those well-known, true Kavyas, the Fathers who sit at the Gharma-vessel.

O Agni, come with the thousand ancient and later fathers who dwell in the heat, who are truthful, eaters of the oblation, drinkers of the oblation, and who occupy the same chariot with Indra and the gods.
O Agniṣvātta fathers, come here; sit each upon his own seat, O excellent leaders. Eat the oblations presented upon the sacred grass, and then bestow wealth consisting of all heroic sons.
O Agni Jātavedas, you who have been invoked, having made the oblations fragrant, you have carried them away;
you have given them to the fathers, and they have eaten them with the *svadhā* call. Now, O God, eat these presented offerings.

Those ancestors who are here and those who are not here, those whom we know and those whom we do not know—you know how many they are, O Jātavedas; accept this well-prepared sacrifice with the *svadhā* offerings.

Those who have been consumed by fire and those who have not been consumed by fire, who rejoice in their own nature in the midst of heaven— along with them, O Sovereign Lord, fashion this body for the journey to the sun according to your will.
Do not burn him up, O Agni; do not consume him with heat; do not scorch his skin or his body.
When you have made him cooked, O Jātavedas, then send him forth to the Fathers.
O Jātavedas, when you have cooked him, then deliver him over to the ancestors;
when he goes to this world of departed spirits, then let him become one who obeys the will of the gods.
Let your eye go to the sun, your breath to the wind; go to heaven and to earth according to the cosmic order.
Or go to the waters if it is beneficial for you there; take your stand among the plants with your bodily parts.
The goat is your portion; consume it with heat. Let your flame consume it, let your radiance consume it.
O Jātavedas, with those forms of yours that are auspicious, carry this man to the world of the righteous.

Release him again, O Agni, to the Fathers—he who, offered to you, moves by means of the *svadhā* offerings. Clothed in life, let him approach his remaining kin; O Jātavedas, let him be united with a body.
Whatever the black bird has pecked at you, or the ant, the serpent, or even the wild beast—
may Agni make all that free from disease, and Soma, who has entered into the Brahmins.

Envelop yourself with the cow-hides as Agni’s armor; cover yourself completely with fat and marrow, so that the bold one, exulting in his heat and seeking to seize you, may not turn you over while intending to consume you.
O Agni, do not overturn this cup, for it is dear to the gods and to those who offer Soma.
This is the cup from which the gods drink; in it the immortal gods rejoice.
I send the flesh-eating Agni far away; let him go to the realm of Yama, carrying off impurities. Let this other Jātavedas remain right here and, knowing the way, carry the oblation to the gods.
The flesh-eating Agni who has entered your house, beholding this other Jātavedas—him I bring away for the sacrifice to the Fathers; may that god promote the Gharma in the highest dwelling-place.
May Agni Kravyavāhana, who shall sacrifice to the fathers who increase the cosmic order,
proclaim the oblations to the gods and to the fathers.
Desiring you, we set you down; desiring you, we kindle you. Desiring them, bring the desiring ancestors here to eat the oblation.
O Agni, that which you have completely consumed, extinguish that again;
let the *kiyāmbu* grow here, along with the *pākadūrvā* and the *vyalkaśā*.
O cool one, O you who possess coolness! O refreshing one, O you who possess refreshment! Come together well with the female frog and gladden this fire.
"Tvaṣṭṛ prepares the bridal procession for his daughter"—saying this, this entire world comes together.
The mother of Yama, being led away, the wife of the great Vivasvat, has vanished.
They concealed the immortal one from mortals; having made her of similar form, they gave her to Vivasvat.
And she brought forth the two Aśvins when that [event] occurred; Saraṇyū abandoned the two pairs.
May Pūṣan, the guardian of the world whose cattle are never lost, lead you away from here, he who is wise.
May he entrust you to these fathers and to Agni, for the sake of the gods who are easy to find.
May Viśvāyu protect your life; may Pūṣan protect you on the distant path ahead.
Where the doers of good deeds dwell, where they have gone—there may the god Savitṛ place you.
May Pūṣan know all these regions; may he lead us by the path most free from fear.
Bestowing well-being, glowing, with all his heroes, may he go before us, watchful and wise.
Pūṣan was born upon the far path of paths, on the far path of heaven, and on the far path of earth. He moves to and fro, knowing well both most beloved meeting-places.

Those seeking the gods invoke Sarasvatī; they invoke Sarasvatī while the sacrifice is being performed. The doers of good have called upon Sarasvatī; may Sarasvatī grant what is desirable to the donor.
O Sarasvatī, you who have come on the same chariot with the Fathers, O Goddess, rejoicing in your own powers;
having seated yourself upon this sacred grass (*barhis*), be exhilarated and bestow upon us food free from disease.
Sarasvatī, whom the ancestors invoke as they approach the sacrifice from the south—
O Iḷā, bestow here a portion worth a thousand, and grant prosperity of wealth to the sacrificers.
May the Waters, our mothers, purify us; may those who cleanse with ghee purify us with ghee. For all defilement, O goddesses, they carry away; from them I emerge bright and cleansed.
The drop has fallen following the first days, into this womb and that which was before;
I offer the drop as it moves along toward the common womb, according to the seven priestly offices.
That drop of yours which falls, that stalk of yours which has slipped from the arms or from the lap of the *dhiṣaṇā*,
or that which [falls] from the hand of the *adhvaryu* or from the filter— that I offer for you with my mind, consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ* call.
Whatever drop of yours has spilled, whatever stalk of yours has fallen— whether near the ladle or far away—
may this god Bṛhaspati pour it together for our prosperity.
The plants are full of milk; full of milk is my speech. Full of milk indeed is the milk of the waters; with that, purify me together.
Go away, O Death, along your own path, which is distinct from the path of the gods;
I speak to you who have eyes and hear: do not harm our offspring, nor our heroes.
Avoiding the path of death as you have come, gaining a longer and more extended life, may you swell with progeny and wealth; being pure and purified, become worthy of sacrifice.
These living ones have turned away from the dead; our invocation of the gods has become auspicious today.
We have gone forward for dancing and laughter, prolonging our lifespan further on.
I set up this boundary for the living, so that no other among them may now go to this goal.
May they live a hundred full autumns; may they place death beyond by means of this mountain.
Just as days follow one another in succession, and just as seasons duly proceed with the seasons, so,
O Ordainer, arrange their lifespans such that the later does not abandon the earlier.
Ascend [to life], choosing old age, striving one after another as you proceed.
May Tvaṣṭṛ, the creator of fair forms, being well-disposed, grant you long life here that you may live.
May these women, not widowed and having good husbands, enter together with ointment and clarified butter.
Free from tears, free from disease, and possessing fine jewels, may these women first ascend to their place of birth.
Rise up, O woman, toward the world of the living; come to this one whose life has departed; lie down beside him.
You have entered into this state of wifehood for your husband, who took your hand and wooed you.
Taking the bow from the hand of the deceased for our sovereignty, splendor, and strength—
right there you remain, while we here, possessed of brave heroes, shall conquer all rivals and adversaries.
Approach this mother earth, the wide-extending, the very gracious Pṛthivī;
may she, the youthful maiden soft as wool for those who give sacrificial fees, protect you from the lap of Nirṛti.
Open wide, O Earth; do not press down upon him. Be easy of access and easy of passage for him. As a mother covers her son with the hem of her garment, so do you, O Earth, cover him.
May the earth, swelling wide, stand firm; may a thousand pillars be set up to support her.
May these houses be dripping with clarified butter, and may they be a refuge for him here for all time.
I prop up the earth for you; placing this clod of earth around you, may I not come to harm. May the Fathers hold up this pillar for you; here Yama shall establish your dwelling-place.
The days have placed me in the western direction like a leaf; I have seized the speech directed toward me, as one holds a horse with a rein.
Turn back, do not go further; follow us, O wealthy ones.
Agni and Soma, you who bring wealth back again, bestow riches upon us.
Bring them back again; bring them back once more.
May Indra restrain them; may Agni drive them hither.
Let these cows return again; let them thrive under this master of cattle.
O Agni, hold them fast right here; let whatever wealth there is remain right here.

The path by which one goes forth, the path by which one returns, that which is the point of meeting, that which is the final goal, the turning away, the turning back— him who is the guardian, him too I invoke.
May the guardian who has reached the point of departure, who has reached the final goal,
and who knows the turning back and the returning, bring us back again.
O Indra, turn them back, bring them back again; give us our cows, O Indra. May we enjoy them while they are still living.
I bestow upon you from every side strength, with clarified butter and milk.
Whatever gods there are who are worthy of sacrifice, may they endow us with wealth.
O Bringer-back, bring them back; O Returner, cause them to return.
From the four quarters of the earth, from those directions, bring them back to us.
May you inspire our minds toward what is auspicious.
I praise Agni, the youngest of those who enjoy, the ruler, the friend who is difficult to resist;
he under whose law the bright ones honor the udder of the mother in the light of heaven.
Him whom they nourish with their mouths as one dwelling in a lowly nest, whose banner is light—
he shines forth with rows of teeth.
The noble one, the path for the people, goes forth when he has reached the ends of heaven;
the seer, shining like a cloud, moves on.
May he enjoy the offerings of man; standing erect, the skillful one presides at the sacrifice, establishing his dwelling and moving forward.
For he is security; the oblation and the sacrifice go forth with speed, for his path is open.
The gods [approach] Agni, who wields the axe.
I have performed worship for the sake of nourishment to Agni, the conqueror in sacrifice, the son of the ancient bliss; they call him the living one, the son of the rock.
Whatever men there may be who belong to us— may they all partake of your favor,
increasing Agni with oblations.
Black, white, ruddy is his course; tawny, dappled, and crimson is he, the glorious one; the progenitor begot him of golden form.
Thus, O Agni, son of strength, Vimada, being in harmony with the immortals, has brought his inspired thought to you;
seeking your favor, he has offered songs of praise, and you have bestowed upon him food, vigor, a secure dwelling, and all prosperity.

We choose you as the Hotṛ priest with our own hymns, like Agni, for the sacrifice upon which the sacrificial grass is strewn—for your exhilaration—O sharp one with purifying luster; you are waxing great.
The self-existent ones, who bestow horses as their gift, adorn you;
the ladle for pouring seeks you. O Agni, in this exhilaration of yours, the straight-flying oblation is proclaimed. You are waxing great.
In you the sacred laws abide, as if pouring forth with ladles.
Black forms and white—O, in your exhilaration—you assume all glories; you wish to speak aloud.
O immortal Agni, whatever wealth you deem fit, O powerful one—bring that to us for the winning of booty at our sacrifices; bring it, the wonderful one, for our exhilaration. You are waxing great.
Agni, born by Atharvan, has discovered all poetic wisdom; he became the messenger of Vivasvat. At your exhilaration, you, the beloved and desirable one of Yama, are being proclaimed aloud.
O Agni, they invoke you at the sacrifices when the ritual has begun;
you bestow all desirable treasures upon the donor—this I declare for you in exhilaration.
Men have established you, O Agni, as the lovely officiating priest at the sacrifices;
with your face anointed with ghee, you, the bright and most wise one, are kindled by our eyes for our exhilaration.
O Agni, with your bright flame you spread yourself out widely and loftily; bellowing, you act as a bull. In your exhilaration, you bestow the germ upon your kin; you desire to speak aloud.
Where is Indra heard of? Among which people today is he renowned like Mitra—whether in the dwelling of the seers or in secret, celebrated through our song?
Hearken here, O Indra; praised by us today, the wielder of the thunderbolt, worthy of hymns, who like Mitra among the people has established matchless glory.
He who is the lord of great and incomparable power, the impeller of mighty manliness,
the bearer of the bold thunderbolt, like a father cherishing his beloved son.
Harnessing the two roaring horses of the wind, O god, wielder of the thunderbolt,
you who flow along the shining path, having been released, shall praise the ways.
You yourself have harnessed those two bay steeds of Vāta to draw [the chariot] by your own power—
[those] for which neither god nor mortal is found to be a driver.
Then Uśanas asked you as you were coming: "For what purpose have you come to our house?
From the distance of heaven and earth, you have approached a mortal."
O Indra, take note of our nourishment; our prayer is uplifted.
We entreat you for that protection, so that you may slay Śuṣṇa, the non-human.
The Dasyu performs no ritual; he is thoughtless toward us, following alien laws, and non-human. O slayer of enemies, strike down the weapon of that Dāsa!
O Indra, hero, you are heroic with your heroes; and we, protected by you, are mighty.
Your many bounties have resounded in many places, like the movements of the peoples.
O Hero, wielder of the thunderbolt, you urged those men on in the slaying of Vṛtra and in the drawing of the sword,
when you were hidden among the sages and the clans of star-like power.
Swift indeed, O Indra, are those gifts of yours, you who possess the prize, O hero, wielder of the thunderbolt,
when you, with your companions, struck down all that was born of Śuṣṇa.
O heroic Indra, let not our excellent aids be held aloof from us;
O wielder of the thunderbolt, may we, each one of us, abide in the favor of these [aids].
O Indra, let those touches of yours be true for us—those which are non-violent; may we know their enjoyment, O wielder of the thunderbolt, like that of milch-cows.
When the handless and footless one grew strong through the powers of the knowable things, you,
moving to the right, struck down Śuṣṇa for every living being.

Drink, drink the Soma, O heroic Indra! Do not fail us, you who possess wealth and are yourself a treasure. And protect the singers and the liberal patrons; make us rich with great and abundant riches.
Let us worship Indra, who holds the thunderbolt in his right hand, the charioteer of the bay steeds that move in various directions;
shaking his beard upward, he stands forth, distributing [gifts] with his armies and with his bounty.
His two bay steeds indeed find the treasure in the wood; Indra, the bounteous slayer of Vṛtra, has become great through his riches.
As Ṛbhu, Vāja, and Ṛbhukṣan, he rules over power; I even erase the very name of the Dāsa.
When he takes up his golden thunderbolt, then Maghavan, renowned from of old, mounts his chariot which his two bay steeds draw along with the patrons;
Indra, the lord of long-famed strength, comes forth.
He indeed, Indra, the lord of the herd, together with his own rain, sprinkles his golden beard;
he seeks the well-housed dwelling at the pressed offering, shaking it like the wind shakes the forest.
He who with his voice struck down many thousands of the malevolent, the discordant, and the foolish— verily,
that very manly deed of his we proclaim, he who like a father has increased his own power and might.
The Vimadas have generated for you, O Indra, a hymn of praise—unprecedented and most abundant—for you, the giver of good gifts;
for we know the enjoyment of this mighty one, when we shall make it our own, like a herdsman driving cattle.
May our friendship never be severed—neither yours, O Indra, nor that of the seer Vimada;
for we know your providence, O God, like that of a kinsman. May your auspicious friendships be with us.
O Indra, drink this honeyed Soma pressed in the vessel;
bestow wealth upon us, O Lord of many riches—thousandfold wealth—in your exhilaration. You are waxing great.
We approach you with sacrifices, with hymns, and with oblations.
O Lord of powers, among all powers, bestow upon us the most excellent treasure in your exhilaration; you are waxing great.

O Indra, you who are the lord of desirable things, the impeller of the feeble, and the protector of those who praise you—protect us from our enemies and from distress at your exhilaration; you wax great.
O powerful ones, masters of illusion, you two churned forth the two united worlds when,
implored by Vimada, O Nāsatyas, you brought them forth.
When the two joined ones were about to issue forth, all the gods felt compassion;
the gods said to the Nāsatyas, "Bring [the child] back again!"
Sweet be my departure; sweet be my return.
O Gods, by your divine power, make both of these for us full of sweetness.
Send us a gracious mind, and skill, and mental power.
Then, in your friendship with the soma-juice, may we rejoice in your exhilaration like cattle in a pasture; you are waxing great.
O Soma, they all dwell touching your heart in all your abodes.
And now, these desires of mine, seeking wealth, spread abroad among you in your exhilaration—you are being celebrated.
Moreover, O Soma, through my simplicity I violate your sacred laws;
therefore, as a father toward his son, be gracious to us in your exhilaration, even from the blow of death—you are waxing great.
Our prayers go forth together like streams from wells. O Soma, for our life, maintain our mental power—just as one fills the cups—at your exhilarating outpouring; you are about to swell.
O Soma, through your powers, these eager ones have opened wide the stall rich in cattle and horses; they, the wise and strong, [have done so] for you—so you proclaim in your exhilaration.
O Soma, you protect our cattle and the moving world spread out in many places. You bring them together so that they may live; beholding all beings, you wax great in your exhilaration.
O Soma, be our protector from every side, you who are invincible.
Drive away our adversaries, O King; let not the evil-minded master us. In your exhilaration, you speak forth.

O Soma, you who possess excellent wisdom, be watchful for us so that we may gain vital strength. You are the one who knows the fields better than man; in your exhilaration, protect us from malice and from distress. You are waxing great.
O Indu, you are our most excellent slayer of Vṛtra, the auspicious friend of Indra.
When they call upon you in the encounter, O Vivakṣaṇa, as you exhilarate them with your juice, they invoke you while fighting for the sake of their offspring.
This indeed is that potent, beloved exhilaration of Indra;
it has increased the thought of the great sage Kakṣīvat for you in your intoxication—you, who desire to speak.
This one sends forth strengths rich in cattle for the inspired singer who offers oblations;
this one, the best among the seven, shall deliver the blind and the lame—so may he further you in your exhilaration, O you who are waxing great.
For the desirable teams of horses advance toward him with inspired hymns;
may the wondrous Pūṣan, whose chariot is drawn by teams, the majestic one, grant us his aid.
The people here have recognized that greatness of his, his capacity for friendship; may the inspired singer win him through his prayers and perceive him through well-spoken hymns.
He knows the beautiful hymns, like the drop, like the bull Pūṣan;
he sprinkles nourishment upon us, he sprinkles it for us as if upon a pen.
O God Pūṣan, may we honor you as our own—
the accomplisher of our thoughts and the protector of the inspired poets.
He is the counterpart of sacrifices, the steed that urges on chariots; he is the seer established by Manu, the friend who protects the inspired singer.
The husband of her who longs for him, and of her who suffers,
and of him who suffers— O weaver of garments, you have cleansed the woolen fleece and the clothes.
Lord of spoils, lord of nourishments, the friend;
the beloved one has vigorously shaken his beard, he who is invincible and moves at will.
O Pūṣan, may goats turn the pole of your chariot;
you are the friend of every seeker, born of old, and unshakable.
May the majestic Pūṣan protect our chariot with nourishment;
may he be the increaser of our strengths and hear this our invocation.

O singer, my impetuous strength is indeed real when I bestow aid upon the sacrificer who presses the Soma. I am the slayer of him who offers no blessing, the one who strikes down the deceiver who follows crooked ways.
If indeed I were to lead forth for battle those godless ones who exult in their own bodies, then at home I would cook for you a powerful bull; I would pour out the sharp pressed juice, fifteenfold.
I do not know him who says "I am he" after having slain the godless in battle; when he has proclaimed his fierce encounter in combat, then indeed they call me "bulls."
When I was among unknown tribes, all the wealthy lords were mine.
Or, I conquer the arrogant one who dwells in security; I strike him down on the mountain, seizing him by the foot.

Neither do the obstacles hold me back in the struggle, nor the mountains, when I set my mind upon it; at my roar, he whose ears are quick shall fear day after day, and even the rays of light shall tremble.

Behold here those who drink the boiled [milk], who are without Indra, who subsist on their arms, and who fall before the arrow—those who have reviled their own bold friend; let the fellies of the chariot now roll over them!
You have grown strong; you have extended life; the former has indeed burst forth, and the latter shall burst forth.
Two filters do not contain him who has penetrated to the further shore of this world-space.
The cows of the nobleman, released, have eaten the barley; I saw them wandering together with their herdsman.
Cries of the nobleman came from all sides; how much of these will the master enjoy?

When we, who eat the fodder of men, and I, who eat the barley within the wide field, come together—then may he, being harnessed, seek out one who provides fodder; and may the winner harness him who was unharnessed.
In this matter, you shall consider my words spoken as truth: I will unite the bipeds and the quadrupeds here;
and whoever should attack the bull with women, I will divide his wealth without a fight.
Whose daughter was ever without eyes? Who, knowing her to be blind, would set his mind upon her?
Which of the two would release his resentment against him—the one who carries her away, or the one who would woo her?
How great is the bride, the daughter-in-law of the mortal, when she is fully gratified by excellent and desirable wealth?
When the bride is auspicious and well-adorned, she herself wins a friend even among the common folk.

The foot has swallowed; he eats him who faces him; with his head he has placed a head as a protection. Sitting upon his lap, he destroys the upright one; turning downward, he follows the outstretched earth.
Great, shadowless, and leafless, the courser stands; the mother is released, and the embryo devours him.
Licking the calf of another, she has lowed; in what world has the cow deposited her udder?
Seven heroes rose up from below; eight came together from above.
Nine came from behind, possessing firmness; ten from the front traverse the ridge of the mountain.
Of ten, they drive forward one who is tawny and common, for the sake of the decisive rite;
the mother bears him, well-placed within her womb, as he grows, bringing him satisfaction.
The heroes cooked a fat ram; the dice were cast and followed the game. Two [dice], possessing filters, move within the vast river, purifying themselves.
Crying out, they have gone in all directions; one half [of the victim] cooks, for the other half does not cook.
This god Savitṛ has told me this: "He who eats wood shall thrive, and he who eats ghee shall thrive."
I saw a village being carried away from afar, moving by its own inherent power without wheels;
the noble one follows the generations of men, instantly destroying the [old] members as he becomes ever new.
These two oxen of Pramarasva are yoked for me; do not drive them away, but rather delight in me again and again.
Even the waters fail to achieve their purpose against him; the sun and the demon have both become his subordinates.

This very thunderbolt which has been hurled in many ways from below the vast mass of the sun—fame indeed is one thing, and beyond that there is another; through it, they overcome old age without distress.
From tree to tree the lowing cow was tethered; from there the man-eating birds flew forth.
Then this entire world was struck with fear; let it offer libations for Indra and provide for the seer.
In the dwelling-place of the gods, the first ones stood firm; from their cutting away, the later ones rose up. Three heat the earth with moisture; two carry the swelling mass of water.
This is your means of life; know that of him as well. Do not hide such a thing from me in the assembly.
He reveals the light and hides the chaff; he is manifest, and his garment is never removed.
Every other kinsman has indeed arrived; alas, my father-in-law alone has not come.
May he eat the parched grain and drink the Soma, and being well-fed, may he return home again.
Roaring like a bull with sharp horns, he stands upon the height, over the expanse of the earth. "I protect him in all his struggles—he who, having pressed the Soma, fills my two flanks."
With the stone, O Indra, they quickly press for you the exhilarating Soma juices; you drink of them.
They cook bulls for you; you eat of them when you are invoked with nourishment, O Maghavan.
O singer, understand this well for me: the rivers carry their curse backward;
the fox assails the lion from behind, and the jackal drives the boar out from the thicket.
How shall I, a simple mortal, comprehend this thought of yours, the wise and powerful one?
As one who knows, declare to us in due season that path which leads to your secure domain, O Maghavan.
For thus they strengthen me, the powerful one; even from the great heaven, my yoke-pole is higher.
I sharpen many thousands all at once, for my progenitor begot me without a foe.
For thus have the gods known me, Indra, as powerful, fierce, and a bull in every deed.
Rejoicing, I slew Vṛtra with the thunderbolt; by my greatness, I opened the enclosure for the donor.
The gods came, carrying axes; felling the forests, they approached with their hosts. Placing Sudrva in the bellies [of the trees], they burn it where the wood-pile lies.
The hare has swallowed the razor that was turned against him; from afar I have split the mountain with a clod of earth.
I shall subject even the great to the lowly; the calf, growing strong, shall gore the bull.
The eagle has thus struck his claw, hemmed in like a lion in an enclosure;
though the thirsty buffalo is trapped, the leather thong drags him helplessly along.
The iguana shall drag away that which belongs to them—those who treat the sacred word with contempt by means of their food.
They devour the bulls let loose, while they themselves destroy the strength of their own bodies.
These have become well-prepared through their labors, they who have impelled their bodies with Soma-hymns.
Speaking like a man, bestow wealth upon us; you have established your name as a hero, O glory in heaven.
Like one who has been placed in the wood and has shone forth, O swift ones, this pure hymn of praise has awakened you both— Indra,
who for many days has been the Hotṛ-priest of men, the manly, most heroic, and protector of men.
May we be at the forefront of this dawn and the next, in the dance of you, the most heroic among heroes.
May the chariot, victorious and accompanied by Kutsa, bring a hundred men hither for Triśoka.
What exhilaration of yours, O Indra, has been delightful? You, the fierce one, have poured forth your songs through the doors.
Or rather, what thought of mine shall bring you hither? May I be able to provide you with the highest gift of food.
When indeed will the glory of one like you, O Indra, come to our men? With what intention will you act?
Why have you not come to us—you who are true like Mitra, wide-striding—so that there may be sustenance and the wisdom of everyone regarding food?
O Hero, drive them toward their goal as if to the further shore—those who have come to fulfill his desire like wives to their husbands;
and those men, O Indra born of many powers, who with their offerings seek to win back your many songs of praise.
O Indra, by your greatness the two well-measured worlds, heaven and earth, were indeed surpassed; by your wisdom, they were outstripped.
For your choice, let the pressed juices mixed with clarified butter be sweet for your drinking; let the honeyed draughts be pleasant.
They have poured out the vessel full of honeyed mead for this Indra, for he is truly bountiful;
he has grown great across the breadth of the earth, preeminent through his wisdom and manly deeds.
Indra, self-strong, has shattered the hostile armies; many seek him for friendship.
Mount his chariot in battles, as one who shall urge it on with auspicious favor.
May the path toward the gods proceed for the sacred prayer, as if toward the waters by the impulse of the mind.
May I offer this well-fashioned hymn to the great sustenance of Mitra and Varuṇa, who possess wide-reaching power.
O Adhvaryus, be possessed of the oblation; desiring [the waters], come hither from afar toward those longing ones.
Those which the ruddy, fair-winged one gazes down upon—those waves, seize them today with your skillful hands.
O Adhvaryus, go forth to the ocean; worship the Son of the Waters with an oblation. May he grant you today a well-purified wave; for him, press the honeyed Soma.
He who shines unkindled within the waters, whom the sages invoke at the sacrifices—
O Son of the Waters, grant us the honeyed waters, by which Indra was strengthened for heroic power.
With those [waters] by which Soma rejoices and exults, like a young man with beautiful maidens—O Adhvaryu, go toward those waters; when you pour them out, purify him with the plants.
Thus do the young maidens bow down to the youth when, desiring him, they come toward him who desires them.
They agree in spirit and are of one mind: the Adhvaryu priests, the Dhiṣaṇās, and the divine Waters.
O Waters, send forth for that Indra a wave rich in sweetness, which gladdens the gods— a wave that made room for you when you were obstructed, and which released you from great calumny.
Send forth for him a wave rich in sweetness, O rivers, which is your offspring and a fountain of honey—sweet-backed and worthy of praise at the sacrifices. O wealthy Waters, hear my invocation!
O rivers, send forth that exhilarating wave for Indra’s drinking, which sets both worlds in motion—
that intoxicating, offspring of the waters, born of the clouds, flowing through the triple-stranded source as it spreads abroad.
Turning hitherward in two streams, like those who fight for cattle wandering toward their stalls—
O Seer, pay homage to the Waters, the mothers and mistresses of the world, who increase us and share a common origin.
Further our sacrifice with the worship of the gods; further our prayer for the winning of riches.
Unbind the udder at the yoking of the Eternal Law; O Waters, be gracious hearers unto us.
O wealthy Waters, for you indeed rule over riches; you bear within yourselves auspicious wisdom and immortality.
You are the mistresses of wealth that consists of noble offspring; may Sarasvatī grant that vitality to the one who praises her.
When the waters were seen approaching, carrying ghee, milk, and honey,
they agreed in spirit with the Adhvaryu priests, bringing the well-pressed Soma for Indra.
These wealthy ones, who bring wealth to the living, have come; O friends, Adhvaryus, set them down!
Place them upon the sacrificial grass, O Soma-offerers, in harmony with Apāṃ Napāt.
The longing waters have come to this sacred grass; seeking the gods, they have settled at the sacrifice.
O Adhvaryus, press the Soma for Indra! Your worship of the gods has become easy to perform.
May the praise of the gods come to us for our protection, worthy of sacrifice along with all the swift ones.
Through them may we become good friends; crossing over all difficulties, may we be secure.
Even a mortal should consider wealth as his own; let him seek to win it through the path of Truth with reverence.
Let him also consult with his own wisdom and grasp a more excellent skill with his mind.

The prayer has been offered; the portions have been poured out. Like helpers at a watering-place, they approach the Wondrous One. We have attained the strength of prosperity; we have become aware of the immortals.
May the eternal Lord of the House, the domestic master whom the divine Savitṛ has brought forth, be pleased with him;
may Bhaga or Aryaman adorn him with cattle, and may he appear beautiful and pleasing to him.

May this [praise] become like the dwelling place of the Dawns, when those possessed of food have come together with power. Seeking the singer's hymn of praise for him, may strengthening gains come to us.
This benevolent thought of his has spread wide from of old like a cow over the earth;
they who dwell together in the womb of this Asura, being sustained in their common nourishment.
What was that forest, and what was that tree, from which they fashioned heaven and earth? Standing together, undecaying, and providing aid, they have caused many days and many dawns to grow old.
There is nothing else beyond this; he is the bull who supports heaven and earth.
Self-dependent, he makes his skin a filter when the bay steeds carry him like the sun.
Like a bird he passes over the broad earth; like the wind he blows through the mist upon the ground, where Mitra and Varuṇa, being anointed, have released their splendor like Agni in the forest.

When the barren cow, being suddenly anointed with oil, brought forth her calf, she who was trembling became free from distress, having found her own protector. When the son was born before his parents, the cow swallowed the sacrificial pin, even as they questioned one another.
And they say that Kaṇva was the son of Nṛṣad; moreover, the swift steed won the prize.
For Kṛṣṇa, the bright udder swelled; here, no one else caused the Truth to flow for him.
May the two who come forth, the companions of the one who meditates, sit down well with their choice gifts toward our choice offerings.
May Indra enjoy both of us, when he takes notice of the Soma juice.
O Indra, much-praised one, you traverse the celestial luminaries and the earthly realms through the mid-air.
May those who repeatedly bring you to the sacrifices overcome the boastful words of the stingy ones.
That indeed shall proclaim to me the most wondrous form of the wondrous one: that the son recites the origin from his parents;
the wife leads her husband with her voice; truly, for a man, the auspicious bridal procession is fully prepared.
I have meditated upon that lovely place of assembly where the cows lowed like milch-cows for their calf;
where the ancient mother of the herd, the sevenfold source of the song, and the people gathered together.
Your footprint has surpassed [all others] as you seek the gods; alone among the Rudras, he goes forth, victorious.
Or rather, among those immortals who grant gifts, let them sing their praise. Pour out the honeyed mead for your protectors.
"That which was being deposited, hidden within the waters—Indra, the knower, has indeed beheld it for me; for he is the guardian of the laws of the gods. Thus instructed by him, O Agni, have I come."
One who does not know the land has indeed spoken to one who knows the land; instructed by the knower of the land, he goes forward.
This is truly the blessing of instruction: one finds the direct path.
Today indeed he has breathed forth; these [beings] have fed and, unobstructed, have sucked at the mother’s udder.
Old age has come upon him, yet he remains young; without malice, the benevolent one has become well-disposed.
O Kalaśa, O Kurusravaṇa, let us perform these auspicious deeds as we bestow gifts.
O bounteous lords, let this be your gift, and let this Soma which I carry in my heart be yours.
The impulses of men have harnessed me; I carry Pūṣan by way of the middle space.
Then all the gods protected me; there was a cry: "A malevolent spirit has come!"
The ribs pain me on all sides like rival wives;
exhaustion oppresses me, and nakedness afflicts me; my mind trembles like a weary bird.
Like rats gnawing at their own tails, they devour me, your praiser, O Śatakratu.
Be gracious to us once for all, O Maghavan Indra; then be to us like a father.
I, the seer, have chosen King Kuruśravaṇa, the son of Trasadasyu,
the most generous among those who offer worship.
I shall praise him whose three bay horses carry me straightway on his chariot— he who bestows a thousandfold sacrificial fees.
Whose songs, like those of Upamaśravas’s father, have tasted the sweetness [of the soma]— [songs] as delightful as a field to one who has spoken [of it].
O Upamaśravas, son of Mitrātithi, come as a grandson;
I am the one who honors your father.
If I were the lord of the immortals, or even of mortals,
then my liberal patron would surely live.
No one, even if possessed of a hundred lives, lives beyond the law of the gods; thus does my companion turn away from me.
The dangling fruits of the great tree exhilarate me, they that were born in the wind and roll upon the gaming board.
Like a draught of Soma from Mount Mūjavat, the wakeful Vibhīdaka nut has pleased me.
She did not scold me, nor was she angry; she was kind toward my friends and toward me. For the sake of a single throw of the die, I have driven away my devoted wife.
My mother-in-law hates me, my wife holds me back; though I am in distress, I find no one to comfort me. Like the worn-out hide of a horse for sale, I find no enjoyment in this gambler.
Others caress the wife of that man whose wealth the die has coveted;
his father, mother, and brothers say of him, "We do not know him; lead him away bound."
When I thought, "I shall not play with these," I was left behind by my departing friends;
and when the brown dice were cast down, they raised their voices, and I go to their appointed place like a mistress to her lover.
The gambler goes to the assembly hall, asking "Shall I win? and trembling with his body;
the dice frustrate his desire, bestowing the winnings upon his opponent.
The dice are indeed like goads, pricking and cutting, burning and causing torment;
they grant boons to children, yet strike down the victor; mingled with honey, they are the instrument of the gambler’s ruin.
Their troop of fifty-three plays like the god Savitṛ, whose laws are true. Even before the wrath of the fierce one, they bow; even a king pays them homage, saying "Salutation! to them.
Moving downward yet leaping upward, handless as they are, they overcome the one who has hands;
like divine coals cast upon the parched ground, though cold themselves, they burn the heart to ashes.
The gambler’s wife is left desolate and suffers; his mother grieves for her son who wanders who knows where.
Borrowing money and filled with fear, seeking wealth, he goes to the houses of others by night.
Upon seeing a woman—the wife of another and her well-fashioned womb—the gambler was tormented.
For in the forenoon he had yoked his brown horses; now, at the edge of the fire, that wretch has fallen down.
To him who was the commander of your great host, the king who became the foremost of the troop—to him I offer no resistance regarding my wealth; for ten days I have spoken the truth toward you.
"Do not play with dice; cultivate the plow instead, and find delight in your wealth, regarding it as abundant.
There are your cows, O gambler, there is your wife. Thus does this noble Savitṛ declare to me.
Make friends with us; indeed, have mercy on us. Do not act with fierce boldness against us.
Let your wrath and hostility now depart; let another fall into the snare of the tawny ones.

The fires, accompanied by Indra, have awakened; bearing light at the dawning of the Uṣas, may the great Heaven and Earth take notice of our work. Today we choose for ourselves the protection of the gods.
We choose for ourselves protection from heaven and earth; we seek the rivers, the mountains, and the marshy lands of Śaryaṇāvat.
We pray to Sūrya and Uṣas for sinlessness; may the well-pressed Soma bring us auspiciousness today.
May Heaven and Earth, the two great Mothers, protect us today from sin for our well-being;
may the dawning Dawn drive away evil. We pray for well-being to the kindled Agni.
May this first Dawn, rich in divine favor, shine forth wealth for us who seek wealth.
May we keep far away the wrath of the malevolent; we pray for well-being from the kindled Agni.
The Dawns that stream forth with the rays of the sun, bringing light at their breakings—may they shine upon us today auspiciously for our renown. We pray for well-being from the kindled Agni.
May the health-bringing Dawns approach us; may the fires rise up with lofty light.
May the Aśvins harness their swift chariot; we pray for well-being from the kindled Agni.
O Savitṛ, impel for us today a most excellent and desirable portion, for you are the bestower of treasures.
I address Dhiṣaṇā, the mother of wealth; we pray for well-being from Agni as he is kindled with fuel.
May that proclamation of the *ṛta* carry me across, which we mortals have meditated upon as belonging to the gods.
The Sun rises, beholding all the dawns. We pray for well-being from Agni as he is kindled with fuel.
Free from hatred today, as we spread the sacrificial grass and employ the pressing-stones, we pray for the success of our thought.
Abiding in the protection of the Ādityas, you move restlessly; we pray for well-being from Agni as he is kindled.
I invoke the gods upon our great sacrificial grass at the shared feast in heaven; I seat the seven Hotṛ-priests.
For the sake of gain, we seek Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Bhaga; for well-being, we pray to the kindled Agni.
O Ādityas, come hither for our complete well-being; with one accord, protect our sacrifice for our prosperity. We pray to Bṛhaspati, Pūṣan, the Aśvins, Bhaga, and the kindled Agni for our welfare.
O Gods, Ādityas, grant us that well-proclaimed protection which is easy to maintain and worthy of being guarded by men;
for our cattle, our children, our progeny, and for life itself, we pray for well-being from the kindled Agni.
May all the Maruts come today with every aid; may all the fires be kindled.
May all the gods come to us with protection; may all wealth and strength be ours.
O gods, whomsoever you protect in the contest for booty, whomsoever you rescue and deliver from distress—
he who knows no fear under your guardianship— may we be such as these for the feast of the gods, O swift ones.

Dawn and Night, the lofty and well-adorned; Heaven and Earth, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—I invoke Indra, the Maruts, the mountains, the waters, the Ādityas, Heaven and Earth, the waters, and the light of heaven.
May Heaven and Earth, the wise ones who follow the cosmic order, protect us from distress and from harm.
Let not destructive Nirṛti, who delights in evil, have power over us; we choose today that protection of the gods.
May Aditi protect us from all distress—she who is the mother of Mitra and of wealthy Varuṇa.
May we attain the light of heaven, free from danger; today we choose that protection of the gods.
May the sounding pressing-stone drive away the demons, the evil dream, destruction, and every devouring fiend.
May we obtain the protection of the Ādityas and the Maruts; today we choose that favor of the gods.
May Indra sit upon the sacred grass; may the sacrificial food swell; may Bṛhaspati, the singer, chant with the Sāman hymns.
Let us fashion a well-enlightened prayer for life; we choose today that protection of the gods.
O Aśvins, make our sacrifice touch the heavens and quicken the rite for the sake of seeking favor;
we choose today that protection of the gods, which is offered with ghee and has its reins directed eastward.
I invoke the well-invoked host of Maruts, the purifying and lofty, who bring bliss for our friendship.
May we obtain an increase of wealth for the sake of high renown; today we choose that protection of the gods.
We bring forth the Soma, the drinker of waters, the source of life, the protector of the gods, the one easily invoked who adorns the sacrifice;
we have restrained the Soma, the lordly power with beautiful rays. Today, we choose that protection of the gods.
May we, living with our sons still living and free from sin, win that through easy victories by means of our gains.
May those who hate sacred prayer bear the guilt away in every direction; today we choose the protection of the gods.
O you who are worthy of sacrifice among men, listen! O gods, grant us that which we implore of you:
a victorious resolve, wealth accompanied by heroes, and glory. We choose today that protection of the gods.
Today we choose for ourselves the great protection of the great gods, the lofty and the invincible;
so that we may obtain wealth born of heroes—that protection of the gods, we choose today.
In the protection of the great Agni as he is kindled, may we be sinless before Mitra and Varuṇa for our well-being;
may we abide in the most excellent impulsion of Savitṛ. We choose today that favor of the gods.
O all you gods who abide in the ordinance of Savitṛ of true impulse, of Mitra, and of Varuṇa—
bestow upon us prosperity consisting of heroic sons and cattle, and grant us manifold wealth.
Savitar from behind, Savitar from the front, Savitar from above, Savitar from below—may Savitar impel all well-being for us; may Savitar grant us long life.
Homage to the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa! Pay worship to that great god;
recite the hymn to Sūrya, the son of Heaven, the far-seeing banner born of the gods.
May that word of truth protect me on every side, as far as heaven and earth extend their days;
everything else that moves goes to rest, yet the waters flow forever and the sun goes forth for all time.
No godless one from of old can stay thee back when thou dost drive upon thy chariot with thy winged coursers.
One realm follows after thee as thou goest forward; with the other light, O Sūrya, thou dost travel.

O Sūrya, with that light by which you dispel the darkness and with which you rise up over the entire world with your radiance— with that, drive away from us all lack of nourishment, lack of offerings, disease, and evil dreams.
For, dispatched, you guard the law of the universe; rising up without malice, you act according to your own nature (*svadhā*).
O Sūrya, whatever intention we declare to you today, may the gods favor that purpose of ours.
May Heaven and Earth, may the Waters, Indra, and the Maruts hear this our invocation and this word.
May we not be deprived of the sight of the sun; living on, may we reach old age in prosperity.
May we, with good minds and clear vision, possessing offspring, free from disease and sinless,
behold you every day as you rise, O Sūrya, you who are great like Mitra— may we live long and gaze upon you.
O far-seeing Sūrya, may we, while still living, behold you as you ascend from the vast expanse— the bearer of great light, radiant, a source of joy for every eye.
O Sūrya, you by whose signal all beings move forth and by whose rays they enter [rest] at night;
O golden-haired one, come day after day with greater and ever greater innocence for us.
Be auspicious to us with your eye, auspicious to us by day, auspicious with your radiance, auspicious with the cold, and auspicious with the heat!
O Sūrya, bestow upon us that wonderful wealth so that there may be well-being on our journey and well-being within our home.
O Gods, grant protection to both our classes of beings—our bipeds and our quadrupeds.
Grant us that which is eaten, drunk, and strengthening; bestow upon us health, well-being, and freedom from affliction.
O gods, whatever grave offense against the gods we have committed with our tongue or through a lapse of mind,
O Vasus, lay that sin upon him who, being ungenerous, seeks to bring ill fortune upon us.
O Indra, protect us in this glorious and vigorous battle-cry for the sake of victory,
where in the struggle for cattle among the bold and armored warriors, the missiles fly in all directions in the conquest of men.
O Indra, at our dwelling, disclose for us wealth abounding in food and swelling with cattle, worthy of renown.
O Śakra, may we be your allies as you conquer; O Vasu, grant us that which we desire.

O Indra, much-praised one, whether it be a Dāsa or an Ārya who intends to challenge us to battle, may those enemies be easily overcome by us; with you as our ally, may we conquer them in the encounter.
He who is to be invoked by the few and by the many, he who in the encounter provides wide space in the struggle for men—
that famous hero Indra, the winner in the contest, we shall today bring hither for our protection.
For I have heard of you, O Indra, as one who follows his own will, the bull who drives away the stingy and impels the weak;
release yourself from Kutsa, come here! How can one like you remain bound by the testicles?

O Aśvins, that well-rolling chariot of yours which travels all around, to be invoked at evening and at dawn by the offerer of oblations—everlasting indeed is that [chariot] of yours; we invoke it here as one whose name is easy to call, like that of a father.
Impel our truthful words; swell our inspired thoughts; send forth our abundant wisdom—this is what we desire.
O Aśvins, make for us a glorious portion; like the Soma, make us dear among the patrons.
Even for the aged, you two become a source of fortune; even for the blind, you are protectors;
even for the destitute, O Nāsatyas, and even for the emaciated, they call upon you two as physicians for his healing.
You two fashioned Cyavāna, who was like an old chariot, into a youth again for the sake of movement;
you carried out Tugra’s son from the waters—all these deeds of yours are to be proclaimed at the libations.
I shall proclaim your ancient heroic deeds among the people; thus you two have been physicians who bring delight.
As such, we now make you both new for our protection, O Nāsatyas, so that this pious man may place his trust in you.
I have called upon you both; hear me, O Aśvins! Bestow your favor upon me as parents do for their son.
I am friendless, ignorant, and without kin; before that calamity strikes, deliver us from this curse!
On your chariot you brought Śundhyū down for Vimada, the maiden of Purumitra. You came to the call of Vadhrimatī; you brought forth fair offspring for Purandhi.
You restored the youthful vigor of the sage Kali, who had reached old age;
you raised Vandana up from the pit, and you instantly enabled Viśpalā to walk.
O Ashvins, you two, O bulls, raised up Rebha who was hidden in a cave and nearly dead;
you two made the heated cauldron a source of protection for Atri and Saptavadhri.
O Aśvins, you gave to Pedu a white horse, powerful with ninety-nine steeds;
a horse worthy of praise, who makes his companion swift, like Bhaga to be invoked by men, the source of bliss.

Neither from any side, O two Kings, Aditi, nor any distress, misfortune, or fear reaches him whom you, O Aśvins— easily invoked, whose path is like that of Rudra— make the foremost in his chariot together with his wife.

Come hither with that [chariot] swifter than thought, which the R̥bhus fashioned for you, O Aśvins— the chariot by whose harnessing the Daughter of Heaven is born, and both the fair days of Vivasvat arise.

O Aśvins, you two went on your circuit and conquered the mountain; you made the cow swell with milk for Śayu. Even the quail that had been swallowed within the mouth of the wolf, you released by your mighty deeds.
O Aśvins, we have fashioned this hymn for you, as the Bhṛgus fashion a chariot;
we have polished it, as one adorns a maiden for her bridegroom, holding it as one holds a constant son and grandson.

Where is your chariot going, O heroes? Who indeed honors you, the radiant one, for the sake of prosperity—that chariot which travels at dawn, all-pervading, and which day after day is brought forth for every clan through prayer and ritual effort?
Where indeed are you at night, O Aśvins, and where by day? Where do you come hither, and where have you dwelt?
Who brings you to your dwelling, as a widow brings her husband, or as a young woman brings her lover?

At dawn you two awaken, like two aged ones through longing; day after day, O worshipful ones, you go to the house. Whose [house] do you, the destroyers, frequent? Or for whom, O heroes, do you go to the libations like two princes?
Like two wild elephants that men desire to capture, we invoke you with oblations at evening and at dawn.
To the man who offers the sacrifice at the appointed time, O Lords of Splendor, you bring nourishment.

O Aśvins, Ghoṣā, the daughter of the king, as she went forth, spoke to you both: "I ask you, O heroes, be present for me by day and be present for the night; grant your aid to the horse-possessor, to the charioteer, and to the steed."
O Aśvins, you two are sages; like Kutsa, bring your chariot to the people, and come to the singer as to our own kin.
O Aśvins, the bee brings honey from you both with its mouth, as a young woman brings her prepared gift.
O Aśvins, you indeed rescued Bhujyu, you [rescued] Vaśa, and you brought Śiñjāra and Uśanas near;
the liberal giver dwells within your friendship; through your protection, I long for your favor.
O Aśvins, you indeed protect Kṛśa, you protect Śayu, and you protect the widow who serves you;
O Aśvins, for the sake of those seeking gain, you throw open the thundering stall with its sevenfold mouth.
The maiden was born; the young man flew forth; the plants sprouted according to his wondrous deeds. For him the rivers flow like valleys; for this day, that state of being a husband comes to pass.
They weep for the living and part at the sacrifice; the men have fixed their thoughts upon a long-lasting lineage.
They who have prepared this [offering] for the fathers have brought forth what is desirable: a joy for the husbands and wives for their embrace.
We do not know that; speak it forth clearly—how the youth dwells within the wombs of the young maidens.
We would go to the home of the beloved bull, the possessor of seed; O Aśvins, that is what we desire.

Your benevolence has come to us, O lords of ample wealth; O Aśvins, desires have been directed toward our hearts. You two have become our protectors, a pair of lords of splendor; may we reach the dear dwellings of Aryaman.

Rejoicing in the dwelling of man, O Lords of Splendor, bestow upon the eloquent singer wealth together with heroic sons. Create a ford with good watering-places; strike down the obstacle that stands in the path and the evil-minded one.
Where indeed today, in which communities, do the two Aśvins, the wonder-workers and lords of splendor, rejoice? Who has detained them? To whose house have they gone—that of a sage or of a sacrificer?

We invoke with well-fashioned hymns that common, much-invoked, praiseworthy three-wheeled chariot which comes to the libations; we call it at the breaking of dawn—the one who traverses all, worthy of the assembly.
O Nāsatyas, you mount at dawn the chariot that is yoked at early morning, which travels at dawn and carries honey;
by means of which, O Heroes, you go to the people who offer sacrifice, even to the sacrifice of the poor man that is attended by the Hotṛ-priest, O Aśvins.
Whether you go to the *adhvaryu* with honeyed hands and skillful fingers, or to the *agnīdh* who is firm in resolve and domestic,
or to the libations of the inspired singer— come from there, O Aśvins, to drink the honeyed draught.
Like an archer aiming at a well-marked target, bring forth this hymn for him as if adorning it.
O sages, cross over the speech of the enemy with your own voice; O singer, cause Indra to settle down within the Soma.
Win over the cow with milking; O singer, awaken Indra, the lover. Like a full vessel overflowing with wealth, bring down the hero for the giving of riches.
Why indeed, O Maghavan, do they call you a liberal giver? Sharpen me; I hear that you are one who sharpens.
O Śakra, let my prayer be effective; O Indra, bring us Bhaga, the finder of wealth.
O Indra, people standing together in the heat of battle call upon you in their desire for possessions;
here, the hero makes him who offers oblations his ally, for he does not seek friendship with one who pours no libations.

Like abundant, flowing wealth, for him who, providing sacrificial food, presses out strong Soma juices for him—early in the day, he strikes down his enemies with swift weapons; he slays Vṛtra along with his followers.
In that Indra we place our hope—whoever the Maghavan has fixed his desire upon us—let his enemy, even though he be far away, tremble; let all human glories bow down before him.
Drive the enemy far away with that fierce *śamba* weapon, O you who are invoked by many!
Bestow upon us wealth consisting of barley and cattle, O Indra; grant the singer a prayer rich in booty.
Into whom the strong-pressing, sharp Somas with abundant ends have entered within—Maghavan does not fail to bestow his gift; he brings much wealth to the one who presses the juice.
Moreover, he wins the stake by playing beyond the limit, when the gambler gathers his winnings at the proper time;
the self-reliant one unites with wealth that man who desires the gods and does not withhold his riches.
O Much-invoked One, may we cross over this evil-minded poverty with cattle, and all hunger with barley;
may we, as the foremost, win riches through the kings and by our own heroic band.
May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind, and from above, and from below, from the one who seeks to harm us;
may Indra from the front and from the middle grant wide space to us, his friends, as a friend.
Toward me, Indra, our thoughts—seeking the light of heaven, all united and longing—have cried out.
They embrace him as wives embrace their husband, as they would a handsome youth, for the sake of his aid, the bounteous Maghavan.

My mind indeed does not turn away from you; O much-invoked one, I have fixed my desire upon you alone. Like a king, O wondrous one, sit down upon the sacrificial grass; let there be a drinking-place for you at this excellent Soma.
Indra is the increaser across [all things], from want and from hunger; he, the Maghavan, rules over wealth and treasure.
These seven rivers in their downward flow increase the vital strength of that impetuous bull.
Like birds to a tree with fair foliage, the exhilarating Soma drops, seated in the vessels, have settled within Indra.
Their vanguard, flashing with power, has found the light of heaven, the Aryan light for mankind.
As a gambler gathers his winnings at play, so Maghavan won the sun as his prize;
no other, O Maghavan, neither one of old nor one of recent times, has been able to equal that heroic deed of yours.
Maghavan has taken his place around every tribe; the Bull gazes upon the lowing of the people.
He at whose libations Śakra rejoices, he overcomes his assailants with the potent Soma juices.
When the Soma juices flow together toward Indra like waters toward the ocean or rivulets toward a lake,
the inspired singers increase his greatness at the place of sacrifice, just as rain increases the barley with a divine gift from heaven.
Like a furious bull, he rushed through the regions of space, he who made these waters the wives of the noble one.
That Maghavan found light for the man who presses the Soma, for the swift-giving one who offers oblations.
