Let the axe be born forth together with light; may it be as a well-milking cow of Truth, as of old.
Let the ruddy one shine brightly with his radiance, pure as the bright heaven; let the Lord of Beings blaze like the clear sun.
O Much-invoked One, may we cross over ill-will with cattle, and all hunger with barley;
may we, as the foremost, win riches through our kings and by our own vigorous band.
May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind, and from above, and from below, against the malevolent one;
may Indra from the front and from the middle grant wide space to us, his friends, as a friend.
May Indra, the lord of the self-ruling ones, come for exhilaration— he who, mighty and impetuous by his own law,
has surged forward across all powers with his boundless and great virility.
Firmly-seated is your chariot, well-governed are your two bay steeds; O Lord of Men, the thunderbolt is fixed in your hand.
Come hither quickly, O King, by fair paths; we shall increase your manly powers once you have drunk.

May the fierce and powerful ones, borne by Indra, bring hither to us this king who wields the thunderbolt— him who is formidable, vigorous, swift of action, a bull of true strength, and our companion at the feast.
Thus you, the bull, desire for yourself a husband who dwells in the wooden vat, who is conscious, the pillar of strength, and the support.
Display your power, gather it within you, so that you may be the lord for the increase of those who drink from the buckets.
May he come to us with riches, for I have praised him; bring the fulfillment of our own desire to the bearer of the Soma.
You are the lord; sit down upon this sacred grass (barhis), for by your law your vessels are inviolable.
The first invocations of the gods went forth separately; they performed deeds for glory that were difficult to surpass.
Those who were unable to board the sacrificial ship remained behind like trembling reeds.

Let those of evil intent go away; let those whose ill-yoked horses have been harnessed depart. Truly, those who are here below for the sake of giving, where there are many provisions and means of enjoyment—let them remain.
He held firm the mountains and the plains as they shook; heaven roared and the intermediate regions trembled.
He props apart the two converging bowls of the universe; having drunk of the bull’s [Soma], he proclaims hymns in his exhilaration.
I carry this well-fashioned goad for you, O Maghavan, with which you shall break those who strike with their hooves.
May there be a home for you at this libation; O Maghavan, be present at the pressed juice and the sacrifice.
O Much-invoked One, may we cross over ill-will with cattle, and all hunger with barley. May we, as the first among kings, win riches through our own heroic band.
May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind, and from above, and from below, from the one who seeks to do us harm;
may Indra from the front and from the middle grant wide space to us, his friends, as a friend.
Agni was first born from heaven; a second time, Jātavedas was born from us;
a third time, he was born in the waters. The manly-minded one, kindling him unceasingly, the pious man praises him.
We know your three forms, O Agni, in three ways; we know your stations distributed in many places. We know your supreme name which is hidden in secret; we know that spring from which you have come.
In the ocean, within the waters, the manly-minded one, the beholder of men, kindled you, O Agni, in the udder of heaven.
While you were established in the third realm, in the lap of the waters, the mighty ones increased you.
Agni roared like the thundering sky, licking the earth and anointing the plants;
as soon as he was born, being kindled, he looked abroad and shines with his splendor between the two worlds.
The noble upholder of glories, the supporter of riches, the inspirer of thoughts, the guardian of Soma;
the Vasu, the Son of Strength, the King in the waters, kindled at the forefront of the dawns, he shines forth.
The banner of the universe, the germ of the world, at his birth filled the two worlds;
he split even the firm rock as he went forth, when the five peoples sacrificed to Agni.
Desiring [oblations], purifying, a messenger, and wise, the immortal Agni has been established among mortals.
Bearing aloft his ruddy smoke, he rises up, striving to reach the sky with his bright radiance.
Visible like a golden ornament, he has shone far and wide, radiant for the sake of glory with an irrepressible life-span.
Agni became immortal through his vital powers when the prolific Dyaus brought him forth.
O Agni, O god of auspicious luster, whoever today prepares for you a cake rich in ghee,
O youngest one, lead him further toward greater wealth, toward the favor bestowed by the gods.
O Agni, grant him a share in glorious deeds; at every hymn being recited, grant him a share.
May he be dear to Sūrya, dear to Agni; may he prevail with what has been born and with those yet to be born.
O Agni, following you day after day, the sacrificers have secured all desirable treasures.
Seeking wealth through you, the desiring ones have opened the cow-filled stall.
Agni has been praised by the seers, the most gracious Vaiśvānara, the guardian of Soma.
We invoke the benevolent Heaven and Earth; O gods, bestow upon us wealth accompanied by heroic sons.
Born as the great Hotṛ-priest, pervading the firmament, he who sits among men has taken his seat in the lap of the waters.
He who was established as the sustainer of your vital powers, he is the protector of your person, the controller of riches for the one who serves you.
Worshipping him in the gathering place of the waters, they followed his tracks like one who has lost an animal;
seeking him with homages as he moved in secret, the wise Bhr̥gus, longing for him, found him.
Trita, the son of Vibhūvasu, seeking him, found him many times upon the head of the cow.
Born as one who increases prosperity within the dwellings, he, the youth, becomes the central point of the radiant realm.
The Usijs, with prostrations, have established the delightful Hotṛ-priest—the leader of sacrifices, who guides the rites forward—as the steward of the people;
they have placed among men the purifier as the bearer of oblations.
The foolish brought forward the great, victorious, wise one who destroys the forts—
the unborn embryo of the woods— bestowing their prayer upon him who has golden beard, like a courser that wins the prize.
Trita, supporting himself within the dwellings, sits enveloped within the womb;
from there, the friend of the people, having gathered [the powers], moves among men by means of his ordinances and restraints.
His are the ageless fires, the rudders of the dwellings, with glowing smoke, purifying;
white-shining, strengthening, restless, seated in the woods like winds, like Soma juices.
Agni bears forth his trembling tongue with wisdom over the expanses of the earth.
Men have established him as the purifying, joyous Hotṛ-priest, the most skilled in sacrifice, who shines brightly.
The Heaven and Earth brought forth that Agni, as did the Waters, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the Bhṛgus with their powers;
Mātariśvan and the gods fashioned him, the first one worthy of praise and worship for mankind.

You, whom the gods have established as the bearer of oblations, you who are much-desired and worthy of worship by men—O Agni, bestow strength upon the one who praises you on your path; for he who seeks the gods becomes glorious through many [ancient] precedents.
We have grasped your right hand, O Indra, seeking wealth, O Lord of treasures.
For we know you, O Hero, as the master of cattle; grant us wonderful, virile riches.
O you who possess excellent weapons, excellent power, and excellent guidance, the support of riches from the four oceans—
you, who are worthy of praise and hymn, the possessor of many boons, grant us wonderful, virile wealth!
O Indra, grant us wonderful, bull-like wealth— rich in sacred prayer, accompanied by the gods, vast, deep, broad-based, renowned as a seer, fierce, and overcoming adversaries.

O Indra, grant us wonderful, bull-like wealth— true, victorious, a hero among the wise, a conqueror, a seeker of riches, ever-increasing, most skillful, the slayer of Dasyus, and the breaker of forts.
O Indra, grant us wealth consisting of horses, chariots, and heroes— wealth in the hundreds and thousands— a brilliant,
bull-like treasure that brings a host of blessings, heroic sages, and the winning of light.
My thought goes forth toward Bṛhaspati, the sevenfold leader, the sage whose mind is fixed on the cosmic order;
he who, as an Aṅgiras, is to be approached with homage—may he grant us wonderful, virile wealth.
My yearning hymns, like envoys, go forth to Indra seeking his favor;
touching the heart and uttered by the mind, O Bull, grant us wondrous wealth.
O Indra, grant us that which I ask of you: a vast dwelling, peerless among men. May Heaven and Earth approve of this; bestow upon us wondrous, bull-like wealth.
I was the first lord of wealth; I win all treasures forevermore.
Living beings call upon me as they would a father; I distribute food to the one who offers oblations.
I am Indra, the dam; for Atharvan and Trita, I brought forth the cows from the serpent. From the Dasyus, I took away their manly strength, bestowing the cow-pens upon Dadhyanc and Mātariśvan.

For me Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the iron thunderbolt; in me the gods placed their will. My splendor is as difficult to overcome as that of the sun; they honor me for what has been done and for what is yet to be done.
I have struck down this cattle-rich, horse-rich, and golden beast, full of vital strength, with my arrow.
I bestow many thousands upon the donor, since the Soma juices, accompanied by hymns of praise, have exhilarated me.
I am Indra; I have never been defeated in battle for wealth, nor have I ever yielded to death at any time.
Pressing the Soma, do you entreat me for riches; O Pūrus, you shall suffer no harm in my friendship.

I struck down with my blow those two who were panting for Indra, who had raised their thunderbolt for battle; calling out to him, I struck them down with my weapon, speaking firm words, I, the one who does not bow, subdued those who offered homage.
I am one, and alone I overcome this one; I overcome two—what can three do? Like a threshing-floor, I strike down the multitude; why do these Indra-less enemies revile me?
I brought Atithigva to the Guṅgus; like nourishing food, I established him among the people as a conqueror of Vṛtra.
When Parṇaya was slain, or when Karañja was struck down, I won renown in the great battle for the slaying of Vṛtra.
Namī Sāpya has come forward for my nourishment and enjoyment; he has formed a friendship with me for the sake of seeking cattle, even doubly.
When I bestowed upon him a missile in the battles, then indeed I made him worthy of praise and fit for hymns.
In one of these two, Soma is seen within; the other stands revealed as a guardian. Desiring to fight the sharp-horned bull, the Deceiver stood bound within the vast expanse.
I do not violate the station of the Ādityas, the Vasus, or the sons of Rudra—the god among gods. They have fashioned me for auspicious power, unconquered, invincible, and unsubdued.
I have bestowed ancient wealth upon the one who praises me; I have made the sacred word (*brahman*) my own means of increase.
I have become the instigator for the sacrificer; in every battle, I am the witness against the non-sacrificer.
The creatures of heaven, earth, and the waters have placed me in the position of the deity named Indra.
I have taken for my own the two vigorous, swift bay steeds that move in different directions, and I have seized the bold thunderbolt for the sake of power.

I struck down Atka for the sake of the sage with my blows; I protected Kutsa with these aids. I am the smiter of Śuṣṇa with my weapon, he who did not yield the Aryan name to the Dasyu, as one yields it to Yama.
Like a father, I subdued the Vetasus for the sake of Kutsa’s assistance, and I delivered Tugra and Smadibha into his hands.
I became the sovereign of the sacrificer when I brought forth [the wealth] for Tuji, so that he might not be overcome by those who seek to assail his dear ones.
I subdued Mṛgaya for Śrutarvan when he did not follow my commands even in succession.
I made Veśa bow down before Āyu; I delivered Paḍgṛbhi as a slave to Savya.
I am he who, like the slayer of Vṛtra, crushed the Dāsa Bṛhadratha of Navavāstva;
when he was growing and spreading forth in due order, I fashioned him as a luminous realm on the far shore of the firmament.
I travel around the sun with my swift steeds, borne along with power by my coursers. When the human presser calls me to the robe of glory, I utterly subdue the Dāsa Kṛtvya with my blows.

I, the slayer of the seven, more powerful than Nahuṣa, have made Turvaśa and Yadu renowned by my might. I have subdued another who possessed a thousand powers, and I have caused ninety-nine mighty ones to grow.
I, the bull, sustain the seven flowing rivers that run swiftly over the earth;
I, the wise one, spread out the floods by my power, and through battle found a path for Manu’s sacrifice.
I have established within these [cows] that bright [milk], which not even the god Tvaṣṭṛ had established before;
the desirable milk in the udders, in the wombs, the honeyed sweetness, the invigorating Soma mixed with milk.
Thus has Indra, the Maghavan whose wealth is true, proclaimed himself among gods and men by his mighty deed;
all these, O Lord of Bay Steeds, O Lord of Power, do the swift ones praise as your own glorious deeds.
Sing forth for the great one who rejoices in the soma-juice, for Viśvānara,
the creator of all— Indra, whose victorious might, great renown, and manly valor both heaven and earth revere.
He indeed, the heroic Indra, when praised, is to be celebrated as a friend by a man like me;
O Lord of the Good, you take delight in all burdens, in deeds for the sake of booty, in Vṛtra, or in the waters, O Hero.
Who are those men of yours, O Indra, who strive for your refreshment and for your wealth-bestowing favor?
Who have urged you on toward heroic power, toward the mastery of the waters, and toward manly valor upon our own fertile fields?

O Indra, through the sacred word (*brahman*) you have become great; you have become worthy of sacrifice at all libations. You have become the shaker of men in every battle, and the supreme mantra for all people, O Lord of the All.
Now indeed, you are the superior one for those who delight in sacrifice; the people know your great protection.
Now indeed, you are the ageless one, and you shall grow; all these libations you have made efficacious.
All these libations you have made effective for yourself, O Son of Strength, which you have established.
For your choice and for the maintenance of the Law, there is the vessel, the sacrifice, the mantra, the sacred formulation, and the word raised up in prayer.
O Sage, those [songs] of yours which were fashioned as sacred prayers (*brahman*) at the pressing, for the bestowing of riches and treasures—
may they proceed with a mind toward the path of your favor, in the exhilaration of the pressed Soma juice.
Great was that womb, firm was it, enveloped by which you entered the waters;
O Agni Jātavedas, the one god beheld all your many forms, O deity.
Who has seen me? Which god was it who beheld my forms in their many aspects? O Mitra and Varuṇa, where do all the fire-sticks that lead to the gods dwell for me?
We sought you in many places, O Jātavedas, you who have entered into the waters and the plants, O Agni.
Yama perceived you, O you of brilliant luster, shining forth from within the ten intermediate regions.
O Varuṇa, I fled from the office of the *hotṛ* priest out of fear, lest the gods should appoint me to it here;
my bodies have entered into many forms, yet I, Agni, did not perceive this purpose.

Come, O Agni! Manu, seeking the gods and desiring sacrifice, has prepared the rite for you; do not dwell in darkness. Make the paths leading to the gods easy to traverse, and, being well-disposed, carry the oblations.
Agni’s elder brothers followed this purpose as a charioteer follows the path;
out of fear of that, O Varuṇa, you went far away, trembling like a wild ox before the archer’s bowstring.
We grant you an ageless life, O Agni, so that once you are harnessed, O Jātavedas, you shall not come to harm;
then, being well-disposed, O noble-born one, you shall carry the portion of the oblation to the gods.

O gods, grant me the fore-sacrifices and the after-sacrifices exclusively, and a strengthening portion of the oblation; grant me the fatness of the waters and the manhood of the plants, and may there be long life for Agni.

May the fore-offerings and the after-offerings be yours alone; may the portions of the oblation be full of vigor. O Agni, let this entire sacrifice be yours; may the four quarters bow down before you.
O All-Gods, instruct me how, having been chosen as the Hotṛ and having sat down here, I may think;
tell me my portion, how [I should act] for you, and by which path I shall carry the oblation to you.
I have sat down as the Hotṛ priest, the most skilled in sacrifice; all the gods and the Maruts impel me.
Day after day, O Aśvins, the office of Adhvaryu belongs to you; the Brahman is the kindling wood, and he becomes the oblation for you both.
Who indeed is this one who is the Hotṛ of Yama? Whom do the gods intend when they anoint him?
Day after day he is born, month after month; therefore the gods have established him as the bearer of oblations.
The gods have established me as the bearer of oblations, moving through many hardships without faltering.
May Agni, the wise one, arrange our sacrifice—five-pathed, threefold, and seven-threaded.
I shall worship you for immortality and heroic strength, so that, O gods, I may create wide space for you.
May I place the thunderbolt in the two arms of Indra, and then he shall conquer all these hostile armies.
Three thousand, three hundred, and thirty-nine gods have honored Agni;
they have sprinkled him with clarified butter, spread the sacrificial grass for him, and then seated him as the Hotṛ priest.

He whom we sought with our mind has arrived—he who knows the joint of the sacrifice and understands its parts. May he, the most excellent sacrificer, worship among the host of gods; for may he sit down within us, closer to us than we are.
The Hotṛ, the most excellent sacrificer, has been successful through his sitting; for he has looked upon the well-prepared offerings.
Let us sacrifice to the gods worthy of sacrifice; come, let us honor with clarified butter those who are worthy of praise.
He has made our feast for the gods successful today; we have found the secret tongue of the sacrifice.
He has arrived, fragrant and clothed in life; he has made our invocation of the gods auspicious today.
May I today perceive that first word of speech by which we gods may overcome the Asuras.
O eaters of strength, worthy of sacrifice, you five peoples, graciously accept my oblation!
May the five peoples enjoy my oblation—both those born of the cow and those who are worthy of sacrifice.
May the Earth protect us from earthly distress; may the intermediate space protect us from celestial distress.
Spinning out the thread, follow the light of the mid-region; guard the luminous paths fashioned by wisdom.
Weave the web without flaw for those who sing your praise; become Manu and bring forth the divine race.
O you who are worthy of Soma, fasten the axle-pins; prepare the reins and polish them.
Bring from both sides the chariot with its eight-seated seat, by which the gods led [Indra] to his beloved [Soma].
The stony river flows; hold fast to one another, stand up, and cross over, O friends!
Here let us leave behind those who were unpropitious; may we cross over toward auspicious strengths.

Tvaṣṭṛ, the most skillful of workers, knows all wondrous powers; bearing the most auspicious vessels for the drinking of the gods, he now sharpens his axe of goodly iron, wherewith Etaśa, the Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati), shall cut away.
O sages, now truly sharpen your axes with which you fashion the existent for the sake of immortality.
Knowing the secret places, perform the work by which the gods attained immortality.

They placed the maiden in the womb and the calf in the mouth, with a secret mind and a tongue; he, being well-disposed toward all things, striving to win through his efforts, gains victory as one who performs sacred acts.
O Maghavan, that fame of yours is truly great through your majesty, since the two worlds, terrified, called upon you.
You protected the gods and overcame the Dāsa’s power, O Indra, because you bestowed your aid upon this progeny.
When you went forth, Indra, increasing in body and proclaiming your powers among the people—that was but a trick of yours;
for those battles of which they speak, you have found no enemy today, nor indeed in the past.
Who indeed among the ancient seers has ever reached the limit of your entire greatness—
from which you brought forth both mother and father together from your own body?
Four are your divine names, O Mighty One, which are invincible; you indeed know them all, those by which, O Maghavan, you have performed your deeds.
You possess all treasures exclusively—those that are manifest and those that are hidden.
O Maghavan, do not frustrate my desire; you are the knower, O Indra, you are the giver.
He who placed light within light, who mingled honey with honey—
he, the maker of prayer, has uttered this dear and powerful hymn for Indra, a lofty song from Bṛhaduktha.

Far away is that secret name, turned away from you, which the two terrified ones invoked as you, the giver of vital strength. You propped up the earth and the sky in close proximity, O Maghavan, shining fiercely against your brother’s sons.
Great is that secret name, touching many, by which you brought forth what has been and what is to be;
the ancient light that was born, which is his beloved—into it the five beloved peoples have entered together.
He filled the two worlds and the intermediate space, and the five classes of gods, seven by seven, according to their seasons.
With his manifold light, which is both uniform and diverse in its movement, he looks out in thirty-four directions.

When you, O Dawn, shone forth as the first of the lights, by which you brought forth the nourishment of nourishment; that kinship of yours which is nearer than the further, and that great, singular sovereignty of yours, O Great One.
The gray-haired one has swallowed the young moon as he hastens in the assembly of many.
Behold the poetic power of the god through his greatness: he who was alive yesterday has died today.
By his own power, the mighty one, ruddy and fair-winged, who is great, heroic, and from of old without a nest;
whatever he has willed is indeed true and not in vain—he is the winner and giver of desirable wealth.
Through these [powers] the wielder of the thunderbolt received manly strengths and virile powers, by which he grew for the slaying of Vṛtra;
those gods who, through the greatness of the rite being performed, arose even before the rite was completed.
Performing deeds with his companion, possessing all vigor, slaying the revilers, all-seeing,
and swift-conquering— having drunk of the Soma and grown strong from heaven, the hero blew the Dasyus away in battle.
This is one [form] of yours, and another is beyond; enter into union with the third light.
Be gracious to our body in this union, beloved among the gods in the highest birthplace.
O vigorous one, may your body, leading your body [to the sacrifice], bestow what is desirable upon us and protection upon you.
Unassailed, for the support of the great gods, may you measure out your own light like [the sun] in heaven.
You are a prize-winner by your prize-winning power; O well-guided one, go to the heaven with a well-guided hymn.
Well-guided, follow the first true laws; well-guided, go to the gods; well-guided, follow the flight of the birds.
Even their fathers could not master their greatness; the gods placed creative power (*kratu*) within the gods. They encompassed all that they kindled, and it entered back into their very bodies.
With their powers, they have traversed the entire expanse of space, measuring out the immeasurable ancient abodes.
They have established all beings within their own bodies and have extended progeny in many directions.

In two ways the sons established the Asura, the finder of heaven, by means of the third act; the fathers placed their own offspring and their paternal heritage among the later ones, like a stretched-out thread.
Like a ship through the waters across the quarters of the earth, may he carry us by blessings past all difficulties.
Bṛhaduktha, by his greatness, has established his own offspring among both those who are near and those who are far.
May we not stray from the path, O Indra, nor from the sacrifice, we who possess the Soma;
may no enemies stand against us.
May we attain that which is the accomplisher of the sacrifice, the thread stretched out among the gods, when it has been offered with oblations.
We now invoke the mind with the Nārāśaṃsa Soma and with the hymns of the Fathers.
May your mind return to you for the sake of will, for skill, and for life, so that you may long behold the sun.
May the divine folk, our fathers, grant back our mind to us; may we be united with the company of the living.
O Soma, may we, bearing our minds within our bodies according to your ordinance, abide together with offspring.
O Yama, son of Vivasvat, that mind of yours which has gone far away to Vaivasvata—
bring it back to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
O mind, that which of yours has gone far away to heaven or to earth— that we bring back to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
O Mind, that which of yours has gone far away to the four-cornered earth, we bring that back to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
If your mind has gone far away to the four quarters of space, we bring it back to you here, that you may dwell and live.
O you whose mind has gone far away to the surging ocean, we draw it back to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
O you whose mind has gone far away to the rays of light and the heights, we cause that [mind] of yours to return here, so that you may dwell and live.
O Mind, that which has gone far away to the waters or to the plants, we bring it back to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
O Sūrya, that mind of yours which has gone far away to the Sun or to the Dawn— that we cause to return to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
O you whose mind has gone far away to the great mountains, we bring it back to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
This entire world that is yours, O Mind, which has gone far away— we cause it to return to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
Your mind that has gone far away to the furthest distances— we bring it back to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
Your mind, which has gone far away— to that which is past and that which is yet to be— we cause it to return to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
May life be further extended, renewed, as by two skillful charioteers of a chariot. Then Cyavāna has attained his goal with great power; may Nirṛti depart to a distance.
Let us now make a storehouse for wealth, and let us create food and manifold glories.
May our singer rejoice in all these things; may Nirṛti depart far away.
May we overcome our enemies with manly deeds, as the sky overcomes the earth, or as mountains overcome the plains.
Our singer has perceived all these things; may Nirṛti depart far away.
O Soma, do not deliver us over to death; may we yet behold the sun rising.
May our old age be set by the days; may Nirṛti depart far away from us.
O Asunīti, maintain the mind within us; extend our lifespan well for the sake of living.
Grant us delight in the sight of the sun; do you strengthen our bodies with clarified butter.
O Asunīti, bestow upon us again sight, again breath, and here give us enjoyment.
May we long behold the rising sun; O Anumati, be gracious to us for our well-being.
May the Earth give back our breath; may the divine Heaven, and the mid-air, give it back. May Soma restore our body, and may Pūṣan restore the path that is well-being.
May Heaven and Earth, the two young mothers of the Eternal Order, bring well-being to Subandhu;
may they carry away whatever blemish there is. O Heaven and Earth, let no harm whatsoever afflict you.

Down from the sky descend the medicines, by twos and by threes. Moving upon the earth, let the single one also bring away whatever blemish there is. O Heaven and Earth, remove the blemish; may nothing whatsoever cause you pain.
Indra, bring together the ox that draws the wagon of the daughter of Uśīnara;
may Heaven and Earth remove whatever blemish there is, and may no harm whatsoever afflict you.
Bearing our homage, we have come to the people of brilliant aspect, who are highly praised among the great ones.
[We invoke] the peerless, bestowing, brilliant, and ever-advancing chariot;
[we invoke] Bhajeratha, the lord of the virtuous.
He who, like a great bull, has surpassed men— whether armed with the spear or even without the spear—
in battle.
He under whose law Ikṣvāku prospers, wealthy and free from disease,
like the five tribes in heaven.
O Indra, maintain sovereign power among those who are peerless, like chariot-seats, so that you may be seen like the sun in the sky.
O Agastya, you have yoked the two ruddy steeds from the rivers;
O King, you have stepped down upon all the Paṇis who offer no gifts.
This is the mother, this is the father; this life-giver has arrived.
This is your path for crawling forth; O Subandhu, come, go out!
Just as they bind the yoke with a leather thong for the sake of support,
even so have I sustained your mind for life and not for death, and for your well-being.
Just as this great earth supports these lords of the forest,
so do I support your mind for life, not for death, but for safety and well-being.
From Yama, the son of Vivasvat, I have brought back the spirit of Subandhu,
that he may live and not die, but attain safety and well-being.
Downward blows the wind; downward the sun shines;
downward the cow yields her milk; let your ailment go downward.
This hand of mine is blessed; this hand of mine is more blessed. This hand of mine possesses all healing remedies; this hand is a propitious touch.
This indeed is the formidable prayer of Raudra, whose speech is praised, fashioned with wisdom and power within the conflict;
when he, acting as the most liberal giver among his parents, rescued the seven Hotṛs on the day of the Paktha-sacrifice.
Seeking to win for the sake of deceptive gifts, Cyavāna prepared the altar with the Sūdas;
Tūrvayāṇa, whose speech is most praiseworthy, poured forth the seed like a flood with his protection.
In whose invocations you two, like swift thoughts, win the sharp inspired hymns with your power;
he who, possessed of great manly vigor, has drawn his arrow from his hand toward the target.
When the dark one settled among the ruddy cows, I invoke you two, O Aśvins, sons of Heaven.
Accept my sacrifice; come to my food, you who have won it, and protect us from those who forget their vows.
He whose heroic deed was extended, who indeed struck down the manly [foe] as it was established;
he, the unassailable one, again drew back that which had been carried away from the maiden’s daughter.

When that which was to be done in the midst had arrived in the encounter, as the father made his desire for the young woman, they both, departing, left behind their thought-filled seed poured upon the ridge in the womb of the well-fashioned work.
When the Father, uniting with her, spilled his seed upon his own daughter upon the earth,
the gods, seeking the good, generated the sacred word (*brahman*) and fashioned Vāstoṣpati, the guardian of vows.
Like a bull, he cast forth foam in the battle; with steady mind, he went forward from there.
He moved like a step, like a sacrificial gift turned away; those dappled mares have not seized me.
Swiftly like a bearer, the one who makes the offspring hear sits near Agni as if naked at the udder;
he wins the fuel and wins the prize; he was born as the sustainer, overcoming with might.

Swiftly the Navagvas came to the friendship of the maiden, speaking the *ṛta* and joined with *ṛta*. Those of double strength who approached the guardian, though giving no sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇās*), desired to milk the unshakable [cow].

Swiftly [I seek] a newer friendship with the maiden; like a gift, I hasten toward the seed, the truth itself—that pure heritage of yours which they offered as the milk of the ever-yielding, ruddy cow.
When he says, "Awakened by the cattle, they have been separated behind," the singer, bestowing gifts, speaks as one who grants.
Through his wealth and lordship over riches, the singer, free from blemish, fashions all wealth and nourishment.
Now indeed his followers have come, sitting in many places, desiring to break through the seat of Nārṣada.
The foeless one has discovered what was hidden in the cave of Śuṣṇa, who is prolific with many offspring.
He whose name is Bharga, and whose gods have sat down in the threefold abode like the sun—he whose name is Agni and Jātavedas, O Hotṛ of Truth, hear us; as the guileless Hotṛ, listen to us!
And may those two Raudras, the radiant Nāsatyas, O Indra, be worshipped for my praise;
being gracious to the man who has trimmed the sacrificial grass, as they were to Manu, may the joyous ones, honored with offered food, be worshipped among the people.
This king, praised and extolled as a wise creator, the inspired singer crosses the waters by his own bridge.
He makes Kakṣīvat tremble, he makes Agni tremble, like the swift-running wheel of a steed.
He of double kinship, Vaitaraṇa, the sacrificer, seeks to milk the cow Sabardhu who yields no horse;
when he encompasses Mitra and Varuṇa with hymns and Aryaman with the highest protections.

A kinsman of that [sacrifice], a patron on high, a bestower of inspired thought, Nābhānediṣṭha speaks forth with longing. This is our highest kinship with him; indeed, was I not among those who followed after him? How many were they?
This is my navel; here is my dwelling place; these are my gods; here am I in my entirety. I am indeed the twice-born, the first-born of Cosmic Order (Ṛta); at my birth, the Cow milked this [world].
Then he, the delightful, radiant, and two-pathed one who dwells in the woods, has settled among these [trees].
When the mother has swiftly brought forth the firm, joy-increasing child, he stands erect like a row [of flames], like a youngling.
Then may the cows follow the example of the maiden of anyone who has sacrificed;
hear us, O possessor of splendid wealth, for you have grown strong through the truthful hymns of Āśvaghnī.
Now, O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, O lord of men, take note of us for the sake of great wealth;
protect our patrons and guard the wise singers, for they are blameless under your protection, O possessor of bay horses.

Then, when the two Kings go forth in the quest for cattle, the swift-moving one hastens to the singer, he who is eager for praise; for he has become their most beloved inspired seer—he shall carry them forward and also bring them across.
Now indeed, for the prosperity of this noble one, we approach you with spontaneous hymns; let us now seek that.
His son is swift, his horse is fleet, and you are a sage in the winning of glory.
If, for the sake of your friendship with us, you have accepted this hymn with reverence for our host—
that host in whom all songs are united, as many paths lead toward the giver of true wealth— then let him pay homage to the Goddess of Bounty.

Being praised with waters, accompanied by the gods, and well-befriended with homage and hymns, may he grow strong through our recitations and words; for now indeed the path is cleared by the milk of the ruddy cow.
O worshipful gods, be you indeed our great protectors for our aid, being of one mind— those who, moving apart, have brought us strength, and those who are the wise perceivers of all.

Those who, perfected by sacrifice and the sacrificial fee, attained the friendship of Indra and immortality—to you, O Aṅgirases, may there be prosperity! O wise ones, accept me, the descendant of Manu.
O Fathers, you who drove forth the wealth of cattle and by the Eternal Law split Vala after a full year—may long life be yours, O Aṅgirases; accept me, O wise ones, as a man of the human race.

O Aṅgirases, you who by means of cosmic order (ṛta) caused the sun to ascend to heaven and spread out the earth, the mother; may there be good offspring for you—O wise ones, accept me, the son of Manu.
This one speaks sweetly for you from the center of your house; O sons of the gods, O seers, listen to that!
May there be excellent Brahman-hood for you, O Aṅgirases; O wise ones, accept the descendant of Manu.
The seers were indeed diverse, they whose inspiration was profound;
they were the sons of Aṅgiras, and they were born from Agni.
Those who were born from Agni, the multiform ones from heaven—
the Navagva, the Daśagva, the best of the Aṅgirases— along with the gods, he bestows great wealth.
With Indra as their ally, the worshippers have released the stall rich in cattle and horses;
those eight-eared mares, giving me a thousand, have won glory among the gods.
May this man now truly be born; may he grow like a young shoot, he who at once bestows for a gift a thousand [cattle] and a hundred horses.
No one can reach him, as if attempting to grasp the ridge of heaven;
the sacrificial fee of Sāvarṇya has spread out like the Sindhu river.
And the two Dāsas, Smaddiṣṭi and Goparīṇasā, served [him];
Yadu and Turvaśa also bestowed gifts upon him.
May the leader, the giver of thousands, not fail; may Manu’s sacrificial fee go forth, striving together with the sun.
May the gods prolong the life of Sāvarṇi, in whom we, unwearied, have won the prize.
May those gods who, from afar, desire kinship, who, pleased by Manu, attend the generations of Vivasvat,
and who sit upon the sacred grass of Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa— may they speak in our favor.
For all your names, O gods, are worthy of homage and worship, and they are worthy of sacrifice;
you who were born from Aditi, from the waters, and from the earth—listen here to my call!
For those whom Mother Aditi, vast as the mountain, pours forth honeyed milk and nectar from heaven;
for those Ādityas, who are strengthened by hymns, who bear the bull, and whose dreams are auspicious—rejoice in them for our well-being!
Beholding men, never blinking, and worthy of worship, the gods have attained lofty immortality.
With chariots of light, possessing the power of a serpent’s illusion and free from sin, they clothe themselves in the height of heaven for our well-being.

Those sovereign kings who, increasing prosperity, have come to the sacrifice and established their dwelling in heaven unassailed—invite them hither with reverence and well-fashioned hymns: the great Ādityas and Aditi, for our well-being.
O All-Gods, who among men offers you the hymn that you enjoy, as many of you as there are?
O you of mighty birth, who shall prepare for you the sacrifice so that it may carry us across distress to well-being?

To whom Manu first offered the oblation with kindled fire and with his mind through the seven Hotṛ-priests—O Ādityas, grant us protection free from fear; make for us easy paths and fair ways for our well-being.
Those who rule over the world, the wise ones, the thinkers of all that is stationary and moving—
O gods, protect us today from committed and uncommitted sin for our well-being.

In battles we invoke Indra, who is easy to call upon, the deliverer from distress, the well-doing divine host; we invoke Agni, Mitra, Varuṇa, Bhaga for our gain, and Heaven and Earth and the Maruts for our well-being.
May we ascend for our well-being the divine ship— well-oared, sinless, and leakless— the good protector Earth, the faultless Heaven, Aditi who provides excellent refuge and excellent guidance.
O all you worshipful ones, speak in our favor for our protection; save us from the assault of the evil-minded.
With a true invocation of the gods, we call upon you, O gods who hear us, for your aid and for our well-being.
Drive away disease, drive away every lack of sacrifice, and keep far from us the malice of the malevolent enemy.
O gods, keep hatred far from us; grant us broad protection for our well-being.
Unharmed, that mortal prospers in every way; he is born again through his offspring according to the cosmic law (dharman).
O Ādityas, whom you lead with your excellent guidance across all difficulties for our well-being.
O Gods, that chariot which you protect in the struggle for booty, which you, O Maruts, protect in the battle of heroes when wealth is staked—
may we mount that early-advancing, victorious, and unassailable chariot, O Indra, for our well-being.
May there be well-being for us on our paths and in the desert wastes; may there be well-being in the waters and in the sunlit assembly.
May there be well-being for us in the wombs that bring forth sons; O Maruts, bestow upon us well-being for the sake of wealth.

Welfare indeed is the best on the distant path, that which is full of wealth and approaches what is desirable. May she protect us at home and in the wilderness; may she be well-disposed toward us, with the gods as our guardians.
Thus has the wise son of Plate increased you all, O Ādityas and Aditi;
the ruling heroes have been praised by the immortal Gaya, as has the divine folk.
In what way, on whose path among the gods who hear our names, shall we meditate? Who will be gracious? Which one will grant us joy? Which one will turn toward us with protection?
The powers of will act as wills; thoughts in the hearts long for them; the seekers fly toward the quarters of space.
No other comforter is found besides these; my desires have been directed toward the gods.
O men, with my song I praise Narāśaṃsa, Pūṣan, and Agni who is not to be hidden, kindled by the gods;
Sūrya and Māsa, the two moons, Yama in heaven, Trita, Vāta, Uṣas, Night, and the Aśvins.
How does the poet, the loud-voiced one, [prosper]? With what song is Bṛhaspati magnified by well-fashioned hymns?
May Aja Ekapād hear our invocation with his well-invoked singers; may Ahi Budhnya hear it at the call.
At the birth of Dakṣa, in the rite when he was invoked, you seek to win over the two kings, Mitra and Varuṇa;
Aryaman, whose paths are unassailable and who possesses many chariots, acts as the seven-priest among beings of diverse forms.
May all those coursers, who hear our invocation and run their measured course, hear our call;
they who, like winners at the sacrifice of wisdom, have by themselves won great wealth in the battles, winning thousands.
With hymns of praise, bring forth Vāyu, who yokes his chariot, and Purandhi, and Pūṣan, for the sake of friendship.
For they, being of one mind and one intent, follow the will of the god Savitṛ under his impulse.
We invoke for our protection the thrice-seven flowing rivers, the great waters, the forest trees, the mountains, and Agni;
we call upon Kṛśānu, the archers, Tiṣya, Rudra among the Rudras—the divine Rudra—from his common dwelling place.
May Sarasvatī, Sarayu, and Sindhu with their waves come with great protection; may the mighty, swelling rivers come.
O divine Waters, mothers, makers of prosperity, purify us; sing for us a song of milk rich in ghee and honey.
May Mother Bṛhaddivā hear our word, and Tvaṣṭṛ with the gods and their wives as father;
may R̥bhukṣan, Vāja, Rathaspati, and Bhaga protect us—the delightful praise of him who exerts himself.
Delightful to behold like a dwelling rich in food, auspicious is the praise of the Rudras, the Maruts.
May we be glorious among the people through our cattle; O Gods, may we ever be united with nourishment.
O Maruts, Indra, and gods—Varuṇa and Mitra—you who have granted this prayer to me, cause it to swell like a cow with milk; will you not carry my songs upon your chariot?
O Maruts, will you not surely take heed of us, as we are your kinsmen?
Wherein we first come together at the navel [of the world], there may Aditi establish our kinship.
For those two great divine Mothers, Heaven and Earth, worthy of sacrifice by virtue of their birth, have come from here to the gods;
both support the two worlds with their sustainings, and together with the Fathers, they pour forth abundant seeds.
May this invocation reach every desirable thing; Bṛhaspati is the most praiseworthy devotion.
Where the pressing-stone, dripping honey, is raised on high, there the wise have caused their thoughts to resound with hymns.

Thus the seer, loud-voiced, knower of the cosmic order (*ṛta*), desiring wealth and longing for riches, has here— through hymns and prayers— the inspired singer (*vipra*) Gaya caused the celestial generations to swell.
Thus has the wise son of Plate increased you all, O Ādityas and Aditi.
You lords, the immortal divine host, have been praised by the mortal Gaya.
Agni, Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, Vāyu, Pūṣan, and Sarasvatī, acting in harmony;
the Ādityas, Viṣṇu, the Maruts, the lofty heaven, Soma, Rudra, Aditi, and Brahmaṇaspati.

Indra and Agni, lords of the virtuous, impelled together by each other’s bodies, sharing the same dwelling, have filled the great mid-air with their might at the slaying of Vṛtra; Soma, adorned with clarity, stirs up his own greatness.

For them, the great and unassailable ones who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*), I, knowing the *ṛta*, send forth hymns of praise. May they, who possess wonderful wealth and whose course is in the waters, grant us boons for our glorification, being well-disposed toward us.
With their might, they have propped up the sun, the mid-regions, the luminous spheres, heaven and earth, and the broad ground.
Like nourishing powers, magnifying [the sacrifice], the gods—those bounteous patrons—extol the wise man as their benefactors.

Give your service to Mitra and Varuṇa, the two sovereign kings who, being worshipped, do not neglect the devotee in their minds; whose high domain shines by the power of cosmic law, and whom both heaven and earth encompass as their protectors.
The cow who goes around the path to the place of sacrifice, yielding milk, observing her vows from below— she,
proclaiming herself to Varuṇa the donor, shall serve the gods with the oblation for Vivasvat.
Dwelling in heaven, with Agni as their tongue, increasing the cosmic Order (*ṛta*), they sit pondering the womb of Order.
Having propped up the sky, they have brought the waters by their might; having generated the sacrifice, they have measured out its bodies.
The two parents dwelling around, born of old, abide together in the womb of *ṛta* as co-dwellers;
Heaven and Earth, acting in harmony with Varuṇa, cause the great, ghee-rich milk to swell for the mighty one.

Parjanya and Vāta, the bulls, the possessors of the soil; Indra and Vāyu, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—we invoke the Āditya gods and Aditi, those who are on earth, those who are in heaven, and those who are in the waters.

We invoke Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, and the Ṛbhus who are honored; the two divine Hotṛ-priests, and Uṣas for our well-being; Bṛhaspati, the wise consumer of Vṛtra, the Soma of Indra, and we seek them as winners of wealth.
They generated the sacred word, the cow, the horse, the plants, the forest trees, the earth, the mountains, and the waters;
raising up the sun in heaven, O bounteous ones, they spread abroad the Aryan laws over the earth.
O Aśvins, you delivered Bhujyu from distress; you restored Śyāva, the son of Vadhrimatī.
You gave Kamadyū to Vimada, and you released Viṣṇāpū for Viśvaka.
The daughter of the thunderbolt, the one-footed Tanyatu, the Unborn, the upholder of heaven, the Sindhu, and the waters of the ocean—
may all the gods hear my words, along with Sarasvatī, together with inspired thoughts and the wisdom that fulfills the city.
May all the gods, together with their insights, with Purandhi, the worshipful, immortal ones who know the cosmic order (*ṛta*) of Manu—
those who bestow gifts, who protect, who find the light of heaven— enjoy our songs, our prayer, and our hymn of praise.
Vasiṣṭha has praised the immortal gods who have extended themselves over all worlds. May they grant us wide space today; and do you [gods] protect us always with your blessings.
I invoke for our well-being the gods of lofty renown, the light-makers who are wise in the sacrifice;
those all-knowing ones who have increased further, with Indra as their chief, the immortals who strengthen the cosmic order (*ṛta*).

Impelled by Indra and directed by Varuṇa, those who have attained a share of the light of the sun—within the host of Maruts, in the assembly, let us fix our thought; in their bounty, the wise have generated the sacrifice.
May Indra with the Vasus protect our household; may Aditi with the Ādityas grant us refuge.
May the god Rudra with the Rudras be gracious to us; may Tvaṣṭṛ with the divine wives (gnās) quicken us toward prosperity.
Aditi, Heaven and Earth, the great *ṛta*, Indra and Viṣṇu, the Maruts, and the lofty sky—these gods, the Ādityas, we invoke for protection; the Vasus, the Rudras, and Savitṛ of wondrous deeds.

May Sarasvat with his prayers, Varuṇa whose laws are firm, Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, Mahiman, Vāyu, and the Aśvins— the immortal, all-knowing makers of sacred prayer— grant us a triple-layered protection from distress.
The sacrifice is a bull; may the worthy of worship be bulls; may the gods be bulls, and the preparers of the oblation be bulls.
May Heaven and Earth, the observers of cosmic order, be bulls; may Parjanya be a bull, and the singers of praise be bulls.

O Agni and Soma, bulls, for the winning of booty I address you, the bulls who are praised by many—those bulls whom the [pious] have worshipped with sacrifice to the gods; may you two extend to us a triple-layered protection.

The Kṣatriyas who uphold their vows, who perfect the sacrifice, who dwell in the great heaven, and who are the glory of the rites— these Agnis, the offerers of oblations, who follow the Truth and are free from guile, released the waters in the conquest of Vṛtra.
Generating heaven and earth according to their sacred laws, [the gods] filled the waters, the plants, and the holy trees;
they pervaded the mid-air and the light for our protection, and the gods fashioned their bodies according to their will.

The upholders of heaven, the R̥bhus with skillful hands, Vāta and Parjanya of the great thundering bull, the waters and the plants—may they further our prayers; may Bhaga, Rāti, and the prize-winning steeds come to my call.
May the ocean, the rivers, the dust, the mid-air, Aja Ekapād, the thundering roar, and the surging flood; may Ahi Budhnya hear my words, as well as all the gods and my wise patrons.
May we, as men, be yours for the feast of the gods; lead our sacrifice forward in the right way.
O Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus, you bounteous givers, quicken these prayers being recited.
I follow rightly the path of Truth, following the two divine Hotṛ-priests, the first appointed.
We pray to the Lord of the Field, our neighbor, and to all the immortal gods who are never heedless.
The Vasiṣṭhas have raised their voice like fathers, praising the gods like seers for our well-being. Like affectionate kinsmen coming to meet a desire, O gods, shake down wealth upon us!
Vasiṣṭha has praised the immortal gods who have extended themselves over all worlds. May they grant us wide space today; and may you [gods] protect us always with your blessings.
Our father discovered this seven-headed, lofty hymn, born of the Eternal Law (*ṛta*). Indeed, the son of all people, Ayāsya, brought it forth while reciting the liturgy for Indra.

Praising the *ṛta*, meditating upon the straight path, the sons of Heaven, the heroes of the Asura, the Aṅgirases— establishing the inspired sage as their station— conceived the first form of the sacrifice.
Like swans, his companions cried out repeatedly as Bṛhaspati cast off the stone-made bonds; he bellowed toward the cows, and knowing the way, he sang aloud and praised them.
With two [steps] he helped [the cows], with one [step] he drove forth the cows that stood hidden behind the dam of falsehood;
Bṛhaspati, seeking light in the darkness, brought up the ruddy cows and indeed disclosed the three [worlds].
Having shattered the western stronghold, Bṛhaspati cut through the three [fortresses] together from the ocean; he found the Dawn, the Sun, the Cow, and the Light, like the thundering sky.
Indra split Vala, the guardian of the milch-cows, with a roar as if with his hand;
seeking the milk-mixture with those whose hands were smeared with sweat, he made the Paṇi weep and stole away the cows.
With his true, radiant companions who seek wealth, he split open the cave that held the cattle.
Brahmaṇaspati, with his bull-like boars sweating from the heat of the *gharma* vessel, attained the treasure.
With truthful minds, seeking the cows, they urged the Lord of Cattle with their prayers.
Bṛhaspati, by means of those who avert mutual reproach and who are his own allies, released the ruddy cows.
Exalting him with auspicious hymns as he roars like a lion in the assembly,
may we rejoice after Bṛhaspati, the bull, the victorious one, in every battle for the sake of heroes.
When he won the prize of every form and ascended to heaven and the higher dwellings,
they, being many and bearing light in their mouths, strengthened Bṛhaspati, the bull.
Make our prayer come true, O Giver of Life; for you protect even the lowly singer with your own inherent ways.
Let all adversaries fall behind us; hear this, O Heaven and Earth, you who encompass all.
By his greatness, Indra split asunder the head of the great ocean, of Arbuda;
he slew the serpent and set the seven rivers flowing. O Heaven and Earth, together with the gods, protect us!
Like birds swimming in the water, guarding themselves, like the thundering sounds of a rain-cloud, like waves breaking from the mountains, the jubilant hymns have roared toward Bṛhaspati.
Approaching with the cattle, the descendant of Aṅgiras led Aryaman away like Bhaga;
like Mitra among the people, he anoints the husband and wife, O Bṛhaspati, as one urges swift horses to the prize in battle.

Bṛhaspati, having overcome them from the mountains, drove out the cows— those who are helpful, hospitable, vigorous, desirable, golden-hued, and of blameless form— just as one winnows grain from the chaff.
Sprinkling the source of the nectar of Truth, casting down the sun like a meteor from the sky,
Bṛhaspati, lifting the cows from the rock, split the skin of the earth as if with water.
With light he drove away the darkness from the mid-air, as the wind blows away the scum from the water; Bṛhaspati, having seized them from Vala, has driven out the cows, as the wind drives the cloud.

When Bṛhaspati shattered the strength of the reviling Vala with fires and glowing hymns, he seized what was surrounded as if by teeth with the tongue; he laid bare the hidden stores of the ruddy cows.

Bṛhaspati indeed discovered that secret name of these lowing cows which was hidden in the cave; having burst them open like the egg of a bird, he himself brought forth the ruddy kine from the mountain.
They beheld the honey fastened by a stone, like a fish dwelling in shallow water; Bṛhaspati, having split it apart with a roar, drew it forth as one takes a cup from a tree.

He found the Soma, he found the sun, he found Agni; with his song, Bṛhaspati drove away the darkness. From Vala, who had the form of a cow, he extracted [the wealth] as one extracts marrow from a joint.
Like forests robbed of their leaves by winter frost, Vala lamented for the cattle because of Bṛhaspati;
he performed an act that cannot be imitated nor undone, since the sun and moon rise from each other in alternation.
Like a dark horse with white spots, the Fathers adorned the sky with constellations;
they placed darkness in the night and light in the day; Bṛhaspati split the mountain and found the cows.
We have offered this homage to the one belonging to the clouds, who roars repeatedly after many [days].
May that Bṛhaspati bestow vital strength upon us through cattle, through horses, through heroic sons, and through men.
Auspicious is the sight of Agni Vadhryaśva’s; his guidance is lovely, and his approaches are delightful.
When the clans, as good friends, kindle him at the forefront, he, offered with clarified butter, awakes and flashes forth in brilliance.
Clarified butter is the strengthener of Agni Vadhryaśva; clarified butter is his food, and clarified butter is his delight.
Offered with clarified butter, he has spread himself far and wide; like the sun, he shines, he whose libation is ghee.
O Agni, that face of yours which Manu and Sumitra kindled—that very same one has been kindled anew here.
As such, shine forth with wealth; enjoy our songs; burst open the prize of victory; and bestow glory upon us here.

O Agni, whom Vadhryaśva, having been invoked, kindled in former times—be pleased with this [offering]. Be a protector of our household and a guardian of our bodies; protect this gift of ours which belongs to you.
Be glorious, O Vadhryaśva, and our protector; let not the malice of men overcome you. Like a bold hero, a shaker, yet a good friend—now I shall proclaim the name of Vadhryaśva.
You have won together the treasures of the plains and the mountains; you have conquered the Dāsa and Ārya Vṛtras.
Like a bold hero, O Agni, you, the shaker of men, shall overcome those who attack us in battle.
Long-threaded, large-oxed is this Agni; he has a thousand stallions and a hundred leaders, skillful and wise.
Resplendent among the resplendent, being cleansed by men, he shines brightly among the pious who possess good friends.
In thee, O Jātavedas, is the cow easy to milk; like one who never fails, she yields her abundance equally.
Thou, O Agni, art kindled by men who possess sacrificial gifts, by the well-disposed Sumitras, and by those who seek the gods.
Even the immortal gods, O Jātavedas, proclaimed your greatness, O son of Vadhryaśva, when the human tribes came to consult you; you conquered with the men who were strengthened by you.
Like a father carrying his son on his lap, Vadhryaśva served you, O Agni; taking pleasure in his fuel, O youngest one, you protected him even from those who were previously powerful.

Evermore has Agni conquered the enemies of Vadhryaśva with his men who have pressed the Soma; O you of brilliant luster, you have burnt up even the common assembly and struck down even the powerful one who increased in strength.

This Agni of Vadhryaśva, the slayer of Vṛtra, kindled from of old, is to be invoked with homage. As such, O son of Vadhryaśva, trample upon our enemies—whether they be strangers or kinsmen—who stand defiant against us.
O Agni, enjoy this fuel of mine; welcome the ladle dripping with ghee at the place of the *iḷā*.
Stand upright upon the height of the earth during the auspiciousness of the days, O wise one, for the sacrifice to the gods.
May Narāśaṃsa, the most divine among gods, come here by the foremost path of the gods with his horses of every form;
may he, the most godlike, prepare the sacrificial food for the gods upon the path of Truth with our homage.
Men, bearing oblations, perpetually invoke Agni for the office of messenger.
With most-swift horses and on a well-rolling chariot, bring the gods here; sit down as the Hotṛ priest.
May the god-loved sacrificial grass spread out crosswise, long in its length, becoming fragrant for us.
O divine *barhis*, with a mind free from anger, worship the longing gods, with Indra as their chief.
Touching the ridge of heaven or expanding further by the measure of the earth, O yearning Doors, hold wide with your greatness; you who seek the chariot, support the divine chariot.
May the two goddesses, Dawn and Night, the daughters of Heaven, well-fashioned, sit down in their proper place. May the desiring gods sit upon your wide, auspicious lap, O longing ones.
Upright is the pressing-stone, kindled is the great Agni; the dear abodes are in the lap of Aditi.
O two priests, the household-priests, most wise in this sacrifice, do you two win for us wealth through the offering.
O three goddesses, sit upon this wide sacrificial grass; we have made it comfortable for you.
Like Manu, may they enjoy the well-placed sacrifice and the oblations—the goddess Iḷā, whose path is ghee.
O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, whatever beauty you have brought forth, and since you became the companion of the Aṅgirases—
being wise, desiring it, and a giver of wealth rich in jewels, do you worship at the path of the gods.
O Lord of the Forest, having bound [the victim] with a cord, bring it to the path of the gods, you who are wise.
May the god make it savory and prepare the oblations; may Heaven and Earth favor my invocation.
O Agni, bring Varuṇa here for our sacrifice; bring Indra from heaven and the Maruts from the mid-air.
Let all the worshipful ones sit upon the sacred grass; let the immortal gods rejoice in the Svāhā-call!

O Bṛhaspati, that which was the first, the very tip of speech, when they sent it forth assuming names— that which was their most excellent and stainless part, hidden in the secret cave, has been made manifest through their love for it.
Where the wise have fashioned speech with their mind, purifying it like groats through a sieve—there friends recognize their friendships; auspicious is the mark placed upon their speech.

By means of sacrifice, they followed the track of Speech; they found her entered among the seers. Having brought her forth, they distributed her in many places; the seven singers celebrate her together.
One man, though seeing, has not perceived Speech; another, though hearing, does not hear her.
But to yet another she has revealed her body, as a longing wife, well-adorned, reveals herself to her husband.
Moreover, they say that in friendship he drinks deeply; they do not urge him on even in contests for prizes.
He wanders with the illusion of one who has no cow; he has heard speech that is without fruit and without blossom.
He who has abandoned a companion who knows the way—of him there is no share even in what is spoken. Whatever he hears, he hears in vain; for he does not know the path of righteous action.
Friends with eyes and ears have become unequal in the swiftness of their thoughts;
some appear like ponds reaching to the mouth or the armpits, while others look as if they have just emerged from bathing.

When Brahmins, as friends, perform the sacrifice together with the speed of thought fashioned by the heart, it is then that they distinguish you through their insights; the knowers of sacred formulation (brahmans) move about, each according to his own understanding.
Those who move neither hither nor thither, who are neither true Brahmins nor performers of the Soma-pressing—
they, having taken hold of speech with its evil aspect, weave a web like that of a spider, lacking all understanding.
All friends rejoice in the friend who has returned with glory, victorious in the assembly;
for he is the remover of their sin, the winner of nourishment, and is well-disposed for the prize of the contest.
One sits nourishing the abundance of the *ṛc*s; another sings the *gāyatra* song upon the *śakvarī* verses;
one speaks as a *brahmán* the knowledge of all that has been born; and yet another measures out the proportions of the sacrifice.
Let us now proclaim with inspired praise the generations of the gods,
so that one may behold them in a future age while these hymns are being recited.
Brahmaṇaspati forged these together like a smith; in the earliest age of the gods, existence was born from non-existence.
In the first age of the gods, being was born from non-being;
thereafter the quarters of space were born, and from him who stands with feet turned upward.
Earth was born from Uttānapad; from Earth the quarters were born;
Dakṣa was born from Aditi, and from Dakṣa, Aditi was born in turn.
For Aditi was born as she who is your daughter, O Dakṣa;
after her were born the auspicious gods, the kinsmen of immortality.
O gods, when you stood there in the waters, firmly grasping one another,
a thick cloud of dust rose up from that place as if from dancers.
When you gods, like ascetics, caused the worlds to swell,
you brought forth the sun that was hidden within the ocean.
Of the eight sons of Aditi who were born from her own body, she approached the gods with seven; she cast Mārtāṇḍa away.
With her seven sons, Aditi went forth to the former age;
for the sake of progeny, she brought back Mārtāṇḍa from death.
You were born fierce for victorious power, delightful, most mighty, and full of great pride;
even the Maruts strengthened Indra on that occasion when his mother bore him as her most excellent son.
The female serpent, though seated in malice, was overcome by your ways; they have strengthened Indra with many praises.
Like embryos enveloped in darkness, those beings have emerged from the deep gloom by means of his great step.
Lofty are your feet; you go forth, and the strengths that are here have increased you.
O Indra, you held a thousand hyenas in your mouth; may you turn the Aśvins hither.
Swiftly you come to the sacrifice from every side; O Nāsatyas, bring us for friendship.
O Indra, you held the Vasāvyā; the Aśvins, O hero, bestowed thousands of gifts.
Rejoicing according to the cosmic order, O Indra, with your vigorous friends, you went toward the purpose for the sake of progeny;
for by means of these wondrous powers you approached the Dasyu and cast down the dark mists and the glooms.
Even those of the same name, the destroyers, Indra struck down for him as he did for the Dawns;
with your lofty and devoted friends you went forth, and you struck down their very heart-firm foundations.
You slew Namuci, the one eager for the sacrifice, making him a captive for the seer;
you made pleasant paths for Manu, like roads leading to the gods for easy travel.
You have filled these names; O Indra, as the Lord, you hold them in your hand.
The gods rejoice in your power; you have made the trees to have their roots above.
That wheel of his which is set within the waters—may he indeed find sweetness for it.
That udder which was fixed upon the earth, you placed its milk within the cows and the plants.
"When they say, 'He has come from the horse,' I consider him to be born of *ojas*;
he has come from *manas* and has taken his stand in the dwellings; from whence he was born, Indra alone knows."
Like birds with beautiful wings, the Priyamedha seers have approached Indra with their supplications.
Dispel the darkness, fill our vision, and release us like those bound in a snare.
Whether seeking to win the Vasus through prayer or through sacrifices to Heaven and Earth;
or those who are like swift steeds possessing wealth in the contest for booty; or those who, being themselves well-heard, have granted a famous boon to the one who prays.
The Asura reached their invocation; with a mind seeking glory, he kissed the earth. Where the gods look on for well-being, they act like the sky with their own desirable boons.
This is the song for these immortals who yearn for treasure in its full perfection; may they, who bring to fulfillment both our devotion and the sacrifice, bestow upon us complete wealth.
Those who long for Indra praise that deed of yours, they who desire to burst open the stall rich in cattle—
those who wish to milk the great, lofty, thousand-streamed earth, the mother of many sons, all at once.
O Śacīs, bring Indra to our aid— he who is unbowed, who subdues those who attack us,
the lord of the Ṛbhus, the bounteous one worthy of fair hymns, who as the possessor of many cattle bears the manly thunderbolt.
Whatever he has accomplished most abundantly in the past, the Vṛtra-slayer Indra has filled with his names.
The powerful Lord of Might has become manifest; whatever we desire him to do, may he perform that.
O Waters, the poet shall proclaim your supreme greatness at the dwelling-place of Vivasvat.
For you have flowed forth in thrice-seven streams; the Sindhu has surpassed the other flowing rivers by her might.
Varuṇa carved out the paths for you to travel, O Sindhu, when you rushed toward the prizes.
You flow along the slope from the earth over its ridges, as you rule over the foremost of these moving creatures.
His roar reaches to heaven above the earth; he raises up his infinite vigor with his radiance.
Like rains from a cloud, the showers thunder forth as the Sindhu flows, bellowing like a bull.
Toward you, O Sindhu, the roaring rivers flow like mothers toward their young, like milch-cows with their milk;
like a warrior-king, you lead the two banks, when you reach the forefront of these rushing torrents.
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī, and Paruṣṇī, accept this hymn of mine;
O Asiknī, Marudvṛdhā, Vitastā, Ārjīkīyā, and Suṣomā, listen well!
First, joined with the Tṛṣṭāmā, Susartu, Rasā, and that Śvitnyā for the journey;
O Sindhu, you travel on one chariot with the Kubhā, the Gomatī, the Krumu, and the Mehatnu—by all these rivers you flow.
Straight-moving, dappled, and bright, she carries her greatness across the expanses and the regions;
the Sindhu, undeceived, the most active of the active ones, is like a wonderful mare, beautiful and fair to behold.
The Sindhu has fine horses, beautiful chariots, and splendid garments; she is golden, well-fashioned, and full of vigor.
The youthful maiden is woolly and possessed of silken finery; the fortunate one clothes herself in that which increases sweetness.

Sindhu has yoked his easy-moving chariot drawn by horses; with it he shall win the prize in this contest. For the greatness of this unassailable one, who possesses his own glory and is overflowing with power, is celebrated as vast.

I draw you hither at the dawning of strengths; O Maruts, anoint Indra and the two worlds—heaven and earth—so that both day and night may be our companions and, as openers of the way, grant us wide space at every session.
Therefore, press out that most excellent libation; like a horse guided by the hand, the pressing-stone is for the presser.
For it provides the noble one with conquering manly power, so that he may overcome great wealth through his swift steeds.

For this very libation of his has opened the waters, just as in the past he established a path for Manu. In the ocean of cows belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ, which was adorned with horses, they have established sacrifices within the sacrifices.
Strike away the treacherous Rākṣasas; hold back Destruction and ward off the assault.
Press out for us wealth consisting of all heroic sons, O stones that favor the gods; bring forth the song of praise!

Even from heaven I sing praise for you who are more powerful than the most powerful, more swift in deed than even Vibhvan; for you who seize the Soma more eagerly than Vāyu, and who provide food more abundantly than Agni.
May our glorious pressing-stones resound as the juice is pressed, with a heavenly voice, divine and celestial,
where the men milk the desirable honey, making a noise all around, vying with one another.
The chariot-borne stones press out the Soma; they milk forth its juice for the seeker of cattle.
Men milk the udder for the purpose of pouring it out; like men preparing oblations, they cleanse [the stone] with their mouths.
O stones, you have become men of skillful hands who press the Soma for Indra;
may every excellence of yours go to the divine realm, and every treasure of yours to the earthly one who presses the juice.
Like rain-drops from the clouds, sprinkle wealth with our speech; like those possessing oblations, let us perform the sacrifices of the wise.
Like a priest for the excellent Maruts, I have praised this host of theirs, as is their due, so that it may be glorious.
For the sake of glory, the youths have prepared their ornaments through many nights, like the host of Maruts.
The sons of Dyaus have come forth like goats; those Ādityas have grown strong like steeds.
Those who by their own greatness have surpassed heaven and earth, like the sun emerging from the clouds;
they are like powerful heroes worthy of praise, like noble youths who destroy the foe and look toward the heavens.
At your foundation, as if on the course of the waters, the great earth trembles and yields;
this all-nourishing sacrifice approaches you. O you who provide nourishment, come hither together like those seated at a common feast.
Like yoked horses at the poles with their reins, you are radiant with light at the dawns;
like falcons, you are self-glorious destroyers of enemies; like travelers on a journey, you are far-reaching and pervasive.
When you Maruts come forth from afar, you who know of the great treasure in the secret place,
O Vasus— granting what is to be won, drive away our enemies even from a distance.

The mortal man who, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, stands firm during the rites and offers gifts to the Maruts—he shall possess wealthy vigor and excellent heroes; may he remain under the protection of the gods.
For they are the ones worthy of sacrifice at the rites, the helpers, most beneficent by their name Āditya;
may they protect our prayer that speeds on the chariot, they who take delight in the great journey of the sacrifice.
Like inspired poets with their hymns, they are skillful in sacred study; like gods who delight in sacrifice, they are seekers of sleep.
Like kings, they are brilliant and beautiful to behold; like blameless youths among the people, they are free from blemish.

Like Agni in their brilliance, with golden ornaments upon their breasts, like winds they are self-yoked and swift in their aid; like the eldest brothers who discern the way, they are excellent leaders; like Soma-draughts, they provide good protection for the one who walks the path of Truth.
Like winds that are shakers and swift-moving, like the tongues of fires, they are radiant;
like armored warriors, they are vigorous; like the praises of the fathers, they are bounteous givers.
Like the spokes of chariots joined at the hub, like victorious heroes gazing toward heaven,
like wooing youths sprinkling clarified butter, they are like singers chanting hymns with perfect praise.
Like the swiftest horses, they are fleet; like chariot-borne lords, they are bounteous givers;
like waters flowing with downward streams, they move forward; like the Aṅgirases, they possess all forms through their hymns.
Like pressing-stones are the wise ones, sons of Sindhu; like mountains they are ever-shattering. Like playful children with good mothers, they shine with brilliance like a great host on its march.
Like the rays of the dawns, they have adorned the sacrifice; like those seeking splendor, they have shone forth with their ointments.
Like flowing rivers, they have moved with glittering spears; like those from afar, they have measured out the leagues.
O Gods, Maruts, increasing us, make us fortunate and well-endowed with jewels, we who are your praisers;
take heed of our hymn and our friendship, for from of old your gifts of treasure have been ours.
I have beheld the greatness of this Great One, the Immortal among mortal clans.
His jaws, spread apart, come together; insatiable, devouring, they consume much.
His head is placed in secret; his eyes are turned away; insatiable, he eats the woods with his tongue.
They bring offerings for him with their feet, with hands outstretched in reverence among the people.
Seeking his mother’s secret place further away, he creeps over the wide plants like a child; he has found him, glowing and licking the raw flesh within the lap of the earth.
This truth I proclaim to you both, O Heaven and Earth: as soon as he is born, the embryo devours his two parents.
I, a mortal, do not understand the god; Agni alone is wise, for he is truly the one who possesses true insight.
He who provides us with food eagerly, who offers oblations of clarified butter and ghee, and nourishes us—for him you look out with a thousand eyes; O Agni, you face every direction from all sides.
O Agni, what offense against the gods have you committed that you abandon us? I ask you now, for I am ignorant.
Playing or not playing, the tawny one has eaten and has cut [the food] joint by joint, like a knife cutting a cow.
The forest-born one has harnessed his horses that move in all directions, held fast by straight-driving reins.
The well-born Mitra, together with the Vasus, has shared out [the portions]; increasing, he has attained success through his joints.
Agni bestows a steed that brings booty; Agni [bestows] a hero, renowned and steadfast in action.
Agni moves between the two worlds (Heaven and Earth), anointing them; Agni [bestows] a woman, a wise one who bears heroes in her womb.
May the fuel of Agni Apnasvat be auspicious; Agni has entered the two great worlds.
Agni impels the solitary warrior in battles; Agni shatters many Vṛtras.
Agni indeed protected that Karṇa as he grew old; Agni burned Jarūtha out from the waters.
Agni rescued Atri within the heated cauldron; Agni brought Nṛmedha together with offspring.
Agni has bestowed wealth adorned with heroes; Agni [bestows] the seer who wins thousands.
Agni has extended the oblation to heaven; the domains of Agni are distributed in many places.
The seers invoke Agni with hymns; men, pressed in their journey, call upon Agni.
Birds flying through the mid-air praise Agni; Agni goes around thousands of cattle.
The human tribes that have sprung from Manu and Nahusha invoke Agni;
Agni [follows] the Gandharva path of Order; Agni’s pasture is established in the clarified butter.
For Agni the R̥bhus fashioned a prayer; we have uttered a great hymn of praise to Agni.
O Agni, youngest one, protect the singer; O Agni, win for us through sacrifice great wealth.
The Rishi who sat down as the Hotṛ-priest, offering up all these worlds, our Father— he,
seeking wealth through his prayer and providing the first shelter, entered into the later generations.
What was the foundation, what was the starting point, and how was it? From what did Viśvakarman, the all-seeing, producing the earth, unfold the sky by his greatness?
With eyes on every side and a face on every side, with arms on every side and feet on every side,
the one God, generating heaven and earth, fans them together with his arms and with his wings.
What was the wood, and what was that tree, from which they fashioned forth heaven and earth? O wise ones, ask this with your mind: upon what did he stand while supporting the worlds?

O Viśvakarman, those stations of yours which are highest, those which are lowest, and these which are intermediate—teach them to your friends at the oblation, O self-dependent one; strengthening yourself, perform the sacrifice for your own body.
O Viśvakarman, growing strong through the oblation, sacrifice yourself to the earth and to heaven!
Let other people around us be confounded; here, let the bountiful one be our patron.
Today, for our protection in the struggle for booty, let us invoke Viśvakarman, the Lord of Speech, who is swift as thought.
May he, the source of all well-being and the performer of righteous deeds, graciously accept all our invocations and grant us his aid.
The Father of the eye, wise in his mind, generated these two [worlds] dripping with ghee as they bowed down;
when their former boundaries were established, then indeed Heaven and Earth spread themselves out.
