Viśvakarman, the wise and far-reaching, the Ordainer and Disposer, the supreme Seer—
whose desired offerings rejoice in nourishment where they say there is one beyond the seven seers.
He who is our father, our progenitor, and our ordainer, who knows all abodes and all worlds;
he who alone is the giver of names to the gods—to him, as the one to be questioned, all other beings go.
The ancient seers, like singers in great number, offered worship to him for wealth— those who,
when the unformed and formed realms were settled, brought these beings into existence.
Beyond heaven, beyond this earth, beyond the gods and the Asuras—
what was that first embryo which the waters received, wherein all the gods beheld one another?
The waters first received that embryo wherein all the gods assembled;
it was fixed upon the navel of the Unborn, in which all worlds abide.
You do not know him who generated these [worlds]; something else has come between you.
Enveloped in mist and idle chatter, the reciters of hymns wander about, seeking only their own sustenance.
O Manyu, wielder of the thunderbolt, he who has honored you nourishes all power and strength in succession;
with you as our ally—made of force, powerful, and possessing might—may we overcome both the Dāsa and the Ārya.
Wrath is Indra; Wrath indeed was the god; Wrath is the Hotṛ, Varuṇa, and Jātavedas.
The human tribes that exist offer praise to Wrath. O Manyu, being in harmony with our fervor, protect us.
Come hither, O Manyu, you who are stronger than the strong; with fervor as your ally, strike down our enemies.
You are the slayer of foes, the slayer of Vṛtra, and the slayer of Dasyus; bring all treasures to us.
For you, O Manyu, possess overwhelming power; you are self-existent, radiant, and the subduer of adversaries.
Belonging to all people, victorious, and full of might, bestow strength upon us in the battles.
Being without a share, O wise one, I have gone away from you, the powerful, through your power.
Therefore, O Manyu, I have provoked you in my lack of resolve; come to me in your own form to grant me strength.
I am here for you; come toward me, O Victorious One, all-sustaining, facing me.
O Manyu, wielder of the thunderbolt, turn toward me; let us two slay the Dasyus, and be mindful of your kinship.
Come toward me; be on my right side, and then we two shall strike down many Vṛtras.
I offer you the foundation, the first of the honeyed [draught]; let us both drink the first [portion] silently.
O Manyu, with you as our companion on the same chariot, may the bold Maruts, exulting and shattering [the foe],—
men with sharp arrows, whetting their weapons, and possessing the form of fire— advance against us.
Like Agni, O Manyu, blaze forth with splendor; as our victorious army-leader, be present when invoked, O Conqueror!
Having slain the enemies, distribute their wealth; measuring out your power, drive away those who oppose us.
Overpower the adversary against us, O Manyu! Breaking, crushing, and utterly destroying, go forth against the enemies!
Your fierce array has indeed been irresistible; O sole-born one, you who are self-controlled, bring them under your control.
You alone, O Manyu, are invoked by the many; sharpen every tribe for battle.
With you as our ally, we, whose luster is unimpaired, raise a brilliant shout for victory.
O Manyu, like Indra, the unopposed maker of victory, be our protector here.
We celebrate your beloved name, O Conqueror; we know that source from which you have arisen.

O Vajra, O Arrow, born together with power, you, the overcomer, bear superior might. O Manyu, invoked by many, through our ritual wisdom, be present with us in strength; let there be a gathering for the great prize.
May both kinds of wealth, gathered together and brought into union, be granted to us by Varuṇa and Manyu.
Let the enemies, conceiving fear in their hearts, lie prostrate, utterly defeated.
By truth is the earth supported; by the sun is the sky supported. By cosmic order (*ṛta*) the Ādityas stand firm; Soma is established in heaven.
By Soma the Ādityas are strong; by Soma the earth is great;
moreover, Soma is placed in the lap of these constellations.
One thinks he has drunk Soma when they grind the plant;
but of that Soma which the Brahmins know, no one at all eats.
O Soma, you stand protected by various arrangements and guarded by the Bṛhatī verses;
hearing the pressing-stones, you remain there, for no earthly being consumes you.
O God, when they drink you up, from that you swell again;
Vāyu is the guardian of the Soma, and the month is the form of the year.
Raibhī was the female attendant; Nārāśaṃsī was the one who led her home. With the Gāthā, Sūryā’s auspicious garment, so well-adorned, was brought forward.
Thought was her pillow, sight her ointment;
heaven and earth were the bridal chest when Sūryā went to her husband.
The hymns were the cross-pieces; the *kurīra* was the head-ornament; the meter was the crest-lock. The Aśvins were the suitors for Sūryā; Agni was the leader of the procession.
Soma became the suitor; both Aśvins were the groomsmen, when Savitṛ gave Sūryā, who was consenting in her mind, to her husband.
The mind was her cart-pole, and the sky was the canopy;
the two bright ones were the draft-oxen when Sūryā went to her husband’s home.
Your two oxen, yoked by the *Ṛk* and *Sāman*, are the two *Sāmans* here;
your two wheels were the sense of hearing, and your path was in heaven, moving to and fro.
Pure are your two wheels as you go; the vital breath is the axle, firmly fixed.
Sūryā, ascending her mind-made chariot, has gone forth to her husband.
The bridal procession of Sūryā has gone forth, which Savitṛ sent away;
on the Aghā days the cattle are slaughtered, and she is carried around between the two Arjunī stars.
When you two, O Aśvins, having inquired, came with a three-wheeled vehicle as the bridal procession for Sūryā, all the gods recognized that deed of yours; Pūṣan, the son, chose you as his parents.
When you two, O Lords of Splendor, went to Sūryā for her choosing, where was one of your wheels, and where did you stand for the sake of the assigner?
O Sūryā, two of your wheels the Brahmins know according to the seasons; but that one wheel which is hidden, only those who see clearly know it.
To Sūryā, to the gods, to Mitra, and to Varuṇa—
to those who are wise regarding all that has come into being— I have rendered this homage.
These two move one after the other by means of their creative power; like two playing children, they go around the sacrifice.
One looks upon all beings; the other, ordaining the seasons, is born again.
Ever new he becomes as he is born; as the banner of the days, he goes at the forefront of the dawns.
Arriving, he distributes his portion to the gods; the moon extends long life.

O Sūryā, ascend the *sukiṃśuka* tree, the *śalmali*, which is multiformed, golden-hued, well-rolling, and has beautiful wheels; ascend to the world of immortality and prepare a pleasant bridal procession for your husband.
Arise from here, for she has a husband; with reverence and songs I implore Viśvāvasu.
Seek another woman who is manifest and dwells among her fathers; that is your portion by birth—be aware of it.
Arise from here, O Viśvāvasu; we bow before you with praise. Seek another woman who is in heat; unite her as a wife with her husband.
May the paths be thornless and straight by which our friends go to choose a bride.
May Aryaman and Bhaga lead us together; O Gods, may the lordship of the household be well-governed.
I release you from the noose of Varuṇa, with which Savitṛ, the kindly one, bound you.
In the womb of Cosmic Order, in the world of well-performed deeds, I establish you, unharmed, together with your husband.
From here I release her, not from there; I make her well-bound from that side.
O bounteous Indra, so that she may be possessed of good sons and be fortunate.
May Pūṣan lead you from here by the hand; may the Aśvins carry you away on their chariot.
Go to the house so that you may be the mistress of the home; as one who has power, may you speak at the assembly.

May what is dear to you here be fulfilled through offspring; in this house, be watchful for the duties of the household. Unite your body with this husband; thus, may you both speak at the assembly until old age.
She becomes blue and red; the attachment of the *kṛtyā* is revealed.
Her kinsmen prosper, while her husband is bound in fetters.
Give away the woolen garment; distribute wealth among the Brahmins.
This sorcery has become footed and enters the husband as a wife.
The body becomes unlovely and pale with this wretched sin,
when the husband seeks to cover his own limb with the garment of the bride.
Those wasting diseases that follow the bride from her people to her bright bridal procession—
may the worshipful gods lead them back again to the place from which they came.
May the highwaymen who lie in wait not find the husband and wife;
may they pass over the difficult path by easy ways, and may their enemies flee away.
Auspicious is this bride; come together and behold her.
Having bestowed good fortune upon her, depart now and go back to your homes.
This is harsh, this is bitter; like a bone, like poison, it is not for eating.
Only that Brahmin who knows Sūryā deserves the bride-price.
The carving, the cutting up, and furthermore the slicing—behold these forms of Sūryā; yet the Brahman purifies them.

I take your hand for the sake of good fortune, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband. Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi—the gods have given you to me for the state of a householder.
O Pūṣan, send forth that most auspicious woman upon whom men sow their seed;
she who, longing for us, spreads her thighs apart, and upon whom we, longing, may cast our member.
For you, in the beginning, they led Sūryā around together with the bridal procession;
O Agni, give the wife back to her husbands along with offspring.
Agni has given back the wife with life and with splendor;
may he who is her husband live for a hundred autumns, possessing long life.
Soma first obtained you; Gandharva obtained you next;
Agni was your third husband; the fourth is born of man.
Soma gave [her] to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave her to Agni;
and Agni has given me both wealth and sons, as well as this woman.
Stay right here; do not be parted. May you both enjoy the full span of life, sporting with sons and grandsons, rejoicing in your own home.
May Prajāpati beget offspring for us; may Aryaman anoint us for long life.
Without ill fortune, enter the world of your husband; be auspicious to our bipeds and auspicious to our quadrupeds.
With eyes not terrible, do not be a slayer of your husband; be auspicious toward the cattle, well-disposed, and full of luster.
A mother of heroes, loving the gods, and pleasant—be a source of blessing to us, to our bipeds, and to our quadrupeds.
O bounteous Indra, make this woman rich in sons and fortunate;
bestow ten sons upon her, and make her husband the eleventh.
Be a sovereign queen over your father-in-law; be a sovereign queen over your mother-in-law; be a sovereign queen over your husband’s sister; be a sovereign queen over your brothers-in-law.
May all the gods anoint our two hearts together; may the waters anoint them together.
May Mātariśvan, Dhātṛ, and the Goddess Deṣṭrī likewise unite our two hearts.
For they have flowed forth from the presser; they did not consider Indra to be a god—at that time when Vṛṣākapi, my friend, took delight among the riches of the noble one. Indra is superior to all.
O Indra, you run far away, past the distress of Vṛṣākapi;
indeed, you find nothing else for the drinking of soma. O Indra, you are superior to all.
What has this Vṛṣākapi done to you, this tawny beast, that you are now jealous of him? Or perhaps it is the nobleman’s flourishing wealth; O Indra, you are superior to all.
O Indra, may the dog that seeks out boars now bite this Vṛṣākapi whom you, O Indra, protect as a dear friend—even in his ear; for Indra is superior to all.
The monkey has defiled those dear and well-fashioned things of mine that were clearly displayed.
I shall surely rend his head; may I not be an easy path for the evildoer. Indra is superior to all.
No woman has been more beautiful than I, nor more skilled in dalliance; no one has surpassed me in agility, nor can raise her thighs higher. Indra is superior to all.
O Mother, O easily won one, it will surely come to pass as I say:
my thighs, O Mother, my hips, and my head seem to tingle all over; Indra is superior to all.
O fair-armed one, O lovely-fingered one, O broad-chested one, O broad-hipped one! Why, O wife of a hero, do you threaten Vṛṣākapi? Indra is superior to everything.
This malicious man regards me as if I were childless;
yet I am the mother of heroes, the wife of Indra, and have the Maruts as my friends. O Indra, you are superior to all.

In former times, the woman went to the common sacrificial feast or the assembly; now, as the ordainer of the Eternal Order, the heroic mother of Indra is exalted as the consort of Indra. Greater than all is Indra.
Among these women, I have heard that Indrāṇī is most fortunate;
for her husband shall never die of old age, nor even later. Indra is superior to all.
O Indrāṇī, I have no pleasure without my friend Vṛṣākapi, whose dear oblation of water goes to the gods; Indra is superior to all.
O Vṛṣākapi’s wife, O wealthy lady, you who have good sons and a good daughter-in-law!
Indra shall eat your bulls, your dear oblation that brings all things to fulfillment; Indra is supreme over all.
"For fifteen bulls they cook for me all at once, even twenty;
and I eat fatness indeed; they fill both my flanks. Indra is superior to everyone."
Like a sharp-horned bull bellowing in the midst of herds, O Indra, this churning-drink is a joy to your heart; it is that which the seeker presses for you. O Indra, you are superior to all.
He does not possess power whose member hangs limp between his thighs;
he alone possesses power whose hairy member expands as he sits. Indra is superior to all.
He does not master him whose hairy member quivers as he sits;
he indeed masters him between whose thighs the penis hangs limp. Indra is superior to all.
O Indra, this Vṛṣākapi found a slain wild beast;
he found a sword, a new slaughter-trough, and a cauldron piled with fuel upon the hearth—Indra is superior to all.
Here I go, looking out and discerning between the Dāsa and the Ārya; I drink of the one who presses the simple juice, and I have gazed upon the wise one. O Indra, I am superior to all.
The desert and the place of slaughter—how many *yojanas* apart are they?
O Vṛṣākapi, come home to our more nearby houses; Indra is supreme over all.
Come back again, Vṛṣākapi; let us two arrange for our well-being.
You who go to your home by the path that destroys sleep—you, O Indra, are superior to all.
When you two, O Vṛṣākapi and Indra, went northward to the house—where was that beast so full of wealth? To whom did it go, the one that brings joy to people? Indra is superior to all.
Parśu by name, the daughter of Manu, gave birth at once to twenty sons.
It was a blessing for her that her womb pained; Indra is superior to all.

I anoint the slayer of demons, the vigorous one; I approach for protection the most extensive friend. Sharpening himself with our sacred rites, Agni, kindled, may he protect us from harm by day and by night.
O Jātavedas, kindled with flame, touch the sorcerers with your iron fangs;
seize the fools who worship false gods with your tongue, and having torn apart the flesh-eaters, cast them into your mouth.
O you who know both, set down your two rows of teeth, you who are destructive, sharpening both the lower and the upper;
and as you travel through the mid-air, O King, seize the sorcerers with your jaws.

O Agni, fashioning arrows with sacrifices, sharpening their points with speech and coating them with thunderbolts—pierce the sorcerers in the heart with these; break their arms as they turn against you.
O Agni, split open the skin of the sorcerer; let the destructive thunderbolt slay him with its heat.
O Jātavedas, crush his joints; let the flesh-eating, flesh-craving [fire] tear apart what has been mangled.
O Jātavedas Agni, whomever you now see standing or moving about,
or whoever is flying through the paths of the mid-air— pierce him with your arrow, sharpening it as an archer.
And, O Jātavedas, snatch away what has been seized from the sorcerer who holds it with his spears.
O Agni, blazing forth, strike him down first; let the ravening vultures devour him as he is raw-flesh-eating.
Speak here, O Agni, which one it is—the sorcerer who does this;
seize him with your fuel, O youngest one, and deliver him to the eye of the one who beholds men.
O Agni, with your sharp eye protect the sacrifice; O wise one, lead it forward toward the Vasus.
Let not the sorcerers deceive you, O watcher of men, as you burn fiercely against the injurious demons.
O watcher of men, look out for the *rakṣas* among the people; crush its three points.
O Agni, burn through its ribs with your heat; tear up the root of the sorcerer in three ways.
Let the sorcerer go three times into your snare, O Agni, he who destroys the Truth with falsehood.
O Jātavedas, thundering with your flame, strike him down before the very eyes of the one who praises you.
O Agni, bestow that eye upon the singer, with which you may see the hoof-smiting sorcerer; like Atharvan, with divine light, burn down the truth-despising, mindless one who causes harm.
O Agni, whatever curse a pair utters today, or whatever harsh speech the singers produce, and whatever arrow is born from the wrath of the mind— with that, pierce the sorcerers in their hearts.
Crush the sorcerers with your heat; O Agni, crush the *rakṣas* with your flame.
Crush the worshippers of false gods with your radiance, burning fiercely against those who subsist on life-breath.
May the gods strike down the wicked man today; may harsh curses return upon him.
May arrows reach the vital organs of that stealer by word; may the sorcerer fall into the snare of everyone.
O Agni, the sorcerer who anoints himself with human flesh, who [anoints himself] with the flesh of a horse,
or who carries off the milk of the cow— tear off their heads with your fiery heat!
The milk of the cow that comes once a year—let no sorcerer, O watcher of men, consume it!
O Agni, whoever should desire to satiate himself with the first-milked cream, pierce him in his vitals from the front with your flame.
O sorcerers, drink the poison of the cattle! May the evil-doers be cut off from Aditi. May the god Savitṛ deliver them over; may they lose their share of the plants. May they be defeated.
From of old, O Agni, you have crushed the sorcerers; the *rakṣases* have never conquered you in battles.
Burn up the flesh-eaters together with their roots; let them not escape your divine missile.
O Agni, protect us from below and from above; protect us from behind and also from the front.
May those unaging and most fierce flames of yours, glowing against the one who intends evil, consume him.
From behind, from before, from below, and from above, O King, as a seer protect us with your poetic wisdom.
O friend, lead your friend to old age, for you, the ageless and immortal Agni, are ours among mortals.
O Agni, O powerful one, we place you around us like a fortress— you, the inspired sage, of bold appearance, the slayer of those who act with treachery, day after day.
Burn up the treacherous ones with poison; O Agni, consume the Rākṣasas with your sharp flame and with spears tipped with fire.
O Agni, burn up the pairs of *yātudhānas* and *kimīdins*;
I sharpen you, the undeceivable one, O inspired sage, with my prayers; remain ever watchful.
O Agni, with your flame, crush the flame [of the enemy] from every side;
shatter the strength and the heroic power of the Yātudhāna and the Rakṣas.
The oblation-drinking, ageless [Agni], who finds the light of heaven, is offered into the sky-touching fire as a welcome guest.
For his support, for the sake of the world, and for the maintenance of the cosmic order, the gods have spread themselves out according to their inherent power.
The world was swallowed and hidden by darkness; when Agni was born, the sun became manifest.
The gods, the earth, the sky, and the waters took delight in his friendship, as did the plants.
Impelled now by the gods worthy of sacrifice, I shall praise Agni, the ageless and vast,
who with his radiance has stretched across this earth and heaven, and has pervaded both the worlds and the mid-air.
He who was the first Hotṛ, beloved by the gods, whom they chose and anointed with clarified butter—
he, Agni Jātavedas, made the winged, the moving, and the crawling world firm.

O Jātavedas Agni, since you have taken your stand upon the summit of the world together with the realm of light, we impel you with our thoughts, songs, and hymns; thus you became worthy of sacrifice, filling both worlds.
Agni becomes the head of the earth at night; from him the sun is born as it rises in the morning.
Indeed, he moves swiftly and knowingly through this wondrous power of those worthy of sacrifice, even through the waters.
He who is visible by his greatness, kindled and shining with light,
born from heaven— into that Agni all the gods, the protectors of their own bodies, offered oblations with the hymn of praise.
First the gods generated the *sūktavāka* and then Agni, and then the oblation; he became their sacrifice that protects the body. Him Heaven knows, him Earth knows, and him the Waters know.
The Agni whom the gods brought forth, in whom they offered all the worlds—
by his flame, straightening himself, he heated this earth and heaven with his greatness.
For by means of praise, the gods generated Agni in heaven with their powers, he who fills both worlds. They made him threefold for the sake of existence; he ripens the plants of every form.
When the worshipful gods placed this Sūrya, the son of Aditi, in heaven;
when the two wandering ones became a pair, then indeed all living beings beheld him.
For the sake of the entire world, the gods made Agni Vaiśvānara the banner of the days;
he who has spread out the shining dawns and uncovers the waters by dispelling the darkness with his flame.
The wise, worshipful gods generated Vaiśvānara Agni, the ageless one—
the ancient, unerring, moving star, the powerful and lofty overseer of the spirit.
We address with hymns Agni Vaiśvānara, the seer who shines forever;
he who by his greatness has encompassed the two wide worlds, the god both from below and from above.
I have heard of two paths for the fathers: that of the gods and that of mortals.
Along these two, all this moving world comes together—that which lies between the father and the mother.
The two joined ones bear him as he moves, born from the head and fashioned by the mind; facing all beings, he stands watchful, crossing over, radiant.
Where the lower and the higher speak together, which of us two, who know the sacrifice, understands?
The friends have been able to reach the common feast; they have attained the sacrifice—who will declare this?
How many fires are there? How many suns? How many dawns? And how many waters? O fathers, I do not speak to you in jest; I ask you, O seers, for the sake of knowledge.
As much as the face of the Dawn, O Mātariśvan, when the fair-winged ones clothe themselves [in light],
so much does the Brāhmaṇa bestow upon the sacrifice as he sits down below the Hotṛ-priest.
I shall praise Indra, the most heroic, who by his greatness has pushed apart the luminous realms and the ends of the earth;
he who, supporting the people with his aids, has filled them and surpassed the rivers in majesty.
May that Sūrya, like Indra, turn around his broad expanses like the wheels of a chariot;
he has struck down the black darkness with his brilliance, like a flowing stream that does not stand still.

Sing forth for him this common, unremitting prayer—new and peerless—a prayer that reaches from the earth to heaven, he who, like the ridges of a mountain, has distinguished the births of the noble ones; Indra does not seek a friend in vain.
For Indra, I have sent forth songs with unrestrained flow, like waters from the depths of the ocean;
he who, by his powers, has propped apart the earth and heaven on all sides, as if with an axle through two wheels.

With his fury stirred, impetuous in onset, roaring, vigorous, armed with the *śaru* weapon, and drinking the dregs—Soma [overcomes] all plants and forests; no counter-measures have ever deceived Indra from his side.
Neither heaven and earth, nor the desert, nor the mid-air, nor the mountains have contained Soma when he flowed;
when his wrath is directed against someone, it shatters the firm and breaks even the solid.
He struck down Vṛtra as an axe fells trees; he shattered the fortresses and dug out the rivers. He split the mountain like a new jar; Indra brought forth the cows with his own companions.
O Indra, wise one, you indeed cut through those crooked things as a sharp sword severs joints;
you strike down those men who violate the law of Mitra and Varuṇa, and thus harm their friend as if he were a companion.
Those of evil intent who violate Mitra, Aryaman, the *saṃgir* (the confederates), and Varuṇa— O bull Indra,
sharpen your fierce, manly, and ruddy weapon against those enemies.
Indra rules over heaven; Indra rules over the earth; Indra is the lord of the waters, and Indra indeed of the mountains.
Indra is the lord of the prosperers, and Indra of the wise; Indra is to be invoked in times of security and in times of exertion.
Indra has surpassed you, O Vṛtra, from the days that have passed, from the mid-air, and from the reservoir of the ocean;
he has surpassed the expanse of the wind, the ends of the earth, the rivers, and all inhabited lands.
Like the banner of the glowing dawn, let your insatiable weapon fly forth, O Indra.
Like a stone hurled from heaven, pierce the deceitful enemies with your most scorching heat.
The months followed him, as did the forests, the plants, and the mountains;
both heaven and earth cried out in longing after Indra, and the waters followed him as he was being born.
When indeed, O Indra, will that manifestation of yours be known, when you shatter the seeking demon?
When those who betray their friends lie scattered upon the earth like cattle at the slaughter, separated from one another by that [dark] night?

O Indra, those who have extended themselves against us as enemies, the arrogant and violent hosts—let those foes be overtaken by blinding darkness; may the nights be filled with brilliant light for us.
For many indeed are the libations of men that have gladdened you, the prayers of the praising seers.
Hearing this joint invocation with favor, come hitherward, passing beyond all who sing your praise.
Thus, O Indra, may we enjoy your ever-new favor;
may we, the Viśvāmitras, singing your praises, find refuge through your protection even now, O Indra.
We invoke for our good fortune the bountiful Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the acquisition of booty—
the fierce one who listens, who comes to our aid in conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras, and who is the winner of riches.
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet;
having pervaded the earth on all sides, he stood beyond it by the measure of ten fingers.
The Person alone is all this—whatever has been and whatever is to be; moreover, he is the lord of immortality, that which grows by means of food.
Such is his greatness, and the Puruṣa is even greater than this. All beings constitute one quarter of him; his three quarters are the immortal in heaven.
With three quarters the Puruṣa rose upward; one quarter of him remained here again. From there he strode out in all directions toward that which eats and that which does not eat.
From him Virāj was born; from Virāj was born Puruṣa. Once born, he extended beyond the earth, both behind and before.
When the gods performed the sacrifice with the Puruṣa as the oblation,
spring was its clarified butter, summer its fuel, and autumn its offering.
They sprinkled that sacrifice, the Puruṣa born in the beginning, upon the sacrificial grass;
with him the gods, the Sādhyas, and the Ṛṣis performed the sacrifice.
From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) was gathered;
from it he fashioned those animals—those belonging to Vāyu, as well as those of the forest and those of the village.
From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the Ṛg-verses and the Sāman-chants were born;
from it the meters were born, and from it the Yajus-formulas were produced.
From him were born the horses, and whatever animals have two rows of teeth;
from him indeed were born the cows, and from him were born goats and sheep.
When they divided Puruṣa, into how many parts did they arrange him? What was his mouth, what were his two arms, what were his thighs, and what are his feet called?
The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya was made from his arms;
that which was his thighs became the Vaiśya; and from his feet the Śūdra was born.
The moon was born from his mind; from his eye the sun was born;
from his mouth Indra and Agni were born; from his breath Vāyu was born.
From his navel the intermediate space arose; from his head the sky evolved;
from his feet the earth and from his ears the quarters; thus they fashioned the worlds.
Seven were its enclosing sticks, and thrice seven were the fuel-sticks made,
when the gods, performing the sacrifice, bound Puruṣa as the victim.
With sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; those were the first ordinances. Those great ones attained the firmament where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide.
He, the domestic lord, being awakened by those who keep watch, is kindled in the house at the place of *iḷā*, seeking nourishment.
The Hotṛ-priest of every oblation, worthy of choice, all-pervading, far-shining, he is a good friend to him who seeks his friendship.
He, of lovely splendor, has taken refuge in every house as a guest, in every forest like a swift hero;
as one who belongs to all people, he does not disdain any person; as one who belongs to the clans, he dwells among every clan.
O Agni, you are most skillful through your skills, most wise through your wisdom; you are a seer through your seer-like power, knowing all things.
As the Vasu among the Vasus, you alone rule over all that heaven and earth nourish.

Knowing it well, O Agni, you have sat down upon your seasonal womb, rich in ghee, at the place of Iḷā. Your movements have become manifest like those of the dawns; they are stainless like the rays of the sun.
Your splendors, like the lightning of the rain-cloud, have shone forth in various ways like the banners of the dawns—
when, released upon the plants and the forests, you yourself gather food for your mouth.

The plants have received him as their timely embryo; the waters, the mothers, have generated him as Agni. Both the trees and the creepers bring forth that same one alike, and they do so perpetually while bearing him within.
Fanned by the wind and impelled according to thy will, when thou spreadest abroad swiftly devouring the food,
thy undecaying hosts, O Agni, strive to burn it as if they were separate chariot-riders.
Agni, the maker of wisdom, the accomplisher of the sacrifice, the invoker, the most pervasive thought—him alone they choose for the small oblation and him likewise for the great; none other than you.
O Agni, here the wise ones, seeking you, choose you as the Hotṛ-priest at the assemblies,
when the god-seeking men, bearing oblations and having spread the sacrificial grass, present the offerings to you.
O Agni, yours is the office of the Hotṛ; yours is the seasonal office of the Potṛ; yours is the office of the Neṣṭṛ; you are the Agnīdh for the one who follows the Truth.
Yours is the office of the Praśāstṛ; you perform the duties of the Adhvaryu; you are both the Brahman and the Lord of the House in our home.

O Agni, for that mortal who offers to you, the immortal, fuel with wood or with the preparation of an oblation—you become his Hotṛ; you go on your mission as messenger; you speak in praise, you sacrifice, and you act as the Adhvaryu.
These thoughts, these words from us, these *ṛc*-verses, songs, and beautiful hymns have come together for him.
Seeking wealth for the wealthy Jātavedas, he in whom they delight—hymns that increase even those already grown great.
This newest hymn of praise, well-fashioned for the Ancient One, I would speak for him who desires it; may he hear us.
May it dwell within his heart so that it touches it, like a longing, well-adorned wife for her husband.
In whom horses, bulls, oxen, barren cows, and rams have been released and offered as oblations—
to that Agni, the drinker of sweet nectar, whose back is sprinkled with Soma, the ordainer, I generate a beautiful hymn from my heart.
The oblation has been poured into your mouth, O Agni, like clarified butter in the ladle, like Soma in the cup.
Bestow upon us wealth that wins booty, rich in heroic sons, highly praised, glorious, and vast.
I praise for you the charioteer of the sacrifice, the lord of the people, the invoker, the guest of the night, the radiant one—
blazing among the dry plants and flickering among the green ones, the bull, the banner, the holy one has reached the sky.
Both [gods and men] have made this Agni the one who flows straight, the upholder of the law, the accomplisher of the sacrifice;
like the young ray of light before the dawns, they kiss Tanūnapāt, the red-hued one, who is placed in front.
We consider his paths to be strong and those of the Pani to be mere thoughts; his branches were offered up for him to devour.
When the terrible ones attained immortality, they then celebrated the divine race of men.
For the extension of Cosmic Order is the sky, wide-expanding; homage to the great Aramati, most worthy of praise.
Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa have come to a common understanding, as well as Bhaga and Savitṛ of purified skill.
The rivers flow forth with the rushing Rudra; they have sped across the great Aramati.
With them, the all-encompassing one, moving around his wide expanse, roars aloud and sprinkles everything within his belly.
The active Rudras and Maruts, who belong to all people, are falcons of heaven, the dwellers of the Asura’s home;
with them—Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, and Indra—shines the swift one together with the swift gods.
Those who strive have obtained enjoyment in Indra, in the sight of the Sun and in the manly power of the Bull—
those singers who, at the assemblies of men, fashioned for him his companion, the thunderbolt, according to its due worth.
Even the sun’s bay horses he caused to halt; everyone fears Indra, the mightiest one. From the belly of the terrifying bull, the unimpeded conqueror bellows day after day with an unrestrained roar.
Today, with homage, offer a hymn of praise to your skillful Rudra, the ruler of heroes— [the Rudra] with whom,
the auspicious and self-reliant one, moves swiftly through heaven with his own glorious, longing companions.
For they have spread their fame among the progeny: Bṛhaspati the bull, and those born of Soma;
Atharvan first established [the rites] through sacrifices, and the Bhṛgus, the gods, became renowned through their skillful deeds.
For they— Heaven and Earth of abundant seed, Narāśaṃsa, the four-limbed Yama,
Aditi, the god Tvaṣṭṛ, Draviṇodas, the R̥bhukṣans, Rodasī, the Maruts, and Viṣṇu— are worthy of honor.
And may that sage Ahi Budhnya hear our call from afar, as he attends to the invocation of the yearning ones.
O Sun and Moon, who move apart and dwell in heaven, through your wisdom, O Śamī and Nahuṣī, take heed of this!
May Pūṣan, who belongs to all the gods, protect our path; may the Son of the Waters and Vāyu aid us in our quest.
Sing forth to the Wind for greater prosperity; O Aśvins, easily invoked, hear this on your journey!
With songs we praise him who dwells over these fearless tribes, the self-glorious one;
with all the divine dames we praise Aditi, the unassailable, and the youthful lord of the night, whose mind is set on men.

There Aṅgiras, the first by birth, sang forth; the pressing-stones, raised aloft, beheld the sacrifice—with them he became far-reaching and all-seeing, while the well-fashioned axe moved upon the wood-filled tree.
O Heaven and Earth, you have become great and wide; like two young women, the two worlds are our constant seat.
With these [powers], protect us in our overcoming; with these, protect us in our strength.
At every sacrifice, that mortal honors the gods who, being most renowned for their fame, seeks to win them over with his prayers for favor.
O you who rule over all, the great treasure of the gods!
For all of you possess universal greatness; all of you are worthy of sacrifice at the rites.
They indeed are the joyous kings of immortality: Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Parijman;
and who among men is Rudra when praised—the Maruts, Pūṣan, and Bhaga?
And may Sūrya and Māsa, the rain-givers of the waters, who share a common dwelling, come to our abode by night,
when the Dragon of the Deep settles among their foundations.
And may the two gods, the Aśvins, lords of splendor, and Mitra and Varuṇa, protect us according to their laws.
He strives for great wealth and crosses over difficulties as one crosses a desert.
And may even the Rudras be gracious to us, as well as the Aśvins, all the gods, Rathaspati, and Bhaga;
O Ṛbhus, Vāja, and Ṛbhukṣans, you who travel around and possess all wealth.

R̥bhu is the lord of R̥bhus; R̥bhu is the exhilaration of the worshiper. May your two bay steeds, swift and vigorous, hasten toward you—the steeds of him whose Sāman is difficult to surpass, like a human sacrifice performed with perfect success.
O God Savitṛ, make us free from shame; he is praised among the wealthy patrons.
Like Indra with his steeds, he has brought down the wheel of these people, as one draws in a rein.
O Heaven and Earth, bestow upon these men, and upon us, great glory that extends over all people;
grant us nourishment for the winning of booty, and nourishment for the attainment of wealth and victory.
O Indra, you who are well-disposed toward us, protect this singer for our aid, wherever he may be, O victorious one; always protect him for our aid, O Vasu, let him be nourished with knowledge.
This hymn of mine, with its radiant course like the sun, has been strengthened for the men; like a craftsman fashioning a horse-harness, it is well-joined and unshakable.
They whose wealth has turned back toward them, whose golden chariot is yoked— like the deeds of heroes in battle, their ends are reached as if in sport.
I have proclaimed this before Duḥśīma, Pṛthavāna, Vena, Rāma, and the Asuras and Maghavans— those who,
having yoked five hundred [horses], have made their path resound for me.
Indeed, here he has bestowed seventy-seven [cows] at once;
Tānva has bestowed them at once, Pārthya has bestowed them at once, and Māyava has bestowed them at once.
Let these speak forth, let us speak forth; utter the speech for the speaking pressing-stones!
O stones, you mountains, swift together, you who possess the Soma, bring forth a song and a sound for Indra.
These speak out with a hundredfold and thousandfold voice; they roar aloud with their tawny horses.
Having performed their work well through their skillful deed, the pressing-stones have first attained the right to eat the oblation even before the Hotṛ priest.
These ones speak, having found the honey; they hum over the cooked meat. As they devour the branch of the ruddy tree, those well-chewing bulls have bellowed forth.
They speak aloud with the exhilarating, intoxicating draught; crying out to Indra, they have found the honeyed food.
Seizing hold together, the wise ones have danced with their sisters, making the earth resound with their rhythmic thumping.

The fair-winged ones have uttered their voice toward the sky; in the cave, the dark, impetuous ones have danced. They go downward to the appointed place of the lower stone; bright as the sun, they have deposited abundant seed.

Like fierce [steeds] rushing forward, they have harnessed themselves together; yoked at once, the bulls bear the poles. When, panting and swallowing, they have bellowed, one hears their snorting like that of racing horses.
Sing praise to those who have ten fingers, ten girths, ten yokes, and ten traces;
to those who possess ten reins and are never-wearying, who carry ten poles and ten yoked [horses].
Those stones, with their ten-fold mechanisms, are swift; their desirable setting revolves around them. They have partaken of the first milk of the stalk, the juice of the pressed Soma plant.
Those Soma-drinkers kiss the two bay horses of Indra; milking the stalk, they sit upon the cow.
Having drunk the Soma-mead milked by them, Indra grows strong, expands, and acts like a bull.
O bulls, your stalk has never failed you; you are always full of joy and well-fed.
Like wealthy lords, you are beautiful in your greatness, you whose pressing-stones have delighted in the sacrifice.
The stones are piercing yet not pierced; they are unwearied, unloosened, and free from death;
they are undiseased, ageless, steadfast, very fat, thirstless, and free from craving.
Firm indeed are you, O Fathers, from age to age; desiring security, they do not leave their seat.
Unaging, accompanied by tawny steeds and tawny horses, they have made themselves heard with their roar across heaven and earth.

At their release, the pressing-stones speak thus on their course with loud clamor, like those who drink the ointment; sowing the seed as grain-gatherers do, they mix the Soma and do not diminish it as they devour it.

When the sacrifice was pressed, they raised their voices, like playful children striking their mother; release well the inspired thought of the one who has performed the pressing, and let the pressing-stones roll forth as they are being honored.
"Come, wife! Stay with me in spirit, O fierce one; let us now exchange words together.
These unspoken mantras of ours shall not bring us joy even on a later day."
"What shall I do with these words of yours? I have set forth like the first of the dawns. Purūravas, go back to your home; I am as difficult to capture as the wind."
Like an arrow from a quiver for the sake of glory, like a swift rush winning cattle and gaining hundreds;
flashing forth when the intention is not toward a hero, the roaring ones make the sound of a sheep known.

Bestowing wealth upon her father-in-law and providing vigor for him, O Dawn, when she desires to depart from the house, she has reached the home where she found delight; day and night she is pierced by the rod of her husband.
"Three times a day you struck me with your arrows, O Vetasena, and yet you continued to satisfy my desire.
Purūravas, I have come according to your will; O hero, you were the king of my body."

She who is well-purified, a row [of beauty], a friend of bliss, moving like an eye in the heart, binding the knot, she has flowed forth like ruddy ointments; for the sake of glory, they have lowed like milch-cows.
When he was being born, the divine dames sat around him, and the self-praising rivers nourished him;
for the gods, O Purūravas, strengthened you for the great battle, for the slaying of the Dasyus.
When I, a mortal, dwelt among these non-human women who cast off their garments, they did not terrify me;
they were like restless waters, or like horses that touch the chariot.
When a mortal, as a seeker, unites with these immortal ones, he joins them with the worlds as if with sacred rites.
Then they adorn their own bodies like birds; they are like playful horses, biting and snapping.
Like a falling flash of lightning that blazes forth, she brought to me the desirable waters of the deep.
A noble son was born from the waters; may Urvaśī prolong her long life.
You were born indeed for the protection of the cow; you bestowed that strength upon me, O Purūravas.
On that very day, I, knowing [the truth], exhorted you, yet you did not listen to me. What do you say now, you who have failed?

When will the son, once born, seek his father; when, like a wheel, will he turn tears from understanding? Who shall separate the husband and wife who are of one mind, while Agni shines among the parents-in-law?

I shall answer him who turns back his tears; let him not cry out like one distressed in his longing for welfare. I will send forth that which is yours among us; go home, O fool, for you have not attained [your goal].
May the good god fly away today, never to return, to go to the furthest distance.
Then may he lie in the lap of Destruction, and there may the impetuous wolves devour him.
O Purūravas, do not die, do not fall away; let not the inauspicious wolves devour you.
There are no friendships with women; these are but the hearts of hyenas.
When, O Virūpā, I dwelt among mortals for four autumn nights, I ate a single drop of clarified butter once a day; even now, I move about satisfied by that very same [act].
Filling the intermediate space, the measurer of the region, I, Vasiṣṭha, entreat Urvaśī.
May the gift of my good deed attend you; turn back, for my heart is burning.
Thus these gods say to you, O son of Iḷā: "Since you have thus become a kinsman of death, let your offspring worship the gods with oblations; you, moreover, shall rejoice in heaven."
I shall proclaim your two bay steeds at the great assembly; I win for you the desirable exhilaration from the one who seeks to conquer.
Like ghee, he who pours forth what is beautiful with his bay steeds—may our songs enter you, whose form is golden-bay.
For those who have sung together toward the golden source, urging on the two bay steeds as if to the heavenly seat;
for him whom they satisfy with bay steeds like milch-cows—sing a strengthening hymn to Indra, the possessor of the bay steeds.
That golden, iron thunderbolt of his is golden, desirable, and golden within his two hands;
radiant, with a beautiful snout, and having golden fury for its arrow—golden forms have been infused into Indra.
Like a beloved banner placed in heaven, the golden thunderbolt has spread itself out with speed.
He of the golden crest struck the serpent; he who is of iron became one with a thousand flames, the bearer of the golden one.
O Indra, golden-haired, you were cherished again and again by the ancient sacrificers who praised you;
you cherish [the offerings], and yours is all that is worthy of praise—the perfect, desirable bounty born of the golden one.
Those two beloved bay steeds carry Indra—the wielder of the thunderbolt, the exhilarating one worthy of praise—to the intoxication on his chariot.
For him, for Indra, many libations are desired; the golden Soma juices have flowed forth.
The bay steeds have flowed readily for the desire of the steadfast one; the bay steeds urge on the two swift bay horses.
He who goes according to his pleasure with his bay coursers—he has attained his desire for the bay steeds.
Tawny-bearded, tawny-haired, made of iron, he who grew strong at the swift draught as the drinker of the tawny juice;
he who, possessing wealth in steeds, with his tawny coursers shall carry us across all difficulties.
Whose two golden jaws fly apart like two ladles as he shakes them for the sake of strength;
when, having drunk of the exhilarating, desirable food, he cleansed his two golden steeds over the prepared chalice.
And indeed, the seat of the beloved one between the two worlds has roared like a prize-seeking steed, the Lord of Bay Steeds;
for even the great *dhiṣaṇā* was won by his might, and you, the beloved one, have established lofty vital power within us.
Desiring both worlds with your greatness, you take pleasure in every newest hymn that is dear to you.
O Asura, make the beloved dwelling of the cow manifest for the golden Sun.
May the draft-horses of men bring you, the longing one with bay jaws, Indra, upon your chariot.
Drink of the offered mead as you please, delighting in the sacrifice at the communal feast where the ten fingers serve.
O Lord of the Bay Steeds, you have drunk of the pressed juices of former times; and now this libation is yours alone.
Rejoice in the honeyed Soma, O Indra; O Bull, pour it all at once into your belly.
Those herbs that were born first, three ages before the gods—
now I take heed of the hundred and seven abodes of those tawny ones.
A hundred, O mothers, are your abodes, and a thousand are your growths;
therefore, you who possess a hundred powers, make this man of mine free from disease.
Rejoice in the plants—those that bear flowers and those that bring forth fruit; like mares that win the prize, may these healing herbs carry us across to safety.
O Plants, my mothers, as such I address you, O goddesses:
may I win back the horse, the cow, the garment, and your very self, O man.
On the *aśvattha* tree is your seat; on the *parṇa* leaf your dwelling has been prepared. You shall indeed be sharers in cattle, if you win back the man.
Where the plants have gathered together like kings in an assembly,
that inspired sage is called a physician, the slayer of demons and the driver away of disease.
I have gathered all the plants— those rich in horses, rich in Soma, invigorating, and full of vital power—
for his well-being and freedom from harm.
The vital breaths of the plants rush forth like cattle from the stall,
O man, as they seek to win wealth for you.
Healing is your mother by name, and so you yourselves are healers; you are winged furrows, for whatever is diseased, you heal it away.
They have passed beyond all obstacles as a thief passes through a pen; the plants have shaken off whatever blemish was upon their bodies.
When I, seeking strength, take these herbs into my hand,
the self of the wasting disease perishes, as if before the seizer of life.
O plants, as you creep through his body, limb by limb and joint by joint, drive away the consumption from there, like a fierce ruler who sits in the midst.
Fly away, O consumption, together with the blue jay, the woodpecker;
vanish together with the rush of the wind, together with the whirlwind.
One of you let another protect; let each one assist the other.
All of you, being in full accord, favor this speech of mine.
Those plants that bear fruit and those that are fruitless, those that blossom and those that are flowerless—
impelled by Bṛhaspati, may they release us from distress.
May they release me from the curse of the oath, and also from that of Varuṇa;
and also from the fetter of Yama, and from every offense against the gods.
As they descended from heaven, the plants spoke:
"The living man whom we shall reach, that person shall not suffer harm."
Of those herbs whose king is Soma, many and hundred-eyed, you are the most excellent; bring healing for my desire and well-being for my heart.
The plants whose king is Soma, which are spread across the earth—
impelled by Bṛhaspati, bestow your power upon this woman.
May he who digs you not be harmed, nor he for whom I dig you;
may all our bipeds and quadrupeds be free from disease.
Those plants that hear this and those that have gone far away— let all the creepers come together and bestow their power upon her.
The plants hold a consultation together with Soma, their king:
"O King, we shall carry across that man for whom a Brahmin performs [this rite]."
O herb, you are the highest; the trees are your subordinates. May he who assails us be our subordinate.
O Bṛhaspati, come toward my divinity, whether you are Mitra, Varuṇa, or Pūṣan;
or if you are with the Ādityas, the Vasus, or accompanied by the Maruts—send down Parjanya for the sake of Śantanu, O Bull.
The divine messenger, swift and wise, has come to me from you, O Devāpi. Turn back toward me; I place this radiant speech within your mouth.

Bestow upon us, O Bṛhaspati, radiant speech from our mouths—speech that is free from disease and full of vitality—by which we two may win the rain for Śantanu; the honeyed drop from heaven has entered [our hearts].
May the honeyed drops enter us; O Indra, bestow upon us a thousand chariots.
Sit down to the office of the Hotṛ, sacrifice in due season, and worship the gods with oblation, O Devāpi.
The seer Devāpi, son of Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, sitting down to the office of the *hotṛ* priest and being skilled in the favor of the gods,
released the celestial waters of rain from the upper ocean toward the lower one.
In this upper ocean, the waters stood encompassed by the gods;
they flowed forth, released by the son of Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, sent by Devāpi among the Mṛkṣiṇīs.
When Devāpi, the domestic priest for Śantanu, was chosen for the office of Hotṛ and meditated with compassion,
Bṛhaspati, bestowing it, granted him speech that is heard by the gods and wins the rain.
O Agni, whom Devāpi, the son of Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, the mortal man, kindled while glowing with fervor—
being celebrated by all the gods, impel Parjanya, the possessor of rain.
The ancient seers approached you with songs; all [of them], O much-invoked one, [approached] you at the sacrifices.
Bring to us thousands of chariots; come to our sacrifice, O you whose horses are ruddy.
These ninety-nine thousand offerings, O Agni, have been poured upon you, each exceeding a chariot-load. With these, O Hero, increase your many bodies; impelled by us, grant us rain from heaven.
O Agni, deliver these ninety thousand as a portion to the bull Indra;
knowing the paths that lead to the gods according to the seasons, place Aulāna also among the gods in heaven.
O Agni, drive away the adversaries; drive away the difficulties, the disease, and the demons.
From this vast ocean, from the great heaven, release for us here an abundance of waters.
Whom among us do you, the wise one, impel—the wide-striding, bellowing [bull]—to grow strong?
What gift shall he give at the breaking forth of his power? He fashioned the Vṛtra-slaying thunderbolt and caused it to swell.
For he, with his flashing lightning, seeks the *sāman*; by his lordly power, he has settled in the broad womb.
Overpowering with those who share his dwelling, he [subdues] the magical powers of this brother, not without the seventh.
He went forth seeking booty on horses that traverse both easy and difficult paths, intending to win it in the contest for the sun;
he, the unassailable one, seized the hundredfold wealth of Śatadurasya, striking down the phallus-worshippers with his wondrous form.
He, the mighty steed, hastens through the streams for the sake of cattle, rushing toward the prizes of war;
where the footless ones, joined together yet without chariots, with horses born from wooden troughs, speed forth like clarified butter and water.
He, the skillful one, whose wealth cannot be cursed, having left his home far behind with its blemishes, has come here.
I believe he has come to expose the pair of Vamra, seeking food and making them weep as he plunders them.
He, the lord of the house, subdued the Dāsa Tuvīrava, the six-eyed and three-headed;
Trita, strengthened by his power, struck the boar with his spear-pointed of iron.
Standing tall against the treacherous man, he hurled his shaft at the one who sought to harm;
he, the most heroic of men, well-born among the Nahuṣas, pierced the fortresses as the worthy slayer of Dasyus.
Like a cloud pouring rain upon the pasture, may he find for us a path to our dwelling;
when he settles upon the soma-drop with his bodies, like a hawk with iron claws, he slays the Dasyus.
He, with his powerful and mighty [deeds], delivered Śuṣṇa to Kutsa in his wretched state;
he led the praised sage Atka, who won for him both [booty] and heroes.
This one, bestowing gifts with his manly deeds, is a wonder-worker like Varuṇa, possessed of magic power;
this youthful guardian of the seasons has been made known—he who measured out Araru, the four-footed beast.
Through his hymns of praise, Auśija Ṛjiśvan burst open the cow-pen of Pipru with his bull;
when the sacrificer had pressed the Soma, his song shone forth, and advancing toward the fortresses, he overcame them with his wondrous form.
Thus, O great Asura, for the sake of your growth, Vamraka has crept near to Indra with his feet.
Seeking him, may he grant us well-being; he has brought us all—food, strength, a secure dwelling, and light.
O Indra, be firm, O Maghavan; one such as you is indeed our enjoyment here. Praised and drinking the pressed soma, be for our increase.
May Savitṛ together with the gods protect us; we choose Aditi for complete well-being.
Bring forth well the seasonal portion for the bearing; offer it to Vāyu, the pure one, who roars at the sacrifice.
He who has attained the drinking of the bull’s milk—we choose Aditi for complete well-being.

May the divine Savitṛ impel strength toward us—toward the one who acts uprightly, the sacrificer who presses the soma—so that we may honor the gods with simple devotion. We choose Aditi for complete well-being.
May Indra be well-disposed toward us at all times; may King Soma attend to our welfare.
Just as they have established the bonds of friendship, we choose Aditi for complete well-being.
O Indra, by means of the hymn and through power, you have joined the joint; O Bṛhaspati, you are the furtherer of this life.
Sacrifice is Manu, our providence, for he is indeed our father. We choose Aditi for complete well-being.
Now Indra’s divine power is well-wrought; Agni, the wise sage, is the singer in the house. And may the sacrifice be dear and most intimate in the assembly. We choose Aditi for complete well-being.

We have not committed many evil deeds against you in secret, nor, O Vasus, have we openly provoked the gods. O gods, let none of us take on the form of falsehood; we choose Aditi for our complete well-being.
May Savitṛ drive away disease; may the mountains push it far down.
Where the pressing-stone, extracting the honey, is raised loudly, we choose Aditi for universal well-being.
May the pressing-stone stand upright for the presser, O Vasus; drive all enmities far away.
May that god Savitṛ be our praiseworthy protector; we choose Aditi for complete well-being.
O cows, eat nourishment and fatness upon the pasture, you who are anointed at the seat of Order in the reservoir.
Let body be the healing medicine for body; we choose Aditi for complete well-being.
The singer is the fulfiller of the will of all; Indra indeed is the auspicious providence for those who have pressed the soma.
His heavenly udder is full for the pouring out [of the rain]; we choose Aditi for complete well-being.

Wondrous is your radiance; your aid fulfills our intentions. There are rivals who are invincible and reach old age. With the straightest line, the worshiper strives to win the foremost prize of cattle.
Awake, O friends, with one mind; kindle Agni together, you many who dwell in the same nest.
I call upon Dadhikrā, Agni, and the goddess Uṣas, along with Indra, for your protection.
Make it pleasant; extend your prayers; fashion a ship that can be steered with oars.
Prepare the weapons; make them ready. O friends, lead the sacrifice forward.
Yoke the ploughs, stretch out the yokes; sow the seed here in the prepared womb.
May our song and the prompt response bring us abundant harvests; may the sickle come closer to the ripened grain.
The seers yoke the ploughs; they stretch out the yokes separately, the wise ones, seeking favor among the gods.
Prepare the buckets; set the straps in place. Let us pour from the water-skin that is full of water, well-dispensing and inexhaustible.
I pour forth the water-bearing, inexhaustible well, which has a well-fashioned opening, excellent buckets, and is easy to draw from.
Gladden the horses; win what is beneficial; make the chariot one that brings well-being.
Pour out the drink for the heroes—the vessel with its trough, the well with its stone wheel, and its quiver-case.
Make a cow-pen; for he is your protector. Sew together many broad shields.
Make iron fortresses, unassailable. Let not your cup leak; make it firm.
I turn toward you your holy thought for aid—the divine, worshipful, and sacred thought, O gods—here.
May it yield for us like a great cow that has gone to pasture, with a thousand streams of milk.
Pour the golden juice into the lap of the wooden vat; fashion it with stone-made axes.
Embrace him with the ten girth-bands; yoke the steed to both poles.
The draft-animal, firmly grasping both poles, moves between them like a bird with two mates within its nest.
Establish the Lord of the Forest in the wood; set him down, digging out the well.
O men, bring forth the filler, the filler; urge him on and stir him for the winning of booty.
O Niṣṭigryas, cause the son to hasten hither; with pressing zeal, bring Indra here to drink the Soma.
May Indra boldly protect your overturned chariot;
O Much-invoked One, favor us in this glorious contest for the winning of wealth.
The wind blew her garment upward when she won a thousand [cows] in the race;
Mudgalānī became the charioteer in the quest for cattle, and Indrasenā won the prize in the contest.
O Indra, hurl your thunderbolt within those who seek to strike us down and those who assail us;
O Maghavan, keep far away the weapon of the Dāsa or the Ārya.
Exulting, he drank from the pool of water; his horn shattered the enemy as he advanced.
Bearing his testicles like a burden, seeking fame, he swiftly extended his forelegs, desiring to win.
They made him bellow as they approached him; they made the bull urinate in the midst of the contest. With him, Mudgala won in the prize-fight a well-bred horse and a hundred thousand cattle.
The bull was yoked for the sake of the *kakardu*; his long-maned charioteer shouted aloud. As the well-yoked horse sped along with its chariot, the footprints reached even unto Mudgalānī.
And the wise one struck out its felly; he harnessed the bull there, seeking to master it.
Indra protected the lord of the cows; the humped one rushed forward with his feet.
Favorably the shaggy one with the goad moved about, being harnessed to the wooden yoke by the leather thong;
performing manly deeds for the sake of many people, he beheld the cattle and assumed his powers.
Behold this yoke-mate of the bull, the mallet lying in the middle of the race-course,
by which Mudgala won a hundred and a thousand cattle in the contests for booty.
Far away are evils; who indeed has seen such a thing? They yoke him and they cause him to stand still.
They bring him neither grass nor water; he bears the burden beyond the yoke-pole, pointing the way.

Like a discarded wife who has obtained a husband, swelling like one pouring from a water-skin with a spout—may we conquer even with a chariot that is just starting its course; may our gain be auspicious and full of wealth.
O Indra, you are the eye of the entire world, the eye of the eye itself;
for as a bull you seek to win the prize with your bull-like companion, urging on even the emasculated one as your ally.
Swift, sharpening his weapons like a terrifying bull, the striker, the agitator of the peoples,
the roaring one who never closes his eyes, the sole hero— Indra has conquered a hundred armies all at once.
With him who is roaring, unblinking, victorious, a striker,
immovable, and bold— with that Indra, O men, conquer and prevail in battle, with the bull who holds arrows in his hand.
He, the controller, with his arrow-handed [attendants] and those bearing quivers; he, Indra, is the one who joins together in battle with his host.
Conqueror of joined forces, drinker of Soma, strong of arm, with a formidable bow, he is the shooter with well-aimed arrows.
O Bṛhaspati, fly around with your chariot, slayer of demons, driving away our enemies;
shattering the armies, crushing them in battle, and conquering, be the protector of our chariots.

O Indra, discoverer of strength, ancient one, preeminent hero, powerful, vigorous, victorious, and fierce; the hero who overcomes, the warrior who overcomes, born of might, winner of cattle—ascend your victorious chariot!
The breaker of enclosures, the winner of cattle, the thunderbolt-armed, who conquers the race and crushes with his might—O kinsmen, follow this Indra; O friends, exert yourselves together after him!

Piercing through the cow-pens with his might, the pitiless hero Indra, possessed of a hundredfold wrath, the unshakable subduer of armies and the invincible warrior— may he protect our hosts in the battles.
May Indra be their leader; may Bṛhaspati, the sacrificial fee, the sacrifice, and Soma go before them.
May the Maruts march at the head of the divine armies as they shatter and conquer.
The fierce roar of the gods has arisen—the host of Indra the bull, of King Varuṇa, of the Ādityas, and of the Maruts; the shout of the high-minded ones who shake the world as they conquer.
O Maghavan, brandish our weapons; rouse the spirits of my warriors!
O slayer of Vṛtra, let the vigor of the steeds be stirred, and let the shouts of the victorious charioteers go forth.
May Indra be on our side when the banners meet; may those arrows which are ours be victorious.
May our heroes be superior; O gods, protect us in our invocations.
Bewildering the minds of these men, seize their limbs, O Apvā;
go away! Attack them! Burn them up with anguish in their hearts; let the enemies be overtaken by blinding darkness.
Advance, O men, and conquer! May Indra grant you protection.
May your arms be mighty so that you may be invincible.
Soma has been pressed for you, O much-invoked one; come quickly to the sacrifice with your two bay horses.
To you the songs of the inspired heroes have flowed, seeking you; O Indra, drink of the pressed juice!
O Lord of the Bay Steeds, drink here of the juice pressed by men and washed in the waters; fill your belly!
O Indra, you for whom the stones have poured it out—be strengthened by them for your exhilaration, O you who are borne by hymns.
I offer a true, forward-moving draught for the bull, for you, O Lord of the Tawny Steeds, as you approach the pressed juice.
O Indra, rejoice here with our songs, being praised by all our prayers and with power.
O Lord of Might, through your aid and your heroic power, the *uśij* who know the *ṛta*, bestowing vitality,
have stood in the dwelling of Manu with progeny, O Indra, praising you as those who share in the feast.

O Lord of the bay horses, through the well-uttered praises of thee, the most gracious and far-shining one, the people, O Indra, bestowing upon thee thy most bountiful aid, have extended their songs of praise through thy gracious favors.
Come near, O Lord of the Bay Steeds, with your two bay horses, to drink of the pressed soma.
O Indra, the sacrifice has reached you who are present; you are the giver and the herald of this rite.

The singer honors with hymns the one of a thousandfold booty, the overcomer of enemies, the Maghavan who brings success in battle; they praise Indra, who is beyond challenge, with reverent salutations.
The seven divine waters, joyous and inviolable, with which you, O Indra, breaker of forts, crossed the Sindhu—
those ninety-nine flowing streams— you found a path for the gods and for man.
You released the great waters from the curse; you alone, O God, were watchful over them.
O Indra, with those [waters] which you won in the conquest of Vṛtra, may you nourish your body for all time.
Indra is the heroic power, worthy of fair praise; even the voice of prayer invokes him who is invoked by many.
Śakra, the helper, struck down Vṛtra, made wide space, and conquered the hostile armies.
We invoke for our good fortune the bountiful Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the acquisition of booty;
the fierce one who listens, for our protection in conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras and is the winner of riches.
O Vasu, when will you desire our hymn?
May the waters flow for the one who has prepared the long-pressed juice for his guest-friend.
He whose two bay steeds, well-yoked and moving in different directions, follow the tail-feathers; he, the lord of the house, is like the two long-maned ones in both realms.
Indra, born of evil, fled from the waters like a mortal who has grown weary and is filled with fear,
when the mighty one harnessed himself for glory.
Indra took pleasure in these two together, honoring them as they were yoked to his chariot;
Indra, the hero, [prevailed] over the two rivers that flow in different directions.
He who has mounted upon the two long-maned [horses] that are wide-spreading as if for nourishment—
he, the possessor of beautiful jaws, wins with his two jaws.
He of lofty vigor has praised; the hero has fashioned [all things] with his might through the lofty ones, like Mātariśvan the *Ṛbhu* with his mental powers (*kratubhiḥ*).
He who fashioned the thunderbolt for the easy slaying of the Dasyu—Hirīmaś, the modest one;
whose jaw is unbreakable, like the wondrous mid-region.
Strike down our crookedness; may we conquer the godless with our hymn.
A sacrifice without prayer does not please you at all.
When your triple flame rose upward at the yoke-poles of the sacrifice in its dwelling, you,
in harmony with the two [Aśvins], mounted the self-glorious ship together with them.
For your glory, may the speckled cow be the vessel for pouring; for your glory, may the flawless ladle be that with which you pour into your own cup.

Whether it was Śatamvā who thus praised you, O Asurya, or Sumitra, or Durmitra who thus praised you; since you helped the son of Kutsa in the slaying of the Dasyus, and since you protected the protégé of Kutsa in the slaying of the Dasyus.
Both of you now surely desire that very thing; you spread out your thoughts like two weavers their cloths. You have awakened him to come together; like two fair days, you bestow nourishing food.
Like two camels at the watering-places, you rest; like two vigorous draft-horses, you come at the command.
For you two stand like messengers among the people with glory; do not stay away like two buffaloes from the drinking-place.
Like the two wings of a bird joined together, like two beautiful beasts, come to the sacrifice with the *yajus*.
Like the blazing fire of the god-fearing man, like those who travel all around, you two worship in many places.
Like kinsmen to us, like sons to a father, like two fierce ones with splendor, like two lords of men for victory;
like two leaders for prosperity, like rays for enjoyment, like two who are swift to hear, come quickly to our invocation!
Like two young bulls with swelling testicles, like Mitra and Varuṇa, the upholders of cosmic order, bestowing hundreds and bringing prosperity;
standing high in the dwelling with strength and vigor, like two rams, they are worthy of worship and full of moisture.
Like two ploughs, you are the supporters; like two swift ones, you are the destroyers; like two hunters, you are the scatterers.
Like two water-born conquerors, you are exhilarating; as such, O two aged ones, grant me agelessness and freedom from death.
Like two Pajras, you move about like a lover; like two plowmen, O fierce ones, you cross over toward your goals.
Like the Rbhus, you possess swift horses; like Vāyu, you scatter [the clouds], bestowing dwellings and riches.
Like two cauldrons filled with honey in their bellies, eager for fortune, they are destroyers of the enemy and scatterers of foes;
like two birds flying through the air, bright-shining, they move with the speed of thought, following the mind as if on a journey.
Like two great ones finding a foothold in the depths, like two feet you find a firm standing for one who crosses;
like two ears, O teachers, remember our instruction, and like two shares, grant us wondrous wealth.
Like two *āraṅgara* bees you bring forth honey; like two honey-bees in a cow that yields downward-flowing milk;
like two laborers sweating from toil, you two accompany the strength of the meadow rich in good pasture.
May we succeed in our hymn; may we win the prize. Come hither to our prayer on your shared chariot!
Like glory, like ripe honey within the cows, the portion of being has fulfilled the desire of the Aśvins.
The great bounty of these [donors] has become manifest; every living being has been released from darkness.
The great light given by the ancestors has arrived; the broad path of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) has appeared.
High in heaven abide those who give sacrificial fees; those who give horses dwell with the Sun. Those who give gold partake in immortality; O Soma, those who give clothing prolong their lives.
Divine is the fulfillment, the sacrificial fee, and the worship of the gods; for those who withhold gifts do not bestow them.
But now, many men, offering their sacrificial fees, bestow them out of fear of reproach.
They who behold with the eyes of men gaze upon the oblation—Vāyu with his hundred streams, the Sun who finds the light.
Those who satisfy and bestow gifts at the assembly milk the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), which has seven mothers.
The giver of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) comes first when summoned; the giver of sacrificial fees goes at the head as the leader of the village.
Him alone I consider the lord of men, who was the first to bring forth the sacrificial fee.
They call him indeed the seer, him the Brahman, the knower of sacrifice, the chanter of Sāmans, the reciter of hymns;
he knows the three bodies of the bright [Soma], he who was the first to succeed through the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
The sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā) bestows the horse; the sacrificial gift bestows the cow; the sacrificial gift [bestows] the moon and whatever gold there is.
The sacrificial gift wins food, which is our very self; the wise man makes the sacrificial gift his armor.
The liberal patrons do not die, nor do they go to ruin; the liberal patrons are never harmed and they never tremble.
This entire world, this very heaven, and all that exists—all this he gives away as sacrificial fees to them.
The liberal patrons have first won the fragrant womb; the liberal patrons have won the bride who is well-robed.
The liberal patrons have won the draught of wine from within; the liberal patrons have won those who go forth uninvited.
For the liberal patron they groom the swift horse; for the liberal patron the maiden adorns herself.
This house of the liberal patron is like a lotus pond, beautifully decorated and as brilliant as a celestial palace.
Well-yoked horses carry the liberal patron; the well-rolling chariot of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) moves forward.
O gods, protect the liberal patron in battles; the liberal patron is the conqueror of enemies in the encounters.
Desiring what has Saramā come here? For the road is far and leads to distant places;
what was our mission, what was the obstacle on the way, and how did you cross the waters of the Rasā?
Sent as Indra’s messenger, I wander about, seeking your great treasures, O Paṇis. Out of fear of my leap, they yielded those up to us; thus did I cross over the waters of the Rasā.
What is Indra like, O Saramā, what is his appearance, he for whom you have come as a messenger from afar?
Let him come here; we shall make him our friend, and then let him be the lord of our cattle.
I do not know him who can deceive; he deceives [himself], for whose messenger I have run from afar.
Deep-flowing rivers do not hide him; O Paṇis, you have been struck down by Indra and shall lie dead.
These are the cows, O Saramā, which you sought as you flew around the ends of heaven, O fortunate one. Who would release them to you without a fight? And our weapons are sharp.
O Paṇis, may your words be without an army; may your evil bodies be proof against arrows. May the path you must travel be unassailable; Bṛhaspati will show no mercy to either of you.
This treasure, O Saramā, whose base is the mountain, is filled with cattle, horses, and riches.
The Paṇis, who are excellent guardians, protect it. You have come in vain to a track that is empty.
May the seers come hither, sharpened by Soma—the Ayāsyas, the Aṅgirases, and the Navagvas.
May they divide for themselves this stall of cattle; then let the Paṇis vomit up these words.
Thus have you come, O Saramā, driven by the sudden power of the gods.
I shall make you my sister; do not go back. O fortunate one, we shall give you a share of the cattle.
I know not brotherhood nor sisterhood; Indra and the terrible Aṅgirases know them.
They, desiring my cattle, looked on as I went; go far away, O Paṇis, from here!
Go far away, O Paṇis, to a wider distance! Let the cows come forth, lowing according to the *ṛta*.
Bṛhaspati, Soma, the pressing-stones, and the inspired sages have found those that were hidden.
They spoke first regarding the sin against Brahman: the boundless ocean, Mātariśvan, Vīḷuhara, the fierce Tapa, Mayobhū, and the divine waters, the first-born by *ṛta*.
King Soma, the first, returned the wife of the Brahman without resentment;
Varuṇa and Mitra were the attendants, and Agni, the Hotṛ-priest, led her away by the hand.
"If they have said, 'This is the wife of a Brahmin; she must be seized by the hand alone as a pledge,' she does not stand for being sent as a messenger; thus is the kingdom of a Kṣatriya protected."
The gods spoke concerning her in the past, as did the seven seers who sat down for ascetic fervor:
"The terrifying wife brought to a Brahmin brings instability even in the highest heaven."
The student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) moves about, performing his various duties; he becomes a single limb of the gods.
By means of him, Bṛhaspati recovered his wife who had been led away by Soma, just as the gods [recovered] the *juhū* ladle.
The gods indeed gave her back, and men as well;
the kings, making their word true, gave back the wife of the Brahmin.
Having restored the wife of the Brahmin and having been freed from sin by the gods,
they partook of the nourishment of the earth and worship the wide-striding Viṣṇu.
Kindled today in the dwelling of man, O Jātavedas, you, a god, sacrifice to the gods.
Bring them hither, O you who are rich in friends and full of wisdom; for you are the messenger, the seer, and the one possessed of profound insight.
O Tanūnapāt, fair-tongued one, anointing the paths that lead along the way of Ṛta with honey, make them sweet;
fulfilling our thoughts through our prayers and our sacrifice, bring our ritual to the gods.
Being invoked, worthy of praise and adoration, come, O Agni, in harmony with the Vasus!
You are the youthful Hotṛ of the gods; as such, being impelled, sacrifice for them as the most skilled sacrificer.

The sacred grass is strewn toward the east upon the earth by its direction, at the beginning of days for her who provides the dwelling. It spreads itself out further and wider, a pleasant seat for the gods and for Aditi.
Let the spacious doors open wide, like women adorning themselves for their husbands; O divine, lofty, all-impelling doors, be easy of access for the gods.
Pressing the juice, the worshipful Dawn and Night, close at hand, have sat down in their place;
the two celestial maidens, lofty and richly adorned, wearing brilliant and radiant beauty.
The two divine Hotṛ-priests, the first, eloquent ones, measuring out the sacrifice for man to worship;
the two poets who impel [the rite] in the assemblies, pointing toward the eastern light by their direction.
May Bhāratī come quickly to our sacrifice; may Iḷā, manifesting here like Manu, and Sarasvatī—may these three goddesses, skillful in their work, sit upon this pleasant sacrificial grass.

O Hotṛ, most skilled in sacrifice, being impelled today, do thou, the wise one, worship here the god Tvaṣṭṛ— he who fashioned these two parents, Heaven and Earth, and adorned all beings with their forms.
