Release [the victim] by yourself, anointing the oblations for the gods in due season;
let Vanaspati, the immolator, and the god Agni sweeten the offering with honey and ghee.
As soon as he was born, Agni measured out the sacrifice; he became the leader of the gods.
At the command of this Hotṛ, in the speech of the Eternal Order (ṛta), may the gods eat the oblation consecrated with Svāhā.
O wise ones, bring forth your inspired hymn, according as the thoughts of men arise;
let us impel Indra with truthful deeds, for he is the hero who loves songs of praise and is well-known.
For from the seat of Truth the inspired thought has shone forth; the bull, son of the Earth, has attained union with the cows.
He has arisen with a powerful roar and has encompassed even the vast regions.
Indra, indeed, knows this by hearsay, for he is the victorious one who prepares the path for Sūrya.
Making himself a companion to the cow, the unshakable lord of heaven—the ancient-born, irresistible one—has become manifest.
Indra, being praised by the Aṅgirases, shattered with his might the ordinances of the great ocean;
he who, through his commitment to truth, established the support and spread out the many regions.
Indra is the counterpart of heaven and earth; he knows all libations and slays Śuṣṇa.
He has overspread even the great heaven with the sun; more firm than the firmest, he has propped it up with a support.

For with his thunderbolt the slayer of Vṛtra struck down Vṛtra and the magical powers of the godless, swelling foe; O bold one, you boldly smote him there, and then, O Maghavan, you became mighty-armed.
When the dawns unite with the sun, his rays find the wondrous light;
when the star of heaven appears, no one truly knows from whence it comes again.

Far indeed have those waters gone, the first of them that flowed forth at the impulse of Indra. Where is their beginning, where is their foundation? O Waters, where now is your middle and where is your end?
You released the rivers that had been swallowed by the serpent; then indeed they rushed forth with speed.
Those seeking to be freed and those already freed—now, once set free, they do not rest.
Like longing women, they have gone toward the river together; from of old, the breaker of forts has been sought as their lover.
O Indra, may your earthly treasures come to our home, and may your many bounties reach us.
O Indra, drink of the pressed juice according to your desire; for the morning pressing is indeed your first draught.
Rejoice, O hero, to slay the enemies! We shall proclaim your heroic deeds with hymns.
O Indra, come with that chariot of yours which is swifter than thought, for the drinking of the Soma.
Let your bay steeds hasten quickly hither, those bulls with whom you come, rejoicing.
With the golden-hued splendor of the Sun, make thy body radiant with the most excellent forms.
O Indra, being invoked by us, thy friends, sit down and rejoice together with us in harmony.
O Indra, since these two great worlds, heaven and earth, could not encompass that majesty of yours in your states of exhilaration,
come now to that home with your beloved, harnessed bay horses, toward the food you love.

O Indra, you who have repeatedly drunk [the Soma] and performed deeds of war against the enemies that cannot be imitated—this [Soma] stirs your abundance and your power; this Soma has been pressed for your exhilaration, O Indra.
This is your cup, O Indra, won by ancient wealth; drink the Soma from it, O Śatakratu!
The vessel is full of the intoxicating mead, which all the gods indeed desire.
For from many sides, O Bull Indra, people who have prepared the sacrificial food call upon you;
may these most honey-sweet libations of ours be yours; take pleasure in them.
I shall proclaim, O Indra, your ancient deeds and those first performed even now— how you,
whose wrath was true, loosened the mountain and made the cow easy to find for the sake of the sacred word.
Sit down here, O Lord of the hosts, among the hosts; they call you the wisest of poets among sages.
Nothing whatsoever is done without you in this world; O Maghavan, sing the great, wondrous hymn!
O Maghavan, look upon us as we implore you; O friend, Lord of Wealth, be mindful of your friends.
O maker of joy, grant us delight; O you of true strength, give us our share even of wealth that has not yet been apportioned.
Heaven and Earth, acting in harmony with all the gods, have aided his vital strength.
When he came, performing his great Indra-power, having drunk of the Soma, he grew strong, possessed of wisdom.
Viṣṇu proclaims that greatness of his, having drunk the stalk of honey with power;
Indra, the bounteous Maghavan, having slain Vṛtra with the gods who accompany him, became preeminent.
When you stood together with Vṛtra the serpent, bearing your weapons for the sake of battle to win the praise,
then all the Maruts, together with you in person, O fierce one, increased your mighty Indra-power.
As soon as he was born, he drove away his rivals; the hero looked toward manly deeds and the field of battle.
He split the mountain, released the flowing waters, and by his skillful work, he propped up the broad firmament.
Then Indra indeed acquired all powers at once; he pushed heaven and earth far apart.
Boldly he brought down the iron thunderbolt, a blessing for Mitra, Varuṇa, and the donor.
Here, before the powers of Indra, the exuberant one, the impetuous ones fled from his wrath;
when the fierce one, by his might, shattered Vṛtra who bore the waters and was encompassed by darkness.

When the two, striving together with their greatness, met for the first heroic deeds to be performed, the thick darkness was cast down; Indra, struck by his own might, prevailed in the first invocation.
Then all the gods magnified your manly powers with eloquence accompanied by Soma;
Vṛtra the dragon, subdued by Indra’s blow, devoured the food greedily like Agni with his jaws.
Proclaim with skillful words and hymns, with friendships, your bonds of friendship!
Indra, subduing both Dhuni and Cumuri, listens to Dabhīti because of his faithful devotion.
Bring us many riches in good horses, by which I may be mindful while reciting my prayers.
May we cross all difficulties by easy paths; find for us today a wide and secure ford.

The two *gharma* vessels have pervaded the threefold world on all sides; Mātariśvan has come to their delight. Desiring to obtain the milk of heaven, they have sought it; the gods have known the hymn of equal power.
Three Nirṛtis wait upon the Ordainer; for the far-famed bearers of the oblation know them well. The seers have discerned their foundation, which lies within the highest secret ordinances.
The young woman with four braids, beautifully adorned, wearing clarity as her garment, has a face of ghee;
upon her two strong-winged bulls have settled, where the gods received their allotted portion.
The single Suparṇa has entered the ocean; he gazes upon this entire world. With a simple mind, I beheld him from nearby; the Mother licks him, and he licks the Mother.
The wise sages, through their hymns, fashion the single Suparṇa in many ways;
establishing the meters at the sacrifices, they measure out twelve cups of Soma.
Arranging thirty-six and four, and establishing the meters up to twelve, the sages,
having measured out the sacrifice with their wisdom, set the chariot in motion by means of the *Ṛk* and *Sāman*.
Fourteen other powers belong to him; seven wise ones lead him forth with speech.
Who here can declare the ford that reaches [him], the path by which they drink of the pressed juice?
The fifteen-fold hymns are a thousandfold; as vast as heaven and earth are, so great is that [Vāk].
A thousandfold are her greatnesses, a thousand; as far as Brahman extends, so far extends Speech.
What wise man knows the application of the meters? Who has attained the inspired speech that belongs to the sacrificial hearths?
Whom do they call the eighth hero among the officiating priests? And who indeed has discerned Indra’s two bay steeds?
Some wander around the edge of the earth; they have stood yoked to the poles of the chariot.
When Yama is established in his home, they distribute the portion of their toil among these [beings].
Wondrous indeed is the growth of the young infant, who does not go away from his two mothers to suckle;
though she who has no udder gave birth to him, he has now grown great, immediately setting out on his mighty mission as a messenger.
Agni has indeed been established by name as the most effective in his work—he who gathers the forests together with his tooth of ash.
With his tongue that crushes all around, he performs the perfect sacrifice; like a powerful stallion snorting in the pasture, he is a bull.
To him, your god, who sits upon the wood like a bird, the drop of Soma juice—panting, scattering [the waters], surging like a flood;
who, like a bearer with his mouth, is full of brilliance through his flame, and like one of great vows, traverses the paths.
O undecaying one, as you spread forth, the unshakable winds cannot encompass you who are burning like fire;
like joyful warriors reaching for a hero, they have reached Trita, urging him forward for his quest.

This very Agni is the best of the Kaṇvas, the friend of Kaṇva; may he overcome the enemies, both those afar and those near. May Agni protect the singers, may Agni protect the patrons; may Agni grant us their favor.
O Supitrya, for Jātavedas, the most powerful and victorious one, who moves swiftly like a thirsty man,
I offer praise— he who, bold even in waterless places, grants his choice to the seeker, and who, though dwelling in the desert, desires to protect the greatest of men.
Thus Agni, the noble son of strength, is praised for wealth by mortals together with patrons and heroes—
those who, like well-established friends, are devoted to the *ṛta*, and who, like the heavens, surpass all men in splendor.
"O Son of Strength, O Victorious One!"—thus does the bull-like voice of Upastuta praise you.
We shall praise you, possessing excellent heroes through you, as we extend our life-span further and further.
"Thus, O Agni, have the seers, the Upastutas, the sons of Vṛṣṭihavya, spoken to you.
Protect them and the praising patrons. 'Vaṣaṭ! Vaṣaṭ!'—thus they have reached upward; 'Homage! Homage!'—thus they have reached upward."
Drink the Soma for great Indra-power; drink, O most mighty one, to slay Vṛtra!
Drink, being invoked, for wealth and strength; drink your fill of the sweet mead, O Indra, and be strong!
Drink of this pressed Soma, O Indra, which is rich in nourishment and has been set forth—the best of what is poured.
Bestowing well-being, rejoice in your mind; turn hitherward for our wealth and good fortune.

May the divine Soma exhilarate you, O Indra; may that which is pressed among mortals exhilarate you. May that by which you have created wide space exhilarate you; may that by which you utterly destroy the enemies exhilarate you.
May Indra, the doubly powerful, tireless bull, come with his two bay steeds to the poured-out soma-juice.
O slayer of Aruṣa, drink your fill of the pressed, offered honey-sweet draught; satisfy yourself completely with it.
Causing their sharp weapons to fall away, loosen the firm bows of those driven by demons.
To you, the fierce one, I grant power and strength; having overcome the enemies, strike them down in their battles.
O Indra, stretch out your glories against the enemy; like the firm bowstring, ward off our assailants. Increasing toward us with your powers, undecaying, cause your own body to grow strong.
O Maghavan, this oblation is offered for you; O Sovereign, accept it without resentment.
For you, O Maghavan, is the pressed juice; for you is the cooked offering. Eat, O Indra, and drink of what has been set forth.

Eat indeed, O Indra, these oblations that have been set forth; take pleasure in them, both the cooked food and the Soma. Providing nourishment, we welcome you; may the desires of the sacrificer come true.
I send forth eloquence for Indra and Agni with hymns of praise, as one propels a boat upon the river.
Like swift steeds, the gods move around us—those who are the givers of wealth and the breakers-through of obstacles for us.
O gods, you have not indeed given hunger as a weapon; even for one who has eaten, deaths approach.
Moreover, the wealth of the liberal giver does not fail, while the one who does not give finds no one to comfort him.

He who, though possessing food, hardens his heart against the needy man who longs for nourishment and has come to him in distress— he may serve those before him, yet he finds no one to show him mercy.
He alone is the liberal giver who bestows wealth upon the suppliant who wanders about, emaciated and desiring food.
He is ready for him when called upon on the journey, and he makes him his friend in future times as well.

He is no friend who does not give food to his friend, who dwells with him and seeks his company. Let such a one depart from us; that is no home. One should rather seek another, even a stranger, who gives.
The stronger man should indeed give to the one who begs; he should look toward the longer path.
For riches turn like the wheels of a chariot, approaching now this one, now another.
The thoughtless man gains food in vain; I speak the truth: that is his own destruction.
He nourishes neither Aryaman nor his friend; he who eats alone becomes the possessor of all guilt alone.
The ploughshare, while ploughing, produces nourishment; he who clears the path with his feet surpasses the one who does not speak the sacred word (*brahman*).
Speaking as a priest, the more eloquent man shall overcome the one who does not give, just as a generous kinsman overcomes the stingy.
The one-footed has stepped out beyond the two-footed; the two-footed follows after the three-footed.
The four-footed comes at the call of the two-footed, standing near and beholding the fivefold rows.
Even two hands that are alike do not perform the same work; even two mother-cows do not yield the same amount of milk;
even twins do not possess equal powers; and even two who are kinsmen do not give gifts in equal measure.
O Agni, you who are pure in your vows, shining among mortals in your own dwelling, you strike down the devourer.
You rise up, well-invoked; you rejoice in the clarified butters when the ladles have been brought together toward you.
Invoked with song, that Agni shines forth, worthy of praise;
his face is anointed with the ladle.
Agni, whose face is honeyed, is anointed with ghee when offered oblations; he shines forth, rich in light.
Being praised, you are kindled for the gods, O bearer of oblations;
mortals call upon you, such as you are.
O mortals, worship that immortal Agni with clarified butter—
the invincible master of the household.
O Agni, burn away the demon with your invincible flame; shine as the guardian of the cosmic order (*ṛta*).
O Agni, with your face do you burn against the sorceresses,
shining brightly among the wide dwellings.
Thee, the bearer of oblations, those dwelling in wide realms have kindled with their songs—
thee, the best at sacrifice among the human race.
"Thus," "thus," so runs my thought: "May I win cattle and horses;
have I not drunk of Soma?"
Like violent winds, the draughts have lifted me up; "Have I drunk of the Soma? I ask.
The draughts drunk have carried me away like swift horses to a chariot; "Have I not drunk of Soma? [he asks].
The prayer has come near to me, like a lowing cow to her dear calf;
"Have I drunk of the Soma? it asks.
Like a carpenter fashioning a chariot-seat, I turn my thought around within my heart: "Have I drunk of the Soma?"—so I ask.
"Indeed, the five tribes have not even glinted before my eyes;
have I not drunk of Soma? he said.
"Neither both heaven and earth together, nor even my other wing, are equal to me; have I not drunk of Soma? he asked.
By my greatness I have surpassed the sky and this great earth;
have I not drunk of the Soma?
"Come, I shall set this earth down either here or there; have I not drunk of Soma? (RV 10.119.9)
"Swiftly indeed shall I strike the earth here or there; have I not drunk of Soma? (RV 10.119.10)
"One wing of mine is in heaven; the other I have drawn down below.
Have I not drunk of Soma? he asked.
I am of great majesty, risen up to the very clouds; have I not drunk of the Soma?
I go to the house, well-prepared, the bearer of oblations to the gods; have I not drunk of the Soma?
That indeed was the eldest in all the worlds, from which was born the fierce one of brilliant valor;
as soon as he was born, he overcomes his enemies—he in whom all his helpers rejoice.
Increasing in power and possessing abundant vigor, you, as an enemy, strike fear into the Dāsa.
Winning both the unbreathing and the breathing, they cry out to you at the offerings during the exhilarations of the soma.
All turn their will toward you when these helpers become twice or thrice as many.
Mix that which is sweeter than the sweet with sweetness; fight well for us with honey against honey.
For thus indeed the sages rejoice after you as you win the treasures at every intoxication.
O bold one, extend your more powerful and firm strength; let not the evil-doing sorcerers deceive you.
Through you we shall prevail in battles, beholding many things worthy of combat. I urge on your weapons with my words; I sharpen your vital powers with my prayer.
I would praise the one of many forms, the skillful, the most powerful Āptya among the Āptyas.
He pierces the seven Dānus with his might and overcomes many adversaries.
You have bestowed that lower and higher [treasure] in the dwelling where you protected us with your aid;
you cause the two wandering mothers to stand firm, and from there you send forth many heroic deeds.
Bṛhaddiva, the foremost winner of light, proclaims these sacred words of power as a hymn of strength for Indra.
As sovereign ruler, he rules over the great stall of cattle; he has thrown open all his own doors.
Thus has the great Atharvan Bṛhaddiva spoken to Indra as his own body;
the stainless sisters dwelling in the mother [the earth] impel him and strengthen him with power.
In the beginning, the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha) arose; once born, he was the sole Lord of all that exists.
He supported this earth and yonder sky. To what god shall we offer our oblation?
He who is the giver of self, the giver of strength, whose command all the gods revere— he whose shadow is immortality and whose shadow is death— to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
He who by his greatness became the sole king of the breathing and blinking world;
he who rules over these bipeds and quadrupeds—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
To him whose greatness these snow-capped mountains proclaim, and to whom they say the ocean belongs along with the Rasa river;
he to whom these quarters belong, and whose arms they are—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?

By whom the formidable heaven and the earth were made firm, by whom the sun was established and the firmament, he who is the measurer of the mid-air and the region— unto what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
To whom the two shouting worlds, supported by his aid and trembling in their minds,
looked up— over whom the risen sun shines forth— to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
When the great waters went everywhere, bearing the embryo and generating Agni, from that there arose the one life-force (asus) of the gods. To which god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
He who by his greatness surveyed the waters as they held creative power and generated the sacrifice—
he who was the one God above all gods— to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?

May he who is the progenitor of the earth, or he of true laws who begot the heavens, and he who begot the great, shining waters—him may he not harm. To which god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings.
Whatever desire we have as we offer this oblation to you, may that be ours; may we be masters of riches.
I praise him who is like a treasure, of wondrous luster—the lovely, auspicious guest who is free from hostility.
May he, Agni, the Hotṛ-priest and lord of the house, grant us all-sustaining riches and heroic strength.
O Agni, graciously accepting my word, take pleasure in it—you who know all ways, O you of noble power!
Clad in clarified butter, prepare the path for our prayer; the gods have brought you forth according to your sacred law.
Wandering through the seven stations, O immortal one, grant gifts to the donor who performs good deeds;
O Agni, be magnanimous toward him who has approached you with fuel, and favor him with wealth consisting of heroic sons and well-disposed attendants.
The seven [priests], bearing oblations, invoke Agni— the banner of sacrifice, the first domestic priest,
the vigorous one— him who hears us, whose back is sprinkled with ghee, the bull, the god who bestows heroic strength upon the giver.
You are the first messenger, most excellent; being invoked for the sake of immortality, take delight therein.
The Maruts have cleansed you in the house of the donor; the Bhr̥gus have caused you to shine forth with their hymns of praise.
Milking the well-yielding cow that provides all sustenance for the sacrificer who loves the sacrifice, O Agni of noble power;
dripping with ghee and illuminating the threefold laws of Truth, you manifest your supreme wisdom as you go around the sacrificial circuit.
At the break of this very dawn, men have sacrificed, making you their messenger.
The gods have magnified you for your greatness, O Agni, as they wiped the clarified butter upon the altar at the sacrifice.
The Vasiṣṭhas, the wise ones, have invoked you, the vigorous one, O Agni, chanting praises at the sacrificial assemblies.
Bestow upon the sacrificers an abundance of wealth; and do you all protect us always with your blessings.
This Vena, enveloped in light, impels the daughters of Pṛśni in the measurement of the mid-air;
at the meeting of the waters and the sun, the sages lick him with their hymns as if he were an infant.

Vena, born from the cloud, raises the wave from the ocean; the back of the beloved one has become visible. Upon the ridge, on the summit of *ṛta*, he shines; the hosts have sung together toward their common source.
Calling out together toward their common goal, the many mothers of the calf stand together in one nest;
moving upon the ridge of Truth, the voices lick the honey of immortality.
Knowing his form, the sages yearned; they indeed went toward the cry of the wild buffalo.
Moving according to the cosmic order (*ṛta*), they stood over the river; Gandharva found the immortal names.
The Apsaras, smiling at her lover, the maiden, bears him in the highest heaven.
Moving among the dwellings of his beloved, being beloved himself, that Vena sits upon the golden wing.
When they beheld you with longing in their hearts as you flew like a well-winged bird toward the firmament—
the golden-winged messenger of Varuṇa, the restless bird in the womb of Yama— then they gazed upon you.
Upright upon the vault of heaven the Gandharva has stood, facing us, bearing his brilliant weapons;
clothed in a fragrant robe fair to behold, he has manifested his dear names like the light of heaven.
As a drop he goes toward the ocean, beholding with the eye of a vulture in the wide expanse; the ray, longing for it with bright luster, has made dear things manifest in the third realm.
O Agni, come to this sacrifice of ours—the fivefold path, the threefold, with seven threads.
Be the bearer of our oblations and our leader; for you have lain for a very long time in deep darkness.
Moving from the godless toward the god, going secretly while perceiving [the truth], I attain immortality;
though I am auspicious, I abandon that which is inauspicious, and I go from my own kinship to a stranger as if to a non-kin.

Beholding the guest of another branch, I measure out many foundations of the Eternal Order (*ṛta*). I proclaim what is auspicious to the Father, the Asura; from that which is unworthy of sacrifice, I go toward the portion worthy of sacrifice.
I have spent many years within him; choosing Indra, I leave my father behind.
Agni, Soma, and Varuṇa—they pass away; I am turning back the kingdom, coming here to protect it.
Those Asuras have indeed become devoid of magic; and you, O Varuṇa, do not desire me. O King, distinguishing the truth from untruth by means of the *ṛta*, come to the sovereignty over my kingdom!
This is the light; this indeed was the lovely thing; this is the radiance, the wide mid-air.
Let us two slay Vṛtra; come forth, O Soma! Being an oblation yourself, let us worship you with an oblation.
The Seer, by his poetic power, fixed his form in heaven; Varuṇa, through his might, released the waters.
Like women making their homes secure, the rivers bear aloft his bright color.
These [waters] attend upon his supreme power; he dwells within them, rejoicing in their own inherent nature.
Like subjects choosing a king, they, shrinking back from Vṛtra, stood apart from him.
They call him the swan, the companion of the loathsome ones, moving in friendship with the celestial waters;
as he moves about following the *anuṣṭubh* meter, the seers have discerned Indra through their inspired thought.
I move with the Rudras and the Vasus; I also [move] with the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas.
I sustain both Mitra and Varuṇa; I [sustain] Indra and Agni, and I [sustain] both the Aśvins.
I bear the crushing Soma; I bear Tvaṣṭṛ, as well as Pūṣan and Bhaga.
I bestow wealth upon the one who offers oblations, upon the sacrificer who presses the juice and is skilled in the rite.
I am the sovereign ruler, the gatherer of treasures, the conscious one, the first among those worthy of sacrifice.
The gods have distributed me in many places, me who have many stations and who cause many things to enter.
Through me he eats food, whoever perceives, whoever breathes, and whoever hears what is spoken. Those who lack understanding dwell near me; hear, O famous one, for I speak to you with faith.
I alone speak this myself, which is pleasing to both gods and men.
Whomever I desire, him I make fierce; him I make a Brahman, him a seer, him a man of great wisdom.
I bend the bow for Rudra, so that his arrow may strike the one who hates sacred prayer. I stir up conflict among the people; I have entered heaven and earth.
I give birth to the Father upon his head; my source is within the waters, in the ocean.
Thence I spread out through all the worlds, and with my summit I touch that very sky.
I alone blow forth like the wind, setting all worlds in motion; beyond heaven and beyond this earth, I have come to be as vast as this in my majesty.
Neither distress nor misfortune, O gods, reaches that mortal whom Aryaman,
Mitra, and Varuṇa lead together in harmony across his enemies.
For that indeed we choose from you, O Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—
by which you protect the mortal from distress and lead him beyond his enemies.
Surely these—Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—are now for our protection;
they are the best leaders to lead us, and the best deliverers to carry us across our enemies.
You—Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—protect the universe on every side.
In your dear protection may we abide, O excellent leaders, beyond our enemies.
May the Ādityas—Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—overcome our adversaries;
may we invoke the mighty Rudra with the Maruts, Indra, and Agni for our well-being, passing beyond our enemies.
May Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman lead us safely across all difficulties,
these kings of the peoples, beyond all our enemies.
May Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman grant us prosperity for our aid;
may the Ādityas, far-extending, grant us wide protection when we pray for it, so that we may overcome our enemies.
Just as you, O Vasus, worthy of sacrifice, released that Gaurī who was bound by the foot, even so release us from this distress; O Agni, further prolong our life.
The goddess Night, approaching, has looked out in many places with her eyes; she has put on all her splendors.
The immortal goddess has filled the wide space, the depths, and the heights;
with her light, she drives away the darkness.
The goddess Dawn, approaching, has driven away her sister, the Night;
indeed, the darkness departs.
May she be ours today, at whose approach we have settled down like birds finding their dwelling in a tree.
The villages have settled down; those with feet and those with wings have settled down;
even the hawks seeking their prey have settled down.
Drive away the she-wolf and the wolf; ward off the thief, O Night. Then become easy for us to pass.
The black darkness, clearly manifesting, has approached me closely; O Dawn, drive it away like a debt.
I have brought these [songs] to you like cattle; O Night, daughter of Heaven, accept this hymn as one who has won the prize.
O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations; kindling you, may we nourish our bodies.
May the four quarters bow down to me; with you as our overseer, may we conquer the hostile armies.
May all the gods be with me in my invocation—the Maruts accompanied by Indra, Viṣṇu, and Agni.
May the wide world of the intermediate space be mine; may the wind blow for me in this desire.
May the gods bestow wealth upon me through sacrifice; may the blessing be with me, and with me the invocation of the gods.
May the divine Hotṛ-priests, the foremost ones, accept [the offering]; may we be unharmed in body and rich in heroic sons.
Let them offer for me those oblations which are mine; let the intention of my mind be realized. May I not fall into any sin whatsoever; O All-Gods, speak in our favor.
O six divine expanses, make wide room for us; O all you gods, display your heroic power here!
May we not be abandoned by our offspring nor by our bodies; may we not fall into the power of the enemy, O King Soma!

O Agni, repelling the fury of our enemies, do you, the undeceived guardian, protect us on every side. Let those who harbor secret malice turn back again; may the minds of these who have awakened perish.
Dhātṛ, the ordainer of ordainers, who is the lord of the world— the god who is our protector and overcomes the assailant—
may both Aśvins and Bṛhaspati protect this sacrifice and the sacrificer from misfortune.
May the wide-striding buffalo, invoked by many, rich in food, grant us protection in this call.
O Indra, Lord of the bay horses, be gracious to our progeny; do not harm us, nor abandon us.
May those who are our rivals be driven away; with Indra and Agni we repel them.
The Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas have made him a high-reaching, formidable, perceiving, and sovereign overlord.
Neither non-being nor being existed then; there was not the atmosphere, nor the sky beyond it.
What did the world-encompassing waters contain, and where? In whose protection was the unfathomable deep? What was there?
There was neither death nor immortality at that time; there was no sign of night or day.
That One breathed, windless, by its own inherent power (*svadhayā*); other than that, nothing else existed beyond it.
In the beginning, there was darkness hidden by darkness; this whole world was an indistinguishable ocean.
That which existed, enveloped by the void and chaotic, was one, and it was born through the power of heat.
In the beginning, Desire arose within that, which was the first seed of mind.
Sages, searching in their hearts with wisdom, discovered the bond of Being in Non-being.
Transversely was stretched their measuring-line; was there below, or was there above?
There were seed-holders, there were powers; self-sustenance was below, impulse was beyond.
Who truly knows? Who here can declare it—from where was it born, from where did this creation come?
The gods are later than its manifestation; so who then knows from whence it first came into being?
From whence this creation has arisen— whether he fashioned it or whether he did not—
he who is its overseer in the highest heaven, he indeed knows, or perhaps even he does not know.

The sacrifice which is stretched out on all sides with its threads, extended by a hundred and one divine acts—these fathers who have come weave it; they sit at the outspread web, saying, "Weave forward! Weave back!"
The man weaves it out; the man unbinds it; the man has stretched it across this firmament.
These pegs have settled near their seat; they have made the *sāman* chants as the warp-threads for weaving.

What was the measure, what the model, what the foundation? What was the clarified butter, what was the enclosing-stick? What was the meter, what the *prauga*, what the hymn (*uktha*), when all the gods sacrificed to the god?
The Gāyatrī became the companion of Agni; Savitṛ was united with the Uṣṇih;
Soma, great through his hymns, was joined with the Anuṣṭubh; and the Bṛhatī aided the speech of Bṛhaspati.
The Virāj is the glory of Mitra and Varuṇa; the Triṣṭubh is Indra’s share of the day.
The Jagatī has entered all the gods; by it the seers and men were fashioned.
By that [sacrifice], when it was born in ancient times, the seers and our human ancestors fashioned it at the sacrifice;
I believe with my mind’s eye that I behold those who performed this sacrifice in the past.

Accompanied by hymns of praise, accompanied by meters, and accompanied by measures, the seven divine seers, having beheld the path of the ancients, the wise ones took hold [of it], like charioteers grasping their reins.
O Indra, O subduer, drive away all our enemies to the east, drive them away to the west,
and drive them away to the north and to the south, O hero, so that we may rejoice in your wide protection.
Just as those possessing barley reap the grain in due order, separating it out,
so do thou bring here the food of those who have not come to the trimming of the sacred grass with their homage.
For there is no chariot that travels according to the seasons, nor has any glory been found in the assemblies.
Desiring cattle, O sages, we seek Indra for friendship; desiring horses, we seek the bull for strength.
O Aśvins, lords of splendor, drinking the Surā together with the Asura Namuci,
you two aided Indra in his deeds.
Like parents for their son, O Aśvins, you both protected Indra with poetic wisdom and wondrous deeds;
when you drank the exhilarating Soma with your powers, Sarasvatī refreshed you, O Maghavan.
May Indra, the good protector, the possessor of wealth, through his aids, be gracious, he who possesses all knowledge.
May he drive away hostility and grant us fearlessness; may we be masters of heroic vigor.

May we abide in the good-will of that one worthy of sacrifice, and likewise in his auspicious favor. May that Indra, the excellent protector and possessor of riches, drive our enemies far away from us.
May the heaven, whose wealth is praised, and the earth, assist the sacrificer;
may the two gods, the Aśvins, increase the sacrificer with their favors.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, upholders of the people, we worship you two who are well-disposed through your inspired guidance. Through your friendship and for your sake, may we overcome the demons.
And now, when we desire to win from you that which is dear—
possessing our own wealth— or when the giver prospers with his riches, let no one withhold his bounties.
That other one, O Asura, was born from heaven; you, Varuṇa, are the king of all. The head of the chariot has taken delight; let him not, for such a sin, be a hater of his end.
In this very man, O Śakapūta, the offender strikes down the heroes who have sought refuge with a friend.
Or when the steed bestows protection upon his own dear and worshipful bodies, he is the one who brings low.
For your mother is Aditi, O wise ones; like the heaven, let the earth be purified with water.
Bestow what is dear upon us; wash away the stains of the sun with your rays.
For you two, O lords of the work, have sat down like one who stands upon a chariot, like one who sits upon the pole, like one who sits upon the tree.
As such, O Nṛmedhas, you protected our lamenting ones from distress; O Sumedhas, you protected them from distress.
Sing forth this strengthening hymn for this Indra, whose chariot is foremost;
he is the maker of space even in close combat, the slayer of Vṛtra in the clash of battles. Be our inspirer! May the bowstrings of our enemies snap upon their bows!
You released the rivers to flow downward; you slew the serpent.
O Indra, you were born without a rival; you nourish every desirable thing. We embrace you—let the bowstrings of our enemies snap upon their bows.
May all hostilities be utterly dispersed; may the prayers of the enemy fail us.
O Indra, you are the hurler of the weapon at the foe who seeks to slay us. May that bounty of yours which bestows wealth be ours; let the bowstrings of our enemies snap upon their bows.
O Indra, whatever person who seeks to harm us like a wolf assails us from any side—cast him beneath our feet;
you are the subduer and the conqueror. May the bowstrings of our enemies snap upon their bows!
Whoever assails us, O Indra—whether he be a kinsman or a stranger—diminish his strength, even as the great heaven [overshadows the earth]. May the bowstrings of our enemies snap upon their bows.
O Indra, we who long for you grasp at your friendship.
Lead us along the path of Truth past all difficulties. May the bowstrings of our enemies snap upon their bows!
O Indra, grant us that boon which yields a choice portion for the singer;
may the great cow, with her flawless udder, flow for us with a thousand streams of milk.

Since you, O Indra, have filled both heaven and earth like the Dawn, the divine Mother has brought you forth—you, the great sovereign of the mighty ones and of all people; the auspicious Mother has brought you forth.
Relax the firm strength of the mortal who seeks to strike us down;
cast him beneath our feet, he who points at us with malice. The divine Mother has brought us forth; the auspicious Mother has brought us forth.

O slayer of enemies, O Śakra, with your powers and all your aids, O Indra, shake down those great, all-glittering refreshments. The divine mother gave birth [to you]; the auspicious mother gave birth.

When you, O Śatakratu Indra, shake off all things like wealth for the one who presses the soma, with your thousandfold aids—O Goddess Mother, you have brought him forth; the auspicious Mother has brought him forth.
Let the missiles fall away on all sides like drops of sweat;
let ill-will depart from us like the threads of dūrvā grass. The divine mother has brought [the child] forth; the auspicious mother has brought him forth.

For you, O wise one, bear a long hook like a spear; O Maghavan, with your forward foot you strike down the branches as Yama does. The divine mother has brought you forth; the auspicious mother has brought you forth.
O gods, we do not diminish you; we do not neglect you. We act in accordance with what is heard in the sacred hymns. With our wings and our armpits, we clasp you closely here.
On that tree with beautiful leaves where Yama drinks together with the gods—
there our father, the lord of the people, looks back upon the ancients.
I gazed upon him with resentment as he wandered in that evil way, following after the ancients; therefore, I yearned for him again.
O boy, the new, wheelless chariot which you fashioned with your mind—
single-seated and facing in every direction— you mount it even though you do not see it.
O youth, the chariot which you caused to roll forth from among the inspired poets—that very chariot followed after the *sāman* chant; thus was it launched from here upon the boat.
Who gave birth to the boy? Who fashioned the chariot?
Who indeed might tell us today how it was that the bride-price was paid?
Just as she became the one to be followed, from that the summit was born;
the foundation was extended in front, and the exit was made behind.
This is the seat of Yama, which is called the dwelling of the gods;
this flute of his is blown, and he is adorned with songs of praise.
The long-haired one bears Agni; the long-haired one bears poison; the long-haired one sustains the two worlds.
The long-haired one is seen as the all-encompassing sun; the long-haired one is called this light.
The sages, girdled by the wind, wear soiled garments of reddish-brown;
they follow the rush of the wind when the gods have entered [them].
Intoxicated by the state of the sage, we have ascended to the winds;
O mortals, you behold only our bodies.
He flies through the intermediate space, beholding all forms;
the sage is the well-disposed friend of every god for the sake of their good work.
The horse of Vāta, the friend of Vāyu, and the sage impelled by the gods—
he dwells in both oceans, the eastern and the western.
Moving in the track of the Apsarases, Gandharvas, and wild beasts, Keśin, the knower of the sacred thought, is a sweet and most intoxicating friend.
Vāyu churned for him;
Kunannamā pounded it, as the long-haired one drank from the cup of poison together with Rudra.
O gods, you raise up again that which has been cast down; O gods, you restore again even the sinner who has committed a transgression.
O gods, you bring back to life once more.
These two winds blow from the ocean and from afar:
may one breathe strength upon you, and may the other blow away whatever is harmful.
O Vāta, blow hither healing; O Vāta, blow away whatever is disease. For you, possessing all remedies, go as the messenger of the gods.
I have come to you with healing remedies and with means for your safety. I have brought you auspicious strength; I drive away your consumption.
May the gods protect him here; may the host of Maruts protect him;
may all beings protect him, so that he may remain free from harm.
The waters indeed are healers; the waters drive away disease.
The waters are the healers of everything; may they provide a remedy for you.
With these two hands of ten fingers, with the tongue as the forerunner of speech—
with these two which cause no illness, we touch you.

In your friendship, O Indra, those priests, mindful of the *ṛta*, rent Vala asunder; there, honoring the dawns and releasing the waters, you performed wondrous deeds for Kutsa and subdued the dragons at his prayer.
You released the plants; you split the mountains apart; you drove out the cows and drank the beloved honey.
You made the trees grow by this wondrous deed; the sun blazed forth through the song born of *ṛta*.
Sūrya unyoked his chariot in the midst of heaven; the Ārya provided a counter-measure for the Dāsa.
Indra, acting together with Ṛjiśvan, shattered the firm fortresses of the wily Asura Pipru.
The bold Ayāsya, having opened up the unassailable treasures, crushed the godless ones.
Like the sun in the month, he took the wealth of the fortresses; being praised, he shattered the enemies with his radiant weapon.
With an army that does not fight, the all-pervading Vṛtra-slayer, piercing through, bestows gifts; he sharpens his impetuous weapons.
He was terrified by Indra’s thunderbolt as it struck him down; the radiant one fled, and Uṣas abandoned her wagon.
These are indeed your famous deeds, unique in that you made one [of the two] devoid of sacrifice;
you established the ordering of the months in heaven, and by you the father bears the wheel-rim that was split apart.
Savitar, with sunbeams and golden hair, has raised up his eternal light in the east.
At his impulse, Pūṣan goes forth, the wise guardian who beholds all beings.
Beholding men, he sits in the midst of heaven, having filled the two worlds and the intermediate space.
He looks toward all the butter-dripping ones, between the eastern and the western sign.
The foundation of wealth, the gatherer of treasures, he gazes upon all forms with his powers;
like the god Savitṛ whose laws are true, he stands like Indra in the clash for riches.
O Soma, when the waters beheld the Gandharva Viśvāvasu, they flowed away according to the cosmic order (*ṛta*).
Indra, hastening after them, perceived that and saw the enclosures of the sun.
May Viśvāvasu, the divine Gandharva who measures the mid-air, sing this to us:
whatever is true and whatever we do not know—may he, impelling our thoughts, protect our prayers.
He found the winner at the foot of the rivers; he threw open the doors of those confined within the rocky enclosures.
Gandharva proclaimed their nectar-like secrets; Indra understood the power of the serpents.
O Agni, yours is glory and vital power; your rays shine mightily, O Lord of Light.
O Sage of lofty luster, through your strength you bestow praiseworthy booty upon the donor.
With purifying luster, with bright luster, with undiminished luster, you rise up with your radiance.
Moving between your two mothers as their son, you protect them; you fill both heaven and earth.
O Son of Strength, Jātavedas, rejoice in our excellent praises and our prayers, for you have been well-disposed toward us.
In you they have gathered many-formed nourishments—those of wondrous aid, born of noble lineage.

O Agni, ruling as sovereign, spread yourself abroad among living beings; bestow wealth upon us, O Immortal One! You shine forth with a form worthy of being beheld; you fulfill our effective will for gain.
The wise ordainer of the sacrifice, who rules over great bounty—
thou bestowest upon him the auspicious gift of beauty, great nourishment, and winning wealth.
Men have placed Agni before them for their welfare—the observer of cosmic order, the mighty one, visible to all;
you, the divine one with hearing ears and most far-reaching fame, through song throughout the ages of mankind.
O Agni, speak here to us; turn toward us and be well-disposed.
Bestow wealth upon us, O Lord of the People, for you are the giver of riches to us.
May Aryaman grant us wealth, may Bhaga grant it, and may Bṛhaspati grant it;
may the gods grant it, and may Sūnṛtā, the goddess, grant us riches.
We invoke King Soma for protection, Agni with our songs of praise,
the Ādityas, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, and Bṛhaspati the priest.
We invoke Indra, Vāyu, and Bṛhaspati, who are easy to call,
here so that every person may be well-disposed toward us in our assembly.
Urge Aryaman, Bṛhaspati, and Indra to bestow gifts;
[urge] Vāta, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, and the vigorous Savitṛ.
O Agni, with your fires, increase our prayer and our sacrifice;
impel us toward the granting of wealth for the sake of the gods.
O Agni, this singer has found refuge in you; for there is no other kinship than yours, O Son of Strength.
For your protection is auspicious and provides triple shelter; keep the weapon of those who seek to harm us far away.
O Agni, your births proceed downward like one seeking food; like a companion, you reach across all beings.
May our steeds and our prayers win the prize; they move forward of their own accord like a herdsman.
Or indeed, O self-dependent Agni, you spare much brushwood as you devour it; even the fallow lands become mere mounds. Let us not provoke your fierce and mighty weapon.
When you go devouring over the heights and down into the depths, you spread out like an army eager for prey;
when the wind blows after your flame, you shave the earth as a barber shaves a beard.
His lines of chariots have been seen returning; there is but one path, yet many are the chariots.
When you, O Agni, stroking your arms, move downward and seek the earth that lies spread out before you.
Let your strength rise up, let your flame rise up, and let your powers rise up, O Agni, as you exert yourself.
Expand upward, bow down while growing strong; may all the Vasus sit upon you today.
This is the gathering place of the waters, the dwelling of the ocean; prepare another path than this, and by that go according to your desire.
In your path of coming and your path of departure, let flowering *dūrvā* grass grow;
let there be lakes and lotuses—these are the dwellings of the ocean.
Even that Atri, who had grown old in the *ṛta*, you made fit for his purpose like a horse for its journey;
when you restored Kakṣīvat, you made him new again like a chariot.
Like that very horse, the prize-winner whom the dustless ones have stretched out—
unloose Atri, the youngest, like a firm knot, from the mid-air.
O Heroes, most wondrous in deed, O radiant ones, bestow your favors upon Atri;
for then, O Heroes of heaven, our hymn of praise shall never cease for you.
O Aśvins, rich in gifts, may that gift and favor of yours reach us,
so that you two heroes may carry us across to our wide dwelling at the assembly.
You two, O Nāsatyas, went with winged birds to Bhujyu, who was tossing about in the ocean at the far end of the region; you brought him success.
Come to us with your favors, O most generous possessors of all wealth, like two who bring peace;
O Heroes, bestow upon us nourishing refreshments that swell like a spring.
For this immortal drop of yours, O Indu, hastens like a steed—
skillful, all-enlivening— for the Ordainer.
This poetic power, this *Ṛbhu*, is this very thunderbolt among us for the liberal giver;
it bears aloft the sharp-edged intoxication, even as the skillful artisan bears his effective draught.
The impetuous bull, having acted for the sake of the falcon, looked down upon these his own [wives],
the Ahīśuvah.
That which the fair-winged one, the son of the falcon, brought from afar— that which has a hundred wheels and whose path is the sky.

That lovely, ruddy measure of the soma-juice, free from predators, which the falcon brought to you with his foot—with that [soma] vitality is extended and life is prolonged; through it, kinship has remained awake.
Thus, O Indra, by means of the drop, you have held back even among the gods that great hostility.
Through wisdom, O wise one, you have extended our strength and our lifespan; through wisdom, this pressed juice has been offered from us.
I dig up this herb, the most powerful of plants,
by which one repels a rival wife and by which one wins a husband.
O you with upturned leaves, auspicious one, impelled by the gods, victorious one:
blow my rival away; make my husband mine alone.
I am the superior one; may I be superior to those who are superior. And let her who is my rival be inferior to those who are inferior.
I do not even utter her name; she finds no pleasure in this man.
We send our rival wife away to the furthest distance.
I am the conqueror, and you are the victorious one;
both of us being powerful, let us together overcome my rival.
I have brought to you the victorious one; I have overcome you with greater power.
May your mind run after me like a cow toward her calf; may it run along the path like water.
O Forest-Dweller, O Forest-Dweller, you who seem to vanish away—why do you not ask the way to the village? Does fear not seize you?
When the cicada chirps in response to the whistling of the wind,
the Forest Woman exults, as if making her way with clashing cymbals.
And it is as if cattle are grazing; it appears like a dwelling house. And the forest-path at evening sounds like the creaking of carts.
"He calls the cow by his own limbs; he has felled the tree with his own limbs.
Living in the forest, at evening he thinks, 'He has bellowed.'"
The forest does not kill unless another approaches it;
having eaten of sweet fruit, it lies down at its own will.
I have praised Araṇyānī, the mother of wild beasts, who smells of ointment, who is fragrant, who provides much food, and who requires no plowing.
I place my trust in your first wrathful deed, when you struck down Vṛtra and set the manly waters free.
When both heaven and earth submit to you, even the earth trembles at your might, O wielder of the stone.
O blameless one, with a mind seeking glory, you crushed Vṛtra—the master of magic—by means of your own magic powers.
Men choose you alone in their quests for cattle; they choose you at all sacrifices where oblations are offered.
O you who are invoked by many, take delight in these patrons, O Maghavan, who have increased and attained wealth as their own.
They sing praises for the sake of offspring and descendants amidst the perils, [praising] the powerful one at the winning of the sacrifice in the contest for undiminished wealth.
He indeed shall take pleasure in well-sustained wealth, he who understands his exhilarating, swift-moving power.
O Maghavan, the one who increases you and performs the sacrifice with offerings quickly brings forth booty and riches through his men.
O Maghavan, being praised, by your greatness grant wide space to our host; bestow wealth upon us.
You are Mitra and Varuṇa, the master of wondrous power; like a father, O wonder-worker, you distribute food to us as its divider.
O Indra, having pressed the soma, we praise you, and having won the prize, O you of many heroic deeds;
bring us prosperity for which we long, so that, protected by you, we may win it ourselves, for ourselves, and for our progeny.
Lofty indeed, O hero Indra, you were born to overcome the Dāsa tribes with the help of Sūrya.
Like Soma at its source, we hold within us that which was placed in secret, hidden, and concealed in the waters.

Or let the wise singer, longing for the favor of the seers, chant his songs toward the noble one. May we be those who take delight in the Soma juices, and likewise in the food offerings borne by your chariot.
O Indra, hero, I have recited these prayers for you; grant strength to men from among men.
Be of one mind with those in whom you take pleasure, and protect both the singers and their dependents.
Hear the call, O hero Indra, from the broad earth; you are praised by the hymns of Venya.
You have roared toward your ghee-filled womb; like a wave through lowlands, your swift-moving powers have rushed forward.
With his supports Savitar has fixed the earth; Savitar has made the sky firm where there is no pillar.
Savitar has milked the roaring atmosphere like a horse, and the ocean bound within the unassailable [vault].
Where the ocean was fixed and roared, Savitṛ, the Son of Waters, knows that;
from there the earth arose, from there the mid-air emerged, and from there heaven and earth were spread out.
Then this other, worthy of sacrifice, came into being through the abundance of the immortal world:
the fair-winged Garuḍa, indeed, was born first from Savitṛ; he follows his law.

Like cattle toward the village, like a warrior toward his horses, like a lowing cow toward her calf while yielding milk with a gracious mind, like a husband toward his wife— may Savitṛ, the upholder of heaven, possessor of all boons, come down to us.
O Savitṛ, just as Hiraṇyastūpa, the Aṅgiras, invoked you for this prize, so do I,
praising and adoring you for protection, remain watchful for you as for a stalk of soma.
Though already kindled, you are kindled again, O bearer of oblations to the gods.
Come to us with the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus; come to us for our mercy.
Accepting this sacrifice and these words, come hither;
O kindled one, we mortals call upon you, we call upon you for mercy.
I praise you, Jātavedas, the possessor of all boons, with my inspired thought;
O Agni, bring hither to us the gods who are devoted to our dear vows, for the sake of their grace, those who are devoted to our dear vows.
Agni, the god, has become the domestic priest of the gods; men and seers have kindled Agni.
I invoke Agni for the winning of great wealth—him who is gracious—for the winning of wealth.
Agni protected Atri, Bharadvāja, Gaviṣṭhira, Kaṇva, and Trasadasyu in battle;
Vasiṣṭha, the domestic priest, invokes Agni for mercy—the domestic priest for mercy.
By faith the fire is kindled; by faith the oblation is offered.
We proclaim faith with our speech upon the summit of fortune.
O Śraddhā, make this which I have uttered dear to the one who gives, dear to the one who desires to give, and dear among those who enjoy and sacrifice.
Just as the gods established faith among the fierce Asuras,
so may you establish this our utterance among the liberal patrons who perform sacrifice.
The gods and those who sacrifice wait upon Faith, with Vāyu as their guardian;
through the intention of the heart they honor Faith, and by means of Faith one finds wealth.
We invoke Faith in the morning, Faith at midday; we invoke Faith at the setting of the sun. O Faith, inspire us here with faith!
Thus, O Ruler, you are truly great, the wondrous devourer of enemies;
he whose friend is never slain nor ever overcome.
May Indra, the bestower of well-being, the lord of the people, the slayer of Vṛtra, the subduer of enemies,
the self-controlled, the bull, the drinker of Soma, and the creator of fearlessness, go before us.
Drive away the Rakṣas, drive away the adversaries; shatter the jaws of Vṛtra.
O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, destroy the fury of the enemy who assails us.
O Indra, strike down our adversaries; cast those who attack us low. Whoever seeks to harm us, send him down into the deepest darkness.
O Indra, turn away the mind of the hater, turn away the weapon of him who seeks to conquer us; grant us wide protection from his wrath and keep his weapon far away.
Swinging him about, the active ones wait upon Indra at his birth,
having obtained excellent heroic power.
O Indra, you were born from strength, from power, and from might;
O bull, you are indeed preeminent as a bull.
O Indra, you are the slayer of Vṛtra; you have extended across the mid-air; by your might, you have propped up the heavens.
O Indra, you bear in your arms the hymn that is in harmony with you,
whetting the thunderbolt with your might.
O Indra, you are the conqueror of all beings by your might;
as such, you have pervaded all the worlds.
Soma purifies himself for some; others attend to the clarified butter;
may he go even to those for whom the honey flows forth.
Those who are unassailable through austerity, those who have gone to heaven by means of austerity,
and those who have performed great austerity— unto them indeed let him go.
Those who fight in great battles, those heroes who lay down their lives,
or those who bestow thousands as sacrificial fees— may he go even to them.
O Yama, may he go even to those ancestors who were formerly observers of the *ṛta*, upholders of the *ṛta*, increasers of the *ṛta*, and performers of austerity.
O Yama, go also to the seers who perform austerities, those born of austerity, and to the poets with a thousand paths who protect the sun.
O one-eyed, misshapen Arāyī, you who follow the track, go to the mountain!
With the warriors of Śirimbiṭha, with them we drive you away.
Chased away from here, chased away from there—let her who has harmed all embryos go!
O Brahmanaspati, you with the sharp horns, go forth and trample the Arayi!
That wood which floats, unoccupied by men, on the far shore of the river—
seize it, O you of evil intent, and go to the furthermost distance with it!
When you went forward, O frogs, with your bellies like copper,
all of Indra’s enemies were slain, they who were as fleeting as bubbles.
These have led the cow around; they have carried Agni around.
They have established their fame among the gods—who would dare to attack them?
May our prayers impel Agni like a swift steed in races;
through him may we win prize after prize.
O Agni, with that army by which we may drive back the cattle through your protection— send that forth for us to win the gift of wealth.
O Agni, bring us solid wealth, broad, consisting of cattle and horses; unbind the aperture, turn back the niggardly miser.
O Agni, you have caused the imperishable star, the sun, to ascend to heaven;
you have bestowed light upon the people.
O Agni, you are the banner of the people, the most beloved and the most excellent, seated upon the sacrificial lap; take note of the singer, bestowing vital strength upon him.
May we now bring these worlds to fulfillment, O Indra and all you gods.
May Indra, together with the Ādityas, fashion for us the sacrifice, our own body, and progeny.
May Indra, together with the Ādityas and the host of Maruts, be the protector of our bodies.
When the gods, having slain the Asuras, went forth, guarding their divine status.
They brought the Sun hither with their skillful arts; then indeed they beheld his vigorous, self-sustaining power all around.
May Sūrya protect us from heaven, Vāta from the intermediate space, and Agni from earthly beings.
Be pleased, O Savitṛ; your flame is worthy of a hundred libations.
Protect us from the falling lightning bolt.
May the god Savitṛ grant us sight, and may Parvata grant us sight;
may Dhātṛ bestow sight upon us.
Bestow sight upon our eye, sight for us to see, and sight for our bodies;
may we behold this world both together and apart.
O Sūrya, may we behold you who are so beautiful to look upon; may we, with our eyes fixed on men, gaze out clearly.
Yonder sun has risen; here has my good fortune arisen. Knowing this, I, the victorious one, have obtained a husband.
I am the banner, I am the head; I am the fierce one who pronounces the verdict.
Let my husband attend to the will of me, the victorious woman.
My sons are slayers of enemies, and my daughter is a sovereign queen; moreover, I am victorious, and my fame with my husband is supreme.
By means of that oblation with which Indra, having performed the rite, became preeminent in glory—O gods, I have now performed this; indeed, I have become free from rivals.
Free from rivals, slayer of rivals, victorious, and all-conquering— may she take away the splendor of the others, just as one takes the wealth of those who are weaker.
I have completely conquered these co-wives, overcoming them, so that I may rule over this hero and over this people.
Drink of this intense, invigorating [Soma]; unyoke your two bay steeds here along with all your chariot.
O Indra, let not other sacrificers detain you; these pressed juices are for you alone.
For you the juices have been pressed, and for you they shall be pressed; the strengthening songs call upon you.
O Indra, enjoying this libation today, you who know all things, drink the Soma here.
Whosoever, desiring the gods, presses Soma for him with a yearning mind and with his whole heart—for him Indra does not give up his cattle; he makes that [Soma] praised and pleasing for him.
He is clearly seen by him who, though wealthy, does not press Soma for him;
Maghavan casts that man down into the pit and slays his haters of sacred knowledge, even without being commanded.
Desiring horses, desiring cattle, and desiring booty, we call upon you to come hither. Serving in your new favor, O Indra, may we invoke you for our good fortune.
I release you with this oblation so that you may live, from unknown consumption and from royal consumption;
if the Grāhi has seized him, O Indra and Agni, release him from her.
Whether his life-span is exhausted, or he has passed away, or has already been led into the presence of Death—I bring him back from the lap of Destruction; I have rescued him for a hundred autumns.
With oblation that possesses a thousand eyes, a hundred autumns, and a hundredfold life-span, I have brought him hither,
so that Indra may lead him for a hundred autumns to the further shore of all misfortune.
Live for a hundred autumns, increasing in strength; live for a hundred winters and a hundred springs.
May Indra, Agni, Savitṛ, and Bṛhaspati restore this man to a life of a hundred years by means of this oblation.
I have brought you back; I have found you. You have returned, renewed.
O whole-limbed one, I have found for you your entire sight and your entire lifespan.
May Agni, in harmony with the sacred word (*brahman*), the slayer of demons, drive away from here that sickness which,
bearing an evil name, has settled upon your embryo and your womb.
Whatever disease of evil name has settled upon your embryo or your womb—
Agni, together with the sacred prayer (*brahman*), has driven that flesh-eater away.
He who kills your embryo as it falls, he who kills it as it lies still,
or he who seeks to kill you once it is born— that one we cause to perish from here.
He who spreads apart your thighs so that he may lie between the husband and wife,
he who licks the interior of the womb— him we cause to perish from here.
Him who approaches you as a brother, having become your husband, or as a lover,
and him who seeks to destroy your offspring— him we cause to perish from here.
Whoever lies down with you after having deluded you with sleep and darkness,
whoever seeks to destroy your offspring— him we cause to perish from here.
From your eyes, from your nostrils, from your ears, and from your chin— I root out the consumption from the head, from the brain, and from your tongue.
From your neck, from your *uṣṇihā* joints, from your vertebrae, and from your spine;
from your shoulders and from your arms, I pull out the consumption that affects your forearms.
From your entrails, from your intestines, from the large intestine, and from the heart;
from the kidneys, from the liver, and from the lungs, I pull the disease away from you.
From your two thighs, from your two knee-caps, from your two heels, and from your two forefeet;
from your two hips and from your buttocks, I tear away the consumption-disease for you.
From your urethra, from your penis, from your body hair, and from your nails—
from your entire self— I now tear away this consumption.
Born from every limb, from every hair, and from every joint— this consumption (yakṣma) from your entire self, that I now tear away from you.
Depart, O lord of the mind; go away and move far off. Look toward Nirṛti from afar; let the mind of the living man wander in many directions.
They choose indeed what is auspicious as their boon; they harness the auspicious right-hand [steed].
Auspicious is the eye in the realm of Vaivasvata; the mind of the living wanders in many places.
Whatever we have committed through a curse, an execration, or an imprecation, whether while awake or while sleeping— may Agni place all those evil deeds and unpleasant things far away from us.
O Indra, O Brahmaṇaspati, whatever offense we commit against you,
may the wise Aṅgirasa protect us from the enmity of our foes and from distress.
We have conquered today; we have prevailed; we have become sinless. May that evil intention, whether awake or asleep, which we hate, fall upon him who hates us; may it fall upon him.

O gods, since the dove, sent as a messenger by Nirṛti, has come here seeking what it desires, let us offer praise to it and perform an expiation; may there be well-being for our bipeds and well-being for our quadrupeds.
May the dove sent to us be auspicious; O gods, may this bird be innocent within our homes.
May Agni, the sage, accept our oblation; may the winged missile pass us by.
The winged missile shall not harm us; it makes its footprint upon the hearth, in the place where the fire is kindled.
May there be well-being for our cattle and for our men; O gods, let the dove not injure us here.
Whatever the owl utters is in vain, as is whatever footprint the pigeon makes in the fire;
to him for whom this has been sent as a messenger—to that Yama, to Death, let there be homage.
Drive away the pigeon with a *ṛc*-verse; driving it forth, rejoicing in the sacrificial food (*iṣ*), lead the cow around.
Causing all misfortunes to vanish, let it fly away most swiftly, leaving us strength behind.
Make me a bull among my peers, a subduer of rivals;
make me the slayer of enemies, a sovereign ruler, and a lord of cattle.
I am here, free from harm and uninjured like Indra, the conqueror of rivals.
All these rivals of mine stand beneath my feet.
Right here I bind you fast, like two ends of a bow with a string. O Lord of Speech, restrain these [words] so that they shall speak what is lower than me.
I have come as the conqueror, with the power of Viśvakarman.
I have won over your mind, your resolve, and your assembly.
Having taken your security and well-being, may I become preeminent among you; I have stepped upon your heads.
Speak up from beneath my feet like frogs from the water—like frogs emerging from the water!
For you, O Indra, this honey is poured out; you are the lord of the pressed vessel.
Bestow upon us wealth consisting of many heroes; you, having heated yourself with fervor, won the light of heaven.
We invoke Śakra, the winner of light, who greatly rejoices in the pressed juice, toward the libations.
Take notice of this sacrifice of ours here; come hither! We pray to Maghavan, the conqueror of rivals.
Under the law of King Soma and Varuṇa, and within the protection of Bṛhaspati and Anumati— O Maghavan, O Dhātṛ, O Vidhātṛ, today in this hymn of praise, I have partaken of your jars.
Impelled, I have made my portion even in the ritual vessel; as the first patron, I have polished this hymn of praise.
O Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni, when I came to you with what was gained at the pressed [Soma] in your dwelling.
Now, the greatness of Vāta’s chariot: it goes breaking [the trees], its roar thundering;
touching the sky, it moves creating ruddy lights, and it goes scattering the dust of the earth.
They hasten along following the various paths of the wind; they go toward him as women to a common gathering.
With them, the god, the king of this entire world, travels on a single chariot.
Traveling by paths through the intermediate space, he does not rest on any day whatsoever.
The first-born friend of the waters, the observer of cosmic order (*ṛtāvā*), where indeed was he born, and from whence did he come into being?
The self of the gods, the germ of the world—this god moves according to his will. His roar indeed is heard, but not his form; to that Vāta we shall offer worship with an oblation.
May the wind blow pleasantly upon the cows; may they graze upon the plants rich in nourishment.
May they drink from the fat, life-bestowing waters. O Rudra, be gracious to our footed cattle for their protection.
Those who are alike, those who are diverse, and those who are of one form—whose names Agni knows through sacrifice;
those whom the Aṅgirases produced here through austerity—to them, O Parjanya, grant great protection.
Those who extended their bodies among the gods, whose every form Soma knows—
grant us, O Indra, those cows that swell with milk, rich in offspring, within our pen.
Prajāpati, bestowing these upon me, in harmony with all the gods and the ancestors, has brought them—the auspicious and true ones—into our cow-pen; may we dwell together with their offspring.
May the radiant, great one drink the Soma-mead, bestowing unimpaired life upon the lord of the sacrifice;
he who, impelled by the wind, protects by his own self and has nourished all creatures, shines forth in many ways.
Radiant, vast, well-sustained, most effective in winning booty, the truth established upon the supporting foundation of heaven;
the slayer of enemies, the slayer of Vṛtra, the greatest slayer of Dasyus, the light that destroys Asuras and rivals has been born.
This is the best of lights, the highest light; it is called the all-conquering, the wealth-winning, the great.
All-shining, with its vast radiance, the mighty Sūrya has spread wide for us to see, along with unfailing, steadfast power.
Shining with light, you went to the sun, to the luminous realm of heaven,
by which all these worlds were brought forth by Viśvakarman, who is favored by all the gods.
O Indra, you protected that chariot of the one who presses the juice and offers oblations;
you heard the call of the Soma-offerer.
You struck off the head of the wildly trembling Makha from his skin; you went to the house of the Soma-presser.
O Indra, you repeatedly loosened for Āstrabudhna that mortal Venya for the sake of the mindful one.
O Indra, place that very sun, though it be in the west, in the east,
even against the will of the gods.
Come hither with thy wood; the cows follow thy path with their full udders.
Come hither with a wealth-bestowing thought, most bountiful, enkindling the sacrifice along with the liberal givers.
Like those who bear the weight of their father, we, the givers of good gifts, take up the thread and perform the sacrifice.
Dawn, by her noble birth, rolls away the darkness of her sister along the path.
I have brought you here; be within, stand firm and unshakable.
Let all the people desire you; let not the kingdom fall away from you.
Be right here; do not waver, as immovable as a mountain. Stand firm here like Indra, and maintain sovereignty here.
Indra has established this man as firm with a firm oblation;
may Soma speak in his favor, and so too may Brahmaṇaspati.
Firm is the sky, firm is the earth, and firm are these mountains;
firm is this entire world, and firm is this king of the people.
Firm is your kingdom, O King Varuṇa; firm is it, O god Bṛhaspati.
Firm may Indra and Agni maintain your kingdom, that it be steadfast.
With the firm oblation, we touch upon Soma with that which is firm;
then may Indra make the clans bring tribute to you alone.
With the *abhīvarta* oblation by which Indra was turned toward victory—
with that, O Brahmanaspati, turn us toward sovereignty.
Turning against our rivals, against those who are hostile to us, stand firm against the one who attacks us and against him who envies us.
May the god Savitṛ turn toward you;
may Soma turn toward you; may all beings turn toward you, so that you may be victorious.
O gods, with that oblation by which Indra, having performed the rite, became preeminent in glory—that very thing I have now performed; indeed, I have become free from rivals.
Free from rivals, a slayer of rivals, a sovereign lord, and all-conquering,
may I rule over these beings and over the people.
O pressing-stones, may the god Savitṛ impel you according to the sacred law; yoke yourselves to the poles and press out the juice!
O pressing-stones, drive away misfortune and ill-will;
make the rays of light our medicine.
The pressing-stones, in unison, exult upon the lower stones,
bestowing manly vigor upon the Bull.
O pressing-stones, may the god Savitṛ now impel you according to the sacred law for the sake of the sacrificer who presses the Soma.
The sons of the Ṛbhus have loudly shouted their great songs of praise;
they who, sustaining all things, have fed upon the earth like calves upon their mother cow.
Bring forth the god Jātavedas with divine prayer;
may he carry our offerings to him in due order.
And this very one, seeking the gods, is led forth as the Hotṛ for the sacrifice; like a well-guarded chariot, he, glowing with heat, takes heed by himself.
This Agni protects us as if from an immortal birth;
he, the god more powerful than power itself, has been established for the sake of life.
The wise behold with their heart and mind the Bird anointed by the magic power of the Asura;
within the ocean, the seers discern him; the ordainers seek his station among the rays of light.
The bird bears speech within his mind; the Gandharva uttered it within the womb. At the station of Cosmic Order (ṛta), the seers guard that shining, celestial wisdom.
I have seen the Herdsman, who never rests, moving hither and thither along his paths;
clothed in converging and diverging rays, he moves repeatedly within the worlds.
Hither let us invoke for our well-being that swift Tārkṣya, the prize-winner urged by the gods, the victorious overcomer of chariots, whose rim is uninjured, who conquers in battle.
Invoking the bounty of Indra as it were, may we ascend you for our well-being as if onto a ship;
O you two who are wide, broad, vast, and deep, may we not be harmed by you when you come near or when you go far away.
He who at once by his might has overspread the five peoples, as the sun with its light overspreads the waters—
he, the winner of thousands, the winner of hundreds, whose impetuous speed no one can restrain, like a young woman or an arrow.
Arise, look upon Indra’s seasonal portion!
If it is cooked, offer it; if it is not yet cooked, wait for me.
The oblation is cooked; come hither, O Indra! The sun has reached the midpoint of its journey.
Your friends sit around you with their offerings, like guardians of a clan surrounding the lord of the herd as he moves about.
I consider it cooked in the udder, cooked on the fire; I consider this newest *ṛta* to be well-cooked.
O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, performer of many deeds, drink with pleasure of the curd from the midday libation.
O much-invoked one, you have utterly subdued your enemies; let your might be supreme and your bounty be here.
O Indra, bring us riches with your right hand; you are the lord of the wealthy rivers.
Like a fearsome beast that wanders and dwells in the mountains, you have come hither from the furthest distance.
O Indra, whetting your sharp bolt and your keen blade, strike down the enemies and drive away those who oppose us.
O Indra, you were born for the sake of desirable dominion and power, O bull among the peoples.
You drove away the unfriendly folk and made wide space for the gods.
From Dhātṛ, Dyutāna, Savitṛ, and Viṣṇu, Vasiṣṭha brought forth the *Rathantara*, that which is the oblation of the oblation belonging to the *Anuṣṭubh* whose names are Prathas and Saprathas.
They found that which had been hidden away, the supreme station of the sacrifice that was in the secret cave;
from the radiant Dhātṛ, Savitṛ, and Viṣṇu, Bharadvāja brought forth the great [song] of Agni.
Meditating with their minds, they found the first *yajuḥ*, the path traveled by the gods;
from Dhātṛ, Dyutāna, Savitṛ, and Viṣṇu, and from Sūrya, these [sages] brought forth the *gharma*.
May Bṛhaspati lead us across difficult passages; may he turn back the thought of the one who speaks evil against us.
May he cast away the curse, strike down the malevolent intent, and then grant well-being and peace to the sacrificer.
May Narāśaṃsa protect us at the fore-offering; may there be well-being for us at the after-offering during our invocations.
May he swiftly strike away the curse and the evil thought, and then grant the sacrificer peace and prosperity.
May he whose head is flaming burn up the demons who hate sacred prayer, so that they may be slain by his arrow.
May he swiftly strike away the curse and the evil thought, and then grant well-being and prosperity to the sacrificer.
I beheld you with my mind, you who are conscious, born of heat, manifested from heat.
Bestowing offspring here and wealth here, be procreated through progeny, O you who desire sons!
I beheld you with my mind as you were meditating, praying for the sake of your own body at the proper time. O young woman, rise up toward me; beget offspring through progeny, O you who desire a son!
I have placed the germ within the plants; I am within all existing beings. I have generated offspring upon the earth; I have produced sons from women yet to come.
May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms;
may Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you.
Bestow the embryo, O Sinīvālī; bestow the embryo, O Sarasvatī.
May the two divine Aśvins, wreathed with lotuses, place the embryo within you.
O Aśvins, that which you two churn out from the golden fire-drills—
that embryo we invoke for you, so that it may be born in the tenth month.
May the great protection of the three—of Mitra, of Aryaman, and of Varuṇa—be ours: heavenly, invincible, and difficult to assail.
Neither at home nor on the paths that ward off enemies,
does the wicked enemy have power over them.
To that mortal man for whom the sons of Aditi bestow imperishable light so that he may live.
May Vāta breathe forth healing for us—beneficent and delightful to our heart;
may he prolong our lives.
O Vāta, you are our father, and you are our brother and our friend;
as such, grant us life.
O Vāta, that treasure of immortality which is placed in your house yonder— grant us from it so that we may live.
Send forth your speech toward Agni, the bull of the peoples;
may he carry us across our enemies.
He who shines forth from the farthest distance across the desert wastes—
may he carry us safely beyond our enemies.
He who, as a bull, consumes the Rākṣasas with his bright, glowing flame—
may he carry us across our enemies.
He who looks out upon all beings and beholds them together— may he carry us across our enemies.
That bright Agni who was born on the far shore of this space—
may he carry us across our enemies.
Now, indeed, urge forth Jātavedas, the spirited steed,
so that he may sit upon this sacred grass of ours.
I offer a great hymn of praise to this Jātavedas, the liberal giver who has heroes among the inspired poets.
Those radiances of Jātavedas which carry the oblations to the gods—
may he further our sacrifice with them.
This spotted bull has come; he has settled before his mother, and advancing toward heaven, he has reached his father.
Moving within the luminous realms, breathing out from his breath,
the Great One has revealed the sky.
He shines across thirty realms; speech is bestowed upon the bird, day after day, throughout the mornings.
From the heat of the kindled fire, *ṛta* and *satya* were born;
from that, night was born, and from that, the billowing ocean.
From the ocean, the billowing sea, the year was born,
ordaining days and nights, the lord of all that blinks its eyes.
The Ordainer fashioned the sun and the moon as they were before;
he fashioned the heaven and the earth, the intermediate space, and likewise the sky.
O bull-like Agni, you gather together all the riches of the noble one;
kindled at the place of libation, bring us treasures here.
Come together, speak together; let your minds be in harmony, just as the gods of old, being in agreement, attend to their share.
Common is the counsel, common the assembly, common the mind, and their thought is united.
I address you with a common prayer; with a common oblation I sacrifice for you.
One and the same be your intention, one and the same your hearts; let your mind be united so that you may act in harmony together.
